# The Legendarium of Dia-thìr

# Aithris a' Chruthachaidh: the Telling of the Making

*Before the count of years*

> *Tha spiorad fa leth san speur, san talamh agus sa mhuir. Meascaich na spioradan agus bidh iad uile-chumhachdach.*
> The sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit. Merge the spirits, and they become almighty.
>
> — said by Coimhdeach na Fine in the grove of Doire ghlas

## I. Of Caoran and the Coals

This is the telling that Coimhdeach na Fine, the Keeper of the Kin, gave in the grove of Doire ghlas to one of the mason's line, who had asked it why the coal of Dia-thìr has colours in it when the coal of the common earth has none. The Keeper answered from the beginning, as the old do when a child asks a short question. The mason's children kept the telling after, father to son and mother to daughter, and said it over at the dark of the year word for word, and long afterward it was written down. It is set here before the Six Books because it is older than any of them.

Before there was a world there were the gods, and they were many, and they were a line. Mother bore daughter and father begot son, back and back into a dark where no name is kept; and every one of that line, when he came to the fullness of his years, went out from the hall of his kin and made a world. That was their coming of age. A god of that line was a child until he had made a thing and kept it, and was grown when it lived.

Each made his world out of what was dearest to him, and each chose a different thing. The eldest of the line, whose name the Keeper would not say, made hers of song: she sang, and the notes hung in the dark and hardened, and the hills of her world are chords and its rivers run in tunes. Another made his of salt and bone. His seas are brine to the bottom and his mountains are the ribs of things that never lived, and he loves that world, though it is hard. Another made hers of wind and the horns of beasts, and nothing in it is ever still. They were all worlds of the elements: each had its earth and its fire, its air and its waters, its life and its spirit, and in each they were made of something else.

In the latest days of that line two of the gods were an Dagda, the Good God, and Danu, the mother; and of them came the Tuath Dè, the people of the gods, whose names are told in their place. Their youngest son was Caoran, whose name is *ember*. He is called an Dia Òg, the Young God, and he is young still, as the gods reckon it.

When Caoran's time came he went about his father's hall a long while and could not choose. He looked at song and found it taken. He looked at salt and bone, at wind and horn, and they were taken also. He went to his sister's forge and to his mother's rivers and to his father's harp, and he came back each time with nothing in his hands. Then one night, when the feast was done and the hall was dark, he sat down by his father's cauldron. The fire under it had burned to its end. The coals lay in the ash, and they had gone black, as coals go when their heat is spent; but when he stirred them, a red eye opened in the heart of one and looked at him.

He took that coal up in his hand. It was black and it was hard, and there was fire in it, sleeping. It had been a tree once, and so it held the memory of life; it had lain under ground, and so it held the weight of earth. It would drink the air and give it back as heat. It was darkness with light folded inside it. And Caoran said to himself that here was a thing in which every element could lie hidden and be woken; and he chose coal.

His brothers and sisters laughed at him, the tellers say, for coal is a mean stuff, the leavings of a fire, and they had made their worlds of finer things. An Dagda did not laugh. He looked at the coal in his son's hand for a long time, and then he said, "It will do." It is said that no word of his was ever dearer to Caoran.

So the Young God went out from the hall into the empty dark, and he made the world.

He breathed on the coal in his hand until it woke, and he cast it out, and it broke into sparks, and the sparks flew wide and did not fall. Those are the stars. The greatest of them he fanned until it was all fire through and through, and it is the sun. One he let burn down to its grey ash, cool and pale, and hung it where the sun could find it at night; that is the moon, and the pocks in its face are where the fire went out. Then out of the black coal, the heaviest and most patient of all, he made the earth, and laid it down in the middle of his sparks. He pressed the hills up with his thumbs. He drew the long valleys with one finger. The seas he poured out of the dark between the stars, and the rivers he let run down from the high places to find them. He set the winds over all. He made the grass and the trees and the beasts after their kinds, and the fish in the waters and the birds in the air, and he was glad of all of it; and it was all made of coal, though nothing in it looked like coal any more.

Last of all, when the wide earth was done, he made the island.

He made it small, and he made it with care, as a craftsman makes the last and dearest piece of a work: a close thing of hills and moor, with mountains at its heart and a grey sea round it on every side. He gave it rivers, and a lake of fresh water, and soft rain, and a mild sky. Then he walked it end to end, and his kin came down to walk it with him and see what the youngest had made; for the gods were on the island before any people were. When they had looked their fill they went up again, and Caoran was alone on his island in the grey before the first morning.

Then he made the godfolk, an Dia-shluagh, the first people of the earth.

He did not bring them from anywhere. He knelt on the heather in the middle of the island and put his hands on the ground and called, and they woke out of the island itself, as the dew wakes on the grass; and when the sun came up they were sitting on the hillsides, blinking, with the heather in their hair. They were a tall people and a quiet one, and their eyes were made to see what he would give them. This is the oldest meaning of the saying of the island, *bha sinn ann*, we were here. The kin did not come to Dia-thìr. They were there on the first morning, because the island was where they were made.

"This is yours," the Young God said to them. "Keep it, and it will keep you."

In the wide lands beyond the sea he let other peoples wake after, each in its own time and place, and he gave them the common coal of the earth, which is black and burns and is only coal. Dia-thìr he did not give to them. Dia-thìr was the godfolk's to care for, and in Dia-thìr he hid his gift.

For the Young God had a secret, and he was glad of it, as a father is glad who hides a present under a child's pillow for the morning. When he laid the island down he took the coal that was deepest under its mountains, and into it he put the elements themselves, each in its own colour, where they would lie asleep until they were found. These are na Seachd Guail, the Seven Coals, and this is what each holds.

The first is *gual dubh*, the black coal, and it holds the earth. It is as black as a wet crow, and it takes a polish like still water at night, and it is heavy in the hand beyond its size. In it lies the patience of the ground: the weight of hills, and the strength of roots that hold.

The second is *gual teine*, the fire coal, and it holds fire. Its colour is the colour of flame itself, red and gold together; when it is turned in the light the colour moves in it, as flame moves when it is seen through closed eyelids. Every fire that was ever to burn on the island was folded into this coal and waited there, for Caoran let no other fire into Dia-thìr.

The third is *gual sneachda*, the snowflake coal, and it holds the air. It is dark and flecked all through with small white stars, like snow falling on black water, and it is the lightest of the seven. In it lie the winds and the breath of the high places.

The fourth is *gual òir*, the gold coal, and it holds the sea. It is black under a sheen of gold, and when it is turned it glints like the sun on the sea at evening. In it lie the salt water and the tides.

The fifth is *gual airgid*, the silver coal, and it holds the river water. Under its sheen of silver it is as dark as a pool in a wood, and it shines as the moon shines on running water. In it lie the springs and the rivers and the rain, which are sweet, and are a different thing from the sea.

The sixth is *gual donn-ruadh*, the mahogany coal, and it holds life. It is the deep red-brown of heartwood and of old blood, warm to look at, and of all the seven it is the most like a living thing. In it lie the quick of the body and the sap of the tree.

The seventh is *gual bogha-froise*, the rainbow coal, and it holds the spirit. All the colours are in it and none of them stays: it shifts as oil shifts on water, as the bow stands in the rain, and no two who look at it see the same. In it lies the spirit that makes the other six more than stuff; and it is the last of the seven, and the hardest to wake.

Together they are called *an gual dathach*, the coloured coal. There is no coloured coal anywhere in the world but on Dia-thìr, for the gift was for Dia-thìr alone. And the Young God set the colours so that only the eyes of the godfolk and their children should see them. To every other eye the coloured coal is black, and it is only coal.

He locked each colour with its own key, so that each should wake only to the thing that it held, and to nothing else. And he told no one what he had done, not the godfolk, and not his own kin. He wanted the island to find it for itself.

Then he set Crom Cruaich, the bent one of the mound, at the door between the mountain and those who would take from it, and went up to his father's hall to wait; and he was patient, though he is young.

## II. Of the Tuath Dè

These are the gods of the Tuath Dè, the people of the gods, the kin of the Young God, who came down with him to see his island in its first days; and they came again, once, on the night the first king of the island was made, as the First Book tells. The Old Faith honours them still, each at their feasts and in need. Caoran made the world and all that is in it, and he is the god of the coal. Yet the island honours an Dagda first, for he is the father of the gods, and it was his word that made the Young God's choice good.

**An Dagda**, the Good God, is the father. His is the cauldron from which no company goes away hungry, and it was from the ash under it that Caoran took the first coal. His is the club that kills with one end and wakes the dead with the other, and the harp that calls the seasons in their order; when the island's first year turned, it was his harp that turned it. He is slow of speech, and generous, and he laughs more than any of the gods.

**Danu** is the mother, and the Tuath Dè are named from her. She gives nothing loudly and asks for nothing. The tellings give her the rivers, and it was from her that Caoran learned to let the water run down from the high places; so the silver coal is hers in honour, though the gift in it is his.

**Brìde** is the lady of the hearth-fire, of poetry, of healing and of smithcraft. When Caoran shut all the island's fire into the fire coal, it is told that Brìde was grieved, for she could not bear to think of a hearth with nothing in it; and he promised her that when the fire was found it should be hers to keep. She has kept it since, and every hearth on the island is swept and relit on her feast.

**Crom Cruaich**, the bent one of the mound, is the god of the vein. When the coal was laid under the mountains, Caoran set him at its door, and so his oldest name is Dòrsair, Uilebheist nan Geataichean, the Monster of the Gates. He is exact. He gives what is asked of the mountain, and he takes his price for it, and his price is measured.

**Manannan mac Lir** is the lord of the sea, and the sea round Dia-thìr is his. When the gods came down to the new island he walked round its coasts in one night, and in the morning he drew up his mist about it, so that no ship from beyond should find it until its time. The gold coal is his in honour. His Cup of Truth breaks at a lie, and is whole again at the truth.

**Lugh Làmhfhada**, Lugh of the long arm, is the master of every craft, and he loves the high places, from which a long arm can reach far. It was Lugh who stood with Caoran on the highest summit of the island on the first evening and named the winds for him, and so the snowflake coal is his in honour. His feast is Lùnastal, when markets open and oaths are sworn before witnesses.

**Macha** is the lady of sovereignty, of kingship and of horses. Two horses draw her chariot, Liath Macha the grey and Dubh Sainglenn the black, and they run as one under one yoke. No king is king until she allows it. When the godfolk woke, Macha looked them over, one by one, and said that there was no king among them yet; and she said it gently, as a mother says that a child has not yet grown.

**Dian Cècht** is the healer of the gods, who made a hand of silver for Nuadha when his own was lost. The life that lies in the mahogany coal is the thing he tends, and he knows it better than any. The warm springs of the island are his.

**Goibhniu** is the smith of the gods, and he knew coal before Caoran did, for there is no smith without it. When the Young God's brothers and sisters laughed at his choosing, Goibhniu kept his face straight, and afterward he was the first of them to praise it.

**Nuadha** is the first king of the gods, who lost his hand in battle and ruled again with the silver hand that Dian Cècht made him. Where a king's right is spoken of, his name is spoken also.

**Ogma** is the lord of letters and of eloquence. The godfolk had no letters, and for a long age they needed none; Ogma was content to wait, for he is patient in the way of those who know that a word, once cut, stays.

**Flidais** is the lady of the deer and of the wild things. When the Young God called the beasts out of the island's heather she went among them, and she keeps them still, and the white stag of the wood is hers.

**The Morrìgan** is the lady of war and the crows. She came down with the rest, and looked at the peaceful island, and said that she would wait; and the others were quiet when she said it. The crows of the island are as black as the black coal, and they are hers.

**Donn** is the lord of the dead. His house is a rock in the sea to the south-west, Taigh Dhuinn, and the dead go to it. In the days of the godfolk no one went to his house for a long time, and he was content with that, for he is in no hurry for the dead.

There are others of the Tuath Dè, and the Old Faith knows them; but these are the ones the Keeper named in the grove.

## III. Of the Keeper of the Kin

When the Young God went up again to his father's hall he did not leave his island unwatched. He took up the smoke that had risen from the first coal he woke, which had hung in the dark all that while and never gone thin, and he gave it a mind and a charge. That is Coimhdeach na Fine, the Keeper of the Kin.

It is neither a god nor a ghost. It was never born, and it will not die while the kin are on the island; it is not one of the Tuath Dè, and it has no feast and no house. It is Caoran's watcher, and it watches for him, as a steward rides round a far holding while the lord is away: it goes where it will, it seldom speaks, and it tells its master what it has seen.

When it shows itself it comes as a figure of smoke, grey and upright, of the height of a tall man. It has no face that anyone has been able to tell of afterward. It stands still in a wind, and the smoke of it does not drift. There is a smell about it of a hearth in the morning when the fire has been banked all night. Its voice is low, and it speaks as fire speaks when it settles; those who have heard it say that they understood every word and could not afterward say whether it had used words at all.

It does not rule the kin, and it does not help them in their work. It will not fight for them. It comes seldom, generations apart, and when it comes it asks after the island as a guest asks after the health of the house. When it is asked a question it answers truly, but it does not always answer the whole of what is asked, for its charge is from Caoran, and some things Caoran has kept for the island to find.

The mason's children say that it came first in the grove, and that it came there to be asked; that it had waited through the whole long life of the kin on the island for one of them to wonder aloud about the colours. And when one of the mason's line did wonder, it came and sat down with him under the oaks in the evening, and it told him all that is written here, from the hall of the gods to the forgetting of the coal. It told him more, and he asked it more, and what passed between them after is told in the First Book.

## IV. Of the Forgotten Coal

In the first days the godfolk lived on the island in peace, and they had no fire.

They did not miss it, for they had never known it. The island was mild to them. The sea gave them its fish and its shellfish on every shore, and the moor gave them its berries and the woods their nuts, and the springs gave them sweet water. They slept in the lee of the rocks and in the long grass, and the rain was soft on them. At night they sat together on the hills and watched the sparks of the Young God's making turn over their heads, and named them, and told each other what they had seen in the day. They did not know that they were keeping the island. They loved it, and that was the keeping.

So many lives went by, the Keeper said, that the godfolk themselves forgot that the island had ever been new.

Then in one year a great rain came down on the mountains. It rained for a month without stopping, and the streams came off the high ground brown and roaring, and one of them tore away half a hillside under the mountains and carried it down into the valley below. When the water went back a child of the godfolk went to look at the new ground. The telling does not keep that child's name. In the raw bank where the hill had broken, she saw stones that were not like any stones she knew.

Some were black, and shone like a crow's wing in rain. Some had a gleam of gold on them. Some had a gleam of silver. One was dark and flecked with white, like the sky on a clear night. One was red-brown and warm to look at. One was the colour of nothing she had ever seen, for it was the colour of fire, and the godfolk had never seen a fire. And one had every colour in it, and would not keep still.

She filled the fold of her cloak with them and carried them home, and all the godfolk of that valley came to see.

They wondered at them a long while. They turned them in the sun. They held them up to their eyes. They struck them together, and the coal did not ring as flint rings, and nothing came of it. One tried to eat a piece and broke a tooth on it, and there was laughter. One tried to cut a shape into a piece with a sharp stone, and it crumbled under his hand and blacked his fingers, and he threw the rest away in disgust. The eldest of the valley said that they were the droppings of the mountain, and that pretty things with no use in them were for children. After that the children kept them for a while, and set them out in rows, and played at games with them on the flat rocks.

That was the whole of the godfolk's first finding. No one asked why the stones had colours. No one asked who had made them so. No one thought to lay them on the sand where the sea came in, or throw them down from a height, or bury them, or take them to the river; and there was no fire on the island to set them near. The gift lay in their hands, and they did not know it was a gift.

The children grew and forgot their games. The stones were kicked into the heather, and the heather grew over them. The stream moved in its bed and covered the broken bank with gravel, and the grass came over the gravel, and there was nothing to show where the hill had torn. The child who had found the coal grew old and died and went over the sea to Taigh Dhuinn, and those who had known her followed. In a few lives there was no one left on the island who remembered that any such stones had been.

When the Keeper told this in the grove, the one of the mason's line was ashamed for his forebears, and he asked whether the Young God had been angry.

The Keeper said that he had not. It said that Caoran had watched it all from his father's hall, and had laughed, as a father laughs who sees his child set aside the finest gift of the feast to play with the wrapping. It said: "A gift that is not opened is still given. He could wait. The coal was in no hurry, and neither was he."

So the coloured coal lay forgotten under the mountains, and the godfolk lived on without fire, and grew many, and spread over the island from the shore to the high moor. The island turned under the Young God's stars through more years than anyone could count; and nobody counted them, for there was no one yet to begin the count.

It began on the day a mason, splitting rock for a well, set his wedge in a seam he had not seen, and struck. That is the beginning of the First Book.


# The First Book: An Aois Àrsaidh, the Ancient Age

*VE 1 – 9,926*

> *Tha spiorad fa leth san speur, san talamh agus sa mhuir. Meascaich na spioradan agus bidh iad uile-chumhachdach.*
> The sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit. Merge the spirits, and they become almighty.
>
> — the Keeper's riddle, as Clann na Ceiste keep it

## I. Of the Mason and the Lightning

The library at Muileann chaol writes the first day of the count as 20 am Faoilleach, VE 1. In the hill country it is only "the night of the lightning", and the tale is told at the hearth in the dark of the year by whoever is oldest in the house; and every hearth that tells it is itself the tale, for before that night there was no hearth on Dia-thìr at all. It goes like this.

Neachdan the mason was sinking a well. He had been at it since the grey of the morning, with a wedge of hard stone and a maul of oak, splitting the rock a hand's depth at a time and lifting the pieces out. It was the dead of the year. The wind came over the heather with sleet in it, and his hands were split at the knuckles from the wet stone, and there was nothing in all the world to warm them but his own breath and the work.

He set the wedge in a seam and struck. The rock broke along a line he had not seen.

Out of every stone he had ever split there had come grey dust and grit, the same dust his father had shaken from his hair. Here the break was black, a hard black that took the light like a wet crow's back; and along the black, where the maul had opened it, lay colour. There was a sheen of gold on one piece, as the sun lies on the sea at evening. There was a piece flecked all over with small white stars, and one that was red-brown like the heart of an old oak, and one with a gleam of silver, and one that seemed, when he tilted it, to hold every colour he had a name for and some he had not. He knelt in the cut with the sleet on his neck and turned the pieces over in his hands until he could not feel them.

He did not know what they were. He filled the breast of his tunic with them, because they were beautiful.

The storm came up the valley at dusk. He took shelter under a lip of rock above the well. Then the sky split with a white light and a noise like the hill breaking, and the light went into the ground.

It went into his well. He saw it strike the broken vein and run along it; and where it ran, the vein began to glow.

The tellers slow here, for the hearth is listening. Neachdan came down out of the shelter with the rain in his eyes and stood at the lip of the well, and something was alive in it. It moved and was not a beast. It breathed out a heat that he felt on his face and his split hands, though the rain was cold; it ate the black stone and gave off a low dark flame, like peat-water moving, with red at its roots. The rain hissed on it and could not put it out. He held his hands over it and they came back to life, and he wept, and was not ashamed to say so after.

He took a flat stone and lifted a burning piece out onto it, and carried it home through the storm under the flap of his cloak, stooping over it the whole way as a man stoops over a sick child. At home he set it on the floor among stones, where the draught would not take it, and fed it with the coloured pieces from his tunic. Each one caught. Each burned the same, low and dark-flamed, and the colours went out of them as they burned, gold and silver and white stars alike, and left only the heat. He saw that, and was sorry a little, and was glad all the same, for his children were sitting round the first hearth on Dia-thìr with their faces red in its light.

So the Dia-thìrich say that fire came to them out of the sky and the stone together.

Three wells claim the crack. Tobar dhìreach, Tobar dhubh and Tobar òg each keep a telling that the mason's well was theirs, and that the lightning fell there. Tobar dhìreach can show a capped shaft with a scorched stain on its lip; the other two can show only the telling. The library holds all three claims and chooses none.

On what the mason's people did next, every telling agrees. They let the fire in the vein burn until it had burned itself out. Then they dug no further. They laid a flat stone over the broken vein, and would draw no water beside it, and cut their well again a stone's throw away. Of all the deeds of the Ancient Age this is the one told most often, to children and to kings, and it is told the same way every time: the people found a wonder in the ground, and they covered it.

## II. Of the Keeper in the Grove

Nine hundred years went by. The fire had gone from hearth to hearth over all the hill country, and no one knew what the coloured coal was. Then the question was asked.

It was asked by **Diarmad**, of the Mason's line, on 17 an Gearran, VE 890, and it was asked in the oak grove at Doire ghlas, far to the north, where the oaks had come in over the old heath. Why he had gone so far from the high valleys the tellers do not agree; the Mason's line says only that he had asked the question of everyone since he was a child, and got nothing for it but laughter.

He had lit a small fire of oak twigs in the lee of a fallen trunk, and he sat with a piece of the rainbow coal in his hand, as he always did, turning it so the colours ran. The wind was blowing hard through the grove. The branches roared with it and the dead leaves went past him in streams.

When he looked up there was someone standing on the other side of his fire.

It was the height of a tall man and made of grey smoke, such as a peat fire gives, and it stood in the middle of the gale and did not stir. Diarmad's own little fire was streaming sideways on the ground, and the smoke that stood beside it was as still as a stone.

He did not run. The tellers make much of that.

"What are you?" he said.

"I am Coimhdeach na Fine," it said. Its voice was quiet and very clear, and the wind did not carry it away. "The keeper of the kin. I watch over the people of this island for the one who made them."

"Are you a god?"

"No."

"A ghost, then."

"Neither. I was made out of the smoke of the first coal he woke. I have watched your line since the mason. You have a question. Ask it."

Diarmad held up the coal in his hand. "Why are there colours in it?" he said. "What are they for?"

Then the Keeper told him. It told him of Caoran, the Young God, youngest son of an Dagda and Danu, and of the long line of gods before him who made their worlds of other things; and how Caoran, coming of age, chose coal, and made of it all that is, and then the earth, and then the first people, an Dia-shluagh, the godfolk; and how he hid in the coal of this one island the seven spirits of his making, each in its colour, as a gift for them to find; and how they found it once, long before the mason, and did not understand it, and let it lie.

All that the Keeper told him the Mason's line kept, and in time the island learned it from them, and the scribes of Muileann chaol have set it before all their books as the Telling of the Making. It is not told twice here.

When it was done Diarmad sat a long time without speaking. The fire had burned down. At last he said: "He hid it. Why would he hide a gift?"

"So that it would be found," said the Keeper. "He said to me once: a gift that is not opened is still given."

"Then how is it opened? The mason burned the coals and they burned like any coal. We have burned them since. The colours go out of them."

"Because you burn them all in the one fire," said the Keeper, "and none of them in its own." And it gave him the riddle, first in the old words and then again, slowly, so that he would keep them:

> *Tha spiorad fa leth san speur, san talamh agus sa mhuir. Meascaich na spioradan agus bidh iad uile-chumhachdach.*
> The sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit. Merge the spirits, and they become almighty.

"That is no answer," Diarmad said.

"It is the one I was given to give," said the Keeper; and the wind, which had gone round it all that while, went through the place where it stood, and there was nothing there.

## III. Of the Seven Lightings

So began the long questioning. The Mason's line took the riddle home to the high valleys and turned it over for four thousand years, with seven coals and three words to go on, sky and earth and sea; and the tellers of Clann na Ceiste give the lightings one by one, as the reciters give kings.

The first was the sea. In VE 1,370 **Aodh** of the Mason's line, who had grown up hearing that the sea was one of the three, carried the seven coals of the vein across the hills to the northern shore, below where Ceann thais now stands. He had never seen the sea. He stood on the shingle a long while looking at it. Then he waded in to his knees and threw the coals out into the swell one after another. Six sank without a mark. The seventh, the one with the sheen of gold, struck the water and took fire, and burned on the heave of the sea with a flame the colour of its sheen, bright gold, rising and falling with the waves, until a breaker rolled it under. That coal is *gual òir*, the gold coal, and its spirit is the sea's. Aodh went home and told it at the hearth, and the old women of the line wept, for it was nearly five hundred years since the grove.

The second was the sky. In VE 2,170 **Fearghas** of the line reasoned that if the sea took one coal by its water, the sky might take one by its air, and that the nearest a man could come to the sky was the highest ground on the island. So he climbed it.

The wind on the top of the bare moor was cold enough to make his teeth ache, and he could see the sea shining at every edge of the island. He took the coals out one at a time and let each drop from the height of his arm over the steep side of the summit.

The fifth coal did not fall far. Halfway down the rock it took fire in the empty air, and burned white, a small fierce white like a star come down in daylight, and struck the stones below still burning and lay there flickering in the wind. It was the coal flecked with white stars, *gual sneachda*, the snowflake coal; and its spirit is the air's. From that day the summit has carried the name of the kindred, Binnean a' Chlachair, the Mason's Point, above where Muileann gheal stands now. The herders of that moor leave a stone on the top when they pass.

The third was the earth, and it was found by a man who took the riddle more simply than the rest. In VE 2,885 **Brian** of the line said that if the earth has a spirit, it lies where the dead lie, deep; and he dug a grave-deep hole beside the slab at Tobar dhìreach and laid the five dark coals in it and covered them over, as the dead are covered, and went home. The next morning he dug them up. Four were as cold as the clay. The fifth, the black one, *gual dubh*, as black as a wet crow, was warm in his hand as a hand is warm, and when the morning air reached it a dark red glow crept over it, and it smouldered. The earth had lit it slowly, overnight, from beneath. Brian kept it burning in a pot for the rest of his life.

The fourth was life, and it came by blood. In VE 3,670 **Cormac** of the line took the four dark coals on the long road north to Doire ghlas, to the grove where the Keeper had first spoken, for he thought the place itself might count for something. He sat under the oaks a month to no purpose, and at last, in a temper, he set the red-brown coal on a stone to break it, to see whether the spirit was inside.

He struck, and the hammer turned on the hard surface of the coal and came down on the back of his other hand, and laid it open to the bone. He swore and fell back, and the blood ran off his fingers and dripped onto the coal. Where it dripped, the coal caught. A flame came up out of it the colour of the coal itself, red-brown, deep and warm like firelight in oak; and Cormac sat in the leaves with his hand in his lap and watched it, and forgot to bind the hand until the flame went out. That coal is *gual donn-ruadh*, and the kindred call it the coal of life. The scar on Cormac's hand is remembered, and his byname with it, Cormac of the Misstrike.

The fifth was the river. Here the tellers of Clann na Ceiste stop and smile, because it is plain enough now, and it took them nearly six hundred years.

In VE 4,225 **Eòghann** of the line was walking home from the northern shore, where he had thrown the three dark coals into the sea once more, to no purpose. He came down tired to the Abhainn ghorm, the river that runs below Tobar dhìreach, and knelt on the stones and drank from his hands.

Then he sat back on his heels with the water running out between his fingers.

"This water tastes different from the sea water," he said aloud, to no one:

> *Tha blas eile air an uisce seo seach uisce na mara.*
> This water tastes different from the sea water.

He had known it all his life, as everyone knows it. He had never thought it before. He took the three coals out of the bag and threw them into the middle of the stream, one, two, three; and the one with the sheen of silver took fire as it went under, and burned on the bed of the river beneath the running water, silver, while the current poured over it and could not put it out. That is *gual airgid*, the silver coal, and its spirit is the river's.

By then the households of the high valleys had grown used to the Mason's line and its long strange business with the coal, and they had begun to call its people **Luchd-ceasnachaidh a' Ghuail Dhìomhair**, the Inquisitors of the Mystic Coal (VE 4,625). It was half a jest when it began. The line took it and kept it, and in the lists the long name is shortened to **Clann na Ceiste**, the Children of the Question; and the older name, Clann a' Chlachair, the Mason's children, is heard less after.

The sixth was fire itself, and it was found by accident, by a man who had given up.

**Seathan** of Clann na Ceiste had sat with the fire coal, *gual teine*, for thirty years. He had put it in every fire the line knew, even the first fire itself, which the line said it had kept alight since the mason's hearth, and it burned in all of them dark and low. Sky, earth and sea, the riddle said; where was fire in that? He had begun to half believe those of the line who said the fire coal had no spirit at all.

On 16 an t-Ògmhios, VE 4,905, a warm evening, he was sitting in his doorway at Tobar dhìreach breaking the fire coal into dust with his fingers, as he often did when he was thinking, and not thinking of the fire coal at all. He was thinking of the mason, and of the lightning that had made the mason's fire out of nothing: a crack, a snap in the sky.

He snapped his fingers.

The dust on them took fire. It went up off his hand in a little rush of flame, and the flame was the colour of the fire coal itself, a clear red-gold that shone through his fingers, brighter than any hearth he had sat at. He yelled and beat his hand against his coat, and the flame went out, and he looked at his fingers and they were whole. There was not a mark on them.

Then he sat in the doorway and laughed until his wife came to see what was the matter. The fire had been in the hand all along, the tellers say, in the hand and in the snap of it, as the lightning is in the sky; and a man cannot go looking in the sea for a thing he carries on him.

There was left the seventh, the rainbow coal, *gual bogha-froise*, that holds every colour; and it was the longest. For more than four hundred years Clann na Ceiste threw it in the sea and the river, dropped it from the Point, buried it, bled on it and snapped over it, and it lay dark through all of them. The tellers do not dwell on those years.

## IV. Of the Line of the Mason

The Line of the Mason is the eldest genealogy on Dia-thìr, older by thousands of years than the lines the common households first recited at the ford, and it is kept by Clann na Ceiste as the other lists are kept, by mouth. It is said standing, at the hearth on the night of the lightning; and before a stranger it is said in this short form, the long stretches between the named fathers given as numbers, for the reciters do not give the rest of the names to a stranger.

A reciter of Clann na Ceiste in the Holy Age gave it thus to a scribe of the Hall, and the scribe wrote it down as he heard it:

"Neachdan the Mason broke the stone, and the lightning came into it, and he carried the first fire home. Neachdan was the father of Conall, who laid the slab over the burnt vein. And after Conall came thirty-four fathers, each the son of the one before, whose names we keep; and the last of them was the father of Diarmad.

"Diarmad asked the question in the grove, and the Keeper answered him, and gave him the riddle. And after Diarmad came eighteen fathers whose names we keep; and the last of them was the father of Aodh.

"Aodh threw the seven into the sea, and the gold took fire on the water. And after Aodh came thirty-one fathers whose names we keep; and the last of them was the father of Fearghas.

"Fearghas climbed to the top of the island and let fall the six, and the snowflake took fire in the air, and the Point bears our name. And after Fearghas came twenty-eight fathers whose names we keep; and the last of them was the father of Brian.

"Brian buried the five like the dead, and the black was warm in the morning. And after Brian came thirty fathers whose names we keep; and the last of them was the father of Cormac.

"Cormac of the Misstrike bled in the grove, and the coal of life took fire from his blood. And after Cormac came twenty-one fathers whose names we keep; and the last of them was the father of Eòghann.

"Eòghann tasted the river, and the silver took fire under the water. And after Eòghann came fifteen fathers whose names we keep; and the last of them was the father of Colla.

"In the days of Colla they called us the Inquisitors of the Mystic Coal, and we took the name. And after Colla came ten fathers whose names we keep; and the last of them was the father of Seathan.

"Seathan snapped his fingers, and the fire was in his hand. And after Seathan came fifteen fathers whose names we keep; and the last of them was Suibhne.

"Suibhne was the father of Ailean, whom men call Ailean Mòr, and he is the first king."

There the Line of the Mason ends, as a line of fathers; for after Ailean it is the list of the Stone Kings, and his daughter comes next in that.

## V. Of the Vigil in the Grove

**Ailean** son of Suibhne was a big young man, slow of speech, with hands like his forefather's, and he had done what no one of the line had thought to do. He left the rainbow coal alone and took up the other six, and lit each one again by its own way, one after another, as the line had lit them over four thousand years: the gold on the sea below Ceann thais, the snowflake off the Point, the black in the earth at Tobar dhìreach, the red-brown with his own blood, the silver in the Abhainn ghorm, and the fire with the snap of his fingers. Each he carried away burning, in a pot of clay with a lid of turf, and he kept them fed. It took him the better part of a year. Then he put the six pots and the dark seventh coal on a pole across his shoulders and walked north, to the grove.

He came into Doire ghlas at dusk on 21 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,324. He set the six pots in a ring under the oaks and took off their lids, and the six fires stood up out of them in their six colours: gold and white and the dark red of the black coal, red-brown, silver, and the clear fire-colour of Seathan's snap. He had never seen them all together. No one had. He set the rainbow coal on the ground in the middle of the ring, and sat down, and waited, for the tellings said that this was where the Keeper came.

It was there before full dark. He saw it through the heat of the fires, the height of a tall man and made of grey smoke, standing among the oaks; and the smoke of his six fires blew past it on the evening wind and it did not stir.

"You have brought them all," it said.

"All I could," said Ailean. "The last will not light."

"No. It is not lit by anything of the sky, the earth or the sea. It is lit when the rest are together." The Keeper came into the ring. It stooped over the rainbow coal, and the coal took fire.

Ailean said afterward that he could not tell the colour of that flame, because it was every colour, and they would not hold still to be named. The six fires round it leaned in toward it, all together, the way grass leans in a wind, and for the first time since the making of the world all seven coals of Dia-thìr burned at once, each from its own spirit, gold and white and dark red and red-brown and silver and fire and the one that is all of them.

"Now listen," the Keeper said. "Stay with them until they are cold. Do not leave them, do not sleep far from them, and eat nothing while they burn."

"Why?"

"So that the spirits, being merged, may know one keeper, and the fire go into no hand but the hand that did not leave it."

He stayed. He kept the watch seven nights, a night for each coal, in the ring of fires under the oaks, and he ate nothing, and drank from the grove's spring only when the fires were steady. The first nights he was hungry and then he was not. The fires did not burn down as fires do. They burned through the nights at their full height and did not need feeding. On the fifth night he thought he heard voices in them. On the seventh he could not tell whether he slept.

On the eighth night, 28 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,324, the fires were cold. He woke, or came to himself, and they were out, all seven: the coals lay in the ring grey and dead, and the grove was dark, and he was very cold.

Then the grove filled with light.

They came in among the oaks as people come into a hall, talking, and the light came with them. First was a young man with hands black to the wrist, as a mason's hands are grey; and Ailean knew him, though he had never been told how, for Caoran, the Young God, who made all that is. Behind him came the Tuath Dè, his kin. An Dagda came, huge and laughing, with his club over his shoulder, and Danu at his side; Brìde with a flame in her hand; Lugh with his spear; Macha, and horses somewhere behind her that he heard but did not see; Manannan, who brought the smell of the sea into the middle of the island; Crom Cruaich, bent, who looked a long while at the slab-country to the south as if he could see it through the hills; and more behind them than Ailean could count or name.

Caoran stood over him in the ring of dead fires. Ailean tried to stand and could not, and the god put out a black hand and held him where he knelt.

"You stayed," Caoran said. "Good." And he said the words that the Line of the Mason keeps, and that no other list has:

> *Rìgh Chlann nan Dè.*
> King of the godkin.

Then he put his hand flat on Ailean's breast, and the heat that had gone out of the seven coals went into him. He said afterward only that it was like the night of the lightning must have been for the mason, if the mason had been the stone.

When he could see again it was morning, and the gods were gone, and the ring of pots lay cold on the leaves.

## VI. Of Ailean's Secret and the First Kingdom

Ailean Mòr, as they called him from then on, told his kin that the gods had come to the grove and named him king of the godkin. That much he never hid, and Clann na Ceiste believed him. What had gone into him with Caoran's hand he told to no one: not his wife, nor his daughter, nor the reciters. How then is it known? The line answers that the Keeper knows everything it watches over, and tells what it chooses to whom it chooses; and there the question stops.

He walked home from the grove and did not stop at the high valleys. He went on east with a few of his kin to the hill where Dùn ìseal now stands, which was held then by households that answered to no one, and on 9 an Lùnastal, VE 5,324, he took it.

The tellers do not say how. They say that the holders of the hill came out against him with spears, many against few, and that when they came near him they stopped, and some sat down on the grass, and some went home; and that none of them could ever say afterward why. They say that the households of the valleys about the hill came in to him one after another that year, and brought him their grazing and their quarrels; and that he judged the quarrels and was feared, and loved a little too; and that no one ever saw him lift a hand. A girl of Dùn ìseal said in her old age that she had once stood near him on a winter night and been warm, as if she stood by a fire, and that there was no fire.

So the first kingdom of the godkin was made: a hill and the valleys round it and the households that came in. Ailean threw up the hill's first bank, a single bank and ditch round some forty houses, the oldest defended place of the hill-folk. With him the reciters at the ford open the oldest spoken king-list, *Rìghrean na Cloiche*, the Stone Kings, and some of Clann na Ceiste say the stone of the name is the mason's stone. The list gives no lengths of reign, and it is older than the name Dia-thìrich.

He was king a long time, and the coals' power was in him all of it, and he used it for nothing but the hill. Of what became of it when he died the tellings say nothing. His daughter Gormshuil stands after him in the list. The coloured coal lay under the slab and in the pots of Clann na Ceiste, and the other households of the hills went on burning it in their common fires, dark-flamed, and never knew what it held.

## VII. Of the Waters and the Woods

The tellers go back now to the first years of the count, for while the Mason's line questioned the coal the island went its own way. In the years after the lightning Dia-thìr was another shape. The snowfields on the central mountains were shrinking, and their meltwater cut the bed that Abhainn uaine follows still; its gravel terraces hold hearth-stones at three heights, each left as the water came up to it. In the bog beneath Doire ghlas the birch and pine of the colder years gave way to oak and hazel, and the grove grew up on the old heath where the Keeper would afterwards stand.

At Achadh dhìreach lie the first hearths of the high valleys, lit from the mason's fire or from fires lit from it: pine and heather charcoal, scrapers of grey flint, the split bones of red deer. There is no coloured coal in them. Whoever sat at them either had none of it or would not burn it, and fed the fire with wood.

And the sea rose. It drowned the low neck that joined Eilean dhubh to the main island, and the island's deer, cut off, grew smaller in the lifetimes after. Out on Eilean mhin seal-hunters pitched their camps a season at a time, reached by boat, and that is the first sure sign that anyone on Dia-thìr crossed open water on purpose. Abhainn ìseal, the longest river of the island, settled into its broad bed, and weirs of hazel were staked across its side channels, and the stakes were renewed in the same holes for generations.

These are small things. A people who leave no words leave their fires and their weirs and their bones, and he who would know them must learn to read those.

## VIII. Of the Seann-Dhaoine

At Seann Dunn there is a mound taller than a man, made of limpet shell and seal bone and burnt weed, laid down over many lifetimes. It is the first sure trace of the **Seann-Dhaoine**, the Old Ones; and no tool in it is shaped as any later Dia-thìreach shaped a tool.

What they called themselves is lost. The name they bear was given afterward, by others, and means only that they were before. Yet they held the shores of Dia-thìr longer than the Dia-thìrich have held their kingdom.

Of them it is told that at Seann Chwen they sank their nets with beach stones, and every stone was notched with the same three strokes, the earliest mark on Dia-thìr made again and again on purpose. At Seann Skell they laid a mole of unmortared boulders out into the river, and every quay wall built there since stands upon it. At Seann Bhral they cut two hundred and twelve steps up the cliff from the shingle to the grazing, and the treads are worn hollow in the middle; no one has counted how many feet that took. At Seann Toll they cut a channel into a river pool with a slot for a gate of wattle, and the slot is still sharp. At Seann Warr they laid a road of crushed shell across the reed marsh, a forearm above the reeds, and it is the first made road on the island that can still be walked. At Seann Mhorn they built seven fish-kilns to dry the catch over peat smoke, the first buildings on Dia-thìr raised for a trade. At Seann Bhrenn they laid long ramps of stone into the water, wide enough for hulls bigger than any hide boat. The hulls are gone, and so is any tale of where they went.

At Seann Tarr they cut rows of signs into the cliff. It is the script that turns up later on the standing stones. It is no Dia-thìris, and it has never been read, and not one sign of it has an agreed meaning.

The Seann-Dhaoine of Seann Vell rowed their dead out to Eilean dhearg and laid them in stone boxes that face the mainland. Forty have been counted. No grave of theirs on the mainland from that time has been found. So the dead of the Old Ones were set to look back across the water at the living.

Their works went up on every coast. Platforms on oak piles stood out in the shallows of Loch chrom, though whether the Old Ones raised them or some other people the timbers do not tell. Below the southern Seann Dunn the ribs of a stranded whale were raised as the frames of round houses. At the eastern Seann Vell there are fourteen house-rings of dry stone. At the north-western Seann Skell stands a hollow-walled tower with a stair in the thickness of its wall, looking over the water where the Sea-Watcher would later be seen. There was a second Seann Mhorn, a headland of oyster and whelk whose lowest oysters are larger than any taken there since, and a second Seann Bhrenn far to the north-east with the same ramps; whether one people built both or the name was carried, none can say. At the eastern Seann Tarr a long house was built into a cleft of the cliff, and the rock behind its hearth is black with soot to the height of a man.

At their height, in VE 3,872, they held every coast: the ten places whose names begin with *Seann*, and the islands off them, and their greatest landing was Seann Skell on the Abhainn naomh, where the mole already stood. At the warm springs of Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh they set stone basins, and the bones buried nearby show old breaks that knitted clean. That is the first place on Dia-thìr where the sick were brought to be made well. Let it be remembered of them also.

## IX. Of the Three Ruins and the Deep Shafts

The three centuries that began in VE 2,524 saw as many works and wonders as any stretch of the age. The tellings hold them together as one time, when great works went up inland and great fears came in from the sea.

On a spur above the ground where Cathair mhòr now stands a walled outpost was raised, which later tongues called Làrach an Dùin-fhaire. Its stones are dressed on the outer face only, and its one gate faces inland, away from the sea. A greater work went up on the height near Ceann mhin: three rings of wall, a cistern cut in the bedrock, and room for four hundred people with their beasts. That is Làrach an Dùin, and whether the outpost's builders raised it too has never been settled. Near Àth fhionn run stretches of a kerbed track, a cart's width and paved with flat slabs, heading toward both; it is the only road the Seann-Dhaoine are known to have built away from the shore.

In the eastern hills a stepped platform was built with an altar block on its top step, and the altar was set square to the central mountains. That is Làrach an Teampaill. Every later temple on Dia-thìr faces some other way. Seers have said since that it faces the vein under the mountains; each who hears it may join the two or leave them apart.

At the eastern Toll-dubh a shaft was sunk straight down through the rock, its walls tooled smooth as far as a lamp can show, and no spoil heap lies beside it. Whatever was taken out of it was carried away, or nothing was. Across the island, at the western Toll-dubh, a second shaft of the same make was cut. Stones thrown into either are never heard to land.

None of these works lasted. The single gate of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire was blocked with rubble from the inside; whoever did it left by another way, or never left. The outpost stood empty, and was a ruin already when the first sure chronicles begin. The cistern of Làrach an Dùin was found choked with the bones of cattle thrown in whole, and no one drew from it again, and the fortress was left in the same state and the same mystery. The top stone of the altar at Làrach an Teampaill was prised off and carried away. The sockets are still sharp. The stone has never been found. Then the temple too was left.

After the high places were given up, every new work of the Seann-Dhaoine lay within sight of salt water, and the middens at the southern Seann Chwen grew as fast as those of Seann Dunn once had. It is as if a people went up into the hills, and built, and were turned back, and came down to the shore and stayed there. That is how the tellers put it, and the stones neither agree nor argue.

Long after, in the days of the Stone Kings, the people of the south-east plaited a rope of hide and brought a youth to the lip of the eastern shaft. The wind came up out of the hole, cool and smelling of wet stone, and lifted the hair from his brow as he sat on the edge with the rope knotted under his arms. He had a lamp of fat in a hollowed stone, and he sat looking down into the dark.

They let him go hand over hand, the men braced with their heels in the turf and the hide creaking through their fists. The lamp went down and grew small, a pin of light on the smooth wall, and then the dark closed over it and there was only the rope going out. The rope ran out to its last knot, and they held it there, and it hung straight and heavy and gave no sign.

Then it jerked twice, and they hauled.

He came up alive. His lamp was out and his face was the colour of ash. They asked him, and he shook his head. He never said what was at the bottom, not then and not in all the years he lived; and after him no one went down again in that age.

## X. Of the Sea-Watcher and the Hollow Man

In those same years the fears of Dia-thìr were born, and two of them have never left it.

Among the coastal families of the Tuathaich, in a far later age, there lives a fragment of a voyaging tale, with a named steersman and a first crossing, which they call the First Canoe. It is the voyage of Naomh Breandan, the saint of their Church, who put out west with his monks and came to the Isle of the Blessed; the families who keep it hold that the isle was Dia-thìr, and set the landing in this age. The druids of the Old Faith call it superstition, and it was put down, and is half-remembered; yet it belongs here, at the beginning of boats. What is sure is smaller. Below Ceann mhòr, in the tidal mud, lie a row of mooring stakes and a scrap of stitched hide, the first sure boats of the north-west coast. Who rowed them, and from where, the mud does not say.

On 1 an t-Sultain, VE 2,990, the Sea-Watcher was first sighted. Old sailors of the north-west speak of a creature vaster than any whale in the water off that coast, and add, before anyone else can, that no wreck has ever been raised to prove them wrong. On the headland where Taigh-solais Baile chrom now stands a fire was kept, and its ash lies a man's height deep. The tellings say it burned to turn boats away from the Watcher's water. The beacon-keepers' word to the boats is kept at Baile chrom:

> *Tionndaidh air ais. Chan ann dhutsa an t-uisce seo.*
> Turn back. This water is not for you.

A telling of that coast counts seven boats gone from Ros ruadh in one calm season, with no storm to blame; that was the first loss laid at the Watcher's door by name. After it the seal-bone thins in the middens of the north-west, and the middens at Caol mhòr and Cuan bheag grow. The hunters were working the southern sides of the headlands now, out of sight of the open sea.

Inland the rock faces of the Doire uaine hills are cut with writing, more than anywhere else on the island, in lines that run for yards; and some of the lines are cut over and defaced by the same kind of tool that cut them. The tellings say they speak of something that walked without breathing and fell upon anyone who lit a fire in its sight. This is the Hollow Man of Doire uaine. How a thing written in a script no one can read came to be known at all is a riddle; yet known it is, in every house of those hills.

After the writing, the hearths of those hills changed. Fires were dug into pits and roofed with slabs, and no open hearth showed on those slopes for many lifetimes. The people stayed. They hid their light. At the hill camp later built over by Muileann chiar nine people lie where they fell inside a hut, beside a hearth of fresh ash, and no wound has been found on any bone. The hut was never reopened, and no one was buried from it.

The fear did not pass. Long after, a herding family new to the hills lit an open fire at Doire uaine against the custom, and their hut was found empty with the fire still burning in it. After that the custom was kept harder.

Later again, two herders were driving beasts home past the Doire uaine hills when the light went. They had stayed too long at the far pasture. Neither had flint or tinder out, for they were hill-bred and would sooner have walked blind; and so they went on in the half-dark with the beasts crowding at their heels.

The younger saw it first and caught the other's arm. Up on the ridge, against the last grey of the sky, a figure was walking, upright and unhurried, along the crest. They watched it for as long as a man might count a score. It was cold enough that the herders' breath hung in clouds before them. Above the walker on the ridge nothing hung at all.

They did not run, for running is noise. They stood among the cattle with their hands over their mouths until the figure passed over the crest. At home they would not let the fire be uncovered until full day. They had no fire lit on the path, the telling says, and that is why they lived.

So the covered hearth spread from the Doire uaine hills to every settlement round Muileann chiar, and the rule that no open fire is lit on those slopes after dark begins there. Mothers in that country still say:

> *Na las teine far am faic e thu.*
> Light no fire where it can see you.

## XI. Of the Groves and the Beasts

A forest near Muileann chiar was hallowed long before any order of the Old Faith laid claim to it: Coille Naomh Muileann chiar. The trees understood, the old telling goes, before the people did. The charcoal in the hearths around it comes from every wood but that one; the families at its edge carried their fuel a half-day's walk rather than cut a branch within it. There, at the edge of the trees, three hunters once saw a white stag, and none of them drew. The stag comes back in the tellings of every age after. The druid schools of later days hold it to be the white stag of Flidais, lady of the deer and the wild; the tellings of this age give it no god at all.

A second forest, older in its feeling than the first, was never settled, never felled, never fully walked: Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag. Paths lead toward it from three sides, and all three end at a low line of set stones short of the trees. Nothing is worn beyond the stones. Lifetimes later a child of Cnoc bheag went past the line and was never found, and the searchers stopped at the stones. The telling does not blame them. The hearths of that country say the sìth took the child, the people of the hills and mounds, whose country begins where the worn paths end.

Near Doire fhionn the red deer were driven down lines of stake and brush into a gully, and the antlers of the greatest stags were stacked apart. At Cnoc fhionn dogs were buried beside people, each with a shell at its head, the first beasts given graves on Dia-thìr; and long after, at Tobar fhiadhaich, wolves were laid in the ground on their sides like people. The grey geese of Eilean ghorm come into the tellings in these years. They come with the first storm and leave with the last, and they are never hunted there.

In VE 5,170 a thing was first marked that is a wonder still: the great cats of the island cross the mountains by fixed roads at fixed seasons. These are the panther roads. The hill-folk learned the cats' timing and kept off the passes while they crossed. A party of eleven from the southern shore went up near Cnoc àrsaidh in the crossing season and did not come back, and their bones were found years afterward along the line the cats still use. The households at Baile dhomhain came to cut a sign on their gateposts at the start of the crossing and scrape it off at the end, the first mark on Dia-thìr made for a season. Herders from Muileann bhàn who drove cattle into the passes out of season lost thirty head in a night and came down with nothing. And once the cats came down the road near Imrich nam Pantar and turned back at the foothills. The hill-folk took it for a sign, and stored double; and the winter was hard.

## XII. Of the Hill-Folk and the Three Stones

In the high valleys around the crack there lived people who were of another kind from the Seann-Dhaoine. They called themselves Clann nan Dè, the godkin, and the Mason's line was one household among them. They buried their dead in the ground, and cut no script. Whether they shared the island with the Old Ones or came after them, no telling knows. Their own answer, given later, is that they were always there. These are the hill-folk, and from them came the Dia-thìrich. They left the green mounds of the valleys unbroken, and built on none of them, and the hearths of every later age give the same reason: the sìth live in the hills and the mounds, and a house on a mound is a house on someone else's roof.

At Àth gharbh, in a hearth of plain peat ash, lies a sliver of the coloured coal burnt to a bead, and the hearthstone round it is stained through with colour. It is the earliest burning of the coal by any hand outside the Mason's line that anyone has found, and it burned as the mason's coals had burned, low and dark; whoever fed it to that fire knew nothing of the riddle. It is also small: one sliver, one fire. In the graves at Achadh dhìreach is wool streaked with colour no plant makes, for the hill-folk rubbed broken coal from the vein into cloth for their dead, one grave in some thirty. And far off on the western coast, in a midden at Seann Bhral, lies a chip of the coloured coal still staining the shell around it. How a piece of the vein came to a rubbish-heap of the Old Ones, by gift or trade or theft, is anyone's guess.

Then the stones were raised; and the Dia-thìrich hold them holier than any temple.

The first is Carragh Cnoc bheag. On its upper face runs a line of the unread script, and lower down, cut with a narrower tool by another hand, are four words of Dia-thìris:

> *Bha teine sa chloich.*
> There was fire in the stone.

When that second hand came, the stone does not say. Clann na Ceiste hold that it was one of theirs, and that the fire in the stone is the mason's.

The second is Colbh Cnoc chiar, and it carries two words only:

> *Cuimhnich an teine.*
> Remember the fire.

Why the command was given, nothing is told. The ground round it is trodden hard in a ring paved with fire-cracked stones, where hearth-sized fires were kept again and again, and nothing else was left.

The third is Calbh Cnoc ghorm, and it carries the doctrine itself, whole: *Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann.* If the doctrine has a birthplace, it may be there. The ground round it holds the post-holes of shelters for some hundreds, used and rebuilt many times. Whatever was said there was said to a crowd.

In those years a burial ground grew about a place that no one remembers hallowing: Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, whose oldest graves are older than its oldest names that can be read. In one of the oldest lies a child with a sliver of the coloured coal closed in one hand. The sliver still stains the cloth it is kept in, and it is the only piece of the vein found buried with the dead in all this age. The graves came to be laid in rows, heads toward the central mountains; the earliest rows are straight, and the later ones bend round graves already there that no one would disturb.

Long lifetimes after, a single dwelling was sealed by chance under three yards of peat. Its hearth is laid with dry wood, and beside the wood lies a slip of the coloured coal, and none of it was ever burned. Whoever laid it went away and did not come back to light it. It is the earliest witness on Dia-thìr of coal that might easily have been burned and was left, and the keepers of later ages call it the Unlit Hearth.

For in those years a custom set in across the hills, that no fire should take more of the coloured coal than can be held in one cupped hand. It was nowhere written and everywhere kept, and the Small-Burning Law of the next age is this custom hardened. The reason is always the same tale, told to children when they first reach toward the coal-box. At Achadh dhìreach, it goes, a household once burned a whole basket of the coloured coal at one time, knowing no more of what was in it than the basket did. The house burned down with three people in it; and when the neighbours came in the grey of morning the hearthstone was cracked through and running with colour. Then the teller cups a hand, and says:

> *Làn na glaice, 's gun tuilleadh.*
> The hollow of the hand, and no more.

And the families near the crack began to sit by the slab laid over it, a household at a time, through the dark half of the year, from Samhain, when the dark half begins, until the light came back. No one ever said what they were watching for.

## XIII. Of the Counting of the Dead and the Silence of the Old Ones

In VE 5,631 the Seann-Dhaoine began to cut strokes on flat stones set at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household. The strokes are simpler than the script: a mark, and then another. They were counting their dead. Before there was a Dia-thìreach people to take up the craft, the Old Ones kept count of their own losses, and the chroniclers of Muileann chaol own them as their first forebears in it, though they cannot name one of them.

At the eastern Seann Warr the counting stones were built into a wall, some three thousand strokes in all, and the wall grew for many lifetimes. At Seann Tarr in the north-east the strokes were cut in fives and the stones set into the floor of a house, and the house was lived in over its own dead. Then the tally stones of Seann Warr, Seann Tarr and Seann Chwen all thicken together, more strokes on each stone, more stones in each course. Whatever killed so many killed on three coasts at once. What it was, the strokes keep to themselves.

At the Seann Chwen near Cuan dhearg, on 5 an Cèitean, VE 5,833, the last tally stone was left half-cut: two strokes finished, a third begun and given up. The chisel marks stop mid-groove.

After the half-cut stone no new work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and their script is never cut again. How they ended, no one knows. Others have guessed in every age, and the library at Muileann chaol keeps their guesses in a press of their own and lends them to no one as history.

There is a lament for them on the south coast. It is young, as such things go, and it says what the stones say:

> *Stràc air a' chloich, is stràc eile;*
> *an treas stràc, cha deach a chrìochnachadh.*
> *Dh'fhalbh iad, is dh'fhàg iad na h-ainmean.*
>
> A stroke on the stone, and another stroke;
> the third stroke, it was never finished.
> They went, and they left the names.

For the hill-folk went on calling the Old Ones' places by the Old Ones' names, putting only their own word for *old* in front: Seann Dunn, Seann Chwen, Seann Skell and the rest. They translated nothing, and the roots are still not understood. Hill-folk families came down the Abhainn naomh and settled the empty river harbour at Seann Skell, using the old mole and mending none of it, the first time they are known to have lived by the water. Long after, a wind-name was cut in the Dia-thìrich manner on a boulder at the central Seann Chwen, over an older mark of the Seann-Dhaoine, and there the marks of the two peoples lie one upon the other. When diggers at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach broke into a grave lined with slabs in the Seann-Dhaoine way, they closed it and moved their row, and no one opened it again.

At the eastern Seann Dunn, near the end of the age, a household set about cutting a floor for a new house into the side of the old midden.

The woman of the house had the spade, a blade of shoulder-bone on an ash handle, and her two sons carried the spoil away in baskets. The midden smelled of salt and long-dead fires. At a man's length in, the spade rang.

She knelt and cleared it with her hands. It was a flat stone, set on its edge, and when she brushed the grit from its face she saw the strokes: one and one and one, row on row, cut clean and close, more than she could count on her hands and her sons' hands together. Beside it was another. Behind that, another.

She knew what they were. Everyone on that coast knew, though no one had ever seen one: the Old Ones' counting of their dead.

They lifted them out one at a time, and she laid them on the turf in the order they had come, the first on the left. She looked at them a long while in the wind off the sea. Then she and her sons put them back, the last first, each in its own place and facing the way it had faced, and they filled the cut and trod it down. They built their house elsewhere, on poorer ground.

So the Dia-thìrich have always dealt with the Old Ones: as a people whose count must not be disturbed.

## XIV. Of the Stone Kings and the Red Hill

In those same centuries the kings begin; and so the last of the Old Ones and the first of the kings stand in the annals side by side, and neither list names the other.

The list of the Stone Kings opens with **Ailean Mòr** and his bank on the hill of Dùn ìseal, and of him enough has been told. A second list was kept in the west, and it opens with **Beathag Ruadh**, who held the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands, and that is the Red Hill. For long the two lists say nothing of each other.

**Gormshuil nic Ailein**, second of the Stone Kings, is the first woman in any list on Dia-thìr, and her telling gives her one deed: in a hard winter she moved the herds of Dùn ìseal down to the warm springs and lost none. **Dòmhnall Clachach**, third, set marker stones along the valley to part the grazing, and some stand yet, and are still quarrelled over. After him came the first named storm, whose name is lost and only the fact of it kept. It broke the shell causeway of Seann Warr in three places and the Seann-Dhaoine never mended it. Then came **Fearchar Bacach**, the lame king, carried to the gatherings in a chair of woven birch, the first ruler on Dia-thìr remembered for a hurt. On the Red Hill **Uisdean Mòr** dug a ditch across the neck of the hill and set a palisade on it, which burned twice and was twice rebuilt; and **Seonag nic Uisdein**, who held the hill after her father, counted her people by pebbles in a bag, one to a household, and knew by the weight when a household had gone.

The first war in either list was a raid for salt. **Mòrag Chruaidh**, fifth of the Stone Kings, went down to the pans at Baile ghorm, shallow clay basins behind a shingle bar and the island's first salt-works, and carried off the salt. Seven died on the hill side, and the telling keeps the number. **Iain Dubh**, sixth, went down to do it again and was killed on the shingle. The list says only that he was brought home.

The land was not quiet under those kings. A sheet of sea sand full of deep-water shells, a hand thick, lies over the hearths of a village on the site of Cnoc chaol, and the village was never rebuilt on that ground. At Cill ghlas a crack a man could fall into opened across the valley and a spring moved a hundred paces downhill; the hill-folk banked it with stones and laid a line of white stones along it, and built no house within a stone's throw. The dwellings on Loch chrom burned to the waterline, and their charred piles were left standing in the shallows.

## XV. Of the Ford of Salt and Wool

**Raghnall Ceannfhionn**, seventh of the Stone Kings, came down to the ford to meet the Red Hill, and the reciters make much of his coming.

He brought only a few with him, for more would have looked like a raid. It was early summer, the river running clear and shallow over its stones, and midges hung in clouds over the water. The Red Hill's holder, whose name the lists do not keep, waited on the far bank with as many, and the two parties looked at each other a long time across the water while the river talked between them.

The two hills had never once spoken. The old salt raids were still sung on the hill side, and a king of Dùn ìseal still lay under his cairn for the salt of Baile ghorm. He also knew his hill had sheep in plenty and too little salt, and that the west had salt in plenty and was short of wool.

So he waded in, alone, to the middle of the ford, with the water to his knees and his cloak held up out of it, and stood there. After a while the other came out to meet him.

What they said the reciters give short. The hill would bring wool; the west would bring salt; neither would bring spears. They clasped arms over the water and waded back, each to their own bank.

Both lists record it, and it is the first time either names the other. The meeting became a yearly gathering where salt, flint, wool, dried fish and pots changed hands and marriages were agreed, and its trodden ground, where the fair of Muileann òg is held now, is the oldest meeting-place on the island that has never been left. **Murchadh Gearr**, who held the Red Hill after Seonag, kept the peace of the ford, and walked the salt road himself every year to be seen on it.

The hill-folk spread in those generations: to Ros bheag on the west coast; to Cathair dhomhain, paying salt to the Red Hill; to Cnoc ghorm with the first cattle of the north-west; to Cathair gheal, where a long-house forty paces long burned and was rebuilt on its footing twice. The first pots were fired at Doire shean. An oak dug-out long enough for six was sunk at Cidhe Beag, the oldest boat on Dia-thìr whose whole shape is known. Seal-oil lamps burned at Caol leathan, the first light on the island that was no hearth.

Hard years came. At the site of Baile chrom in the north-west the pots are found full of boiled bark and seaweed and the grave-rows doubled: the oldest hunger on Dia-thìr with a place to it. The springs of Achadh shean ran dry, and its fields were given up to the grass. **Sìleas Bhàn**, eighth of the Stone Kings, held Dùn ìseal through years of failed grazing, and her telling gives her no deed but that. She held, and the list goes on after her. **Tormod Liath**, ninth, outlived three heirs, and in his time Dùn ìseal got its second bank.

Things were fixed in those lifetimes that have never been unfixed. Flint was dug at Cnoc àrsaidh, the only good flint on Dia-thìr, and the road of those who carried it is sunk a yard deep near Àth leathan. A hawk was carved on a lintel at Àth mhòr, wings closed, head turned, the oldest carving of any bird on the island. The Hawk order of later ages claims it for the Hawk of Acaill, the grey hawk as old as Fionntan; the lintel keeps its own counsel. Someone began to mark the high-water line against a fixed rock, at intervals too regular for a fisherman's habit, and the practice was carried to Ros dhomhain with the interval unchanged; and there the marks crept upward from keeper to keeper, until by the age's end the lake stood a hand higher than at the first cut. The keepers kept cutting. And the eight winds were named, with names that translate awkwardly and have never been replaced. Eight stones were set in a ring on the point at Ceann leathan, one to each wind, and sailors of every age since have touched the stone of the wind they want before they go out.

## XVI. Of the Dia-thìrich Name and the Sharing before the Storms

By VE 7,524 the hill-folk had begun to call themselves **Dia-thìrich**, and their island **Dia-thìr**. The first mouth to say it is forgotten. The oldest tellings already take both names for granted, and the doctrine goes with them.

With the name came the first forbidden marriage, two lineages refused to each other for reasons none can now give: the earliest sign that the Dia-thìrich ordered themselves by bloodline before the coal gave them any cause to. At the ford, households began to recite their lines seven names back on each side before a marriage was agreed, and those are the first genealogies of the common households, for only the Line of the Mason is older. None of them survives whole.

In the same years they went looking for another vein. Diggers from Dùn ìseal opened a trench near Cnoc dhubh and gave it up when two of them were crushed by a fall. A second opening elsewhere struck ordinary rock with nothing beneath it, and so it was first shown that the vein under the mountain stands alone. No one in this age tried a third. The Dia-thìrich took it that the vein chooses where it lies, and that the choosing is not theirs to test.

Then came the custom that later ages lean on more than they admit: that any household with food to spare must share it before a storm season. At Dùn ìseal it was shared in the open within the bank, by count of mouths. At Àth shean a household hid its grain in a pit beneath the floor and brought nothing, and when the pit was found the household was put out with what it could carry, the first known punishment under the custom.
