A boy of the harbour sat that night on the wall of the west quay with his knees drawn up to his chin and watched the lamps come out along the strand, one and then another, until the whole curve of the water was pricked with light. It was the moon of Bearnach, the gap between the last of the stores and the first of the green, and the air was sharp. Below him the hulls lay against the new stones, so close that he could have dropped a pebble onto a deck. He smelt pitch and wet hemp and the sheep's fat the crews had rubbed into the blocks. Somewhere aboard, someone was singing under her breath, and someone else told her to hush.

He was to be one of the counters. The harbour scribe had given him a hazel stick and a knife, and told him: one notch for each hull as she passes, and no talking.

On 19 an Giblean, LE 40, in the grey before sunrise, the volunteers departed.

They did not go straight down to the sea. The first hull came off the quay and swung, and the next came after her, and the boy saw that they meant to go round the river pool, sunwise, *diosal*, as you walk round a well or a new-built house for luck. He cut his notches. The hulls went by so near that he knew faces on them, and he did not look at the faces long, because he was counting.

At the foot of the pool the fleet straightened and went away down the Abhainn naomh toward open water, and there the harbour scribe's account of them ends, as if his pen had been lifted from the leaf. Of the crowd, or the weather, or who wept, the chronicles of the island say nothing. The harbour songs go a little further. They say the fleet stood out west into Manannan's sea, toward the Otherworld of the tellings, Tìr nan Òg and Magh Meall, and that a mist came down on the water behind the last hull and did not lift until it was gone.

Whether the boy's stick said nineteen or twenty-one, no one thought to ask him.

## V. Of the Two Landfalls and the White Sorrow

For nineteen centuries the years of Dia-thìr were counted from that turn, though not at once, and not for ever. In LE 44 Donnchadh mac Thormoid, scribe of the vein-house, began to number the years from the sunwise turn at Seann Skell and called them the years of the Diosal. The crown's scribes took up his count only a generation later. So an island that had reckoned its time by kings and harvests began, in one clerk's hand, to reckon it by an absence.

That same year a report of the fleet came into Seann Skell. By whom it came, or in what boat, the custody-book will not say; only that the harbour scribe copied it in a hand that shook. The copy came down to later keepers stained by water, and its end is gone.

It tells of two landfalls, two separate coasts reached, and the keepers have read in it the seed of two later peoples where one had sailed. Which hulls went to which shore, and whether storm or quarrel or purpose parted them, is dark. Sixteen centuries later Beathag nic Thòmais of Muileann chaol found three copies of the report, and they differed in the order of the coasts and in the number of hulls. She wrote all three out side by side and chose none of them, and the library has followed her ever since.

In LE 46 Queen Beathag struck her sister Mòrag, and Mòrag's children, from the order of succession, as persons no longer on Dia-thìr. The act stands in the roll without comment, between a grain ruling and the mending of a bridge. It is the last time the crown of Dia-thìr wrote Mòrag's name, and it wrote it in the ordinary way.

What befell across the water after that, the island learned in pieces, if it learned it at all. The chronicle calls it the thinning. Cut off from the vein, whatever strength the crossing had asked of the departed faded in their children, and by the third generation abroad nothing was left that Dia-thìr would have known for its own.

Then came the second silence. Some twelve years after the thinning is first written, men spoke of a second and smaller crossing: fewer ships, bound for a shore nobody named. Nothing that survives either bears it out or gives it the lie, and the keepers enter it and let it stand.

In LE 53 the vein-house counted again the households that held the right to the coal, and set the loss down as one hand in five. Beside the figure Donnchadh mac Thormoid wrote that the vein itself answered no differently for those who stayed. Donnchadh never said whether he meant it as comfort or complaint, and men have argued over it since.

The next year the queen made a rite for the departed, and she kept it first for her sister. Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill came into her own hall in a gown of undyed wool, pale and rough as a fleece off the hill, and sat at the head of the board. Beside her a place was laid with no one in it: a cup, a trencher, a knife set straight. The meal that followed was neither feast nor fast. The court did not know what to do with its face, so it ate. The queen did not look at the empty place, and she did not look away from it either.

The court called the custom an Tùrsa Geal, the white sorrow, and the chronicle calls it the Mourning Custom. By the next generation it was kept in every harbour town on the island. Long afterward it would be taken up again, uneasily, for a very different leaving, and that belongs to its own book.

The year after, the island shaped itself around what was left. With part of the coal-bonded people gone the custodian class grew smaller and closer, and every later aristocracy of Dia-thìr was cast in that mould. In LE 55 the remaining custodian households were gathered into seven houses, each answerable to the vein-house for its share of the coal and of the measured burning: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. Mark those names. Until that day the right to the coal had been earned by apprenticeship; from it, the right passed by house.

Queen Beathag died at Cathair dhearg in the summer of that year, the last ruler of Dia-thìr to have seen the fleet. Her son Raghnall mac Uilleim was crowned in the same hall.

## VI. Of the Empty Harbour

The net-menders of Seann Skell tell the years after the leaving on winter nights with the door shut, and they tell them so.

A ceremony grew up around the berth the ships had left from, the empty-harbour rite, and it is kept still, in a lesser form, on an anniversary no one can now fix to the day. By LE 64 the harbour-master was writing his berths down at half their old use, because the fishing households that had crewed the fleet were simply gone, and the rope-walks at Cuan shean laid off hands for the first time. On the north-west coast the fishers of Ceann mhòr kept a watch from the headland for returning sails, household by household in turn. The watch lapsed within a generation. No sail came.

By LE 67 Seann Skell had found a way to go on trading. The berth of the departure was given a new name, so that common trade could keep the old one without the memory clinging to it; the chronicle calls this a forgetting done on purpose. In the harbour rolls the berth became Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn, and the name Cidhe an Iar passed to the new fish-wharf at the north end of the strand, where within a few years the fishers used it without a thought.

The tongue kept what the harbour put away. From LE 67 the custody-book writes *roghnaich*, to choose, with nothing after it, meaning to have chosen the crossing, and the scribes of the next century write it so and never gloss it. By that same year a generation had grown up that had never seen the harbour with those ships in it, and for them the leaving was already history. A saying of the western shore claims to come from about this time:

> *Is fhada an cuan, is goirid a' chuimhne.*
> Long is the sea, and short is memory.

Alasdair Saor died at Seann Skell at the end of that summer. His last work was a coasting trader of the old sewn-plank kind, built for a fish merchant of Inis àrsaidh. Seventeen years later his fellowship came quietly apart, since no one wanted ocean-going hulls any more, and its craft was half forgotten before anyone thought to need it again. In a hard season after that, its patterns and keel-moulds were broken up and burned for firewood. The harbour-master wrote down the loss of the shed and said nothing of what had been in it.

In LE 109 the seven houses drew lots at the vein-house for the galleries each would keep. The lot-stones went into a bag at Muileann dhearg, and for centuries the keepers there tipped them out into the hands of visitors. Doire fhionn, its oaks gone to the fleet, began to cut its woods by coppice, and the law spread to every shire with a *doire* in its name.

Every year on the eve of the empty-harbour rite the waterfront of Seann Skell kept the night of lamps. The children were told the lamps were for ships coming home, and the priests let them believe it. The children's verse is still known on the west coast:

> *Solas air an uinneig,*
> *solas gus an tig iad dhachaigh.*
> A light on the window,
> a light till they come home.

Donnchadh mac Thormoid died at Muileann dhearg in LE 109. His last entry is a list of the coal burned that season, household by household, in the same hand as his first. Sixteen years on, in LE 125, King Raghnall died after a long reign in which little happened, and his son Ìomhar mac Raghnaill was crowned. The custody-book gives Raghnall a single line. After the shaking of its first years the age seems to have wanted no more than that.

## VII. Of the Hawk and the Firlot

The centuries that followed were quiet as a well-kept house is quiet: much afoot, and most of it small. The silver of Muileann chiar, mined since the Holy Age, was beaten into neck-rings for the heads of the seven houses, and the smiths' fellowship of the seam shut its craft up within four families. Inis mhòr built barges for its grain, to go down the Abhainn ghorm and along the coast, sewn-plank boats of the old kind that never slept out of sight of land. The road-house of Am Buabhall Fortanach burned to its footings, and its keeper, Eilidh nic Chaluim, raised it again in stone. The account of her rebuilding already speaks of the jugged buffalo it was known for.

Beathag's line ended in LE 180 with King Ìomhar, who died childless. The heads of the seven houses were summoned to the capital, and in LE 182 they chose Fearchar mac Lachlainn of Baile Mòr dhomhain, of Clann Fhearchair. He was the first king in the record crowned by the choosing of the custodian houses. His son Fearchar Donn followed him, and no one gainsaid it.

In those years the orders of the Old Faith began to take their shapes. At Cnoc bheag the dawn-hawk rite of the Holy Age was still kept, and there in LE 229 the priestess Gormshuil nic Artair taught that the hawk of the rite was Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, the oldest of men, and remembering all things with him; and that the vein was the Hungry Hawk, who must be fed the measured handful and no more. A hawk overfed will not hunt, she said, and a hawk starved will turn on the hand. Her followers gathered the old rite into the first house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig, the order of the Hawk of Acaill, and her pupils raised a second at Ros gheal. After her death her sayings were written down as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the Book of the Hawk. The copyist, Ùisdean mac Pàdraig, marked every saying he had not heard from her own mouth, and the marked sayings outnumber the rest. The first in the book is one he heard:

> *Beathaich an seabhag, ach na sàsaich e.*
> Feed the hawk, but do not glut him.

In LE 261 Clann Ìomhair walled Dùn dhearg in stone, the first walls on the island that any custodian house had raised. That same year Sìleas nic Fhearchair, crowned after her father, fixed one measure for grain across the whole island, the firlot of Cathair dhearg, so that barter between shires need no longer begin with a quarrel over the size of a basket. She sent firlots of oak bound with iron to every shire seat. Later she set a tally-house in each royal granary, where every trade of grain for cloth, salt or labour was cut on paired sticks. It was the first account of trade to run the length of the island, and not one coin passed through it. She reigned more than half a century, and her son Uisdean mac Dhùghaill followed her in LE 324.

It was a good time to be a carter. Near Imrich nam Pantar the herders began clearing the panther roads on the days the great cats crossed, driving their flocks aside beforehand, and those crossing days were the first thing the southern shires ever agreed on in writing. At An Leòmhann Buidhe on the northern mining road the coal-carters were served oatcakes fried in linseed oil, and fire water, and the keeper was fined for watering the fire water. Ros fhionn laid out salt pans at the brine springs on its river flats, and its salt, carted inland over Drochaid Ros fhionn, became the common measure of worth in the north-east.

## VIII. Of the Forbidden Question, the Stone and the Two Horses

In LE 314 Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn, a druid of the schools of Flidais, lady of the deer, whose teaching the old rolls call Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, founded a house of disputation at Dùn thais. There the schools' old question, *Carson an làmh seo?*, why the vein answers some hands and not others, was argued by rule, and pupils came to hear it from as far as Caol bheag.

Ten years later Coinneach stood up in his own hall to ask the thing he had been carrying.

The benches were full, and the air was thick with wet wool and tallow smoke. Coinneach was old enough by then to know which questions were safe. He had turned this one over on the road, to the knock of his stick, and it had grown no safer for the turning.

"We ask why the vein answers this hand and not that one," he said. "Then let us ask it of the hands that went. Were they the hands it answered best? And if they were, does it answer fewer now?"

No one spoke. A bench creaked. Somewhere at the back a young man laughed, once, and then thought better of it. Coinneach waited, as the rule of disputation bade him, for someone to answer. When no one did, he sat down.

The answer came from the seven houses. They forbade the question at their own tables. The record notes that until then they had forbidden only deeds, and that this was the first question they forbade.

The skills of the fleet were slipping already. In LE 344 a merchant of Inis àrsaidh paid for a deep-keeled hull, but the wrights could no longer remember how Alasdair Saor had scarfed his keels, and she listed so badly at her launch that she was broken up for timber.

Aonghas mac Uisdein, crowned in LE 394, was the first king who learned his letters as a child, and in his reign two more orders took their shapes. In LE 409 Dòmhnall mac Ailein, a net-maker of Inis thais, where the wolf-sworn's stone stood, gave that stone its name and its order. He called it Clach, the Stone, and said it was Lia Fàil, which cries out under the rightful king; and he called its sworn guards the Fianna, who keep the island as a wolf keeps its range. So began Òrd na Cloiche, the order of the Stone, and the tales of Fionn and his band, which every hearth on the island knew, the Fianna took for their own. When the Hawk and the Stone both laid claim to the harbour shrine at Caol leathan, the king's reeve divided its days between them as the Holy Age had divided the sacred woods, and the sharing held.

In LE 441 Aonghas himself took up the wood-watchers' rite of Macha, which keeps the two horses of one chariot, foaled on one night: Liath Macha the grey and Dubh Sainglenn the black. Two horses, one yoke, the rite says; dark and light are two powers in balance, and the vein belongs to both. The court followed its king, and Òrd Mhacha, the order of Macha, became the order of Cathair dhearg. From Aonghas on, the kings of Dia-thìr were made by Macha's rite.

In LE 484 Eilidh nic Iain of Doire chiar, called Eilidh Dhubh, raised again the Holy Age's rival teaching, that the vein answers effort and cares nothing for birth, and her tracts were read aloud at harvest gatherings across the north-east. The vein-house ordered every copy brought to Muileann dhearg and burned, and some hundred were given up. Eilidh herself was never punished. She died at Doire chiar, still teaching.

Aonghas died that winter and was the first king buried by the rite of Macha. His son Iain reigned a short while, and Iain's son Tormod mac Iain, called Tormod Bàn for his white hair, was sworn to without dispute. On the central mining road the ox-teams of the mountain now waited out the snow at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, whose keeper, Iain mac Mhurchaidh, built them a second byre and kept a book of the teams that lodged.

## IX. Of the War of the Three Claimants

In LE 534 both sons of King Tormod Bàn were drowned when a ferry overturned crossing Abhainn fhionn in spate. The king had no other child. Thirteen years later he died at Cathair dhearg without naming an heir, and three claims were laid before the houses at once. Catrìona nic Aonghais of Inis thais was the dead king's niece. Dùghall Garbh of Baile Mòr dhomhain was his half-brother. Raghnall Ruadh was head of Clann Raghnaill and master of the vein-house. The seven houses split among the three, and in LE 552 the War of the Three Claimants began.

So small a cause, and so long a war: the keepers have wondered at it. Perhaps, having held the coal by inheritance for five hundred years, each house had come to believe that a crown could be inherited the same way.

Seann Warr, the port nearest the capital on the west, shut its gates on all three and declared for none. It was besieged twice and taken by neither. At the ford of Àth shean, the northern town of that name and no kin to the granary town, Dùghall Garbh's host broke Raghnall Ruadh's, and the custody-book counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned in the ford. Raghnall's men burned Doire mhin and its granary as they fell back, and the villagers wintered at Cathair mhòr on the charity of Macha's priests. Catrìona laid siege to Cathair dhomhain, which had declared for Dùghall, and took it after forty days, when the dead of the siege lines had fouled its wells; and she let the garrison go free on their oath.

Snow lay on the mountain on 24 am Faoilleach, LE 558, when Raghnall Ruadh came out into the yard of the vein-house.

The carriers were waiting there with their baskets and their sealed measures, as carriers had waited every season since before there were kings, stamping against the cold. Beyond the gate the road wound down toward the shires, white and empty.

Raghnall had a list in his hand. His clerk had drawn it up the night before: the shires that stood against him, and every hearth and temple in them that took the handful. It was a long list. He read it through once more in the thin light, and then he gave it to the master of the store.

"None of these," he said.

The master of the store looked at the list, and then at him. Since the Small-Burning Law began it had measured the coal out; no one in that yard had ever seen it used to hold the coal back. "Lord," the man said, and got no further.

"None of these," said Raghnall again, and went in out of the wind.

Down in the shires that stood against him, hearths that had been lit with the coal for generations burned low, and grey, and then went cold. The chronicle says the deed turned more against him than any battle. A verse from the cold shires survives, with no name to it:

> *Cha do chaill sinn blàr, ach chaill sinn an teine.*
> We did not lose a battle, but we lost the fire.

Catrìona and Dùghall joined their hosts against him, and on 14 am Faoilleach, LE 560, in the dead of another winter, they met Raghnall below Muileann chrom. He was killed on the field. The next day his own custodians opened the vein-house, and the carriers went down the white road with their baskets full. Dùghall died of his wounds at Baile Mòr dhomhain in LE 561, and his followers went over to Catrìona without another blow. She was crowned at Cathair dhearg in LE 562, and was called ever after Catrìona Bhuadhach, Catrìona the Victorious. The war had lasted some ten years.

Three years later she did the deed she is remembered for. With the vein-house she fixed it in law that no claimant, house or king might withhold the measured handful from any lawful hearth. This was the ruling of the hearth, the first law in the record written to bind the custodians themselves. To Seann Warr she granted the right to keep its own gates and tolls, in memory of its standing aside, and had the grant cut over the landward gate. When she died in LE 604 the houses swore to her son Lachlann mac Iain in a single day, and the record remarks on it.

In LE 624 Seònaid nic Coinnich, a clerk of the late queen's household, wrote the history of the war from the custody-book and from the mouths of those who had fought. It is the oldest history on Dia-thìr told as one tale from end to end, and every later history of the island descends from it, this book among them. That same year a spotted fever killed some three hundred at Inis chrom. The Fianna of the Stone nursed the sick, and many of them died of it, and after that the town was the Stone's for good.

## X. Of Manannan's Mist, and the Crown Joined to the Vein

So the fishing families of the west coast tell the coming of Manannan's order, as an old woman of Ros bheag once told it to a keeper of Muileann chaol over her nets.

In LE 654 a preacher named Mànas mac Ruairidh stood up at Seann Skell, of all places, where the sting-creed of the Holy Age had first called itself the only true faith, and proclaimed its one power: Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, whose Cup of Truth breaks at a lie spoken over it and bears the yellow scorpion for its sign. Manannan, he said, had shut the western sea behind the fleet with his mist, and hid the island in it from every ship beyond; and what the fleet had done must never be tried again. Those who heard him on the quay were the first congregation of Òrd Mhanannain, the order of Manannan. A month later, in the autumn of LE 654, Lachlann mac Iain died at Cathair dhearg and his daughter Anna was crowned. The record calls his reign quiet, and means it as praise.

The teaching went down the west coast with the fishing families. At Cuan shean the rope-makers, whose walks had been laid out for the fleet, were among the first to take it up. In LE 694 Manannan's priests at Ros bheag laid it down that no boat of the faithful might go beyond sight of the headlands. The west coast kept that rule for centuries, and there the steering of boats by the stars, half lost already, was lost entirely. Of all the orders of the Old Faith the keepers have been least easy with Manannan's, the one order whose teaching stands on the Sundering; and what it teaches is that the island must never again do what the fleet did.

In LE 739 the vein-house and the crown's scribes found that their counts of years since the Setting-Out disagreed. They settled the difference by agreement, and by the same agreement fixed the day of the empty-harbour rite, which the two counts had placed differently. Later scribes gave up pretending it had been fixed by evidence. Every year counted from the Diosal stands on that bargain between two offices, and whoever reads the old rolls should know it.

Eilidh Bhàn, fifth ruler of the house of Catrìona, was crowned in LE 769, and the record of her long reign is nearly all harvests. The north-west had no share in them. From LE 784 boats out of the small islands off that coast fell on the coasting traders and took their fish and grain. The sea-thieves were Dia-thìrich of the north-west shore, and the harbour rolls give some of their names. Baile chrom reported half its houses empty, and the crown remitted its grain dues. In LE 801 a force sent by Eilidh Bhàn landed on Eilean dhubh and burned the thieves' boats on the strand, and their leader, Uilleam Ruadh, was hanged at Cathair dhearg. It did not save the coast. In LE 819 a run of failed harvests brought a dearth to the north-west shore that the shared-meal custom could not carry. Families went inland and east, and the north-west stayed thinly held until the age was out.

In LE 829 the queen's scribes recopied the king-list from its oldest surviving roll and added the rulers since the Sundering. The new copy opens the present age with the Choosing, ahead of the fleet, and this book keeps that order. Twelve years after, Eilidh Bhàn died childless, and the seven houses met to choose; this time they met at the vein-house, and the capital waited on their word. They named Dòmhnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill, a descendant of the claimant killed at Muileann chrom, and he kept the mastery of the vein-house together with the crown. In LE 859 his reeves wrote into the custody-book that the ruler of Dia-thìr is also master of the vein-house. From then on the heads of the seven houses sat as the king's council, and custodians and court were one body. What Raghnall Ruadh had seized in war, his descendant now held by law. The ruling of the hearth still bound the custodians; the custodians, now, were the crown. Dòmhnall Ruadh was buried at Muileann dhearg, under the mountain, far from the capital.

The Hawk split in LE 889 over whether Mòd's measure might ever be raised. Those who held it fixed for ever kept the name of the Hungry Hawk and the house at Cnoc bheag. Those who said a larger flock might be fed a larger handful were called the Fed Hawk, and they went to Seann Skell on the north coast, the other town of that name. In LE 919 they petitioned the council to raise the handful by a quarter for the northern hearths. The council refused. It was the first recorded asking to change the Small-Burning Law, and the custody-book enters the Fed Hawk's teaching as an error, at length.

## XI. Of the Stair under the Hill

In LE 929 a second tremor in the hills of Cill ghlas brought down a gallery of the vein and killed fourteen labourers. The vein-house closed the gallery and set a stone at its mouth with the fourteen names cut on it. The last shepherds left the high pastures of Doire uaine. They said it was for the grazing, and every one of them who was asked also spoke of the Marbh-bheò.

In LE 979, north of the capital, a quarry face gave way under the hammers and opened on darkness.

Air came up out of the hole, cold as well-water, and it smelt of nothing at all, which was worse than any smell. One of the quarrymen held a lamp in at arm's length, and they saw steps: a stair cut in the living rock, each tread worn hollow at the middle, going down and down past where the light would reach. Someone said the name before anyone else could, Toll-dubh, the shaft of the old tellings, long lost. After that nobody said anything.

One of them went down. His fellows watched his lamp go, turning and dropping and dwindling, until the rock swallowed it. They waited. One who was there said afterward that they waited long enough to be ashamed of how glad they were when the light came back.

The man climbed out, sat down on the spoil heap and said nothing, and whatever he may have said later went unwritten. The custodians came down from the vein-house and had the entrance walled up.

Twenty years later Ailean mac Dhùghaill of the druid school at Dùn thais measured the ruin of Làrach an Teampaill and wrote that its altar faced the central mountains, with its back to the sea. Who had set it so, he would not guess. By LE 1,011 he had finished his tables of the three old ruins, Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin and Làrach an Teampaill, with their measures and their stone and the lie of each, and he concluded that he could not say whether one people had built all three. Because of his tables no one after him could say either.

Mòrag Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill was crowned in LE 1,019, the first ruler whose household accounts survive whole. On 15 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,039, in the dark of the year, the vein-house marked the thousandth year of its count with a single measured burning of the coal on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell, and the queen stood by. The flame burned the colour of the vein, the record says, and the crowd went home without a word.

## XII. Of Things Forgotten, and the Brothers' War

After the thousandth year the island began, plainly, to lose what it knew.

A sickness that closed the throat, the swallowing cough, broke out at Muileann dhomhain in LE 1,079 and killed nearly a third of the town. When it reached Seann Bhral the townsfolk shut their own harbour and kept the shared-meal custom by leaving food at the gate. Queen Beathag Fhionn, daughter of Mòrag Ruadh, closed the coast road between the two towns and set reeves at the fords to turn travellers back, and the cough went no further west. Her son Ailean followed her, the first of four kings of that name in the house of Raghnall.

The dyers of Baile ghorm had made a fast blue from a marsh plant and a mordant of their own, and it was the feast-day dress of the seven houses. In LE 1,139 the last dyer who knew the mordant died without apprentices, having quarrelled with both of hers, and the blue that came after was the common blue of the rest of the island.

The Abhainn bheag silted behind a shifting bar below Ros fhionn, and the salt-masters moved their trade to Caol gharbh on the coast. The carts stopped crossing Drochaid Ros fhionn, and the bridge-keeper's office was done away with. Fishers of the thinned north-west saw the Sea-Watcher, Uilebheist na Mara, close enough to foul their nets, and the few boats left there drew further in.

In LE 1,209 Raghnall mac Chaluim of the druid school at Dùn thais set out a table showing that the heads of the custodian houses lived, on the average, a few years longer than the tenants of their lands, and he asked whether the vein answers the hand that holds it. The record notes the finding uneasily and gives it no answer. The council forbade the table to be copied and shut the house at Dùn thais for a generation. Raghnall's own copy went into the vein-house and was entered in its inventory.

In LE 1,266 King Ailean mac Raghnaill died and left two sons by different mothers, Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, each of whom had been told he was the heir. Four years after, Alasdair Bàn's men seized Cnoc naomh and Iain Ciar took it back. The houses split four to three, and the Brothers' War, Cogadh nam Bràithrean, took its name from that fight. Alasdair's ships burned the waterfront of Ceann mhin, which held for his brother; the fire took the rope stores and the granary, and the town had to beg its bread from Cathair mhòr. In LE 1,274 Iain Ciar beat Alasdair below Muileann ghlas, took him alive, and let his captains go home. The field comes into the record again two ages on.

The peace was made in LE 1,276 at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, the road-house where the ox-teams waited out the snow, on neutral ground between the brothers' lands.

The keeper of the house had been given a day's warning and had spent it scrubbing. She set the long board in the common room with a bench on either side, the benches the same length to a finger's breadth, for she had heard that great men quarrel over such things, and she put the same bread and the same ale at each end. Then she stood by the fire and tried to look as though she were not listening.

Iain Ciar came in first and sat. Alasdair Bàn came after him, stiff as a man is who has lately been a prisoner, and sat down across the board. For a long while neither spoke, and the keeper could hear the oxen shifting in the byre. What passed between them she never told. Alasdair gave up his claim and took the lordship of Seann Chwen for his life. Iain Ciar was crowned. When they rose, both loaves had been broken and neither eaten.

Alasdair kept the peace he had made and died at Seann Chwen. Because he had seen Ceann mhin beg its bread, Iain Ciar ordered every shire seat to keep a year's grain against the next war. The law held while he lived and lapsed within a few years of his death, as he had foreseen in a note in his own hand. His clerk Pàdraig mac Ruairidh wrote the account of the war. It praises the king at every turn, and it is the only account that survives, which later readers have found inconvenient.

The road-houses come back into the record here. In LE 1,319 the crown chartered the seven great road-houses of the mining circuit and made their keepers answerable for the roads between them, and the keepers met once a year at An Sligeanach Fad' às to settle their accounts. At An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the bare northern road a party of reeves was snowed in for a whole season and lived on pickled spinach and fire milk. Their complaint to the charter-roll is set down in full.

In LE 1,359 Seumas mac Iain of Seann Skell tried to build a deep-keeled hull again from what the strand still remembered of the Sundering fellowship's lore. She filled and sank at her launch, and Manannan's priests preached on her for a year.

Thirty years later Iseabail nic Lachlainn, a folk-collector of the royal household, came to Cuan shean for the songs of the rope-makers. She found them at the end of a walk that had lost half its length to barley, going backward in a line as they twisted the strands and singing to keep the pace. Most of it was the common stuff of work-songs. Then the leader struck up a song she had never heard, and the others fell in behind him, and she caught *druim* and *aisne*, keel and rib, and began to write fast.

Afterward she asked what the song was about. Rope, they told her. And the words further on? They looked at one another. Nobody knew. They were the words of the song.

It names the parts of a deep keel. It is the only record of the fleet's craft that survives in any shape. Its first lines can still be understood:

> *Druim fon aisne, aisne fon chlàr,*
> *clàr ri clàr is an cuan fodhpa.*
> Keel under rib, rib under plank,
> plank to plank and the sea beneath them.

After that the song runs on in words no one can read. The rope-makers who kept it were of Manannan's order by then, and they sang it anyway.

## XIII. Of the Last Lamps

The last four centuries of the age are the longest stretch in the record and have the least to tell, and the keepers will not dress them up.

The order of the Stone split over whether the dead, who are Donn's, might be prayed for at Clach, and its two houses, at Inis thais and Baile gheal, were not reconciled in this age. Catrìona Bheag of Clann Raghnaill was crowned in LE 1,429, the first queen in more than three centuries. The record notes that she was small, and that no one said so twice. In LE 1,449 she had the heads of the seven houses swear to the ruling of the hearth in her presence, the first renewal of that oath since Catrìona Bhuadhach. Clann Choinnich swore last.

More was forgotten. The potters of Muileann gheal made a grey-green glaze no other kiln could match, and the custodian houses bought it for their tables. The secret stayed in one family, and in LE 1,509 the last of them died without passing it on. The smiths of Dùn dhearg lost the last man who knew how their layered steel was folded, and afterward the blades of Dùn dhearg were ordinary. In the east, charcoal-burners found again the eastern Toll-dubh of the old tellings, with the same cut stair as the first. The custodians walled that one up as well, and the scribe cross-referenced the two entries.

At Àth shean the granary found that its firlot had worn smaller than the standard of Cathair dhearg, and had been so for generations. The reeve corrected the accounts as far back as anyone could reckon.

Sìleas Òg, named for the queen of the firlot, was crowned in LE 1,529, the first ruler to visit every shire seat. She ordered a new count of the households holding the right to the coal. It came out smaller than any before it, for the right had narrowed into fewer and larger households, and she had it entered without comment. In LE 1,559 Clann Choinnich asked leave to burn the coal beyond the measured handful to smelt silver at Muileann chiar, arguing that it burned hotter than charcoal. The council refused. Until then the coal had been burned only for worship, and this was the first asking to burn it for work. The keepers know where that asking leads in the next age, and here they only set it down.

Ailean the Fourth had the shortest reign in the king-list. His sister Mòrag nic Ailein, who followed him, reigned forty years, and her entries record nothing but good harvests and the rite. In LE 1,590 the priests of Manannan met in synod at Seann Skell, restated the rule of sight-of-land, and added a prayer to be said at the foot of the river pool:

> *A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte.*
> Manannan, keep the sea shut.

The library that keeps this record begins here. In LE 1,659 Beathag nic Thòmais, a mill-owner's widow of Muileann chaol, began buying up old copies of the custody-book and the harbour rolls from houses that no longer read them, and stacked them in a loft over her mill. Soon a mill in the same town began making paper from rags, the first on Dia-thìr, and the custody-book was copied onto paper for the first time. Among her papers were the three copies of the landfall report. She died in LE 1,699 and left the loft to the town on condition that nothing in it be burned. The town kept that condition, and very little else of her wishes.

The crown sent a reeve to list the households of the north-west coast between Baile chrom and Ceann mhòr, and he counted fewer households than harbour berths. Tormod mac Ruairidh, crowned in LE 1,709, reigned more than fifty years. In LE 1,714 Manannan's priests at Seann Skell began saying their prayer to keep the sea shut on the same day as the empty-harbour rite, so that the two were kept together on Cidhe an Diosail. Neither side was pleased.

In LE 1,749 a visiting scribe found the rite at Seann Skell kept by the harbour priests and a few old families, and wrote that none of them could say on which day the fleet had truly sailed. The house of disputation at Dùn thais, shut and opened more than once since the table of years, opened again in LE 1,759 on condition that the question of longer lives was not raised. The scholars agreed, and argued about the vein instead.

Tormod's daughter Gormshuil nic Thormoid, crowned in LE 1,766, rode a progress round every shire seat. Her clerks wrote down each shire's grievances, and she answered none of them in writing. On the eastern road An Taigh-òsta Grianach fed her company on pan-fried spinach and black wine, and its keeper, Peigi nic Dhonnchaidh, was let off her road dues for a year. It is the last warm entry of the age. In LE 1,776 Clann Choinnich asked again to burn the coal for the silver smelt, with three of the seven houses behind it now, and Gormshuil's council refused by one voice. The record names the member who changed his vote and keeps his reason to itself. In LE 1,791 the vein-house counted the households of the right for the last time in this age. They were fewer than ever, and larger, and three of the seven houses held more than half the right between them.

In LE 1,794 a worked timber came ashore at Ceann mhòr on the empty north-west coast, from beyond Manannan's mist, as the fishers said. It was longer than any tree on the island and fastened with nails of a make no smith on Dia-thìr knew. They carted it to Seann Skell and showed it to Manannan's priests, and the priests burned it.

By then fewer and fewer houses on the Seann Skell waterfront kept the night of lamps, and at last none did. An old woman set a lamp in a window of the harbour-house, and the scribe wrote that it was she who kept it, and not the town.

On 25 an t-Samhain, LE 1,803, the harbour scribe of Seann Skell went down to Cidhe an Diosail with his board and his pen for the empty-harbour rite. The dressed stones of the old quay were green at the foot, where the river had been working at them for eighteen centuries. He counted the people standing on them, and it did not take him long. There were eleven. When the rite and Manannan's prayer were said and the people had gone home, he looked at the sky and at the water, and wrote down the number, the weather and the state of the tide. He sat a while with the pen in his hand before he closed the board.

Clann Choinnich did not bring its silver petition to the council again, for the member who had turned the vote had died. The petition lay in the vein-house unanswered, and the record of the age ends with the Small-Burning Law still kept.

In those last winters the priests of Manannan at Seann Skell wrote that the mist on the western sea, which had hidden Dia-thìr from every ship beyond it since the fleet sailed into it, lay thinner each year. On 27 an Dàmhair, LE 1,813, they set it down in so many words, and they said their prayer at every tide.

A fisher of the west coast, putting out before dawn on one of those still mornings, rested on her oars off the headland where the rule of sight-of-land told her to turn. All her life the grey had stood out there on the water like a wall of wet fleece, and the sea ran into it and did not come out. That morning she could see through it. Beyond the grey lay a line, hard and dark and level, ruled across the edge of the world: the open sea, going on. She looked at it for a long time. Then she turned for home as the rule said, and from the quay she heard the priests at their prayer. Manannan, keep the sea shut.

Eighteen centuries after a queen at Cathair dhearg said she would keep no one back, Dia-thìr had kept the vein and kept the law, and had let go of nearly everything else the fleet had meant: the keel and the stars, the far coast, all but eleven keepers of the rite. The houses were fewer and richer. The north-west was nearly empty. For two hundred years the prayer to keep the sea shut had been said, and no one had tried the sea. Then the mist lifted, and sails came in over that water from the far side, and they were no sails of Dia-thìr. The people under them had crossed the water the Dia-thìrich once crossed. Whether any of them came down from those who chose to go, no one on Dia-thìr knew then, and no one knows now. With their coming begins the Age of Strangers, and the next book tells it.


# The Fourth Book: An Aois Choigreach, the Age of Strangers

*AE 1 – 151*

> *Thàinig na coigrich air an t-sàl, agus dh'fhàg iad an cnoc falamh.*
>
> The strangers came over the brine, and they left the hill empty.
>
> — a line sung in the camps, as the copyists at Muileann chaol set it down

*Here is told the history of Dia-thìr from the Crossing to the Severance: the hundred and fifty years in which men from over the western sea ruled the island, first by leave and then without it. It is drawn from four witnesses: the rolls of the custodians, most of which live now only in the copies made in a cellar of Muileann chaol; the letter-books of the humans' Administration, left lying in the Residency when its masters fled; the daybooks of the beacon-keepers, who wrote down every sail they saw; and the songs of the camps, which were forbidden, and were written down for that reason. Where the witnesses quarrel, both are heard. Where they fall silent, the telling falls silent with them.*

## I. Of the Three Ships and the Leave to Stay

The age begins with the Crossing, on 5 am Faoilleach, AE 1, when the humans first made landfall on Dia-thìr. That winter Manannan's mist lifted, which had lain on the western sea since the fleet of the Sundering sailed into it and had hidden the island from every ship beyond. The fishers of Achadh àrsaidh saw it go, and theirs is the first telling.

Two boats were out that morning, working the lines off the north-west cape, where the old men say the Sea-Watcher rises when it pleases. The mist stood on the water as it had stood all their lives, a grey wall a few oar-lengths off. But that morning the wall had gone to gauze, and behind the gauze there was a paleness that moved.

It was sail; then three sails, heaped high on masts taller than any tree the fishers knew, and under them black hulls, wet and shining, coming on slowly out of the west with the mist tearing off their bows in rags. A voice called down from high up in a tongue that was no tongue at all.

The steersman stood and gave back the old hail of the north-west boats. The voice answered. Neither understood a word of the other. Nothing in all the customs of Dia-thìr told a fisherman what to do when the sea opened. At last the steersman put his tiller over and turned south for Cuan shean, where there were custodians whose business it was to know. When he looked back, the three ships were following.

The place of that meeting is called Coinneachadh nan Long, the meeting of the ships (13 am Faoilleach, AE 1), and the boats of Achadh àrsaidh slow there still.

The roll of Cuan shean, which is the fuller witness, first sets the ships down on 5 an Gearran, AE 1: three hulls out of the west riding at anchor off the town, the first of their size seen from any shore of the island since the fleet of the Sundering went out sunwise from the harbour and did not come back. Their master came in through the surf in a small boat with eleven men and no weapon among them that anyone could see. The roll calls him Edmund Harrow. He waded the last of the way, stood on the shingle in front of the custodians of the town, and held out an empty cask and tipped his hand to his mouth.

They gave him water. More than that they would not give on their own word, for no custodian living had ever been asked such a thing, and they sent a rider inland to the capital for counsel. For forty days the strangers were fed on the beach and kept below the dunes.

On 11 am Faoilleach, AE 2, the Council of Custodians at Cathair dhearg gave the strangers leave to stay. The council had sat in the crown's place since the crown fell vacant at the close of the Age of Sundering, and its high custodian in those years was Tormod mac Ailein. The roll enters the vote as unanimous. In the margin a later hand has written that three custodians were absent. The copyists kept the note, for it is the first of many places in the record of this age where what was written and what was so do not quite meet.

Soon the old sailors of Cuan shean began to say that the strangers had come in from the very quarter of the sea into which the Sundering fleet had sailed. The council forbade the remark in its hall. It was written down anyway, and never answered. Whether the humans were children of the departed, or of some other people of those waters, or of no one the Dia-thìrich ever knew, the island has never learned.

## II. Of the Season of Words

The strangers had a name for their homeland in their own tongue, and no Dia-thìreach scribe troubled to set it down. From the first season the rolls call it *an Tìr Thall*, the land beyond, and call its people simply the humans; and so they are called in this book. They had brought their god with them over the sea: Crìosd, one God and no other, with priests and a Bible and a great company of saints. The Dia-thìrich called that faith *an Eaglais*, the Church, after the word its clerics used, and the name has held.

Then came the season of words, when the clerics of the Church and the custodians sat down together to make a common tongue out of two. What was agreed in that season neither side has handed down whole. Two lists were kept, side by side.

The custodian Gormshuil nic Fhearchair kept the Dia-thìreach list. Through that season she sat across a table from the cleric Samuel Wren, a thin, courteous man who coughed in the damp, and the two of them pointed at things. He held up a cup and said his word, and she wrote it; she held up bread and said *aran*, and he wrote that. Before the season was out they had some hundreds of words each.

Then one morning Gormshuil tipped a basket of broken coal out on the table where the window-light fell, a double handful from the vein, black as a wet crow and bright with a sheen, the colours shining at the edges where it had split.

She began to name the colours. There was the green that lies under the black like deep water under weed, and the red at the break that deepens if you breathe on it, and the grey-violet of old cuttings, and the brown that means the piece came from near the surface; and she laid a finger on each and gave its word, as any child of the hills could have done. She gave forty, and there were more, and she stopped because Wren had stopped writing.

He picked up a piece and turned it in the light with his eyes narrowed, and looked at her in a puzzled, kindly way. Then he said a single word, and wrote a single word, and tapped the whole heap with his pen to show that the word stood for all of it.

When she understood the word she sat very still. It was the word for the fuel his people burned at home.

She waited for him to ask for hers. He smiled, and set the coal aside to make room on the table, and held up a candle.

Wren's list lies still in the Administration's letter-books. Gormshuil's was lost, and only its first leaf lives on, in a copy: forty words for the colours of broken coal. Her copyist wrote beneath it a thing the chroniclers have since set at the head of the whole age. The humans had one word for the coal of the vein, and it was their word for the black fuel of their own hearths. No Dia-thìris word in either list answered to it, for to Dia-thìreach eyes no coal of the vein is only black. And the humans did not ask for one.

## III. Of the Years of Fair Exchange

Let it be told plainly, since what came after has thrown its shadow back across them: the first years were good. The island had been alone for eighteen centuries and lacked much that the strangers had, and the giving ran both ways. For a few years the bargain looked as if it would last, and those who trusted it were no fools.

The humans set up a trading post at Ros dhomhain, the capital's harbour on the lake. Iron tools went across its counter, and window glass, lamp-oil and paper; wool came back, and salt fish, hides and dyed cloth. Its first tally-book, kept by the trader Thomas Pike, balances to the last line across its first year. The smiths of Cathair dhearg took the humans' bar-iron gladly and learned to temper it in a single winter, and within a few seasons the old bronze hoes of the capital's fields were melted down for bells. The salt-pans of Seann Warr sold to Pike by the barrel, and theirs was the first Dia-thìreach trade the humans came back asking for twice.

Harrow sailed west with hides and cloth in his holds and came back with four ships in place of three. He brought carpenters, and a surgeon, and a letter from a trading house in an Tìr Thall asking what else the island had. The surgeon, Jonas Tull, set the broken leg of a Cuan shean fisherman whom the whole town had given up for lame, and the custodian of Cuan shean entered it in the roll as the first debt owed to a stranger.

In AE 5 the small port of Baile dhìreach, on the south-west coast, took Dia-thìrich and humans alike under one council of six, three of either people. Its founding compact was written twice, once in each tongue, and it is the only such compact of the age. The chair passed in alternate years between the fisherman Iain mac Chaluim and the human carpenter William Rook, and the harbour dues went half to the custodians and half to the humans' post.

At Baile dhìreach the net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh married the human cooper Samuel Hale. The council entered the marriage in both its books. The custodians at Cathair dhearg, asked for a ruling on it, sent none. No other town tried what Baile dhìreach had tried, and the tellers will come back to that marriage when they reach the years in which the humans' law found a use for it.

In AE 6 a human supply ship struck the western reefs in fog and nine of her crew were drowned. Her master had been sailing, the letter-books complain, by a chart drawn from memory on a coast lit only by the old driftwood fires. The human navigators asked for beacons, and the Dia-thìreach engineers agreed, and did not yet see what the asking would bring. The navigator James Fenn and the Dia-thìreach mason Torcall Clachair walked the coast together that year to choose the ground. They marked the five headlands of the old fires. Fenn's chart survives. Torcall's cairns, for the most part, have gone back into the hills.

## IV. Of the Treaty in One Tongue, and the Company

In AE 8 the terms of the humans' presence were set down in writing for the first time, in the humans' tongue only, and no one on the Dia-thìreach side is known to have spoken against it.

Tormod mac Ailein came to the council hall at Cathair dhearg on the day of the signing, 7 an Cèitean, AE 8, and sat down at the long table across from Josiah Pell, newly come over the sea as the humans' first Commissioner. Between them lay the treaty, covered edge to edge in the strangers' close black writing.

Tormod could not read a word of it. The letters stood on the page like a fence of thorn. Someone read it to him, and he sat with his hands folded and listened as the voice went down the sheets, and once he asked for a line to be read again. Outside the rain was coming off the lake.

When the reading was done Pell turned the last sheet round and held out a pen. Tormod took it. He looked a long moment at the place where his name should go, as a man looks at a ford before he wades it. Then he wrote, and Pell signed after him for the Administration.

The treaty was dated by the humans' day, month and year. The custodians' clerk entered it in the roll under its year of the Diosal and the moon in which it was signed, and left the day empty, having nothing to put there. It was the first of many such pages. Within a generation every clerk on the island wrote two dates at the head of his page, and the crews in the Company's pits had learned the humans' week before they learned their prayers, because they were paid by it.

Pell built a house of dressed stone on the rise above Ros dhomhain and called it the Residency, and from it the humans governed Dia-thìr for a hundred and forty years. Harrow went back to the sea, and with Pike he founded a trading house licensed by the Administration, which the island knew only as the Company. Its charter gave it first refusal on "all fuels, ores and minerals the island may yield." Its first building of its own was a stone warehouse at Cathair dhomhain, along the lake shore, where it kept its tools out of reach of the harbour thieves. The copyists ask the reader to remember that warehouse.

The strangers' fever came ashore at Cuan shean with a crowded ship in AE 9 and ran down the west coast. Ninety-one Dia-thìrich died of it, by the custodians' count, and eleven humans. The custodians shut Cuan shean to ships for a season, and Pell protested in writing.

In AE 10 the Company sent two prospectors, Abel Stone and Hugh Mercer, into the hills east of the capital, the country of Muileann chrom. They came down again with sacks of broken coal on their backs and word that the black seam ran "further than can be walked in a day." The custodians demanded the coal back, to be laid in the rock again with the proper words. The Company gave back half. The roll enters the other half as "carried west."

In AE 11 barter gave way to contract. Under the first contracts of extraction Dia-thìreach hands began to cut the vein on a scale that no reverent keeping had ever used. A crew of thirty opened the first pit at Muileann chrom, paid by the ton in iron tools and lamp-oil, where the custodians' own cuttings had never once been measured by weight. The Company built a coal quay at Ceann fhada, a fishing hamlet below the hills, and paid the fishermen for their foreshore in iron nails, by weight. Wren finished his grammar of Dia-thìris for the Mission, which was the Church's mission to the island. It is careful and right in most things, and it turns the name of the vein's custodians into "keepers of the coal." The Mission raised a chapel on the quay at Ros dhomhain and hung in it the first iron bell on Dia-thìr, and the custodians asked that it not be rung before the fishing fleet was out.

In AE 14 one settlement would not sign.

The Company's agent climbed to Doire mhòr, in the hills above Muileann chrom, with the contract under his coat. The custodian, Beathag Dhubh, met him at her door and did not ask him in. She let him say all he had come to say, and answered him in a few words, and shut the door.

Her words live only in his report, where he set them down in his own tongue: that the hill was not hers to sell, and not his to buy.

Doire mhòr was not punished. The Company opened its next working at Cnoc fhiadhaich instead, and ran its cart-road round Doire mhòr's fields rather than through them. The annals add two words: *for now*.

The first of the new beacons was finished in AE 15 on the southern headland at Tobar dhearg, a round tower of grey stone raised over the old fire-tower and paid for by the Company. Torcall Clachair built it and Fenn set its lens.

In AE 17 the humans brought in their coin beside the barter of the island, for convenience, they said: the mark and its hundred pence, struck at Ros dhomhain from metal shipped in from an Tìr Thall, with a ship on one face and nothing of Dia-thìr on either. At the capital the custodians' clerks began to keep two sets of books, and complained of it in both. Within ten years nothing that came across the sea could be had for anything but marks.

Wren spent a winter at Dùn thais among the druids of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, the school of the deer. He asked them why the vein should be holy. They asked him why his fuel should be burned. Neither side's account names a winner. Wren wrote home that the druids told of a voyage west to an isle of the blessed very like his own Church's telling of Naomh Breandan, told from the other shore, and that he did not know what to make of it.

The Harbour Articles followed, written like the treaty in the humans' tongue alone, and they fixed the dues at Ros dhomhain in the Company's favour. This time two custodians refused to sign. The council granted the Administration upland grazing in the north-west, around Muileann àrsaidh, for human families who would not work in the pits. The grant was for grazing. The families built houses of stone.

Tormod mac Ailein died at Cathair dhearg in AE 20, and the council chose Coinneach Glas of Ceann àrsaidh to follow him, a man who had never met a human before the Crossing and had dealt with little else since. In AE 21 Edmund Harrow's ship did not come home from the western crossing. The Company passed wholly into Pike's hands, and the letter-books mourned Harrow as the man who found Dia-thìr.

## V. Of the Lapse of the Law, and the First Steward

The keepers at the hearths of the hills tell the end of the Small-Burning Law as they would tell of a fire that went out for want of feeding. That Law had been kept since the Holy Age: that the vein be cut and burned sparingly, and that what the hill could give in a year be counted and never exceeded. The Age of Sundering ended with it still kept. Within a generation of the Crossing it was gone. No council repealed it. It stopped being enforced when it stopped paying to enforce it. At Dùn dhearg the custodian Fionnghal nic Artair wrote to the council the only defence of the Law that has come down. The Law, she wrote, was made for the people more than for the coal, for a people becomes whatever its burning makes it.

At Seann Skell the hawk-priest Murchadh Seabhag preached that Mòd, the Hungry Hawk of Acaill, starves those who eat faster than the land can feed them. The sermon was copied and carried into the camps, and it was the first Dia-thìreach writing the Company's agents were told to seize. At Muileann chrom the Company burned coal by the cartload to drive its pumps, and when Coinneach Glas's council asked that the old tally be kept, it was sent a copy of the Company's accounts.

Pell sailed home in AE 24 and did not return. Henry Maddox came in his place, with orders to double the yield and a letter in his pocket promising him a share of it. In AE 25 a gallery at Cnoc fhiadhaich, driven forward faster than any Dia-thìreach crew would have chosen and without the timbering the crews had begged for, came down and killed eleven. The custodians' roll names all eleven. The Company's report names none, and calls the gallery "unsound ground." Then a dry cough ran through the camps and killed thirty-eight, most of them boys who broke coal at the pit-mouth. The Mission's surgeon called it a winter complaint. It lasted through the summer.

The second beacon was lit at Baile ìseal on the eastern shore, with Torcall Clachair directing the work from a chair at the foot of the headland, too old now to climb. The Company founded a camp of timber huts at Àth ìseal, the first settlement on Dia-thìr built for no purpose but the pit. It dammed the stream that watered Doire mhòr to wash its coal. No order for it was ever found. Beathag Dhubh's people carried water up by hand for two summers, and then they began to leave. In AE 30 the hill villages lost their oats to rain that no one was home to cut ahead of, and the Company sold them meal for marks, and they had few marks.

From AE 31 the mountain was worked by the ton. The Company was chartered anew in an Tìr Thall under a name the Dia-thìrich never used, and at Ros dhomhain its agents outnumbered the Administration's clerks four to one. Coal barges loaded at Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine, where the old canoe landing was widened with cut stone and its shrine carried uphill out of the way. Within a few seasons the green river ran black with slurry and the salmon at its mouth failed, and the fishermen kept the river's name and said it bitterly. Baile dhomhain was laid out on a grid by a Company surveyor, the first Dia-thìreach town drawn on paper before a stone of it was set. On the coal road the old carters' house at the halfway stage was rebuilt and kept its name, An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, and its keeper Seònaid Bhàn took marks and barter both, the only keeper on the road who would. Seann Toll was made a coal landing for the barges on the Abhainn uaine, and its fishing boats were moved to the next reach.

In AE 36 a Dia-thìreach was set over Dia-thìreach miners to answer to human masters, and the chroniclers count it the first crack within the Dia-thìrich themselves. He was Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill of Muileann chrom, a crew-leader since the first contract. The Company gave him its staff and a house with a slate roof, and the Dia-thìrich gave him his byname: Raghnall Maor, Raghnall the steward. Soon there were overseers at every working in the district, and the roll stopped giving their names and gave only their number. At Cnoc mhòr the overseer Seumas Dubh was killed by his own crew after a boy was crushed on a haulage he had ordered hurried, and the Company hanged two men at Ros dhomhain. It was the first hanging the Administration did on Dia-thìr.

Maddox barred the priests of the hawk from the camps in AE 38, on the ground that their preaching slowed the work. The overseers enforced it; several of them were hawk-faithful themselves, and the roll says so. A spotted pox came up the coal road from the quays of Ros dhomhain. The Mission counted four hundred and six dead. The custodians counted more, and wrote the difference in the margin of the Mission's list. The Administration moved its customs house from Baile dhìreach to Ros dhomhain, and the mixed council there, left with half an income, shrank from six to four. In AE 41 Maddox left Dia-thìr a rich man, and Arthur Lisle, a lawyer, came to the Residency. His first act was to have every agreement since the treaty copied into a single bound book.

## VI. Of the Silver Compact, and the Things the Clerks Could Not File

Reading that book closely, Lisle found in it nothing whatever about silver.

When the Company's surveyors came up the valley to Muileann chiar with their chains and pegs, Ùna nic Choinnich was waiting for them at the mouth of the adit. Behind her, filling the yard and the slope above it, stood the whole membership of the guild in their leather aprons, not one of them speaking, and two of the eldest held the guild's ledgers open across their forearms.

The chief surveyor began to read out his authority. Ùna let him finish. Then she turned the first ledger toward him, and the second, and asked him, in his own tongue and quite pleasantly, to find the humans' name anywhere in either.

He looked. The yard waited, and the wind came down off the hill with the smell of the smelting-floors in it. After a while the surveyor closed his book, and the Company's men went back down the valley.

On Là Fhèill Brìde of AE 44 Lisle signed a compact that left the seam to the town. It was the first writing of the age in which the Dia-thìreach side kept the better terms, and Muileann chiar held its silver in its own hand through all the rest of the age. When a Company coal ship was taken off the eastern coast by raiders in low black boats and burned to the waterline, the Company said the guild had paid them. The guild said nothing.

The third beacon was lit at Àth dhearg in AE 45, and its keeper, Tormod mac Pheadair, kept a daybook of every ship he saw. From his book, and the books of the keepers after him, the sailings of the humans in this age are known; and the copyists have leaned on the daybooks more than on any other witness, for a keeper has nothing to gain from a ship that is not there.

In AE 47 the council of Baile dhìreach broke up in a quarrel over a boundary wall and never sat again. The human families went to Ros bheag and Ros dhomhain; the Dia-thìrich stayed. The households that were both split, or went quiet. The next year the rain failed for a single season around Achadh shean, and it was a warning nobody heeded.

At Dùn thais in AE 49 the Deer master Aonghas mac Coinnich put to his students a question the register calls new: why the humans could not see the colour in broken coal that every Dia-thìreach child sees. He did not answer it, and told them it was the wrong question. Its form in the Deer books has been quoted in every age since:

> *Carson a chì sinne an dath, is iadsan dall air?*
>
> Why do we see the colour, and they blind to it?

On the concession the human families founded a market town at Cathair gheal under a charter that made no mention of the custodians. In AE 51 the family of Eachann Mòr, a custodian of Ceann àrsaidh who had lost his seat, sent their son Calum west on a Company ship hoping his schooling would buy them better treatment. He never came home. The Mission opened a school at Ros dhomhain in the humans' tongue, and most of its pupils were the children of overseers. The Company rebuilt the old bridge over the river at Ros fhionn for its eastern coal road.

Two things the Administration's clerks never knew where to file. The crew of a Company brig reported a beast larger than their ship off the north-western headlands; the clerk put the report in with the complaints about pirates, and the sailors of that coast said they had wondered when the humans would see it. And two Company surveyors went up into the hills at Doire uaine against the villagers' advice and were not seen again.

In AE 57 the Administration's share of the coal rose sharply, and what the Dia-thìreach towns received did not rise with it. Lisle's schedule took the portion from one part in five to one part in three, and the custodians received it in the humans' tongue with a translation made by a Mission pupil. A bloody flux broke out on the Ros dhomhain quays; the Mission's nurse Anne Colby turned the chapel into a sick-house, and the record credits her with keeping the dead under two hundred. Lisle died at the Residency in AE 61, and Walter Crane, the Company's chief agent at the pits, took the seal after him, the first man to hold both offices in turn.

Raghnall Maor died in AE 62, and the Company gave his staff to his son Dòmhnall. The custodians had hoped the office would die with the man. It became a family's inheritance instead.

The fourth beacon was lit at Muileann bheag in AE 63. It was the first to burn coal in place of oil, and its flame laid a colour on the water that no oil lamp ever had. The Mission cleric Edwin Lowe dug that season at Làrach an Teampaill and found cut stone, burnt bone and marks he could not read, and wrote that the ruin's builders "were not the present race." The custodians agreed with him, and added nothing. What became of the Seann-Dhaoine his spade did not turn up.

In AE 67 the Company agent Martha Gale offered the silver guild a partnership, on terms its own ledger calls generous. Ùna nic Choinnich was very old by then. She had the offer read aloud twice in the guild hall, slowly, and then put it to a show of hands, and the hands refused it. That same year a new camp was opened at Achadh dhomhain for the deep galleries. Its houses were built of spoil.

## VII. Of the Child in the Camps, and the Green Death

When the women of the camps tell of the Green Death, they begin with a child, for she was born in the same years and the same dust, and the one tale has grown into the other.

On 7 am Màrt, AE 69, a girl was born in the mining camps. Her whole life long she was steeped in more raw coal than any Dia-thìreach in living memory, and she did not age as the people around her aged. Her name was Aisling, and she was the first of the generation that would be called immortal. Of her the rolls give three things, her birth, her name and her condition, and the tellers are content to leave her there.

The next year the Company set up a great steelyard on the quay at Ros dhomhain, and from then on the island's yield was known by the ton, and the custodians' old count, kept in seasons of labour, was no longer entered. What was happening to the child had no name in any tongue on the island, and decades passed before anyone tried to find one. At Cill ghlas the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde kept the old rites of the flame and the stone at the mouth of the oldest cutting, while the pits deepened all around them. It was the last shrine in the district the crews still climbed to on the old feast days, at Samhain and Imbolc, Bealltainn and Lùnastal. Remember it.

In AE 73 came A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death.

It showed first at Achadh dhomhain. A man would go pale with a greenish cast, like a candle seen through bottle-glass; then came a cough that brought up dark dust; then weakness. The camp buried forty in the first month, in a field beyond the spoil-heaps that is called the green acre to this day. It went out along the coal roads from the camps at Muileann chrom, Àth ìseal and Cnoc fhiadhaich, and it fell hardest on Ros dhìreach, Ceann òg, Inis ìseal, Baile dhomhain, Achadh fhada, Cnoc bheag, Muileann uaine, Cuan àrsaidh and Inis bhàn. Twenty-six settlements set down cases. The roll lists them, and leaves a blank line after the last, as though waiting for another. At Àth ghlas the custodians burned every hut in which anyone had died, bedding and all, over the Company's protest at the loss of its property, and there the sickness stopped sooner than anywhere else.

The dust was blamed, and no study was ever finished. The Administration's physician Nathaniel Bright began one at Muileann chrom, weighing the dust in the lungs of the dead. He fell ill in its second season, and his notebooks break off in the middle of a table. Commissioner Crane, who had walked the camps through the worst of it, died of it at the Residency in AE 75, and Martha Gale held his seal until George Tolley came over the sea, with orders that the yield must not fall. Tolley never visited the camps. His letter-book blames the dust, the Dia-thìreach habit of sleeping near the fire, and the custodians' shrines, in that order.

The hawk-priests were still barred, so the crews carried the sermons in their own mouths, and the overseers' reports of those years list hawk-feathers nailed above hut doors as a matter for discipline. The saying of the feathered doors outlived every report:

> *Ithidh Mòd an neach a dh'itheas an cnoc.*
>
> Mòd will eat whoever eats the hill.

Anne Colby opened sick-houses at Àth ìseal and Achadh dhomhain and nursed in them until the sickness ebbed. Of all the humans on the island she is the only one the camp people name in their own tellings of the plague, and they name her kindly.

## VIII. Of the Eleven Days of Baile thais

Catrìona nic Eachainn called the halt on a grey morning in AE 77, standing on an upturned coal-tub at the pithead of Baile thais with the whole shift below her.

She had asked the Company to close the galleries where the Green Death had been worst, and had been told that the yield must not fall. So she told the crews what she had told the agent, and then she stepped down off the tub and sat on it, and folded her arms, and did not go below.

Nobody went below. By noon the word had gone round every hut in the town, and the winding-gear stood still, and the coal-carts stood in a line on the rails with nothing in them. The agent came up and shouted in two tongues, and the crews sat on the spoil-heaps in the thin rain and listened to him politely.

For eleven days no coal left Baile thais. Each evening Catrìona walked the town and counted the loaves in the windows, and knew what the agent knew: that there was one store in Baile thais, and it was the Company's. Each day the shelves were barer. On the twelfth morning she went down to it herself and looked through the shutters at the empty shelves, and then she walked back up to the pithead and told the crews to go below.

After it the Company built its own granary at Muileann chrom and forbade the camps to keep more grain than a week's ration, and the order was signed by Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor. Catrìona was turned out of Baile thais and refused work at every Company pit. She went east over the hills to Muileann chiar, and the silver guild took her on as a refiner. The Company asked for her back. The guild's answer was filed, and has not been kept.

The Administration built a new bath-house at the hot springs near Muileann ruadh for officials recovering from fevers. The Dia-thìrich, who had bathed there for centuries, were let in on certain days for a penny. The silver town grew, for the humans wanted both metals, and in AE 82 the guild founded a daughter town to the west for its refiners and carters, under the same name; the record calls them the old town and the new, and does not always say which it means. The guild sold bar silver to the Company at a price the guild fixed, and it was the only thing on Dia-thìr in all the age priced by Dia-thìreach hands.

At Tolley's asking the priests of Òrd Mhacha at Cathair dhearg, the capital's own order and the crown's, blessed the Residency's new coin. Macha's priesthood teaches that the two horses of her rite, Dubh Sainglenn the black and Liath Macha the grey, each have their due, the dark and the light; the dissenting priests said the coin was only one of them. In AE 86 barter was cheapened against the mark a second time, on terms set wholly by the Administration. In AE 87 the dissenting priests left the capital's temple for the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag, where custodians who had lost their seats found a welcome. And Dòmhnall Maor died, and his son Iain took the staff: the first overseer schooled at the Mission, who kept his reports in the humans' tongue and his household in Dia-thìris.

## IX. Of the Levy, the Ring of Beacons, and the Great Hunger

The hunger of Baile chrom is told in the north-west by the beacon-keepers' families, and they begin it with a piece of paper. On 4 am Faoilleach, AE 88, Tolley issued the ordinance the Dia-thìrich called simply the Levy. Every farming village in the west and north was to send one in five of its able men and women to the pits for two years, and be paid for them in marks, at the new rate. It fell hardest on the villages round Baile chrom and on the northern concession, which had never sent crews to the pits. The Dia-thìrich of the concession were taken. Its human farmers were exempt.

Tolley closed the hall of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh at Dùn thais in AE 89, over a lecture on whether the humans' blindness to the colour of the coal might be a kind of sickness. The masters went on teaching in their own houses, to smaller rooms each year, and some went out under the trees of the sacred forest of Flidais near Muileann chiar, where there was no hall to shut.

Work began on the fifth and last beacon at Baile chrom, and the masons were taken by the Levy from the very villages whose fields they left unworked. The ring was finished in AE 91: Taigh-solais Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag, Àth dhearg and Tobar dhearg. It had been asked for so that ships should not be lost on the reefs. By the time it was done it served a trade that was plunder in all but name. The Baile chrom beacon was lit with a coal flame in AE 91, and the daybooks show the sailings doubling in the years after.

In AE 94 the harvest failed. Gorta Baile chrom, the Great Hunger, went across thirty-four settlements, and it bit the deeper because the Levy had stripped the countryside of the hands to farm it. It was worst at Baile chrom itself. From their empty fields its people could see the coal flame of the new tower moving on the sea at night; and the custodians recorded that more died at Baile chrom than anywhere else, and the Administration, which kept its own count, did not dispute the figure. A relief ship from an Tìr Thall lay a month at Ros dhomhain with her holds full of grain while the Residency and the Company argued over who should pay to unload her. The Mission opened kitchens meanwhile at Cathair gheal and Baile chrom, and Anne Colby, come back to the island, ran the one at Baile chrom. The Levy was suspended in the famine districts in AE 97, too late for the harvest. It was never repealed, and never used again, and the custodians note that it never needed to be, since the villages had learned what it meant.

Tolley retired with honours in AE 98. Robert Haskins, who came after him, ordered that the custodians' council be consulted on the tithe, and then set the tithe before the council had met.

In AE 99 the custodians acted together for the first time. Nineteen settlements sent their custodians to Ceann àrsaidh, and there, meeting as one body, they drew up a formal grievance to lay before the Administration.

Peigi Ghlas, the custodian of Cill ghlas, carried it to the Residency. She was kept waiting on a bench in a stone passage that smelled of lamp-soot, and at last was shown to a young clerk at a high desk. He took the petition from her, and thanked her, and laid it on a pile, and bent to his work again. She stood a moment longer. Then she went home.

It was not answered.

From these years come the oldest Dia-thìreach writings of grievance that survive. They are grievances as yet and no more, the first written word that something had gone wrong. The earliest is Leabhar Baile thais, a book of complaints kept by many hands over some years: wages, deaths, the granary, the stream at Doire mhòr. At Muileann dhearg the poet Fearchar Bàrd, who had broken coal since boyhood, made songs of the Levy and the famine. The overseers forbade them, and the forbidding is why several were written down.
