They were sung in the roadside houses of the east, and An Taigh-òsta Grianach became known for them, and the Company's own carters sang them over their ale without always knowing what they sang. When the Company built its deep-water quay at Ros dhomhain for the new iron steamships, which burned the island's own coal to carry it away, Fearchar made the song that is quoted most of all his songs:

> *Tha an long ag ithe a' chnuic*
> *gus an cnoc a ghiùlan air falbh.*
>
> The ship is eating the hill
> to carry the hill away.

The Company walled its pithead at Baile thais and set a gate in the wall and a watchman at the gate to count who went in, and it was the first working on Dia-thìr walled against its own crews. Catrìona nic Eachainn died at Muileann chiar in AE 104, a refiner of the silver guild to the end, and when the camp people of Baile thais sent a delegation to her burying, the Company docked each of them a day's pay. In AE 105 a fire in the Company's coal sheds burned three days and took two streets of the harbour quarter with it. The Company's inquiry found no cause. The harbour quarter's own account has several. That year the council, on the death of its high custodian, could not agree on another, and sat for years with the seat empty, and Haskins wrote to an Tìr Thall that this made it easier to deal with.

## X. Of the Long Drought, and the Law of One Line

In AE 106 came Tiormachd Achadh shean, the Long Drought: three dry seasons one after another, the dry year of the east come back threefold. At Achadh shean the wells failed, and the cattle were driven west in a column the roll says was a day long and fewer than half of them reached water. The roll counted ten districts as drought country, worst at Achadh shean, Àth uaine, Achadh àrsaidh and Muileann chiar, and reaching down to Cuan ruadh and west toward Baile chaol. The Administration kept no count of its own.

The spring of Allt an Àigh, which is said never to have failed, did not fail. Pilgrims of Na Seann Spioradan came to it from all across the east, the first of them at Bealltainn. The Administration posted a watchman at the spring to charge for the water. He was called back after a single season.

A fever of bad water followed the drought into the towns. It was worst at Baile Mòr ruadh, where the wells had been dug deeper into the old middens, and two hundred and sixty died there. The Mission's report was the first to name the cause rightly, and the Mission bored deep wells at Achadh shean and Àth chrom that held. The custodians of the east entered the Mission's wells and the Company's quotas on facing pages, and wrote nothing beside either. For the quota was not lowered. The custodians petitioned Haskins one by one, and he wrote back to each that the matter was under consideration.

In AE 111 a case came before the Administration that fixed the law of inheritance on Dia-thìr for the rest of the age. The claimant was Thomas Hale, grandson of the Baile dhìreach marriage of Eilidh nic Ruairidh and Samuel Hale, and he claimed a share in a customary cutting through his Dia-thìreach grandmother. The magistrate at Ros dhomhain, Oliver Dunstan, ruled that customary rights descend only through the line the Administration recognises, and that it recognises only its own. Within a few years that ruling had passed eleven customary cuttings to the Company, each because some owner in the line had married a human or been born to one. The custodians stopped entering such marriages in the roll. And so the marriage that Baile dhìreach had written into both its books became, a century on, the reason marriages were written into neither.

In AE 113 a society of pit crews that called itself the Lamp-Watch began to meet at Baile thais and Cnoc chaol under cover of a burial club. The first thing it is known to have done was to bury an old breaker who had died in the Company's lock-up.

Haskins was recalled in AE 114 after a quarrel with the Company over steamship berths, and Edward Vane came to the Residency. He was the first Commissioner born on Dia-thìr, at the Residency itself. He spoke Dia-thìris badly, but he spoke it. He laid the mule-drawn tram-road to Ros dhìreach, and before he died the Company's railway ran from the pits at Muileann chrom to the quay at Ros dhomhain, its engines burning the island's coal (22 am Màrt, AE 120).

In AE 116 came the night-shift order, and from then on the mountain was given no season of rest. It was felt first at Cnoc chaol, in the newest galleries, where the crews worked by coal-lamp in two shifts. The custodians' roll records that the hill was given no silence at all, and leaves the rest of the page empty. The crews at Cnoc chaol refused the night shift and were replaced within a week by crews brought from the coast. The Lamp-Watch paid the strikers' families for a season, and then its money ran out. The Mission's minister at Ros dhomhain, Matthew Dunne, preached from the chapel pulpit that the Dia-thìrich were right, and that even the ground must rest. The Company complained, and Dunne was called home to an Tìr Thall, and the Lamp-Watch copied his sermon and read it aloud in the camps.

A wasting sickness of the lungs spread among the night crews of Cnoc chaol and Baile thais. Unlike the Green Death it killed slowly. The Company paid the widows a pension for a year, and then stopped. In AE 119 Iain Maor wrote to the Company that the night shift was killing his crews faster than it paid for them. The letter survives because it was filed with his dismissal, which was reversed a month later for want of anyone else to do the work.

## XI. Of the Second Child, and the Word that was Coined

In AE 121 a second child was born who showed the same bond with the coal that Aisling had shown half a century before. His name was Fionnan. To those who kept the rolls his birth meant that the first had been no single mischance, and that the thing was being made by the pits themselves.

Seònaid nic Dhùghaill, the last master of the Deer to teach openly in the age, died at Dùn thais in AE 123, and the school's register ends with her. Nobody took it up again until long after the humans had gone.

In AE 124 the custodians of the east began to send copies of their rolls to Muileann chaol, which still kept Beathag nic Thòmais's loft of papers, well out of the Residency's reach. The copying was done in the houses of three families and the copies were kept in a cellar. The library at Muileann chaol, which keeps this book among its others, grew out of that loft and that cellar together.

On 23 am Faoilleach, AE 126, the custodians met at the shrine of Cill ghlas to give the thing a name.

They came up the path in ones and twos through the evening, past the spoil-heaps, to where the oldest cutting still stood open in the hillside with Brìde's lamp burning in its mouth. They sat on the benches of the shrine with their cloaks steaming, and all around them in the dark they could hear the pumps of the Company's pits.

There were two cases now, and nobody could call it chance. A wonder that comes twice is a sickness, and a sickness must have a name if a physician is to write it down.

They argued late. Some wanted an old word out of the tellings; some wanted none, for a name is a door. At last one of them put forward the plainest word there was: *fuil-ghuail*, coal-blood. It was meant for a physician's register, a word to be written in a column, with no song in it. They took it by vote. In the humans' tongue it was rendered *coal-touched*.

It did not stay in the column.

The Residency, hearing of the word, ordered every Dia-thìreach child who showed the condition to be reported to the Commissioner's office. The custodians complied by reporting none.

In AE 129 barter was abolished as lawful tender, and every bargain on the island from then on ran through the humans' coin. The barter houses of Ros dhomhain and Cathair dhearg were shut by order, and a Residency clerk wrote that the ledgers were now "complete for the first time." The hill villages borrowed marks from the Company's stores to buy seed, at interest, and within a few years most of them owed the Company more than a year's crops.

Iain Maor died in AE 131, and his daughter Mòrag took the staff, the first woman to hold it. The Company approved her in a letter that calls her "a safe pair of hands." Vane died at the Residency that year, and Charles Merriman came with a small company of armed constables, the first standing force the Administration had kept on Dia-thìr. His first posts were at Muileann shean, which the townsfolk called the humans' second Residency and did not mean it kindly, and at Tobar ghorm.

In AE 133 the Mission at Cathair gheal reported that human labourers near Baile chrom had been meeting at night in the fields to keep a silent vigil under the sign of a grey goose. They were of the Church, and took the goose for an Gèadh Fiadhaich, the wild goose of the Holy Spirit. The Mission called the vigil irregular, and supposed it a superstition picked up from the Dia-thìrich. The Dia-thìrich of Baile chrom disowned it. Manannan's priests at Ceann mhòr said the Mission was half right: the practice came from the Dia-thìrich, from Manannan's own harbours; Baile chrom had nothing to do with it. The human fishing families of Ceann mhòr had learned from them the night prayer to keep the sea shut, and the labourers inland had made of it a night of silence to a grey goose. The priests called it their prayer gone astray, and would not have its keepers in their house.

That year the dockers of Ros dhomhain, Dia-thìrich and human alike, refused for nine days to load coal over the new berth charges. It was the only strike of the age in which the two peoples stood together. Merriman's constables broke it, and the human dockers were shipped west.

In AE 134 a third child of the condition was born, Lorccan, the first of them born in a mining town outside the camps, and the custodians knew from it that the thing had outgrown any one place. In AE 135 a fourth was born, Cian, within a year of the third: the nearest the generation of the coal-blood ever came to being born together.

## XII. Of the Rending of Cill ghlas, and the First Blood

In AE 136 the Company began to drive galleries under the hills around Cill ghlas with blasting-powder shipped from an Tìr Thall. The custodians of the shrine asked that no charge be set within sight of the old cutting. The Company's engineer marked their request on his plan, and set the charges below it.

On 9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 137, in the course of an ordinary day's work, the hills east of the capital broke.

The tellers of Cill ghlas say the ground spoke first, a long grinding under the feet like a quern turning, and then the fault tore open. That was Scàineadh Cill ghlas, the Rending. It killed dozens and shut a whole mining district for a generation. The old cutting where the rites had been kept through all the age, where Brìde's lamp had burned and the word *fuil-ghuail* had been agreed, went down into the earth with its shrine and was not seen again. The custodians' roll sets down the loss of the shrine before the loss of the dead, and a later copyist has put the order right; the copyists of Muileann chaol let both hands stand. The Company fenced the district and left Cill ghlas and its hamlets without work, and the closed country went to thorn.

Within days came the first blood between the two peoples. The fuller account of it in the roll, written up at the year's end, sets it at Muileann chrom.

Mòrag nic Iain Maor was at the pithead when they brought the seven up.

The pumps had been stopped the day before to save fuel, and in the night the gallery had filled. Now the seven lay on the wet boards in a row, and the women of the camp were coming up the track, and there was no sound but their feet and the rain.

At noon the Company's agent rode up with his constables and began to speak about the loss to the working.

The first stone took him on the shoulder. Then the air was full of them, and the constables were shouting, and Mòrag was shouting too. She saw a constable raise his rifle. She saw the smoke before she heard the sound. When it was over four Dia-thìrich lay in the mud beside the seven, and one constable with them.

At the inquiry she stood up in her good dark dress with the Company's staff in her hand, the staff her great-grandfather had taken from the Company, and testified that the pumps had been stopped on the agent's order. The clerk wrote it down, and then was told to strike it out.

The Lamp-Watch got a copy anyway.

In AE 138 the grey fever came in on the ships, a fever of the chest that took the young and strong before the old, and it ran from the capital to the eastern farms. The camps, already hungry, buried more than the towns.

In AE 139 a second petition went to the Residency, and where the first had held a plea, this one held a warning. It was drafted by Eilidh nic Raghnaill, a crew-leader of Baile thais and a member of the Lamp-Watch, and signed by custodians and crew-leaders of thirty-one settlements, and its last sentence was underlined at the Residency: that the hill would not be worked by people who were not asked. It was the first Dia-thìreach writing the Administration troubled to answer. It answered with constables. In AE 140 Merriman tripled the constabulary and posted companies at Muileann chrom, Baile thais, Ceann fhada and Cnoc chaol, each with a fortified store, all paid for out of the tithe; and a barracks for two hundred at Dùn chrom stood empty most of its first year for want of men to fill it.

At Seann Skell, where Murchadh Seabhag had preached the hawk's hunger in AE 22, the hawk-priest Ìomhar Seabhag now preached that Mòd's hunger had turned at last toward those who had eaten the hill. The hawk-shrines of the west became meeting-houses for the Lamp-Watch, and the constables did not yet know it.

The grey fever came back in AE 140 and settled in the north-west, and there it killed humans as readily as Dia-thìrich. In the Mission's crowded hospital at Cathair gheal the two peoples lay in the same wards for the first time.

## XIII. Of the Houses on the Roads, and the Day the Pits Stopped

The carters of the old coal roads tell these years as a tale of inns. From AE 141 the roadside houses of the mining routes began, unbidden, to serve as waystations for a nameless militia in a war not yet declared. The singing house, An Taigh-òsta Grianach, walled its yard and set a watch on its gate. Am Buabhall Fortanach on the south-western road barred its gates at dusk and kept a man on its roof, and its keeper Tormod Buabhall sent a list of travellers up the road every week, and never told the constables whose hands it reached. At An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the northern road the stables were rebuilt with a loft for sleeping men, and the carters noticed that the loft was never empty and never held the same men twice. An Sligeanach Fad' às, near the silver country, became the post-house through which the Lamp-Watch sent word to Muileann chiar and the silver guild paid its rent. And An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, the carters' house that Seònaid Bhàn had opened in the first years of the extraction, was kept now by her great-grandson Aonghas. It was the busiest of the fortified houses, the one the constables searched most often and found least in.

In AE 143 the pits stopped.

That morning the Company's chief agent stood at his window over the Ros dhomhain quay to watch the first coal-trains come down to the steamships. None came. By noon the ships still rode high at their moorings with their holds open to the rain.

Word came in by rider and by rail. Every working in the Muileann chrom district had halted at once. So had Baile thais, and Cnoc chaol, and the silver town, and the eastern pits at Ros fhionn. The signal had been a fire on the hills above Doire mhòr, which the Company took for a heath fire.

For six days the steamships lay at Ros dhomhain with empty holds. The agents wrote home that they had never known the harbour so quiet, and that the quiet frightened them more than the crowds ever had.

The stoppage was broken as the strike at Baile thais had been broken, when the constables shut the Company stores in every district at once. Forty crew-leaders were taken. Thirty-two were let go without charge. Eight were shipped west to an Tìr Thall for trial, and were never heard of again. The beacon of the stoppage had been lit on Doire mhòr's hill by the children's children of Beathag Dhubh's people, and the constables burned the heather there so that no fire could be lit on it again.

The keepers' daybooks were showing by now fewer ships from an Tìr Thall each year, and older ones. The Company's letters speak of troubles at home and do not say what they are. Of whatever was happening beyond the sea, the island saw only the emptiness in the daybooks.

In AE 146 the Administration began to issue its orders with no Dia-thìreach counsel sought at all, and the polite pretence of permission, kept up since the council's vote of AE 2, was put away. Merriman left in ill health, and Lionel Strake, a soldier, took his place. His commission, read aloud at the Residency, made no mention of the Council of Custodians, and he did not call on it. He brought a flying machine over in the hold of a Company steamship and had it flown over the coal country to count the workings from the air. The Dia-thìrich called it *eun-iarainn*, the iron bird (27 am Màrt, AE 147). He had the council hall at Cathair dhearg locked and its keys lodged at the Residency. The custodians met instead in the temple of Macha, whose priests had once blessed the humans' coin and now sheltered those who had petitioned against it.

In AE 147 the Administration claimed the right to take any Dia-thìreach dwelling it judged needful for the widening of the workings. Of all the wrongs of the age, the edict of seizure is the one named most often in every telling of what came after. The first houses taken under it were those of Doire mhòr, for a new shaft beneath the hill, and the last households there were carried out by constables. The village that had refused the first contract was the first to be emptied by the last. At Baile dhomhain, the first camp laid out on paper, two streets were pulled down for a spoil-tip.

## XIV. Of the Breaking of the Staff

In AE 148 the order came to Mòrag nic Iain Maor to clear the houses of her district.

She read it twice at her table in the steward's house under the slate roof. Then she took down the staff from over the hearth, the staff Raghnall had carried, and Dòmhnall after him, and her father Iain, and walked down through Muileann chrom to the Company's office, with the townsfolk coming out of their doors behind her.

At the Company's door she broke it across her knee. It was old wood and it went with a crack like a shot. She laid the two halves on the step and walked home.

Three other overseers resigned that month, and the Company put humans in their places. So ended the office that Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill had taken up more than a hundred years before, Raghnall, Dòmhnall, Iain and Mòrag each in turn; and the custodians' hope that it would lapse with the first of them was granted at last by the fourth.

That summer the silver guild of Muileann chiar, still holding its seam under the compact of a century before, began to buy rifles from the raiders of the eastern waters, where no gunboat had patrolled for years, and paid them in bar silver by weight. Its ledger enters the rifles as refining tools. Custodians, crew-leaders of the Lamp-Watch and the dissenting priests of Macha met in the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag and made themselves one council for the mining country, and chose Eilidh nic Raghnaill to speak for it. No human hand wrote down that meeting. Strake learned of it all the same, and ordered the arrest of Eilidh and the forest council; and the constables went to Baile thais, and found her house empty and the town silent.

## XV. Of the War of the Hills

On 20 an Gearran, AE 149, the grievance of the Dia-thìrich, joined at last under one council across the mining country, became war.

It opened in the hills. At first light crews under Mòrag nic Iain, who had broken the staff, rushed the fortified store at Muileann chrom, and its eleven constables gave themselves up without a shot; before noon the rifles and the grain were gone. Crews from the camps took the coal quay at Ceann fhada and sank two barges across its mouth, and no coal left the hills by water again in the age. At Baile thais the constables held the walled pithead for eleven days, the span of Catrìona's strike a lifetime before, and on the twelfth, their water gone, they came out. Eilidh nic Raghnaill sent them under guard to the coast unharmed. The Residency had not looked for that, and did not return it in kind. The northern pits at Baile gharbh rose in the same season, took the constable posts at Muileann shean and Tobar ghorm, and sent the constables south on foot. Aonghas shut the gates of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr across the coal road, and the men in its loft came down armed, and the road between the capital and the hills was cut at its halfway stage and stayed cut. At Muileann dhearg the smith Uilleam Gobha made grenades of the Company's own blasting-powder cased in tin from the coal sheds, and pike-heads from the rails of the galleries, and the council's roll says it could not have fought its first season without him.

Then the capital rose. The custodians broke the Residency's locks on their hall at Cathair dhearg and sat in it again. The townsfolk held the stone bridge against the constables sent up from the harbour, the bridge the Company had rebuilt for coal-carts, and they barricaded it with the carts. At Cathair dhomhain the townsfolk broke open the Company's warehouse, the first building the Company had ever owned on Dia-thìr, and carried its tools to the council's companies. Strake drew the Administration back into the Residency and fortified the Company's quarter of the harbour. The city below it, Dia-thìreach almost to a soul, neither joined the rising nor stood against it, and the constables did not trust it enough to leave their walls.

A column of constables and Company guards under Major Peter Ashdown marched up the coal road to relieve the hills, and on 5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 149, it came to the ford of Àth chiar and found the rebels on the far bank. The water was high and brown, and his men went into it to the waist with their rifles over their heads, and the fire from the far bank came down on them. Ashdown lost forty men there and all his baggage, and turned back. The rebels lost nineteen, and the council's roll names every one, as the custodians' roll had named the eleven of Cnoc fhiadhaich when the Company's report named none. Ashdown's column halted a night at the barracks of Dùn chrom, and in the morning found the town's gates shut behind it, and went on to the coast without its wounded, whom the townsfolk kept and nursed.

In the east the silver guild declared for the council, opened its armoury, and escorted the Company's agents to the coast with their papers. The guild's ledger notes that this was the one place on the island where the rising took nothing, because the humans had never held anything there to take. The constables' post at Dùn ìseal gave itself up to the guild's riflemen after a single exchange of fire, and the east was clear of human arms. Dùn dhearg declared for the council and sent it grain, and its declaration quotes the defence of the Small-Burning Law that its custodian Fionnghal nic Artair had written a hundred and twenty-seven years before. The crews of the eastern workings at Ros fhionn stopped the pumps and walked out, and let the lower galleries flood, and the bridge on the eastern coal road fell silent.

The humans struck back from the sea. In the first month of AE 150 a Company steamship came up the Abhainn uaine and shelled the coal stage at Seann Toll to keep it from the rebels, and set the fishing town behind it burning, and twenty-three townsfolk died. It was the first time the humans turned the island's own coal, burning in their boilers, against a Dia-thìreach town. Fishing boats from Seann Chwen and Ros ruadh, sailing by night along the south coast, boarded a Company coaster at anchor and burned her, and the Company drew its coastal shipping back into Ros dhomhain and Ros bheag.

On the concession, Cathair gheal shut its gates and raised a militia and sent none of it south. Its magistrate asked both sides to leave it alone; the council granted it, and Strake did not reply.

That spring the council's letters to the Hawk coast went north by the hands of seven hawk-faithful crewmen of the river towns. They waited nine hours for the letters at An Cupa Dàna in Cuan dhearg (17 an Giblean, AE 150). Each wore at his throat a hawk cast in lead from the cartridges taken at the store at Muileann chrom, and the record calls them Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, the Leaden Hawk company. They left at dark.

They went on foot, past the burned stage at Seann Toll, over the hills by Achadh dhomhain, down the Abhainn ìseal to Cnoc bheag and along the Hawk coast to Inis mhin. At every hawk-house on the way one of them stood up among the benches and read the letter aloud. At Inis mhin they heard that Strake's constables rode the western roads out of Ros bheag every day, so they hired a carriage and left the roads altogether. In the grasslands above Tobar dhomhain they lay eleven hours in the long grass over the road from Ros bheag and counted the constables' riders as they passed (23 an Giblean, AE 150). There were forty-one, and none of them going north.

They came down to Inis thais eight days after they had set out. The priests of the Stone, the keepers of Clach, heard the letter in their temple and would send no men; but they shut the harbour of Inis thais to the Company's ships (25 an Giblean, AE 150), and gave the hawk-faithful the use of the Fianna's roads. At Seann Skell Ìomhar Seabhag declared that the war was Mòd's own hunger turned back on those who had fed it, and the hawk-shrines of the west became recruiting-houses.

The keepers at Tobar dhearg put out their beacon, and Àth dhearg and Baile ìseal followed. Company ships feeling their way along the coast by night ran onto the reefs the beacons had been built to light, and two were lost. The Administration begged an Tìr Thall for troops and ships. One ship came in the war's first year, with dispatches and a few crates of cartridges, and sailed again within the week.

Through the first winter the council held the hills, the east and the capital, and Strake held the Residency, the harbour quarter below it and the western ports, and neither had the strength to break the other. Cathair dhearg went short, its harbour held against it, and the custodians shared out the grain by household; and the roll records that they took the same share as everyone else.

In that stalemate the ledgers burned.

The first fire was at the Company's counting-house on the Ros dhomhain quay, inside Strake's lines. Dùghall Dubh and the men of the harbour quarter came to it over the roofs on a night of low cloud, in their stocking feet, and in at a garret window and down the stair in the dark. The tithe books stood in rows in the long room, calf-bound, heavy as flagstones. They carried them out into the yard in armfuls and heaped them on the cobbles, and Dùghall struck the light himself. The sentry at the front door never turned round until the whole yard was lit.

The second raid burned the tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh, where the portion owed by every settlement of the hills had been entered since the first schedule. The clerks were let go. The custodians of Ceann àrsaidh asked that one ledger be spared for the record, and their own people refused them, and the library at Muileann chaol has been sorry for it ever since. The third burned the weigh-house at Muileann chrom, with the steelyard ledgers in which the coal of the hills had been set down by the ton since the first contract. The rebels' own chronicler writes that the fire burned green. Later chroniclers hold those fires great in what they meant, if small in what they did. The camps made a verse of them:

> *Loisc iad an leabhar, ach cha do loisc iad an cnoc.*
>
> They burned the book, but they did not burn the hill.

On 25 an Lùnastal, AE 150, Company guards and constables sallying from the harbour to win back the eastern road were driven back at Cnoc ghorm, in the hills beyond the capital, and it was the Administration's last attempt of the war to reach the mining country. The next day the Dia-thìrich of the Ros dhomhain harbour quarter opened the lower gates to the council's companies, and Strake held only the Residency and the Company's quays. On 21 an t-Sultain, AE 150, Strake took his officials, the Mission's clergy and the Company's agents away by water to Ros bheag. The council's companies came into the Residency the next morning and found it stripped of everything but its furniture and the letter-books, from which so much of this history is drawn, and which the humans had not troubled to take.

## XVI. Of the Truce of Àth àrsaidh, and the Closing of the Crossing

Ros bheag, the western port the humans had used since the early years, became the last seat of the Administration, and the human families of the west and south, a few thousand in all, gathered behind its walls. With the roads cut and no ships from the west the town went short within months, and Strake ordered the Company's stores opened to the human families and the Dia-thìreach townsfolk alike. It is the one deed of his that the Dia-thìreach rolls give him credit for.

The custodians of Cuan shean, the town where the first humans had waded ashore to beg for water, shut their harbour to Company ships. The council's roll marks the turn of it and says no more, and neither shall the tellers. At Baile dhìreach the descendants of the old joint council, many of them of both peoples, were asked by each side which people they belonged to. Most of them would not answer, and neither side made them.

On 1 an t-Samhain, AE 150, on Samhain, the last ship known to have come from an Tìr Thall anchored at Ros bheag. She brought no troops and no grain, only a sealed letter for the Commissioner, and she sailed on the next tide with as many passengers as she could hold. What the letter said, Strake kept to himself. On 2 an t-Samhain, AE 150, envoys of the council and the Administration met at Àth àrsaidh, on the edge of the northern concession, and agreed a truce: the humans remaining on Dia-thìr would withdraw into the north-west under the council's safe-conduct, and the council would leave the concession towns standing.

On 29 an t-Samhain, AE 150, the columns went north. The human families of Ros bheag, Cuan shean, Baile dhìreach and the south-west walked up the western roads with their carts and bundles under the guard of the council's companies, and few of them had ever lived in the north. The roll records that no column was attacked, and that none was helped. At Àth chrom the custodians stood at the ford and counted them over, and that count was the last the Dia-thìrich made of the humans on Dia-thìr in this age. At Àth leathan, the last stage before the northern country, the columns camped a night, and the custodians of the town record that the humans asked the name of the place, and that several of them wrote it down.

The keeper of the beacon at Baile chrom saw the last of it.

He was on the gallery of the tower on 5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150, with his glass to his eye when the ship came up along the coast. She had sailed from Cuan shean with Lionel Strake, the last Commissioner, and his officials, and she was the last ship on the island that could make the crossing. How the harbour that had shut itself to the Company came to let her go, the men of Cuan shean never said. The keeper watched her stand out to the west, smaller and greyer, until the sea had her. Then he went in out of the wind and wrote her down.

Nothing on Dia-thìr records her arriving anywhere.

The council ordered the five beacons lit again, from Baile chrom round to Tobar dhearg. The keepers kept their daybooks as before, and there was nothing to put in them. The line that stands in them, in the hands of five keepers, is this:

> *Cha tàinig long.*
>
> No ship came.

At the year's end the custodians sent what was left of the age's rolls down to the cellars at Muileann chaol: their copies of the petitions, the book of Baile thais, and the letter-books left in the Residency. What the Administration's own clerks carried west with Strake, no one on Dia-thìr saw again.

On 1 am Faoilleach, AE 151, the war ended with the crossing itself closed. Whatever had let the humans reach Dia-thìr shut behind them. No one on the island knows what it was, or why it opened, or why it closed, and the chroniclers set it down as a thing that befell the sea. The humans still on the island were brought into the northern country their descendants hold today. This was the Severance. Cian and Lorccan, neither yet twenty, grew up in its wake.

*The masters of the humans on Dia-thìr, as the letter-books give them.* Edmund Harrow, captain, from the Crossing until the treaty; then the Commissioners at the Residency: Josiah Pell, AE 8 to AE 24; Henry Maddox, AE 24 to AE 41; Arthur Lisle, AE 41 to AE 61; Walter Crane, AE 61 to AE 75; George Tolley, AE 76 to AE 98; Robert Haskins, AE 98 to AE 114; Edward Vane, AE 114 to AE 132; Charles Merriman, AE 132 to AE 146; Lionel Strake, AE 146 to AE 150, the last.

*The Stewards of Muileann chrom, as the custodians' roll gives them.* Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill, Raghnall Maor, AE 36 to AE 62; Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill, AE 62 to AE 87; Iain Maor, AE 87 to AE 131; Mòrag nic Iain, AE 131 to AE 148, who broke the staff.

Thus ended the Age of Strangers. It began with a vote that three custodians did not attend, and with forty words for the colours of the coal that the strangers never asked to learn; and it ended with the hill cut to its roots, the Small-Burning Law a hundred and thirty years forgotten, and the tithe ledgers burning green at Muileann chrom. What was lost the rolls can count only in part: the shrine at Cill ghlas and the water of Doire mhòr, the salmon of the green river, the Deer school's hall and the barter houses, the eight who were shipped west, and all the names the Company's reports never gave. What was kept is shorter to tell: the silver of Muileann chiar, the copies in the cellar at Muileann chaol, and the four children of the coal-blood, whom the strangers' pits had made and the strangers' registers never held. The hill was the island's again. But the island knew no way to use it save the way the strangers had taught, and of that, and of the kingdom restored at Cathair dhearg, and of the same digging under new masters, and of the northerners in their new country, the next book tells, which is the book of An Aois Rìoghachd, the Age of the Kingdom.


# The Fifth Book: An Aois Rìoghachd, the Age of the Kingdom

*SE 1 – 71*

> *Tha e scrìobhte a-nis.*
> It is written now.
>
> — a minute of the Moot at Caol mhòr, 6 an t-Samhain, SE 64, entire, as the library renders it

## I. Of the Severance and the Settling of the North

*So the old people of the north tell it, at the hearths of Doire ghlas, when the fire is low and the children will not sleep.*

In the last days of the Age of Strangers, whatever road had brought the humans over the western water shut behind their last ships, and those still on Dia-thìr were marched north under the council's guard. That was the Severance, and it fell on the first day of AE 151, in the dead of winter, when the roads north were mud to the knee.

On 22 am Màrt, SE 1, with the lambs coming, the homeland of the Tuathaich was fixed. The children of the stranded humans were settled in the north by the council's word, and its guard stood at the head of the roads. It was a confinement, and everyone on both sides of the guard knew it. Their grandchildren would call it home all the same, having no other. Cian and Lorccan of the immortal generation grew up in the wake of those days; of them the chronicles of this age tell nothing further.

The victors began by putting things away. At Cathair dhearg the war-companies of the Severance were stood down, and their rolls went into the council's chests instead of the fire. Nobody ever abolished the companies. They lived on as names on a list, and the list lay quiet for nearly ninety years. On the roads running north, at Caol mhòr and elsewhere, stones were set to mark where the Tuathaich country began. No wall came after them. Many still stand at the roadside, since nobody has ever been paid to shift them.

That first year the north went hungry alone. The stores that had come over the water from an Tìr Thall came no more, and the grain ran out before the spring. At Doire ghlas, the old people say, more than two hundred were buried that winter; they had it from their grandmothers, and it was written down long afterwards. The Dia-thìrich made no count.

Meanwhile the council's clerks went through the humans' counting-houses at Cathair dhearg, Ros dhomhain and Seann Skell like rooks through stubble, and carried off every written leaf. The tithe ledgers, or what the raids of the war had left of them, they boxed unread, for few of them could make out the humans' hand. In the north-west things went otherwise. At Ceann mhòr, Cathair gheal and Inis àrsaidh the human harbour officers had sailed with the last ships and taken their keys with them. The Tuathaich fishermen took hammers to the locks of the harbour stores and shared out what they found, house by house. The north tells that part with some relish.

## II. Of the Moot and the Kingdom

In the south the kingdom was making itself. On 27 an t-Iuchar, SE 2, in the high summer, the state styled itself Rìoghachd Dia-thìris: a kingdom in its form, whatever it was in its working, and its own records carry that contradiction still.

A month before the council was seated, the householders of the northern towns came to Caol mhòr.

They came on foot and in carts at the tail of a wet summer, and crowded into a long low room that smelt of damp wool and fish-scale. Walter Hale stood at the back with his hat in his hands. He had been a harbour clerk under the humans, and there was still ink in the creases of his knuckles.

They argued most of the afternoon over who should speak for them. Somebody said his name, and it went round the room like a bucket passed along a line, and it stopped with him.

"We've no standing," said a man by the door. "Not in their law. They needn't hear a word of it."

"Then we'll say it where we can hear it ourselves," said Walter Hale. He sat down at the trestle, opened a book that had nothing in it yet, wetted his pen and wrote the day.

That was the Moot. It had no standing in Dia-thìrich law. It met all the same, and it kept minutes, and they run unbroken from that wet afternoon to the present year.

That autumn a royal council of twelve was seated at Cathair dhearg, drawn from the custodian families and the captains of the Severance war. Its minute-books are the oldest unbroken record of the state in this age, younger than the Moot's by a month.

At Ros dhomhain the first Dia-thìrich harbour-master, Dùghall mac Iain, kept the humans' tariff in force for want of another, and spent years turning it into Dia-thìris, clause by clause.

In the early summer of SE 3 a ship was sent out past the western capes to seek the crossing the humans had used. She came home after a month of open water. She had seen no land and no sign of any passage, and no second ship was sent. At Seann Skell the priests of Manannan said that the lord of the sea had shut his sea again, as they had begged him to ever since the Crossing, and they said the old prayer at the harbour mouth:

> *A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte.*
> Manannan, keep the sea shut.

## III. Of Niall, the Shires and the Great Wave

In the long light of midsummer, on 19 an t-Ògmhios, SE 3, Niall was crowned at Cathair dhearg by Macha's rite, as the kings before the humans had been crowned. He was the first ruler of the restored kingdom and the first name in the line that the state's chronicles have kept without a break ever since. So smoothly did the crown pass to him that *mar a thàinig Niall*, "the way Niall came", became a saying for any handing-over of power that went without a quarrel. The first place it is found written is a tavern ledger in the capital, set against a debt paid without argument.

The council drew the kingdom into shires, each *siorrachd* named for its seat, and drew them on the humans' district lines, for the humans' surveys were the only whole surveys of the island there were. The kingdom used them and did not say so. Over each shire went a *maor* to gather the Crown's dues: the head-due on every household, counted by its heads, and the market-due on every sale. Where the humans' lines stopped, at the edge of the great moss of the far north-west, the shires stopped too, and the windy coast beyond was left in no shire at all. In the Tuathaich shires the maoir were Dia-thìrich. At Ceann mhòr the maor moved into the old human magistrate's house, and the townsfolk went on calling it by its old name.

Then the sea came in.

The Great Wave came in the short night of early summer, on 3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 4, and it gave no warning at all. The south calls it Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol. In one night it wrecked Cnoc chaol, Cuan dhearg and Achadh mhin.

The relief party out of Cathair dhearg came down the coast road to Cuan dhearg, and the young clerk who carried its tally-book smelt the town before he saw it: salt, and torn weed, and something under both that he did not want to name. Where the harbour had stood there was brown water and a row of broken piles like bad teeth. He looked for the boats, until a man of the party touched his arm and pointed inland. The boats of Cuan dhearg were in the fields behind the town, keeled over among the barley, and one sat upright in a furrow with her mast still stepped, as if she had been sailed there in the dark. The clerk wrote that down, not knowing what else to do with it, and went on counting.

When the tallies from Cnoc chaol and Achadh mhin came in and were added to his, the dead of the three towns came to a little over nine hundred. The wave had run on up the gulf as far as Ros gharbh and broken its quays. That town stood high and lost few of its people, and nearly every boat.

It was the first disaster the new state met on its own terms, and it met it well. The council moved the survivors of Achadh mhin off their salted fields and paid for their seed out of the treasury, the first relief the restored kingdom ever gave. The old site is called an Tràigh Bhàthte, the drowned strand, and nobody builds there. From the survivors the south took a word: *tonn*, wave, for anything sudden and overwhelming. *Tha e san tonn*, they say, he is in the wave of it. The south would have need of the phrase again.

In SE 5 the human coinage was called in. In the old counting-house at Cathair dhearg, Fearchar mac Dhòmhnaill, whom men called Fearchar Bonn, set up the mint and struck the coin of the Rìoghachd. He pressed each coin's seal with an ink ground from coal dust, so that a clipped coin showed the coal's colour at its edge. The coin was honest and holy, and the kingdom liked it both ways.

The north paid for it. The Tuathaich households had put by their savings in human coin, and those savings were now worth their weight as metal and no more. The Moot petitioned for an exchange. The petition was received and filed. It is the first petition in this book to end that way, and not the last. At Doire mhin a smith named Joseph Marlow gathered up his neighbours' dead coin, melted it down and cast it into ploughshares, and sold the shares back to them for the price of the charcoal. The Tuathaich sing of him still in their own tongue. A library clerk once set down a verse of the song in plain prose: *he turned the king's silence into iron, and the iron into bread.*

## IV. Of the Rite, the Orders and the Law

In the spring of SE 6, Òrd Bhrìde, the order of Brìde's flame and Crom's stone, which had kept the Hall's rite since the Binding, was drawn up into ordered doctrine, where before there had been only a wide and loose reverence. It was built about the leyline and the unbroken line of the coal-touched, and the kingdom calls it simply the Rite. Dòmhnall mac Thormoid was named Àrd-choimheadaiche, the first high custodian of the Rite, and seated at Seann Skell on the southern coast, where the order's greatest house stands. His first labour was to write down an order of worship. In all the long keeping of the flame no one had ever written one.

The Hawk houses round Cnoc bheag would have none of it. Òrd an t-Seabhaig, the older form of the Rite, had never needed a custodian above the local altar, they said, and had no need of one now. Nobody forced them, and here begins the long quarrel between the two forms of the Rite. Only the southernmost hawk-house, at Muileann naomh, far from Cnoc bheag, took up the written order, and it has been a house of the Rite ever since. The houses of the Stone in the south-west, whose Clach was never Crom's stone, sent no witnesses, only a letter wishing the Rite well. Òrd Mhacha, the capital's own order, which makes the kings, was given the coronation regalia to keep, as it had kept them before the humans came, and it gave the high custodian no share in them. Within a year the orthodox Rite had one house that disowned it, one that ignored it with great courtesy, and one that outranked it at court. The orders of the Old Faith stood so for the rest of the age.

In the north the Church was kept quietly. The Tuathaich held to an Eaglais, the faith their grandparents had carried over the sea, and to the fragment they call the First Canoe, the voyage of Naomh Breandan, which the Dia-thìrich priesthood calls superstition. The library has never been shown the fragment. It knows only that it is kept. At Baile chrom the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane kept the vigil of Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise, the Mystery of the Grey Night, in the open for the first time since the Severance. The sect keeps one night of silence in the year for Sìne, the Peaceful Goose, which is its name for the wild goose of the Holy Spirit, and it tells no outsider which night that is. The Church's bishops call the vigil irregular, and they have never put it out. In the towns of the west coast, where the Tuathaich lived beside the Dia-thìrich of Manannan's harbours, many congregations came to preach in the humans' tongue and to read the Bible in Dia-thìris. How that came about the west coast has never troubled to explain.

In SE 10 a wall between the two peoples was proposed, and the council threw it out as needless, since the peoples were keeping apart well enough without one. The minute that rejects it runs to four lines. The fourth reads *They do not come south.* Five of the twelve initialled it, and the other seven did not sign against it. The library keeps that minute under glass. It is a small leaf, and a good deal of the age is written on it.

The law came north in the same fashion. In SE 8, at Seann Bhral, Eilidh nic Leòid, first of the circuit justices, ruled that land held by the Tuathaich under human title passed to the Crown, while the right to work it stayed with the holders and their heirs. The Leòid ruling is cited in nearly every land case of the age.

Seven summers later she carried it north herself.

The court at Ceann mhòr sat in the heat of an t-Iuchar, late in the month, in SE 15, with the windows open on the square and the flies drifting in. Eilidh nic Leòid had nineteen cases before her. Seventeen were Tuathaich suits over land, and in each the same kind of paper came up to the bench: a human title, brown at the folds, under the seal of a magistrate who had sailed west. She read every one to the end, and would not be hurried, while the suitors stood in their best coats and sweated. Then she took up her own ruling and read that too, aloud, so that the room should hear what the law was, and gave judgment.

In fifteen of the seventeen she found for the Crown. She was exact. The law she was exact about had been made for one people, and she had made it. Her rulings became the kingdom's first law-book.

Some years before, in SE 7, Walter Hale had asked leave to open schools in the north that taught in the humans' tongue. The council answered that the kingdom's schools taught in Dia-thìris and it had no others. The Moot's minute calls the answer "clear, at least." In the middle of the winter of SE 15 Agnes Pike opened such a school at Doire ghlas anyway, with Moot money and without leave, and within ten years there were nine. The council never licensed them and never shut them. For most of the age that was the kingdom's way with the north: it forbade little there, and helped with less.

## V. Of the Mountain, the Guilds and the Fair

By SE 11 the mine was yielding as much as it had under the humans, and then more. The work was the same work. Only the owners had changed.

The Crown granted the Sloc Mòr, the great shaft at Achadh dhomhain, to Uisdean mac Ùisdein of Cathair mhòr, whose house had held an overseer's post under the humans. The Crown took a fifth. Those were the humans' terms with the names changed. The council would not end the day-and-night working the humans had ordered, and so the mountain was still given no season of rest. The custodians entered a protest, and then went down and blessed the shafts. The hewers had a saying for it:

> *Cha d' fhuair a' bheinn fois a-riamh,*
> *is cha d' fhuair sinne.*
> The mountain never got its rest,
> and neither did we.

Families from the hungry east came to the vein-towns for wages, and Muileann dhearg doubled in three years. The humans' railway was mended to the pithead, and in an Dàmhair of SE 12 the first coal train ran from the Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg, under the kingdom's name, on the humans' rails. At Muileann chrom the families who worked the little shunting engines were counted apart and lived apart, in rows beside the lines. For forty years the public buildings of the south went up in the Sloc Mòr's grey spoil-stone, sold under the Mac Ùisdein quarry-mark.

In SE 13 the apprentice-binding of the Holy Age was taken up again, and this time the charters said in so many words that it was for Dia-thìrich applicants. The Guild of Hewers came first, its oath sworn with a hand laid on a lump of coal, and the shipwrights, chandlers, lamp-makers and weavers came after. The Tuathaich boys already bound to Dia-thìrich masters were released from their indentures. Some went north. Most stayed on as day-labour, outside the guilds and beneath their wages. The rule kept them where the pay was worst.

Off Cathair gheal, ships that flew no flag began to raid the north-western coast, and some of their crews were men who had served the human administration. The Tuathaich towns suffered first, undefended. In SE 20, having asked twice and been sent nothing, the fishermen of Cathair gheal armed their own boats and drove the raiders out of the bay. The council then fined the town for bearing arms without a licence. The town paid.

On 16 an Dàmhair, SE 21, in the reddening of the year, the fair at Muileann òg was established, and it grew to be the greatest recurring gathering on the island. Its first toll-mistress, Oighrig nic Mhathain, set down its rules, and one of them was this: that Tuathaich goods be sold only through Dia-thìrich factors. They are still read aloud when each fair opens. Two years after, the Còmhrag began at Ceann leathan, a yearly melee that the south called an old custom of arms, and where, more and more, men who had nowhere else to spend their anger spent it. Two men died in the first one that anyone remembers.

On 7 an t-Ògmhios, SE 24, in the green of early summer, there was a cluster of births among the shunting families, the generation called Splatter and Dodge's. Seachran and Brean were among them. They would grow up to be the closest allies of a man not yet born.

## VI. Of the Library at Muileann chaol

On 1 an Cèitean, SE 16, which was Bealltainn, the fires were lit on the hills round Muileann chaol to bring the summer in, and their smoke hung over the town all day. Ailean mac Iain spent that day in a cellar.

He had been named first keeper of the new library, and had brought the council's minute-books with him, and the remains of the humans' tithe ledgers in their boxes. Now the townsmen led him down a stair to the custodians' rolls, which had lain there since the Severance war, stacked on planks above a wet floor, the lowest gone as soft as bread. He untied one and read three lines by the light from the stair. Then he sent for lamps, and a table, and a boy to fetch and carry.

He spent years having them read, and as they were read he had every date in them turned into the civil calendar, the day and month the humans had brought, and set in the years of its age as the copyists' table of the ages divided them. He had come to dislike the count of the Diosal, which ran backwards into the thousands for everything older than the sunwise turn, and he said that a people should not have to name every year of its life after the day its kin went away. Before the year was out, *a chur san Leabharlann*, to put it in the Library, meant to make a thing settled and beyond dispute. A clerk once used it in his hearing.

"The library settles nothing," said Ailean Leabhar, for so they called him by then. "It only keeps."

The phrase outlived him all the same. The library now keeps the fullest surviving record of everything told in this book, and the reader should bear that in mind.

In SE 18, as the nights drew in, an office was made to keep the kingdom's record, and from its books this book is drawn. The first royal chronicler, Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, a council clerk, kept her record at Muileann chaol and would not keep it at the capital. She wrote in her first entry that a record kept beside the throne is kept for the throne. The same order that made her office bade the kingdom's records count their years as Ailean Leabhar counted them, each age from its own first event, and Gormshuil headed her first year the eighteenth of the Severance Era. It was the first year so written in the kingdom's own record, and the years of the Diosal went into the old books. She sent clerks to every shire to copy parish books, grave-lists and harbour rolls. The south filled forty chests. The northern shires filled one, for few of the Tuathaich would talk to the clerks.

The five lighthouses of the humans were given Dia-thìrich keepers. At Baile chrom, on the Tuathaich coast, the keeper's warrant bade him report what he saw by land as well as by sea. In time he reported that the Grey Night sect kept its vigil in the lighthouse's own shadow. The council took no action.

The library also dug. At Làrach an Dùin its trenches turned up walls older than any Dia-thìrich building and no writing at all, and the finds were catalogued as belonging to the Old Ones, purpose unknown. At Làrach an Teampaill the houses of the Seann Spioradan asked it not to dig, and the keeper entered the ruin as *measured and let be.* The obelisk near Cnoc bheag bore signs that matched no script known on the island. In this age as in every age, the Seann-Dhaoine appear only in what they left, and in what the living will not do near it.

When Ailean Leabhar died in SE 40, Mòrag nic Coinnich became keeper. She began the practice, kept ever since, of writing beside each item where it came from. In SE 42 Gormshuil laid down the chronicle. Her last entry is a list of what the record did not hold: the northern towns' own accounts, the humans' treaties in their own tongue, and the Board's surveys. Her successor, Tormod mac Sheumais, called Tormod Pinn for the speed of his hand, copied that list into the front of his first book and added nothing to it. He struck nothing out, either.

## VII. Of Brìghde and Eòghan, and the First Word of the Depletion

Niall died, and his daughter Brìghde was crowned on 31 an Lùnastal, SE 22, at summer's end, and no one contested it. It was a mortal succession in an aristocracy that stood very near the undying. It seemed nothing strange then. Gormshuil wrote that the succession came *mar a thàinig Niall*, and that is the only idiom she let into the chronicle in all her years.

On 12 am Màrt, SE 26, in the raw end of winter, the survey reports first began to say, very quietly, that the vein's yield was falling.

Iain mac Ruairidh of the Mine Board, whom the hewers called Iain Mapa, had spent long months crawling the faces of the Sloc Mòr with a lamp and a chain, and he knew what he had found before he had finished finding it. The vein was thinning to the east and to the south, and it was thinning in a way that did not argue.

He carried his survey to the Board himself, rolled and tied, and laid it on the table in front of three men who did not unroll it while he was in the room.

"It will be considered," said the one in the middle.

"I should like a receipt," said Iain Mapa.

The clerk looked at him as though he had asked for a kiss. But he wrote one, and signed it, and Iain Mapa folded it into his pocket-book and went home. The survey was filed and never circulated. Soon after, he was sent to the silver works at Muileann chiar.

The next year the Board moved its clerks to Cathair mhòr and made a rule that its surveys were to be kept there and not sent to the library. The state did nothing for years. The library could not know what it was never sent. It knows now, and it counts those years as part of the Depletion.

Brìghde's reign ended young, and no cause was ever made public. Her cousin Eòghan was crowned on 11 an Gearran, SE 28, amid the first true strife over a succession that the restored kingdom had known. The chronicler's entry gives the fact and nothing more, and no chronicler since has added to it. In an Dùbhlachd of that year the council's minutes recorded votes against a succession for the first time. They name the councillors and not their reasons. Two of them did not sit again.

On 9 an Cèitean, SE 29, in the green of an Cèitean, Dubhan was born, mortal, into the confinement the Severance had made, decades after the war that had shut the island to the people his line came from. No chronicle of that year mentions him, and none could have.

The kingdom went on round the Depletion it had not announced. In SE 33 the second census measured, for the first time, the gap between Dia-thìrich and Tuathaich living. The report was never made public. A census clerk, Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire, left a note among her papers saying that she had asked to see it and had been refused, and that note is the only mention of the report outside the council.

That year Walter Hale died, and the Moot chose Mary Coyle, a fisherman's widow, the first woman in its chair. The Còmhrag grew bloodier. In SE 36 six fighters died, and the custodians asked for it to end. The fair-wardens of Ceann leathan, whose town lived off the crowds, refused.

On the first day of an t-Iuchar in SE 39 a gallery gave way under Muileann dhearg, in the reopened Cill ghlas district, along a line the surveyors had marked as sound. Thirty-one hewers died. It was small beside the Rending. It was the same fault. New rules for digging followed. They were written for Dia-thìrich workers, and near the Tuathaich country they were kept loosely, and by intent. At the pits round Àth leathan, where Dia-thìrich overseers worked Tuathaich hands, the timbering rules were posted on the pit-head door and never paid for. The overseers' books show the timber ordered and never delivered. Àth leathan will come into this book again.

## VIII. Of the Search for a Second Vein

After Muileann dhearg the Guild of Hewers bound sixty apprentices to fill its rolls, and not one of them was Tuathaich. On Samhain eve of SE 40 fire ran through the fair at Muileann òg. Its court sat in a field the next morning, and the fair went on, and Oighrig nic Mhathain died of her burns. That winter the Rail Board refused to carry the Moot's goods, and the north's wool went south by cart, a week on the road. The north calls that way the Carters' Road. The south has no name for it.

In the dark of the year's end in SE 41 the Moot began a register of Tuathaich hewers killed or maimed in the western pits, since no Dia-thìrich book counted them. It has been kept ever since, and never sent south. In those years Dubhan was a child in the north, watching a caste that did not age hold every true advantage on an island to whose edge his own forebears had been pushed. The coal was never his to inherit.

The age had its good keepers too. When the dry years came back to Achadh shean in SE 43, the council sent grain up the coal line out of the Sloc Mòr's share, and nobody in the shire died of hunger. The maor had twelve wells dug to the rock, and four of them are still drawn from.

Of Ciorstaidh nic Artair it is told at Tobar dhearg that her father, the keeper of the light there, drowned going out to a boat on the reef, and that she went out after him and brought the boat's crew in. She took his warrant, and set a belled post on the reef. While she kept the light, no boat went aground there.

On 12 an t-Samhain, SE 46, when the leaves were down, the druid schools, Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, whom many still call Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, woke out of their long sleep. Their founding question, why the vein answers some hands and not others, mattered again now that the vein was running short. Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain lectured in Flidais's sacred wood near Muileann chiar, and at Caol shean her students copied the census line on the coal-touched and argued over it in the open, which the Rite did not do. They set the old pillars and the obelisk side by side and found signs in common, and no meaning. Seonaid wrote that the Old Ones had been here and had said so, and that nobody living could hear them.

In SE 50 Alasdair mac Ùisdein, grandson of the first holder of the Sloc Mòr, borrowed against his house's share to go looking for a second vein. The Board lent its surveyors and the Crown lent its name. Seonaid wrote to the Board that the search asked the wrong question. Her school had always asked why the vein answered some hands; nobody had asked why there was only one vein. The Board filed the letter.

The search failed. Forty-one shafts went down between the hills above Dùn dhearg and the moors south of Baile ruadh, and none of them struck the vein. Afterwards Mòrag nic Coinnich found in the library a list from the Holy Age that named those same hills as searched and barren. The kingdom had repeated a failure that its own library could have warned it of, had anyone thought to ask. The house of Mac Ùisdein paid part of Dùn dhearg's damages and sold half its share back to the Crown. The dry shafts at Baile ruadh were left open to the sky, and sheep fell into them, and one child, before the shire fenced them at its own cost.

In SE 55 Mary Coyle laid down the chair, and Daniel Frayne of Muileann leathan came after her, the first speaker born after the Severance. He had taught young Tuathaich to bind books when the southern guilds would not take them. That winter the fair gave one day to northern goods. They were still sold through factors, but under the makers' own marks, and it was the first time a Tuathaich name had been written on anything sold there. The first such mark was the Doire ghlas weavers' grey twill, with a white thread at the selvedge. Within the year the weavers of Baile chiar were weaving a white thread into theirs.

On 11 am Màrt, SE 56, the Depletion could no longer be denied.

Catrìona nic Neacail, the surveyor-general, had drawn the last untouched sections of the vein, and they were smaller than anyone wished to admit. When the drawing was finished it fitted on one sheet. Because a sheet so small wanted explaining, she went down into the Board's files at Cathair mhòr to learn how long the thinning had been going on.

It took her the best part of a week, by a smoking lamp. Near the bottom of a press she found a survey of the faces of the Sloc Mòr, rolled and tied, in a hand she did not know. It showed the vein thinning to the east and the south, and it was thirty years old.

She published her map. She sent the library a copy of Iain Mapa's survey, with a note of the day the Board had received it, and within the year she resigned. Iain Mapa died at Muileann chiar the next spring. His own copy of the survey was found among his papers with the Board's receipt pinned to it. He had kept the proof that he told them.

Muileann dhearg lost a third of its households. Its Fèidh hall was shut, and its bell was sold to Caol shean, where it still rings the students in to their lectures.

## IX. Of Mairead and the Failing of the Coal

Mairead was crowned on 29 an Dàmhair, SE 58, in the fall of the leaf. Eòghan's reign had ended in the decade the Depletion came into the open, and she was heir to a kingdom whose founding wealth was plainly failing. That year the Guild of Hewers bound no apprentices, for the first time since its charter.

The north began building things that did not hang on the mountain. In SE 59 wool mills went up at Doire ghlas with Moot money. The Rail Board refused to carry their cloth, until the circuit justice at Seann Bhral, Ruairidh mac Phàdraig, ruled that the Board was a carrier of the Crown and must carry for anyone who paid. It was the first ruling the Moot ever won in a Dia-thìrich court. The Board appealed, and the council let the appeal lapse without a reason given.

In SE 60 the Crown bought the last of the house of Mac Ùisdein's working shafts, and from then on the Board worked the vein in the Crown's name alone.

On 1 an t-Iuchar, SE 61, Dubhan began his experiments, trying to make a fuel to stand in for the coal out of what the mines threw away. They all failed, and the record of those years scarcely troubles to name them. In that same month the lowest galleries of the Sloc Mòr were let flood, because the pumps cost more to run than the coal beneath them was worth. The Board's minute calls it a pause.

The chronicle of those years is full of small alarms. Panthers came across the south-west, beasts named in the Holy Age lists and not seen in living memory, and the old list named the year after them as a hungry one. At Muileann chrom the yard families stopped the coal trains for three days over cut wages; the Board settled on the fourth day and dismissed eleven men on the fifth. Then the harvest after the panthers came in good, and Tormod Pinn drew a line through his own note of the year before. This book has always liked him for it.

In the autumn of SE 64 the third census published its figures openly, the first census in the kingdom's history to do so. It was a small reform, and nothing in the frame of the kingdom moved because of it.

A month later the figures were read at Caol mhòr. Daniel Frayne sat in the Moot's chair with his hands flat on the table, the way he sat when he meant to keep them still. The clerk read the columns in a flat voice. In every column the census clerks had chosen to take, the northern towns stood at about half the Dia-thìrich measure. Nobody in the room was surprised. They had simply never heard it read aloud from the kingdom's own paper.

When the clerk had done, there was a long quiet. Then Daniel Frayne drew the minute-book towards him and wrote two words, and the words are the whole of the minute: *Now written.*

The census carried a line for the coal-touched, as the first one had, giving a number and nothing else. Tormod Pinn copied it into the chronicle without comment, as Gormshuil had done before him.

Tormod Pinn died at his desk in SE 65 and Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh became royal chronicler. She was the first to add, at the foot of each year, a note of what the record could not learn. Her first concerned the northern shires. The census clerks there had been told the figures and had not counted them, and the figures they were told were the Moot's. So the kingdom's first honest census was honest in the north because the Moot had supplied the numbers.

Mòrag nic Coinnich now called the shires' record-chests in to Muileann chaol. At Seann Tarr the shire keeper burned his chest in the yard sooner than send it, saying that the shire's record belonged in the shire, and that chest is lost. In SE 67 the library doubled its holdings, and from then on the history of Dia-thìr was kept in one place instead of many.

No Tuathaich record was called in. The Moot's minute-books, the schools' registers and the vigil-books of Baile chrom stayed in the north in private keeping. The new wing was built of Sloc Mòr stone. The shires' chests filled three floors, and the fourth was left empty for what had not been sent. It is empty still, or near enough.

In the west the Board was drawing back. In SE 68 it closed the branch line to Àth leathan, citing the falling yield of the western pits. The Tuathaich hewers there kept working under their own pit captains and paid the Crown's fifth by the Leòid ruling, and the Board took the payments and entered them as arrears. At Cnoc thais the pits passed to their hewers in the same way. The south did not notice; it wanted nothing in the western hills any longer.

In SE 70 Raghnall mac Mhuirich became keeper of the library. The price of coal-fuel at the fair doubled, and at Cnoc fhiadhaich households were found picking coal off the spoil-heaps to burn. The Board posted watchmen from the town, who saw nothing.

## X. Of the Eve of Dubhan

The summer of SE 71 came in dry and dear. The poorer streets of the capital were darker than they had been since the humans first lit them, the Guild of Hewers bound no apprentices, and the fair's court could not hold its price. So far as the kingdom's own record knew, its seventy-first year held nothing larger than a watch set on the spoil-heaps, whose watchmen saw nothing.

In the north Dubhan was at his work still, as he had been for ten years, boiling and burning what the pits threw away. Nobody in the capital was watching him, and nobody in the Library knew his name. One night near midsummer, the tellers of the north say, he banked his fire and slept beside it, as he had on a hundred nights before, and did not know that the morning would open a new count of the island's years, which no one would begin to keep for fourteen years yet.

Here the Fifth Book ends, on the eve of dubhan. The Library closes the Age of the Kingdom on that night and not an hour after it, and the Severance Era with it. The Sixth Book begins in the morning.


# The Sixth Book: An Aois Dhubhain, the Age of Dubhan

*DE 1 – 27*

> *Bho latha a' chiad dubhain cunntar na bliadhnaichean às ùr.*
> From the day of the first dubhan the years shall be counted anew.
>
> — the council's proclamation of the Dubhan Era, 5 an Cèitean, DE 15

## I. Of Dubhan's Fire

On 19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1, about midsummer, the first working dubhan was made, and from that morning the island counts the years of its sixth age, the Dubhan Era, though nobody counted them so for fourteen years. It was crude, and it burned. Nobody yet traded in it; for the while it was one man's answer to a crisis that the caste in power had still not faced. At the foot of that year Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh wrote that a fuel made without the vein was reported from the north, and that she had not seen it. That is the first mention of dubhan in the royal record, and she spelled the word three ways in two lines.

In the capital the poorer streets were left dark to save coal. By DE 3 coal was sold at the fair only by the sack, and at last only by the lump, for altars.

Cathal was crowned on 1 an Lùnastal, DE 3, the feast of Lùnastal, by Macha's rite. Mairead's reign had ended while Dubhan's experiments still failed more often than they worked, and Cathal did not yet know how near his kingdom's answer lay. The new dies at the mint still pressed the coal ink into the seal.

The fuel came south within three years. In DE 4 a company of shipmasters set up a dubhan works at Seann Skell on the southern coast, the first outside the north, and how they came by the making of it they never told. The high custodian wrote to the houses of the Rite that the new fuel was not forbidden, since it was not coal, and not blessed, since it was not coal. It sold its first year's making to the south-coast boats and the capital's lamp-houses, and the dark streets were the first to be lit again.

In DE 6 the five coastal beacons, which had burned coal-lit flame for more than a century, were the first works of the kingdom to be turned over to dubhan by decree.

Ciorstaidh nic Artair was grey by then, but nobody else was let carry the lantern. Inside its thick glass the flame of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg burned with the dark, coloured edge that only the island's coal gives. She carried it into the Rite's house at Seann Skell in the late spring, down the hall between the custodians of four shires, who stood in their rows and did not speak. Her boots were loud on the flags.

At Brìde's altar she set the lantern down and opened its little door. The flame leaned towards the air, and steadied. Nobody told her to go, so she stayed, and so did they, while the last of the coal burned down. It took longer than anyone had thought. When the flame shrank to a blue bead and then to nothing, a thread of smoke went up and hung under the roof, and one of the custodians let out a breath as if he had been holding it the whole while.

The south coast has a song of that day in more than one form. This is the shortest:

> *Dh'fhalbh an lasair às an tùr,*
> *tha solas ann, ach chan ann leinn.*
> The flame has gone out of the tower;
> there is a light there, but it is not ours.

At Baile chrom, on the Tuathaich coast, the change was made by Tuathaich fitters from Caol mhòr, because the Lighthouse Board had none of its own to send so far. The keeper's report names none of them.

After that the change came to everything, and it came fast. On 1 an Cèitean, DE 8, Bealltainn, the Rail Board ran its first dubhan engine on the coal line. It carried no coal. The drovers sold their oxen for lorries. On 25 an t-Ògmhios, DE 9, the fitters at Seann Skell set a lorry's engine under a closed carriage for the high custodian of the Rite, the first carriage on the island that needed no horse, and on 5 an t-Iuchar, DE 13, buses began to run out of the capital to Inis mhòr and Cathair mhòr. The roadside inns put in dubhan lamps, and centuries of oil and wick were gone within a decade. At An Leòmhann Buidhe the landlord kept one wick lamp burning over the door beside the new ones, and a wick lamp over an inn door is still called a Leòmhann.

In DE 8 Daniel Frayne died, and the Moot chose Martha Greaves of Doire ghlas, a mill manager. His old pupils rebound the Moot's minute-books from the first meeting onward. The Moot's minute says that a second set was made and hidden elsewhere. The library notes this and has not gone looking.

In DE 10 the last working face under Muileann dhearg was closed. Its families were moved to the Hewers' Row at Seann Toll, and most of them went to work on the dubhan tanks at the river landing. Muileann dhearg was left with its chapel, its graves and a caretaker.

By DE 11 *dubhan* meant the fuel and no longer the man, years before the trade built on it was whole. A letter of the Fèidh school at Caol shean coined *dubhan-tùsail* for a first attempt that looks like a dead end until it turns out to be the road. On 30 an Cèitean, DE 12, the Guild of Hewers dissolved itself. Its rolls, its oath-stone of coal and its sick-roll went to the library. Its last master, Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh, wrote that the guild had outlived the mountain's patience.

By DE 13 the markets, the army's supply lines and the shipping were all going over to the new fuel. The coal caste watched its own source of power fail and did not object. The house of Mac Ùisdein sold the last of its share in the spoil and put its money into dubhan shipping at Ros dhomhain, the only family of the vein that moved before the vein failed it.

In DE 14 the fitters of dubhan engines were chartered as a guild at Seann Skell. Like every guild before it, its rolls were open to Dia-thìrich only, and the Tuathaich fitters were let go. They went home and fitted engines without a guild. That winter the Moot voted to take up the new fuel, and the delegates of the western pit towns got up and walked out. When the northern depots opened, Martha Greaves wrote in the minute that the north now bought its fire from the south, and she did not say whether that was good.

On 5 an Cèitean, DE 15, the coinage was pegged to the making of dubhan in place of the coal reserves, which was a quiet way of owning which of the two now ran the kingdom. At the same sitting the council proclaimed that the Age of the Kingdom had ended with the first working dubhan, and that the kingdom's years were counted anew from that day. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh re-headed fourteen years of her chronicle, and wrote at the foot of the page that she had never before had to move a year she was living in. The coal ink was left out of the seal, and the seal was plain. Fearchar Bonn's first dies went to the library, where they lie beside the Hewers' oath-stone. The high custodian protested that a plain seal showed the vein was no longer held sacred. The council answered that the kingdom had never said it did. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh copied both letters into the chronicle. It is one of the few places in the whole record where the kingdom said plainly what it was.

The north has a rhyme from those years, heard there in both tongues. This is its Dia-thìris form:

> *Dubh an gual, 's dubh an dubhan,*
> *ach cò leis an teine?*
> Black the coal, and black the dubhan;
> but whose is the fire?

## II. Of the Holdouts of the Western Hills

In the spring of DE 16 the western pit towns met at Muileann àrsaidh, apart from the Moot, and agreed to go on working their seams and to sell their coal to any household in the north that would buy it. Àth naomh, with only a few old shafts to its name, joined them, saying it would rather be cold with its neighbours than warm alone. So a knot of northern towns refused to fold themselves into the new trade. They kept to the last workable coal seams sooner than hang their fires on one man's fuel. They were Àth leathan, Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg, and their spokeswoman was Ruth Calder, a pit captain's daughter from Àth leathan. The Moot neither joined nor condemned them. At Cnoc thais Tom Varley opened again two shafts that had lain abandoned since the humans' time. The coal was poor. It was theirs, and it kept the town warm.

In DE 17 Ellen Marsh, a schoolteacher of Doire ghlas, finished eleven books of Tuathaich accounts of the Severance and the settling, taken down from the old people of the north. She asked Leabharlann Muileann chaol, formally, to keep the Tuathaich tellings beside the Dia-thìrich record. The request was tabled, and it lies on the table yet. Raghnall mac Mhuirich replied that it awaited the council's view on the standing of spoken witness. The council has never given one.
