Ellen Marsh wrote back that spoken witness had been good enough for the census clerks when they took the Moot's figures. Her letter is filed with the request. It is short, and nobody has answered it.

The holdout pits undersold dubhan across the north, and the Moot's own mills bought their coal. In DE 18 the Board's northern revenue fell by a quarter, the first fall since the Severance, and its report named the western pits as the cause and the Leòid ruling as the cure. Eighty years after Eilidh nic Leòid gave it, her ruling was put to the use the north had always feared. The Board declared the western seams Crown property, holding that the right to work them had lapsed when the holders stopped paying the fifth. The holders answered that they had stopped paying when the Board stopped carrying the coal. Both were true. The pits were ordered shut.

A company of enforcers was posted to Seann Skell in the west, which is another town from the Rite's Seann Skell in the south. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh noted that it was the first armed company the kingdom had sent toward the north since the Severance. Martha Greaves wrote that the western towns would not shut their pits because of a letter, and asked for a year while the Moot talked with them. Her letter was received and filed.

In the autumn of DE 19 the first skirmishes began. Each was too small to name and none was written down, and together they ran straight into open war. At the foot of that year Beathag wrote that clashes were reported in the west, and that she had asked for the Board's reports of them. They were not given. At Muileann àrsaidh the pit-heads were walled and the road from the south was dug across. On 25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 19, which was Christmas Day, Ruth Calder wrote to the council for the western towns and offered the Crown's fifth in coal, if the Board would carry it and let the pits work until the seams were spent. The letter reached the library. No answer to it did.

In DE 20, in the depth of winter, the Moot resolved by nine votes that it was no party to the quarrel and would feed anyone who came to its towns hungry. That summer it filled its granaries at Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas beyond the usual. The minute gives no reason. It needed none.

In an Lùnastal Beathag laid down the office, and her clerk Sìleas nic Rath became royal chronicler. It is her record of the war that the library would later seal. In an Dàmhair came the order to mobilise. Regiments that had not been called out since the Severance were formed again and armed again, openly, months before anyone in power would admit that a war was coming. Command went to Somhairle mac Lachlainn, who had risen among the Board's enforcers. The rolls of the Severance companies were brought out of the council's chests to name the new regiments, and the old names were read aloud before new men. The list had been kept for nearly ninety years. Now it was used.

On 25 an Dùbhlachd, DE 20, Christmas Day again, Martha Greaves came to Cathair dhearg with the Moot's petition.

She had kept the feast on the road, in a cold carriage, and she came into the capital in the grey forenoon with the frost still white on the bridge. The Dia-thìrich keep no feast that day, and the council was sitting. She waited on a bench in a passage for most of an hour, the petition on her knee. Then a clerk said her name, in the Dia-thìris way, so that for a moment she did not know it for hers.

She was the first speaker of the Moot ever to walk into the council chamber. It was smaller than she had thought, and warm with a dubhan stove. Twelve faces turned to her. She read the petition standing. It asked that the western pits be let alone to work out their seams, which would be spent within a few years in any case. She read it to the end without hurrying, and laid it on the table.

"Received," said the clerk, and wrote.

It was filed. That winter the Rail Board carried arms and dubhan west to Seann Bhral, and the yard at Muileann chrom worked on the trains day and night.

## III. Of An Cogadh Fada, the Long War

*What is told here of the war comes from the open record, the towns' reports and the Tuathaich tellings; the rest is sealed.*

Late in am Faoilleach of DE 21 the hewers of the five towns came together at Àth leathan, where the road from the south goes up into the hills. In the north they tell it like this. It was bitter weather, with a thin snow blowing that would not lie, and the men and women came in by the hill paths with their pit-lamps lit at noon, the sky was so dark. They slept in the pit-sheds, and in the byres with the cattle for the warmth. Ruth Calder went from fire to fire with a list, asking who was here, and who was coming. The Board's lists name her among them, and Tom Varley too.

From Cathair dhearg the regiments marched west, and their carts and lorries ran on dubhan.

The Battle of Àth leathan was fought on 11 an Giblean, DE 21, in the spring, the first great battle of An Cogadh Fada. The state, already leaning on Dubhan's fuel to prop its fading power, moved against the holdouts with its own hand. The open record counts the kingdom's dead and not the holdouts'. The Tuathaich tellings put theirs in the hundreds. Ruth Calder's name does not appear in the open record after that day. Whether she fell there, no teller in the north will say for certain. Her name simply stops.

The holdouts gave up the southern pits and fell back into the hills round Muileann àrsaidh and Cnoc thais. The pits of Àth leathan were flooded on the Board's order, and the field was left unploughed. The seventh regiment was raised on the west coast to hold the road behind the army. Before the month was out a wartime tithe was laid on every sale of dubhan in the kingdom, for the war's sake. It was never lifted. Fleets were raised and sent round the western cape to close the Tuathaich ports of the north-west to every boat but the fishing boats, and to search those.

In an t-Ògmhios the regiments invested Muileann àrsaidh. The town held out for weeks on stored coal and potatoes, and its pit-heads were taken one at a time. Sìleas nic Rath's open record gives the day it fell and nothing more. The army's dubhan was served before any other use, and the capital's poorer streets went dark again, as they had been before the fuel came.

The families of the western pits came into Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas with what they could carry. The Moot fed them from its own stores, as it had resolved to. The council sent nothing and forbade nothing. The Moot's minute records the families' names, and it is among the few Tuathaich records of the war that the library does not hold. Agnes Pike's old school at Doire ghlas was given over to them, and Ellen Marsh, who taught there, took down their accounts. This book would give a good deal to read them.

In an Lùnastal Cnoc thais was taken, after the regiments cut the road to its pits, and Tom Varley's two shafts were fired and sealed. The open record gives the number of holdouts taken and not the number who went on into the hills. Some went on past the hills and out onto the windy coast, beyond the shire lines, and the regiments did not follow them there. With the fleets away in the north-west, raiders out of the east took two salt-boats off Àth bheag and burned a third.

Through the autumn the kingdom went on raising regiments, as if it looked for a longer war. The fourth regiment was quartered at Ceann mhòr in the old human magistrate's house, and the Moot's protest was received.

In an Dùbhlachd the regiments came to Baile chrom on the night of the vigil.

The corporal at the head of the file had come up the coast road expecting shutters and dogs and shouting. There was nothing. Not a lamp showed in any window. No dog barked. The only sound was the sea on the stones and his own men's boots, and even they began to tread softer without being told.

He tried the first door. It was unlatched. Inside, by the grey of the window, a man and a woman and three children sat round a cold hearth with their hands in their laps. None of them spoke. He asked them, in Dia-thìris and then in the humans' tongue, who else was in the house, and whether there were arms. The man only shook his head, once, slowly, as a man does at a child who has asked a foolish thing in church.

It was the same in the next house, and the next, until the small hours. He wrote in the end that the whole town had been dark and silent, and that it had been searched and nothing found. The regiments' return for that month says as much, and no more.

That month Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg opened their roads without a siege. Their pits were flooded. The open record names no holdouts taken at either.

Late in an Dàmhair of the next year a column of holdouts, several hundred strong, came out of the western hills, and through an t-Samhain it moved south-east through the middle of the island toward the capital. The reason lies in the sealed archive. The Tuathaich tellings give its leader the name Owen Barrow; the open record gives him none. On 6 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22, the column passed Muileann òg and made camp on the fields by Muileann ghlas, a day's walk from Cathair dhearg, and the first and third regiments were brought down the fair road to meet it. The booths of the fair-ground were cleared for their camp, and the fair court's books for that year end without a closing entry.

The Battle of Muileann ghlas was fought on 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22, four days after, in the short grey days before midwinter. It was the second great battle of the war, and the last. The holdouts were broken in two summers' campaigning. They were the children of humans once pushed to the island's edge, and now they were pushed back again, and the fuel that drove the lorries against them had been made by one of their own. The open record lists the first and third regiments on the field and does not count the column's dead. When word reached the hills, the holdouts still there came down to the seventh regiment's posts on the Àth leathan road. They were disarmed and sent home, and the open record counts their weapons.

So An Cogadh Fada ended on 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22, twenty months after it began, and it has been called the Long War all the same. Nine regiments and four fleets were raised in it. All are under arms yet, and each is named for the town where it is stationed.

Before the year was out the Tuathaich had a new saying. *Chaidh am fadachadh*, they got long-warred, was said first of the defeat in the west, and then of any defeat that comes after holding out too long. It is said as a joke, and the people who say it do not laugh.

## IV. Of the Peace, and of the Present Year

The regiments were not stood down. The council kept each at the town where it had been raised and paid them out of the wartime tithe. With the last organised resistance gone, Dubhan's fuel became, in all but law, compulsory across the whole island. The last western seams were flooded and capped with concrete, and after that no coal was dug on Dia-thìr outside the Board's own works. The holdouts taken at Muileann ghlas were marched north as far as the boundary stones, the stones set in SE 1 that nobody had ever been paid to move. The Moot's register gave their names a column of their own. Somhairle mac Lachlainn was given a seat on the council, the first soldier to sit there since the captains of the Severance war.

In DE 23 the kingdom raised a stone at Cathair mhòr, beside the Mac Ùisdein market cross, with the names of the regiments' dead. On the field of Àth leathan the Tuathaich families built a cairn without leave. The seventh regiment's patrols have let it stand, and it grows by a stone or two every time they pass. At Muileann ghlas the field was sown again, and for years its farmer turned up weapons in the furrows and handed them to the first regiment, which keeps a list.

On 14 am Faoilleach, DE 24, the library's whole record of the Long War was sealed from the public for fifty years. It is the only sealed archive in the kingdom's history. What is still open for the war years is Sìleas nic Rath's list of places, the regiments present, and the counts she was allowed to give. Her full record went into the sealed room with everything else. Ailean Leabhar said once that the library settles nothing and only keeps. He never thought it would one day keep a thing it was not let read.

The war left its accounts. The Treasury carried the wartime tithe forward as a standing line under the regiments' pay, and no council minute records a decision to keep it. The fuel-fitters took the contract for the regiments' engines and doubled their rolls, and every new fitter was Dia-thìrich.

In an t-Ògmhios of DE 25 Anna nic Phàil, councillor for Cathair dhomhain, brought the Moot's petition before the council: that the Tuathaich towns be paid for what they had lost in the war. She spoke for it once. On 10 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25, the proposal was raised in the capital and quietly let die without a vote. The Moot's minute on it is one line long: *Allowed to die.* Martha Greaves laid down the chair that year, and the Moot chose Peter Hale, great-grandson of its first speaker. The fourth regiment left the magistrate's house at Ceann mhòr. The Moot asked that the house be given to the town. It was given to the maor.

By DE 26 the Tuathaich had one name for the tabled request and the dead motion together: *seann-chunntas*, an old reckoning that nobody in power will settle and nobody has struck out. Official Dia-thìrich usage has not taken up the word. This book uses it, since the record should hold the words of both peoples.

That year the mountain was shut, or nearly. The Board closed the upper galleries of the Sloc Mòr and kept one face open, in the Rite's custody, to cut coal for the altars. Twelve hewers were kept on to work it, the last of their trade on the island. On 10 an t-Sultain, DE 26, the last coal train ran to Cathair dhearg. The coal line has kept its name and carries dubhan, wool and soldiers. The second regiment set a guard at the library over the sealed archive, and Raghnall mac Mhuirich wrote to the council that the library had not asked for one. On the northern road, where the boundary stones stand, the sixth regiment keeps posts, and Tuathaich going south show a pass for the first time since the Severance. The council's minute calls the passes temporary. The reader will know by now what the kingdom's temporary measures tend to become.

The last year and this one have been like other years. Tuathaich wool was sold at Muileann òg on its northern day, through Dia-thìrich factors, as at the first fair. The Còmhrag was fought with staves and fists, and one man died. Ellen Marsh's eleven books have been copied by hand in the northern schools and are kept there; the library's catalogue lists the tabled request and not the books. The Moot met at Caol mhòr under Peter Hale, its minute-books unbroken since Walter Hale's wet afternoon, with no standing in Dia-thìrich law and no request for any. Every lamp and engine on the island, every ship and every lorry, runs on dubhan; the coinage is pegged to it, and the tithe is taken on every sale. The Treasury's roll for the year stood at 9,568 purses, two parts in three of it from the head-due. In the summer the Rite's twelve hewers cut the year's altar-coal. It filled four baskets, and the high custodian shared it among the houses by lot.

On 7 an t-Sultain, DE 27, as the summer went out, Dubhan himself, an old man now in his sixty-ninth year, won from the council at Cathair dhearg the right to sell dubhan off the island. He had written to the council for a year and sat before it three times. It is the first leave the kingdom has given for any good of Dia-thìr to go beyond its waters since the Severance, and it is narrowly drawn. The Treasury sets each year's measure. The fuel is loaded only at Ros dhomhain, where a clerk of the Treasury takes the tithe on every barrel. The kingdom's depots and the Moot's are served first. The custodians of Òrd Bhrìde seal every hold, since nothing of the vein may be sold, and the Small-Burning Law is not touched by it. Dubhan has told neither the council nor the chronicler who his buyers are. The first tank-hull loaded under the charter went out past the western capes in the autumn, and at Seann Skell the priests of Manannan said the old prayer to keep the sea shut on the day she sailed. Dubhan goes out under that charter and no other.

On 22 an t-Samhain, DE 27, with the lamps lit by mid-afternoon at Muileann chaol, Sìleas nic Rath wrote at the foot of the year that the kingdom's record is whole in every part but two: the war, which is sealed, and the north, which was not asked.

So the account stands on 21 an Dùbhlachd, DE 27, at the turning of the year's shortest days. The coal is all but gone. The kingdom's trade runs on a name that once belonged to one man, and since the autumn a little of it has gone out past the western capes under his charter. The Dia-thìrich hold the capital and the sea. The Tuathaich hold the north, and their Church, and a grievance five years old, and a memory of the First Canoe that the people who twice defeated them still call folklore. The restored kingdom promised the island its own again. It kept the humans' tariff, their surveys, their rails and their terms for the mountain, and it kept the humans' children where the humans had put them. It kept faith as well with the drowned towns of the south, and its wells at Achadh shean still draw water.

Here the Sixth Book stops, at the present year, for the chronicle itself goes on. The age that follows has no name yet, because nobody can yet say what began it. It is left to the next chronicler, who will be handed the whole record and, with it, the things still missing from it: the war in its guarded room, which is to be opened fifty years from its sealing if the kingdom keeps its word; the fourth floor at Muileann chaol, built for what was not sent; the eleven books in the north; and the Moot's minutes with their hidden second set. The old reckoning is still owed. Whoever writes the next book should begin by asking for them.


# The Annals of Dia-thìr

## Age I · An Aois Àrsaidh

*The Ancient Age · the Vein Era, VE 1 – 9,926*

- **20 am Faoilleach, VE 1** — *The crack in the stone*. Neachdan, a mason splitting rock for a well, breaks into a vein of hard coal that shows every colour in the break. That night a storm comes over the hills, and lightning strikes the broken vein, and it takes fire. He carries a burning coal home and lays the first hearth: it is the first fire of the Dia-thìrich. On it he tries the other coals he broke out, and all burn alike, with a low black flame; he is glad of the fire all the same.
- **17 an Giblean, VE 76** — *Three wells claim the crack* (Tobar dhìreach). Tobar dhìreach, Tobar dhubh and Tobar òg each tell that the mason's well was theirs, and that the lightning fell there. Tobar dhìreach can show a capped shaft with a scorched stain on its lip; the other two have only the telling. Between the three no chronicler has ever judged.
- **19 am Màrt, VE 151** — *The slab over the burnt vein* (Tobar dhìreach). When the fire in the vein has burned itself out, the mason's people dig no further. They lay a flat stone over the broken vein, draw no water beside it, and cut their well again a stone's throw off. In this all the tellings agree.
- **14 an t-Ògmhios, VE 227** — *The high snowfields shrink* (Abhainn uaine). Meltwater off the central mountains cuts the bed that Abhainn uaine follows still. On the gravel terraces of its lower reach lie hearth-stones at three heights, each left as the water rose to it.
- **16 an Cèitean, VE 303** — *The first hearths of the high valleys* (Achadh dhìreach). Hearths are made at Achadh dhìreach, of pine and heather charcoal, with scrapers of grey flint and the split bones of red deer about them. There is no coloured coal in them: those who sat there had none of it, or would not burn it.
- **11 an Lùnastal, VE 378** — *The oak comes to the lowlands* (Doire ghlas). The birch and pine of the cold years give way to oak and hazel, as the pollen in the bog under Doire ghlas shows. The grove that names the place stands on ground that was open heath when the vein was first broken.
- **22 an Lùnastal, VE 451** — *The bare north-west*. The oak never reaches the north-western horn of the island. The gales off the north-western sea keep it bare, low heather and blanket bog behind the shore without a tree, as it is still. No hearth of that age has been found there.
- **13 an t-Iuchar, VE 506** — *Eilean dhubh cut off* (Eilean dhubh). The rising sea floods the low neck of land that joined Eilean dhubh to the main island. The hearths of the neck lie drowned under the sand of the sound, and the deer of the island, cut off, grow smaller in the lifetimes after.
- **1 an t-Iuchar, VE 551** — *Hunters on Eilean mhin* (Eilean mhin). Seal-hunters pitch camps on Eilean mhin, coming there by boat: the first sure sign that anyone on Dia-thìr crossed open water of set purpose. The camps are kept a season at a time and left.
- **30 an t-Sultain, VE 611** — *Seals on the skerries* (Eilean fhada). Hunters of the north shore go out in skin boats in the autumn gales to the skerries off Eilean fhada, where the grey seals haul out to pup, and take them there. The seal bones in the middens of the north coast bear the same cut-marks as those of Eilean mhin. On Eilean fhada a hard year is counted by the boats the gales kept ashore.
- **2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 681** — *The flood-plain of Abhainn ìseal* (Abhainn ìseal). Abhainn ìseal, the longest river of the island, settles into the wide bed it keeps now. Fish-weirs of hazel stakes are set across its side channels, and the stakes are renewed in the same holes for generations.
- **28 an Lùnastal, VE 751** — *The middens of Seann Dunn* (Seann Dunn). The Seann-Dhaoine begin the great mound at Seann Dunn: limpet shell, seal bone and burnt weed, laid down over many lifetimes until it stands taller than a man. It is the first sure trace of them. No tool in it is shaped as any later Dia-thìreach shaped tools.
- **26 an t-Sultain, VE 820** — *The notched net-weights of Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). At Seann Chwen the Seann-Dhaoine sink their nets with beach stones, and every stone is notched with the same three strokes. It is the eldest mark on Dia-thìr made again and again of purpose.
- **17 an Gearran, VE 890** — *The Keeper in the grove* (Doire ghlas). In the oak grove at Doire ghlas a figure of grey smoke comes to Diarmad of the Mason's line, who has asked why the coal of the vein has colours. It names itself Coimhdeach na Fine, the kin's keeper, and tells him of the making of the world by Caoran, the Young God, and of the gift hidden in the coal. Asked how the colours may be opened, it gives a riddle: the sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit; merge the spirits, and they become almighty. From Diarmad's line the telling of the making goes to every hearth.
- **1 an t-Iuchar, VE 951** — *The mole at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). A mole of unmortared boulders is laid out into the Abhainn naomh from the bank at Seann Skell, long enough to shelter a dozen boats from the current. Its foot lies under water still at the lowest tides, and every quay wall built there since stands on it.
- **30 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,027** — *The steps of Seann Bhral* (Seann Bhral). Two hundred and twelve steps are cut up the cliff at Seann Bhral, from the shingle to the grazing above. Their treads are worn hollow in the middle. How many feet that took, none has reckoned.
- **4 an Cèitean, VE 1,096** — *The dead of Seann Vell go to Eilean dhearg* (Eilean dhearg). The Seann-Dhaoine of Seann Vell row their dead out to Eilean dhearg and lay them in stone boxes facing the mainland. Forty boxes are counted there. No grave of theirs of this time is found on the mainland.
- **2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,170** — *The fish-channel of Seann Toll* (Seann Toll). At Seann Toll a channel is cut through a shelf of rock into a pool beside the Abhainn uaine, with a slot for a wattle gate. When the river falls the gate is dropped and the pool emptied by hand. The slot is sharp still.
- **7 am Màrt, VE 1,233** — *The shell causeway of Seann Warr* (Seann Warr). A road of crushed shell is laid across the reed marsh at Seann Warr, on the western shore of Loch chrom, a little over a mile long and raised a forearm above the reeds. It is the eldest made road on the island that may still be walked.
- **5 an Giblean, VE 1,301** — *The script appears at Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). Rows of signs are cut into the cliff above Seann Tarr, in the script that is found afterwards on the standing stones. It is not Dia-thìris, and none has read it. No sign of it has a meaning that all accept.
- **14 an t-Sultain, VE 1,370** — *The gold coal takes fire on the sea* (Ceann thais). Aodh of the Mason's line carries the seven coals of the vein down to the northern shore, below where Ceann thais now stands, and throws them into the sea one by one. The coal with the sheen of gold takes fire on the water and burns gold until the waves put it under; the other six sink. It is the first of the Seven Coals to be lit from its own spirit.
- **17 an Giblean, VE 1,443** — *The fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn* (Seann Mhorn). Stone-lined pits with short flues are built above the beach at Seann Mhorn, to dry the catch over peat smoke. Seven are known. They are the first buildings on Dia-thìr made for a trade, and not for sleep or for the dead.
- **16 an Cèitean, VE 1,515** — *The slipways of Seann Bhrenn* (Seann Bhrenn). Long ramps of flat stone are laid down into the water at Seann Bhrenn, wide enough for hulls greater than any hide boat. Of the hulls nothing is left, nor any telling of where they went.
- **7 am Màrt, VE 1,588** — *The lake dwellings of Loch chrom* (Loch chrom). Platforms on oak piles are raised in the shallows of Loch chrom and joined to the shore by plank walks. Whether the Seann-Dhaoine built them, or some other people of those years, is not known.
- **6 an Gearran, VE 1,670** — *The whale-rib houses of Seann Dunn* (Seann Dunn). A whale strands below the southern Seann Dunn, and its ribs are raised for the frames of three round houses roofed with turf. The ribs are set up again in new houses at least twice before they rot.
- **8 am Faoilleach, VE 1,734** — *The round houses of the eastern Seann Vell* (Seann Vell). At the eastern Seann Vell the Seann-Dhaoine build round houses of dry stone, each with a hearth sunk in the middle of the floor and a drain running out under the wall. Fourteen house-rings are counted there.
- **10 an Dùbhlachd, VE 1,806** — *The tower at the north-western Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). At the least of the Seann Skell places, on the north-west coast, a single round tower of dry stone is raised, hollow-walled, with a stair in the thickness of the wall. It looks out over the water where the Sea-Watcher is afterwards seen.
- **1 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,879** — *The huts of the northern Seann Toll* (Seann Toll). At Seann Toll on the north coast a cluster of stone huts is built in the lee of a dune. The dune afterwards buries them whole, and the sand keeps them.
- **2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,951** — *The eastern Seann Bhral* (Seann Bhral). At the Seann Bhral of the south-east coast the Seann-Dhaoine keep a landing and a line of fish-kilns like those of Seann Mhorn. The two places lie within a day's rowing of each other.
- **4 an Cèitean, VE 2,025** — *The shell beds of the southern Seann Mhorn* (Seann Mhorn). At the second Seann Mhorn, on the southern coast, oyster, whelk and cockle shell is heaped over a whole headland, and there is little else. The oysters of its lowest layers are larger than any taken there since.
- **5 an Giblean, VE 2,097** — *The twin landings of Seann Bhrenn* (Seann Bhrenn). A second Seann Bhrenn, far to the north-east of the first, has the same long ramps into the water. Whether the two were of one people, or only the name was carried, is not known.
- **2 an t-Sultain, VE 2,170** — *The snowflake coal takes fire in the air* (Binnean a' Chlachair). Fearghas of the Mason's line climbs to the highest ground of the island, above where Muileann gheal now stands, and lets the six unlit coals fall from the top. The coal flecked with white stars takes fire as it falls and burns white in the air; the others strike the stones cold. The summit is called after the kindred Binnean a' Chlachair, the Mason's Point.
- **25 an Dàmhair, VE 2,241** — *The cliff-house at Seann Tarr in the east* (Seann Tarr). At the Seann Tarr of the north-eastern headlands a single long house is built into a cleft of the cliff, with the living rock for its back wall. The rock behind the hearth is black with soot to the height of a man.
- **26 an t-Sultain, VE 2,312** — *The north-eastern Seann Vell* (Seann Vell). The Seann Vell on the Abhainn bheag, a short way above its mouth in the north-east, is a small place of four houses and a boat-shed. No Seann-Dhaoine dwelling on the main island is known further to the north-east.
- **22 am Màrt, VE 2,382** — *The northern Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). At the Seann Skell below the later Ros gheal, on the north coast, the Seann-Dhaoine lay a second breakwater, shorter than the southern one and curved against the swell of the open sea. The two moles are built the same way, stone by stone.
- **20 an Giblean, VE 2,451** — *The western Seann Vell* (Seann Vell). At the Seann Vell of the west coast the Seann-Dhaoine dig a line of storage pits into the dune, lined with clay and lidded with slabs. Some held fish bones still when they were opened.
- **19 an Cèitean, VE 2,524** — *Làrach an Dùin-fhaire raised* (Làrach an Dùin-fhaire). On a spur above the ground where Cathair mhòr now stands, the Seann-Dhaoine build the walled outpost afterwards called Làrach an Dùin-fhaire. Its stones are dressed on the outer face only, and its single gate looks inland, away from the sea.
- **17 an t-Ògmhios, VE 2,576** — *Làrach an Dùin raised* (Làrach an Dùin). A greater work is raised on the height near Ceann mhin: three rings of wall, a cistern cut into the bedrock, and room within, as it was later reckoned, for four hundred people and their beasts. Whether the builders of the outpost built this also has never been settled.
- **16 an t-Iuchar, VE 2,627** — *The kerbed way between the forts* (Àth fhionn). A kerbed track, a cart's width and paved with flat slabs, is laid through the ground near Àth fhionn toward both strongholds. It is the only road the Seann-Dhaoine are known to have made away from the shore.
- **14 an Lùnastal, VE 2,679** — *Làrach an Teampaill raised* (Làrach an Teampaill). A stepped platform of fitted stone is built in the eastern hills, with an altar block on its top step. The altar is set square to the central mountains. Every later temple on Dia-thìr faces some other way.
- **12 an t-Sultain, VE 2,730** — *The shaft of Toll-dubh in the south-east* (Toll-dubh). A shaft is sunk straight down through the rock at the eastern Toll-dubh, its walls tooled smooth as far as a lamp will show. No spoil lies beside it. Whatever was taken out was carried away, or nothing was.
- **11 an Dàmhair, VE 2,782** — *The shaft of Toll-dubh in the west* (Toll-dubh). A second shaft of the same making is cut at the western Toll-dubh, far across the island from the first. Stones thrown into either are not heard to land.
- **9 an t-Samhain, VE 2,833** — *The First Canoe*. Among the coastal Tuathaich families a half-forgotten telling of a voyage is kept, long hushed: a steersman with a name, and a first crossing to an isle of the blessed. Their church tells it as the voyage of Naomh Breandan. The druids of the Old Faith call it idle belief.
- **17 an t-Sultain, VE 2,885** — *The black coal warm in the ground* (Tobar dhìreach). Brian of the Mason's line buries the five unlit coals deep in the ground beside the slab at Tobar dhìreach. When he digs them up on the next day the black coal, as black as a wet crow, is warm in his hand and smoulders as the air comes to it; the other four are as cold as the clay.
- **8 an Dùbhlachd, VE 2,937** — *Stakes in the mud below Ceann mhòr* (Ceann mhòr). The first sure boats of the north-west coast leave their trace in the tidal mud below Ceann mhòr: a row of mooring stakes and a scrap of stitched hide. Who rowed them, and from where, is not known.
- **1 an t-Sultain, VE 2,990** — *The Sea-Watcher first sighted* (Uilebheist na Mara). Old sailors tell of a vast creature dwelling in the waters off the north-western coast. No wreck has ever been brought up to prove them wrong.
- **3 an Lùnastal, VE 3,042** — *The beacon on the Baile chrom headland* (Taigh-solais Baile chrom). A fire is kept on the headland where Taigh-solais Baile chrom now stands, and its ash lies a man's height deep. The tellings say it was lit to warn boats off the water where the Sea-Watcher was seen, and never to bring them in.
- **29 an Dàmhair, VE 3,094** — *Seven boats lost off Ros ruadh* (Ros ruadh). Seven boats are lost from Ros ruadh in one calm season, with no storm to blame. It is the first loss laid at the door of the Sea-Watcher by name; before this it was feared only in general.
- **30 an t-Sultain, VE 3,147** — *The seal hunt moves south* (Caol mhòr). The hunters of the north-west leave the open water and work the southern side of the headlands, out of its sight. The seal bones thin in the middens of the north-west and grow at Caol mhòr and Cuan bheag.
- **8 an Cèitean, VE 3,199** — *Signs cut in the Doire uaine hills* (Doire uaine). Inscriptions are cut on rock faces all across the Doire uaine hills, more than anywhere else on the island, in lines that run for yards. Some lines are cut over and defaced with the same kind of tool that made them.
- **9 an Giblean, VE 3,251** — *The Hollow Man of Doire uaine* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). The inscriptions of the Doire uaine hills tell of something that walked without breathing, and fell upon any who lit a fire in its sight.
- **5 an t-Iuchar, VE 3,304** — *The hill fires go under the ground* (Doire uaine). After the inscriptions the hearths of the Doire uaine hills are dug into pits and roofed with slabs. No open hearth shows in those hills for many lifetimes. The people stay, and hide their light.
- **6 an t-Ògmhios, VE 3,351** — *The nine at the hill camp* (Muileann chiar). Nine people die inside a hut at the camp where Muileann chiar was afterwards built, and lie where they fell beside a hearth of fresh ash. No wound is found on any bone. The hut is never opened again, and none is buried from it.
- **21 an Giblean, VE 3,408** — *Coille Naomh Muileann chiar set aside* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). A forest is held sacred long before any order of the Old Faith claims it. The trees knew it first, the old telling says, and the people after.
- **23 am Màrt, VE 3,470** — *No axe in the grove* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). The families at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar carry their fuel a half-day's walk sooner than cut a branch within it. The charcoal in their hearths is of every wood but that one.
- **11 am Màrt, VE 3,513** — *The white stag of the grove* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). Three hunters see a white stag at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, and none of them draws. This is the first telling of it. The stag returns in the tellings of every age after, and the druids of later ages name it the white stag of Flidais; in this age it has no god.
- **9 an Giblean, VE 3,570** — *Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag left unclaimed* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). A second forest, that seems older than the first, is never settled, never felled, and never walked from end to end.
- **12 am Faoilleach, VE 3,618** — *The paths that stop at a line of stones* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). Tracks are worn toward Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag from three quarters, and all three end at a low line of set stones some way short of the trees. Beyond the stones the ground is not worn.
- **20 an t-Samhain, VE 3,670** — *The blood of the misstrike* (Doire ghlas). Cormac of the Mason's line carries the four unlit coals to the grove at Doire ghlas, where the Keeper first spoke, and sets about breaking them there. His hammer misses and opens the back of his hand, and where the blood falls on the red-brown coal it takes fire. The kindred call it the coal of life.
- **10 an Gearran, VE 3,720** — *The deer-drives of the eastern forest* (Doire fhionn). Lines of stakes and brush are set to drive the red deer of the eastern woods into a gully near Doire fhionn, where they are killed with spears. The antlers of the greatest stags are stacked apart from the rest.
- **5 an t-Iuchar, VE 3,771** — *The first dog graves* (Cnoc fhionn). At Cnoc fhionn in the east dogs are buried beside people, each with a shell at its head. No beast was given a grave on Dia-thìr before.
- **3 an Lùnastal, VE 3,821** — *The geese of Eilean ghorm* (Eilean ghorm). The grey geese that winter on Eilean ghorm come into the tellings for the first time. They come in with the first storm and leave with the last, and none hunts them there.
- **8 an Cèitean, VE 3,872** — *The widest reach of the Seann-Dhaoine* (Seann Skell). At their height the Seann-Dhaoine hold every coast of the island: the ten places whose names begin with Seann, and the islands off them. Their greatest landing is at Seann Skell, up the Abhainn naomh, where the mole already stands.
- **6 an t-Ògmhios, VE 3,922** — *The warm springs used* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). Stone basins are set into the springs at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh. The people buried near them have old breaks that knitted clean. Here the sick of Dia-thìr are first brought for healing.
- **29 an Dàmhair, VE 3,973** — *The gate of the outpost walled up* (Làrach an Dùin-fhaire). The single gate of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire is blocked with rubble from within. Those who did it left by another way, or did not leave.
- **27 an t-Samhain, VE 4,023** — *Làrach an Dùin-fhaire abandoned* (Làrach an Dùin-fhaire). The outpost is deserted. It lay in ruin before the first trusty chronicles, and it is older than any dwelling of the Dia-thìrich. Who built it none knows.
- **4 an Giblean, VE 4,074** — *The fortress cistern fouled* (Làrach an Dùin). The cistern of Làrach an Dùin is choked with the bones of cattle, thrown in whole. Its water had served four hundred people. No one draws from it again.
- **6 am Màrt, VE 4,124** — *Làrach an Dùin abandoned* (Làrach an Dùin). The fortress is deserted in like manner, and is as much a riddle as the outpost. Whether both had the same builders has never been settled.
- **5 an Gearran, VE 4,175** — *The temple altar stripped* (Làrach an Teampaill). The top stone of the altar at Làrach an Teampaill is prised off and carried away; the sockets that held it are sharp still. It has never been found, and what was cut on it, if anything, is not known.
- **21 an Dùbhlachd, VE 4,225** — *The silver coal in the river* (Abhainn ghorm). Eòghann of the Mason's line drinks from the Abhainn ghorm below Tobar dhìreach and says, 'This water tastes different from the sea water.' He throws the three unlit coals into the stream, and the coal with the sheen of silver takes fire in the current and burns silver under the water. The coal of fire and the rainbow coal lie dark.
- **7 am Faoilleach, VE 4,275** — *Làrach an Teampaill abandoned* (Làrach an Teampaill). The temple is deserted. It is older than any faith that has a name, and its altar looks to the central mountains and the vein beneath them, away from the sea.
- **9 an Dùbhlachd, VE 4,325** — *The Seann-Dhaoine keep to the shore* (Seann Chwen). The high places are left, and every new work of the Seann-Dhaoine is made within sight of salt water. The middens at the southern Seann Chwen begin to grow as fast as those of Seann Dunn once did.
- **7 am Faoilleach, VE 4,375** — *The ancient sea-way* (Seann Dunn). The boats of the Seann-Dhaoine keep a lane along the south-east coast, from the river mouth below Seann Dunn round the cape where Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg now stands to the bay of Ceann chaol. Flat landing-stones lie along it a day's rowing apart, some grooved still by hauled keels. The Dia-thìrich call it Slighe-mhara àrsaidh, the ancient sea-way, and the fishers of that coast keep to it yet.
- **10 an t-Samhain, VE 4,425** — *The hill-folk of the vein* (Àth gharbh). In the high valleys about the crack dwells a people other than the Seann-Dhaoine, who call themselves Clann nan Dè, the godkin. They bury their dead in the ground and not on islands, and they cut no script. Whether they shared the island with the Seann-Dhaoine or came after them, no telling knows; their own word, later, is that they were always there.
- **12 an Dàmhair, VE 4,475** — *The first small burning* (Àth gharbh). At Àth gharbh a sliver of the coloured coal is burnt to a bead in a peat fire by a household not of the Mason's line. It burns black-flamed like any other coal, and the hearthstone round it is stained through with colour. No older burning of the coal by other hands is known. It is a small thing: one sliver, one fire.
- **13 an t-Sultain, VE 4,525** — *The stained cloth of Achadh dhìreach* (Achadh dhìreach). At Achadh dhìreach the hill-folk rub broken coal from the vein into the wool of the dead, and it takes streaks of a colour no plant dye makes. It is seldom done: one grave in some thirty.
- **15 an Lùnastal, VE 4,575** — *A sliver in a Seann Bhral midden* (Seann Bhral). A chip of the coloured coal, still staining the shell about it, is thrown on a midden at Seann Bhral on the far western coast. By gift, by trade or by theft a piece of the vein came to the Seann-Dhaoine; which, is not known.
- **18 an t-Iuchar, VE 4,625** — *The Children of the Question* (Tobar dhìreach). The households of the high valleys begin to call the Mason's line Luchd-ceasnachaidh a' Ghuail Dhìomhair, the Inquisitors of the Mystic Coal, for their long questioning of the two dark coals; the lists shorten it to Clann na Ceiste, the Children of the Question. The kindred take the name, and Clann a' Chlachair is heard less after.
- **17 an t-Iuchar, VE 4,672** — *Carragh Cnoc bheag raised* (Carragh Cnoc bheag). A standing stone is raised, on which four words are afterwards found carved: Bha teine sa chloich, "there was fire in the stone."
- **11 an Lùnastal, VE 4,718** — *The older face of Carragh Cnoc bheag* (Carragh Cnoc bheag). On the upper face of the stone runs a line of the unread script. The four Dia-thìris words lie lower, cut with a narrower tool by another hand. When that second hand came is not known.
- **9 an t-Sultain, VE 4,770** — *Colbh Cnoc chiar raised* (Colbh Cnoc chiar). A second stone is raised, bearing only two words: Cuimhnich an teine, "remember the fire." Who is bidden, and why, none has ever said.
- **8 an Dàmhair, VE 4,812** — *A ring of fire-stones round the pillar* (Colbh Cnoc chiar). The ground about Colbh Cnoc chiar is trodden hard in a ring and paved with fire-cracked stones. Fires the size of hearths are kept there again and again. Nothing else is left.
- **6 an t-Samhain, VE 4,851** — *Calbh Cnoc ghorm raised* (Calbh Cnoc ghorm). A third stone is raised, and on it the whole of the saying: Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann. Here, it may be, the belief was first spoken.
- **16 an t-Ògmhios, VE 4,905** — *The fire in the fingers* (Tobar dhìreach). Seathan of Clann na Ceiste, who has handled the coal of fire all his days to no end, snaps his fingers when a thought strikes him, and the coal-dust on his hand takes fire. He beats it out against his coat and is not burned. So the sixth coal is lit, by the fire that is in the hand itself.
- **17 an Giblean, VE 4,951** — *The gatherings at the column* (Cnoc ghorm). People come to the column at Cnoc ghorm in numbers. The post-holes of shelters for some hundreds lie about it, used and rebuilt many times. Whatever was said there was said to a crowd.
- **16 an Cèitean, VE 5,010** — *Tuam Cnoc dhìreach consecrated* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). A burial-ground grows about a place that none remembers hallowing. Its oldest graves are older than the oldest names that can be read there.
- **14 an t-Ògmhios, VE 5,070** — *The black chip in the child's grave* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). A child is buried at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach with a sliver of the coloured coal closed in one hand. The sliver stains still the cloth it is kept in. No other piece of the vein is found with the dead of this age.
- **13 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,114** — *The rows at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). The graves at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach begin to be laid in rows, heads toward the central mountains. The first rows are straight. The later ones bend round older graves that no one will disturb.
- **22 an Dùbhlachd, VE 5,170** — *The panther roads*. The great cats of the island are first seen to keep their roads, crossing the mountains by fixed ways at fixed seasons. Why they do so no one has learned.
- **20 am Faoilleach, VE 5,219** — *The crossing season kept* (Imrich nam Pantar). The hill-folk learn the panthers' seasons and keep off the high passes while the cats cross. The camps in the passes stand empty at the same point in every year.
- **7 an t-Sultain, VE 5,272** — *Eleven lost on the panther road* (Cnoc àrsaidh). A party of eleven from the southern shore goes up into the hills near Cnoc àrsaidh in the crossing season and does not return. Years afterwards their bones are found along the line the cats use still.
- **21 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,324** — *The rainbow coal lit by the Keeper* (Doire ghlas). Ailean of Clann na Ceiste, having lit each of the six coals again by its own way, carries them burning to the grove at Doire ghlas with the last coal, which his kindred have tried for more than four hundred years. The Keeper comes to him there and lights the rainbow coal, and for the first time all seven burn together, each from its own spirit. It bids him stay with them until they are cold.
- **28 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,324** — *The vigil and the crowning* (Doire ghlas). Ailean keeps watch by the seven fires for seven nights, fasting, a night for each coal. On the eighth night the coals are cold, and Caoran comes into the grove with the Tuath Dè about him. He names Ailean Rìgh Chlann nan Dè, king of the godkin, and puts into him the power that was in the coals. Of that power Ailean tells no one while he lives.
- **9 an Lùnastal, VE 5,324** — *Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings* (Dùn ìseal). Ailean Mòr, crowned in the grove, comes down to the hill where Dùn ìseal now stands and takes it, and brings the households of the valleys about it under his hand: the first kingdom of the godkin. How he won, none who stood against him could say. He throws up the hill's first ring of bank. With him opens the eldest of the spoken king-lists, afterwards called Rìghrean na Cloiche; it gives no lengths of reign, and it is older than the name Dia-thìrich.
- **4 an t-Samhain, VE 5,332** — *The bank of Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). The first earthwork is raised on the hill at Dùn ìseal: a single bank and ditch, enclosing room for some forty houses. It is the oldest defended place of the hill-folk.
- **6 an Dàmhair, VE 5,341** — *Beathag Ruadh of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag Ruadh holds the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands. With her opens a second spoken list, kept in the west. The Red Hill list and the list of the Stone Kings make no mention of each other until late in both.
- **1 am Faoilleach, VE 5,350** — *Gormshuil nic Ailein* (Dùn ìseal). Gormshuil nic Ailein, second of the Stone Kings, is the first woman named in any list on Dia-thìr. One deed is told of her: in a hard winter she moves the herds of Dùn ìseal down to the warm springs and loses none.
- **3 an Dùbhlachd, VE 5,430** — *Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones* (Dùn ìseal). Dòmhnall Clachach, third of the Stone Kings, sets marker stones along the valley below the hill to part the grazing of Dùn ìseal from its neighbours'. Some stand yet, and are argued over yet.
- **30 am Faoilleach, VE 5,470** — *The first named storm*. A tempest comes so great that the eldest spoken king-lists give it a name. The name is lost; only the memory of the naming remains.
- **28 an Gearran, VE 5,470** — *The shell road broken* (Seann Warr). The storm breaks the shell causeway of Seann Warr in three places and floods the marsh behind it with lake water. The Seann-Dhaoine do not mend it, and the broken ends may be seen still.
- **27 an Giblean, VE 5,550** — *Fearchar Bacach* (Dùn ìseal). Fearchar Bacach, the lame king, rules at Dùn ìseal after the storm and after Dòmhnall Clachach, and is carried to the gatherings in a chair of woven birch. He is the first ruler on Dia-thìr remembered for a hurt.
- **29 am Màrt, VE 5,590** — *Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). Uisdean Mòr, second of the Red Hill list, digs a ditch across the neck of the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands and sets a palisade on it. In his time the palisade burns twice and is twice rebuilt.
- **31 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,631** — *Strokes on the midden stones* (Seann Chwen). The Seann-Dhaoine begin to cut single strokes on flat stones set at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household. The strokes are not the script. They are simpler: a mark, and then another.
- **29 an Lùnastal, VE 5,671** — *The counting of the dead begins*. The Seann-Dhaoine, whoever they were, who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin, begin to keep count of their dead. They keep it before ever there were Dia-thìrich to take up the custom.
- **3 an t-Ògmhios, VE 5,712** — *The tally wall of Seann Warr* (Seann Warr). At the eastern Seann Warr the counting stones are built into a wall, each cut with its strokes, some three thousand strokes in all. The wall grows for many lifetimes.
- **2 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,751** — *The count at Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). The counting comes to Seann Tarr in the north-east. There the stones are cut with strokes in fives and set in the floor of a house, and the house is lived in over its own dead.
- **6 an Giblean, VE 5,793** — *The bad years in the counts* (Seann Warr). The tally stones at Seann Warr, Seann Tarr and Seann Chwen thicken together: more strokes to each stone, more stones to each course. Death comes on three coasts at once. What it was the strokes do not tell.
- **5 an Cèitean, VE 5,833** — *The half-cut stone of Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). At the Seann Chwen near Cuan dhearg the last tally stone is left half-cut: two strokes finished, a third begun and forsaken. The chisel marks stop in mid-groove.
- **7 an Gearran, VE 5,874** — *The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent*. After the half-cut stone no work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and their script is cut no more. How they ended no telling knows.
- **8 am Màrt, VE 5,914** — *The old names kept* (Seann Skell). The hill-folk keep the names of the Seann-Dhaoine places and set before them only their own word for 'old': Seann Dunn, Seann Chwen, Seann Skell and the rest. They turn nothing into their own tongue, and the roots of those names are not understood.
- **11 an Dùbhlachd, VE 5,951** — *The old landings taken up* (Seann Skell). Families of the hill-folk come down the Abhainn naomh and settle in the empty river harbour at Seann Skell, using the old mole and mending none of it. They are not known to have dwelt by the water before.
- **9 am Faoilleach, VE 5,995** — *Mòrag Chruaidh and the salt-flats raid* (Baile ghorm). Mòrag Chruaidh, fifth of the Stone Kings, raids the salt-pans on the southern shore at Baile ghorm and carries off the salt. It is the first war in either list. Seven fall on the hill side, and the number is kept.
- **12 an Gearran, VE 6,006** — *The salt-pans of Baile ghorm* (Baile ghorm). Shallow clay basins are made behind a shingle bar at Baile ghorm, the first salt-works of the island. From this time their salt is found in the hill settlements.
- **13 am Màrt, VE 6,017** — *Seonag of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). Seonag nic Uisdein holds the Red Hill after her father. It is told that she counted her people by pebbles in a bag, one to a household, and knew by the weight when a household was gone.
- **11 an Giblean, VE 6,028** — *The first pots at Doire shean* (Doire shean). Pots of coiled clay, fired in open bonfires, are first made at Doire shean on the south-west coast. Within a few lifetimes the whole southern shore uses them.
- **10 an Cèitean, VE 6,039** — *The dug-out at Cidhe Beag* (Cidhe Beag). A boat hollowed from a single oak trunk, long enough for six, is sunk and left at the landing on Abhainn uaine now called Cidhe Beag. No older boat on Dia-thìr is known in its whole shape.
- **8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 6,050** — *Iain Dubh killed* (Baile ghorm). Iain Dubh, sixth of the Stone Kings, goes down to raid the salt-pans as Mòrag Chruaidh had done, and is slain on the shingle at Baile ghorm. The list says only that he was brought home.
- **7 an t-Iuchar, VE 6,100** — *The wave at Cnoc chaol* (Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol). The sea comes far inland over a village on the site of Cnoc chaol and leaves a sheet of sand a hand thick upon its hearths, with the shells of deep-water creatures in it. The village is not rebuilt on the same ground.
- **5 an Lùnastal, VE 6,150** — *The ground opens at Cill ghlas* (Scàineadh Cill ghlas). A crack a man could fall into opens across the valley at Cill ghlas, and a spring moves a hundred paces downhill. The hill-folk bank the crack with stones and build on neither side of it.
- **3 an t-Sultain, VE 6,170** — *The fault-line kept clear* (Cill ghlas). A line of white stones is laid along the old crack at Cill ghlas, and for the rest of the age no house is built within a stone's throw of it. Part of the line remains.
- **2 an Dàmhair, VE 6,225** — *The unlit hearth*. In a single dwelling a hearth is laid and never lit. Peat keeps it by chance. It is the eldest sign that someone here chose not to burn what could easily have been burned.
- **31 an Dàmhair, VE 6,279** — *Peat over the unlit hearth*. The house of the unlit hearth lies under three yards of peat, its hearth laid with dry wood and a slip of the coloured coal beside it, none of it burned. Whoever laid it went away and did not come back to light it.
- **5 an Lùnastal, VE 6,334** — *The measured handful* (Àth gharbh). In all the hill settlements a custom takes hold that no fire shall have more of the coloured coal than one cupped hand can hold. It is nowhere written and everywhere kept. From it the Small-Burning Law of the next age is made.
- **7 an t-Iuchar, VE 6,389** — *The basket burning at Achadh dhìreach* (Achadh dhìreach). A household at Achadh dhìreach burns a whole basket of the coloured coal at once, knowing nothing of what it holds. The house burns down with three within, and the hearth-stone is found cracked through and running with colour. Ever after the tellings use it to show why the handful is kept.
- **8 an t-Ògmhios, VE 6,443** — *The watchers of the slab* (Tobar dhìreach). Families near the crack take turns to sit by the slab laid over it, a household at a time, through the dark half of the year. What they watch for, none ever says.
- **10 an Cèitean, VE 6,498** — *Raghnall Ceannfhionn makes peace* (Fèill Muileann òg). Raghnall Ceannfhionn, seventh of the Stone Kings, meets the holder of the Red Hill at the ford where the fair of Muileann òg is held now, and they agree on salt for wool. Both lists tell of the meeting, and in neither is the other named before it.
- **29 an t-Samhain, VE 6,531** — *The ford gathering* (Fèill Muileann òg). The meeting at the ford becomes a yearly gathering. Salt, flint, wool, dried fish and pots change hands there, and marriages are made. No meeting-place on the island has been used longer without a break.
- **31 an Dàmhair, VE 6,570** — *Murchadh Gearr of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). Murchadh Gearr holds the Red Hill after Seonag and keeps the peace of the ford. It is told that he walked the salt road himself every year, to be seen upon it.
- **2 an Dàmhair, VE 6,597** — *Hill-folk on the western shore* (Ros bheag). Households from the hills settle the bay at Ros bheag, the first of their kind on the west coast. They build in the hill manner, round and turf-roofed, a little back from the beach, and fish from the shore and not from boats.
- **8 an Gearran, VE 6,629** — *Amber from the Hawk bay* (Seann Skell). Amber is gathered from the wrack on the strands of the Hawk bay and drilled for stringing; lumps of it lie in the middens below Seann Skell. A bead of the same amber lies in the oldest ground of the ford gathering, carried there the length of the island.
- **3 an t-Sultain, VE 6,670** — *The first houses at Cathair dhomhain* (Cathair dhomhain). Round houses are built by the harbour where Cathair dhomhain now stands, near enough the Red Hill to pay it salt. The Red Hill list counts them among its holder's households.
- **25 am Màrt, VE 6,702** — *Cattle in the north-west* (Cnoc ghorm). Cattle come to Cnoc ghorm in the north-west, where the settlements had lived on seal, fish and deer. The herds must have been walked up the flint road.
- **24 an Gearran, VE 6,739** — *The long-house at Cathair gheal* (Cathair gheal). A long-house forty paces long, with byre and hall under one roof, is built on the rise at Cathair gheal. It is the greatest building of the age in the north-west. Twice it burns, and twice it is rebuilt on the same footing.
- **21 an t-Iuchar, VE 6,775** — *A youth let down into Toll-dubh* (Toll-dubh). A youth is let down on a rope of plaited hide into the eastern Toll-dubh, to the rope's end. He is drawn up alive and never tells what lay at the bottom. No one goes down again in this age.
- **19 an Lùnastal, VE 6,812** — *A fire lit in the Doire uaine hills* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). A herding family, new to the hills, lights an open fire at Doire uaine against the custom. Their hut is found empty, the fire still burning. Thereafter the covered hearth is kept more strictly.
- **24 an Cèitean, VE 6,848** — *The lake dwellings burn* (Loch chrom). The platforms on Loch chrom burn to the waterline, and the charred piles are left standing in the shallows. No one builds on the lake again in this age.
- **22 an t-Ògmhios, VE 6,885** — *Seal-oil lamps at Caol leathan* (Caol leathan). Stone lamps with a hollow for seal oil and a wick of moss are used at Caol leathan. They are the first light on Dia-thìr that is not a hearth, and they give little smoke.
- **27 am Màrt, VE 6,921** — *The fish-traps of Caol fhiadhaich* (Caol fhiadhaich). Wattle fences are staked across the river-mouth at Caol fhiadhaich to trap salmon on the ebb. The same line of stake-holes is used again and again through the rest of the age.
- **25 an Giblean, VE 6,951** — *The upright looms of Muileann leathan* (Muileann leathan). At Muileann leathan in the north cloth is woven on standing frames, no longer twined by hand. The loom-weights of fired clay lie in rows in the houses, where they fell from the warp.
- **28 am Faoilleach, VE 6,994** — *The first tide-count*. Someone begins to mark the high-water line against a fixed rock. Why is not told; but the marks are cut at intervals more even than a fisherman's need would ask, as later scholars observe.
- **26 an Gearran, VE 7,031** — *A second tide-rock at Ros dhomhain* (Ros dhomhain). The high-water marking is copied at Ros dhomhain on a boulder in the harbour mouth, the marks cut at the same intervals as on the first rock. Someone carried the practice there, and the interval with it.
- **10 am Màrt, VE 7,070** — *The lake is higher* (Ros dhomhain). The marks on the Ros dhomhain rock creep upward from keeper to keeper, and by the end of the age Loch chrom stands a hand higher on the rock than at the first cut. The keepers go on cutting.
- **8 an Giblean, VE 7,104** — *The flint of Cnoc àrsaidh* (Cnoc àrsaidh). A pit is worked for flint on the hill of Cnoc àrsaidh in the north-west, the only good flint on Dia-thìr. Its grey flakes are carried to hearths from one end of the island to the other.
- **11 am Faoilleach, VE 7,140** — *The flint road* (Àth leathan). A track is worn by the flint-carriers from Cnoc àrsaidh south and east toward the ford gathering. Near Àth leathan their feet sink it a yard deep.
- **13 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,176** — *The hawk lintel at Àth mhòr* (Àth mhòr). A hawk is carved on a lintel over a house door at Àth mhòr in the north, wings closed, head turned. It is the oldest carving of a hawk on the island, and of any bird.
- **10 am Màrt, VE 7,213** — *Wolves at Tobar fhiadhaich* (Tobar fhiadhaich). At Tobar fhiadhaich wolves are buried whole and with care, laid on their sides as people are. No other beast is so buried in this age.
- **9 an Gearran, VE 7,250** — *Sìleas Bhàn and the hungry years* (Dùn ìseal). Sìleas Bhàn, eighth of the Stone Kings, holds Dùn ìseal through years of failed grazing. No deed is told of her but that she held, and the list goes on after her.
- **7 an Cèitean, VE 7,289** — *The hunger at Baile chrom* (Gorta Baile chrom). Hunger comes to the settlement on the site of the north-western Baile chrom. Its pots are left full of boiled bark and seaweed, and its grave-rows are doubled. No older hunger on Dia-thìr is tied to a place.
- **8 an Giblean, VE 7,329** — *The drought at Achadh shean* (Tiormachd Achadh shean). The springs of Achadh shean in the east run dry so long that the field banks are forsaken and grown over. When people return they cut new fields on another line.
- **4 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,370** — *The naming of the wind directions*. The eight winds are named, and every Dia-thìreach sailor after uses the names. Their meaning is dark even to those who speak them, and they have never been changed.
- **5 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,407** — *The wind-stones of Ceann leathan* (Ceann leathan). Eight tall stones are set in a ring on the point at Ceann leathan, one for each of the named winds. Sailors of every later age touch the stone of the wind they want before they put out.
- **24 an Cèitean, VE 7,447** — *The wind-names carried to the islands* (Eilean fhada). The eight wind-names are used on Eilean fhada as on the main island. The markers on its high point bear eight cut notches, one facing each way.
- **25 an Giblean, VE 7,486** — *Tormod Liath* (Dùn ìseal). Tormod Liath, ninth of the Stone Kings, outlives three heirs, and is remembered as old. In his time Dùn ìseal is given its second bank, and its ground is doubled.
- **4 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,524** — *The Dia-thìrich name*. In this age the hill-folk begin to call themselves Dia-thìrich and the island Dia-thìr. The first use is not known; the eldest tellings take both names for granted. With the names goes the belief: they did not come; they were here.
- **2 an Lùnastal, VE 7,546** — *The first forbidden marriage*. A marriage between two lineages is forbidden, for a reason no surviving telling gives. Already the Dia-thìrich order themselves by blood, long before the coal gives them cause.
- **31 an Lùnastal, VE 7,570** — *Lines recited at the ford* (Fèill Muileann òg). At the ford gathering households begin to recite their lines aloud before any marriage is made, seven names back on either side. These are the first genealogies of the common households; only the Line of the Mason is older. None survives whole.
- **29 an t-Sultain, VE 7,590** — *The first seeking of another vein* (Cnoc dhubh). Diggers from Dùn ìseal open a trench on a hill near Cnoc dhubh in the east, seeking coal like the vein's. They leave it unfinished when two of them are crushed by a fall. The trench stays open, and what it would have found is not known.
- **10 am Màrt, VE 7,612** — *The stone that would not break*. A second opening for a new vein is made elsewhere on the island and fails wholly: common rock, and nothing beneath it. So it is first known that the vein under the mountain is alone of its kind.
- **8 an Giblean, VE 7,635** — *The prospecting ends*. No one tries a third opening in this age. The Dia-thìrich hold that the vein chooses where it lies, and that the choice is not theirs to try.
- **7 an Cèitean, VE 7,651** — *The first shared meal law*. A custom arises, unwritten, that any household with food to spare shall share it before the storm season. Later it is made law, and later ages lean on it more than they own.
- **5 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,679** — *Surplus shared at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). At Dùn ìseal the sharing before the storms is done in the open: every household brings its surplus within the bank, and it is divided by the count of mouths. The custom has no earlier place that is known.
- **14 an t-Samhain, VE 7,701** — *A household turned out at Àth shean* (Àth shean). A household at Àth shean hides its spare grain in a pit under the floor and brings nothing to the sharing. When the pit is found the household is put out of the settlement with what it can carry. It is the first punishment under the custom that is remembered.
- **13 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,723** — *Eilidh Ghlas* (Dùn ìseal). Eilidh Ghlas, tenth of the Stone Kings, sends her younger son to the Red Hill to be fostered, the first fostering in either list. The son's name is not kept; only that he went, and that the peace of the ford held while he was there.
- **25 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,724** — *Lachlann Ruadh takes the fosterling* (Cathair dhearg). Lachlann Ruadh, holder of the Red Hill, takes the son of Eilidh Ghlas into his house. For it he is named Lachlann an Altraim, 'Lachlann of the fostering', and the Red Hill list calls him so more often than by his own name.
- **26 an t-Samhain, VE 7,726** — *Oighrig, first keeper by lot* (Tobar dhìreach). The families who watch the slab agree to choose one keeper at a time by lot, and no longer to take turns by household. The first lot falls to a woman called Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill, and she keeps the slab for the rest of her life.
- **28 an Dàmhair, VE 7,727** — *The keepers' house* (Tobar dhìreach). A house is built beside the slab at Tobar dhìreach for the holder of the lot, its door facing the stone. It is rebuilt on the same footing many times. It is the first building on Dia-thìr made only to be near the vein.
- **29 an t-Sultain, VE 7,728** — *The stone cup* (Tobar dhìreach). Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill has a cup ground out of grey stone to the size of her own cupped hand, that the handful of coal may be the same for every household. The cup is carried round the hill settlements. Whether it outlasts the age is not known.
- **31 an Lùnastal, VE 7,730** — *The stone cup copied* (Cnoc chaol). Copies of the keeper's cup are ground at Àth gharbh, Achadh dhìreach and Cnoc chaol, each tried against the first by filling it with water. Thereafter the hill settlements measure the coal with one measure.
- **28 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,731** — *The meeting of the cups* (Coinneachadh nan Cupan). The keeper's cup and its three copies are carried to a spring on the moor between Àth gharbh and Tobar dhìreach, set side by side on a flat stone and filled from the spring in turn. The place is called Coinneachadh nan Cupan, the meeting of the cups. The hill settlements return to it whenever a cup is broken and a new one must be tried.
- **2 an Lùnastal, VE 7,732** — *Gilleasbuig Beag takes coal* (Eilean chrom). A keeper by lot, Gilleasbuig Beag, is found with a basket of broken coal from the vein in his own house. The households of the hills sit in judgement at the slab, row him out to Eilean chrom, and leave him there without a boat. He is the first known to be exiled for the vein.
- **4 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,734** — *The coal returned to the crack* (Tobar dhìreach). The coal from Gilleasbuig Beag's house is neither burned nor kept. The keeper after him carries it back to the slab and lays it beneath, piece by piece. The tellings make much of it: the coal went home.
- **4 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,735** — *Calum Ciar asks for the lot* (Dùn ìseal). Calum Ciar, eleventh of the Stone Kings, asks that the keeper's lot be drawn at Dùn ìseal in his sight. The households at the slab refuse him. The list sets down the refusal, which is more than it sets down of most things.
- **7 an Cèitean, VE 7,739** — *The kings and the keepers* (Dùn ìseal). After the refusal of Calum Ciar the lot is still drawn at the slab. The Stone Kings rule the grazing and the gatherings but not the vein, and the line between the two holds for the rest of the age. It is not yet written anywhere.
- **1 an Gearran, VE 7,740** — *A' Ghaoth Dhubh* (Cuan ruadh). A storm called A' Ghaoth Dhubh, the Black Wind, strips the thatch from every house on the east coast from Cuan ruadh to Ceann chiar. Of all storms it is the eldest whose name is kept.
- **8 an Giblean, VE 7,740** — *The sharing holds after the Black Wind* (Ceann chiar). The settlements of the east coast feed the people of Cuan ruadh through a whole winter out of their shared surplus. None on that coast is known to die of hunger that season.
- **2 am Màrt, VE 7,741** — *The beacon at Baile ìseal* (Taigh-solais Baile ìseal). A fire is built on the eastern cape where Taigh-solais Baile ìseal now stands, kept by the households of the coast in turn. It is lit to bring boats home in a storm, the tellings say, and not to warn them off.
- **3 am Faoilleach, VE 7,742** — *The beacon at Muileann bheag* (Taigh-solais Muileann bheag). A second shore-fire is kept on the north coast, on the point where Taigh-solais Muileann bheag stands now. Under the tower the ash goes down through three yards of fire-reddened soil.
- **5 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,742** — *The beacon at Àth dhearg* (Taigh-solais Àth dhearg). Households of the north-east coast keep a fire on the cape where Taigh-solais Àth dhearg now stands, and cut steps up to it from the shore. The steps are narrower than those at Seann Bhral, and less worn.
- **28 an Cèitean, VE 7,743** — *The beacon at Tobar dhearg* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). A fire is kept for the boats of the south coast on the southern cape where Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg stands. With Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag and Àth dhearg the coasts of the island are lit at five points.
- **31 am Màrt, VE 7,744** — *The Sea-Watcher seen from Seann Skell* (Uilebheist na Mara). Four watchers on the north-western tower at Seann Skell see a back as long as three boats rise and go under off the point. It is the first sighting of the Sea-Watcher tied to a named place and a count of witnesses.
- **26 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,744** — *Wreckage in the western water* (Spùinneadairean-mara). For a season planks of stitched boats, broken small, wash up along the western shore below the waters where raiders are afterwards seen. No bodies come with them, and no settlement on that coast lacks a boat.
- **29 an Giblean, VE 7,745** — *Anndra Breac says 'we came'* (Fèill Muileann òg). At the ford gathering Anndra Breac, a teller of the western coast, recites a telling in which the people came to Dia-thìr over the sea. The households of the hills shout him down, and he is put out of the ford for the rest of his life. His telling is not kept; only the memory that he told it.
- **21 an t-Sultain, VE 7,746** — *The doctrine said at the column* (Calbh Cnoc ghorm). After Anndra Breac, the saying cut on the column at Cnoc ghorm is spoken aloud at the opening of the ford gathering: we did not come; we were here. From this time it is said as a rule, and not only held as a belief.
- **25 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,747** — *The keepers of the Ros dhomhain rock* (Ros dhomhain). The tide-rock at Ros dhomhain passes to Seònaid Mhòr, who cuts her marks in pairs, one for high water and one for low. Her pairs can be read still. The keepers after her go back to single marks.
- **20 an Dàmhair, VE 7,747** — *A third tide-rock at Inis thais* (Inis thais). Households at Inis thais cut their own high-water marks on the harbour rock, at the interval of Ros dhomhain. So three rocks are kept side by side. None tells why the interval is what it is.
- **26 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,748** — *Ros dhomhain grows* (Ros dhomhain). Ros dhomhain becomes the greatest settlement on the shores of Loch chrom, some sixty houses round the tide-rock. Its people fish now from boats and not from the shore.
- **23 an Lùnastal, VE 7,749** — *The Red Hill's harbour* (Cathair dhearg). The households of the Red Hill build a landing of laid stone at the river-mouth below the hill, where the harbour of Cathair dhearg is now. It is the Red Hill's first way onto the water, and by the lake and the Abhainn gheal to the sea.
- **21 an t-Sultain, VE 7,749** — *Peigi Dhubh of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). Peigi Dhubh holds the Red Hill after Lachlann an Altraim. She sends the fostered son of Dùn ìseal home grown, with gifts of salt, and the peace of the ford holds a generation more.
- **31 am Màrt, VE 7,750** — *The foster-son returns* (Dùn ìseal). The son of Eilidh Ghlas comes home from the Red Hill to Dùn ìseal, bringing the salt-songs of the west. The Stone Kings' list gives him no name and no reign; he is remembered only as the one who went.
- **2 am Màrt, VE 7,751** — *The first songs kept* (Baile ghorm). The salt-songs of the south and west are sung at the raking of the pans. They are the oldest songs on Dia-thìr whose words are said to survive: a refrain of four lines, which no one can now wholly construe.
- **14 am Màrt, VE 7,751** — *Bone pipes at Cnoc àrsaidh* (Cnoc àrsaidh). Pipes of hollow bird-bone, bored with four holes, are made in a house at the southern Cnoc àrsaidh near the panther road. They are the oldest instruments of the island.
- **29 an Giblean, VE 7,751** — *The panthers turn back* (Imrich nam Pantar). The great cats come down the panther road near Imrich nam Pantar and turn back at the foothills without crossing. The hill-folk read it for a hard winter and store double. The winter is hard.
- **28 an Cèitean, VE 7,751** — *The cattle lost in the passes* (Muileann bhàn). Herders from Muileann bhàn drive cattle into the passes out of season, against the custom of the crossing. The panthers take thirty head in a night, and the herders come down with nothing.
- **15 am Faoilleach, VE 7,770** — *The panther season kept at Baile dhomhain* (Baile dhomhain). At Baile dhomhain in the south the households cut a sign on their gateposts at the start of the crossing season and scrape it off at its end. It is the first mark made on the island for a season.
- **13 an Gearran, VE 7,770** — *The wind-stone at Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). One of the eight wind-names is cut in the Dia-thìreach manner on a boulder at the central Seann Chwen, over an older mark of the Seann-Dhaoine. In few places do the marks of the two peoples touch.
- **14 an Gearran, VE 7,770** — *Boats named for the winds* (Caol bheag). The fishing households of Caol bheag, who fish the north coast from the mouth of the Abhainn ghorm, name their boats for the winds they fish in. A boat named for the wrong wind is held unlucky, and the name of a boat that sinks is never given again.
- **14 am Màrt, VE 7,770** — *The Tuam keepers* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). A family dwelling by Tuam Cnoc dhìreach takes on the clearing of thorn from the old graves. They bury none of their own there. They only keep it.
- **12 an Giblean, VE 7,770** — *A grave at Tuam opened* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). Diggers laying a new row at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach break into a grave older than any they knew, lined with slabs cut in the manner of the Seann-Dhaoine. They close it and move the row, and none opens that grave again.
- **11 an Cèitean, VE 7,772** — *Pilgrims at Coille Naomh Muileann chiar* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). People begin to walk to the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and sit a night at the line of the trees without entering. Their small fires, each of a single night, lie all along the edge.
- **9 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,774** — *A child lost in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). A child of the settlement at Cnoc bheag goes past the line of stones into Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag and is not found. The searchers stop at the stones, and the telling does not blame them.
- **8 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,776** — *The first house at Cnoc bheag* (Cnoc bheag). Settlers from the Red Hill build at Cnoc bheag, near the edge of the forest. They take their timber from the far side of the river, and never from the unclaimed wood.
- **6 an Lùnastal, VE 7,778** — *The spring at Muileann ruadh* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). Pilgrims come in numbers to the warm springs at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, and a ring of shelters is built there. Here is set the eldest healing-tale of Dia-thìr: a herder came lame and walked home.
- **28 an Cèitean, VE 7,780** — *The Hollow Man seen again* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). Two herders passing the Doire uaine hills after dark see a figure walk the ridge with no breath showing in the cold. They had no fire lit, and so, the telling says, they lived.
- **26 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,783** — *The covered hearth spreads* (Muileann chiar). The covered hearth, pit-dug and roofed, spreads from the Doire uaine hills to the settlements about Muileann chiar. From this comes the later rule that no open fire is lit on those slopes after dark.
- **31 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,785** — *Settlers at Caol mhòr* (Caol mhòr). Dia-thìreach households settle at Caol mhòr in the north-west, on the strait where the Seann-Dhaoine once hunted seal. They find the old middens and build on them.
- **2 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,787** — *Settlers at Baile chrom in the north-west* (Baile chrom). Households from Cnoc ghorm settle again the ground at Baile chrom that the old hunger had emptied. They dig their storage pits deeper than any others on the coast.
- **3 an t-Samhain, VE 7,789** — *Muileann àrsaidh settled* (Muileann àrsaidh). Houses are built on the stream at Muileann àrsaidh in the north-west. Their flint comes from Cnoc àrsaidh, and their salt from the south, carried the length of the island.
- **5 an Dàmhair, VE 7,791** — *The salt road to the north-west* (Muileann àrsaidh). A salt road runs from the pans of Baile ghorm by the ford gathering to the north-west. At Muileann àrsaidh the salt costs three times its price at the pans, and is paid for in flint and seal-skins.
- **26 an Giblean, VE 7,793** — *Doire ghlas settled* (Doire ghlas). Households settle under the oaks at Doire ghlas in the north. The settlement grows in rings, each built outside the last as the wood is cleared back.
- **28 am Màrt, VE 7,796** — *The east settled at Dùn thais* (Dùn thais). The hill-folk push east and build a banked enclosure at Dùn thais, on a hill above good grazing. It is the first stronghold of the Dia-thìrich away from Dùn ìseal and the Red Hill.
- **27 an Gearran, VE 7,798** — *Achadh chaol cleared* (Achadh chaol). Fields are cleared at Achadh chaol in the east by fire and by picking stones. The picked stones are laid in banks round each field, and those banks bound the fields still.
- **29 am Faoilleach, VE 7,800** — *Cuan ruadh rebuilt* (Cuan ruadh). Cuan ruadh, stripped by the Black Wind, is rebuilt in stone to the height of the eaves. It is the first settlement of the east coast to build its walls against the wind and not only the cold.
- **13 an Cèitean, VE 7,846** — *Cathair fhada on the south coast* (Cathair fhada). Cathair fhada is founded on the south coast, between the old Seann Dunn and Seann Chwen. It draws its water from a well the Seann-Dhaoine dug, and never speaks of where the well came from.
