- **14 an Giblean, VE 7,893** — *Caol ruadh on the southern strait* (Caol ruadh). Fishing households settle Caol ruadh on the south coast and take the cod of the strait on long lines. Their middens are the first on the south coast to hold more fish than shell.
- **13 an t-Sultain, VE 7,939** — *Baile Mòr mhòr in the north* (Baile Mòr mhòr). Houses are built at Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern plain, round a spring that never freezes. At its height it has some eighty houses, a great place for the age.
- **15 an Lùnastal, VE 7,985** — *Baile gharbh in the north-east* (Baile gharbh). Households settle the rough ground at Baile gharbh and live by sheep, not cattle. Their wool goes south along the coast to the ford gathering.
- **17 an t-Iuchar, VE 8,032** — *Baile fhiadhaich on the west coast* (Baile fhiadhaich). Settlers build at Baile fhiadhaich on the western coast, where boars run in the thickets. They hang boar tusks over their doors, and boar is their chief meat for the rest of the age.
- **18 an t-Ògmhios, VE 8,078** — *Cuan shean settled* (Cuan shean). Dia-thìreach households take up the harbour at Cuan shean on the west coast, beside an old landing of unknown builders, and use the landing without mending it.
- **7 am Faoilleach, VE 8,124** — *Dùn chrom raised* (Dùn chrom). A banked hill-fort is raised at Dùn chrom in the midst of the island, between the Red Hill and the hills of the vein. Its bank faces both ways.
- **9 an Dùbhlachd, VE 8,170** — *Cathair mhòr below the old outpost* (Cathair mhòr). Households settle on the ground below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, where Cathair mhòr now stands. They take no stone from the ruin above them, though it is the nearest quarry.
- **10 an t-Samhain, VE 8,217** — *Cnoc naomh* (Cnoc naomh). Households come to settle on a hill for its spring, and the hill is already called Cnoc naomh, the holy hill. Why, is not known.
- **12 an Dàmhair, VE 8,270** — *Tobar dhearg on the southern cape* (Tobar dhearg). The keepers of the beacon at Tobar dhearg build their settlement on the cape itself, round a well whose water runs reddish from the rock. It becomes the greatest place on the south coast.
- **24 am Faoilleach, VE 8,309** — *Muileann naomh founded* (Muileann naomh). Muileann naomh is founded near the south coast, between the beacon at Tobar dhearg and the old Seann Skell. Its first houses stand on stilts over a marsh, and are afterwards moved to firm ground.
- **26 an Dùbhlachd, VE 8,351** — *Ceann mhin on the south-eastern shore* (Ceann mhin). The south-eastern Ceann mhin is settled near Làrach an Dùin. Its people are the first to live in sight of the fortress ruin, and they will not go up to it.
- **23 am Màrt, VE 8,402** — *Seann Skell of the south* (Seann Skell). Dia-thìreach households take up the old harbour at the southern Seann Skell and keep its old name. Within a few generations it is the busiest landing on the south coast.
- **21 an Giblean, VE 8,448** — *Achadh shean resettled* (Achadh shean). Households return to Achadh shean after the drought and cut new fields on the higher ground. They sink a deep well first and plant after, and the well does not fail again in this age.
- **20 an Cèitean, VE 8,495** — *Inis mhin settled* (Inis mhin). A few households settle at Inis mhin on the eastern coast. They live by the eggs and birds of the cliffs, and trade feathers inland.
- **18 an t-Ògmhios, VE 8,541** — *Muileann chaol on its hill* (Muileann chaol). Households settle on the hill at Muileann chaol, above the upper reaches of the rivers. Where the library stands now there is a cattle-fold.
- **17 an t-Iuchar, VE 8,587** — *Cairns on the hill at Muileann chaol* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). At Muileann chaol a cairn is raised for each head of a household at death, on the slope above the fold. By the end of the age some forty stand there.
- **15 an Lùnastal, VE 8,634** — *Baile Mòr ruadh in the east* (Baile Mòr ruadh). Baile Mòr ruadh grows up near the eastern Seann Dunn, on land its people call empty. The middens of Seann Dunn lie a morning's walk away, and the settlers do not dig into them.
- **13 an t-Sultain, VE 8,680** — *The temple ruin avoided* (Làrach an Teampaill). The Dia-thìrich of the eastern hills pass Làrach an Teampaill without stopping and take no stone from it. A path is worn round it at a distance.
- **12 an Dàmhair, VE 8,726** — *Ceann leathan's contests* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). At Ceann leathan the gathering by the wind-stones ends with wrestling and the lifting of stones. The heaviest, a black boulder, lies on the point still, and few have raised it.
- **3 an Lùnastal, VE 8,773** — *The ford gathering grows* (Fèill Muileann òg). The ford gathering at Muileann òg now draws households from every coast. Its ground is parted by custom: the salt people downstream, the hill people upstream, the flint people on the far bank.
- **1 an t-Sultain, VE 8,819** — *Stone axes from the north* (Àth àrsaidh). Axes of polished green stone from a quarry near Àth àrsaidh in the north-west are carried all over the island. They are too fine for work; most are laid unused in graves or under house floors.
- **13 an Giblean, VE 8,870** — *The quarry at Àth àrsaidh* (Àth àrsaidh). The green-stone quarry at Àth àrsaidh is worked by a few households who trade in nothing else, and the chips about it lie knee-deep. Before the age ends the quarry is forsaken, and the axes cease.
- **19 an t-Sultain, VE 8,911** — *The moor takes the north* (Doire ghlas). The oak falls back, as the pollen in the bog under Doire ghlas shows. Heather, birch and bog-moss spread over the northern lowlands, and the groves that give the north its many Doire names shrink to the sheltered valleys, where they stand yet. In the north this is remembered as the time the winters lengthened.
- **15 am Màrt, VE 8,951** — *The river crossings of Abhainn fhionn* (Abhainn fhionn). Stepping-stones are laid across Abhainn fhionn at its shallows, the first made crossing of any river on the island. They are older than the first bridges, and in places lie beneath them.
- **10 an t-Ògmhios, VE 9,003** — *A drowning at the fords of Abhainn chaol* (Abhainn chaol). A spate on Abhainn chaol takes a party of twelve crossing its fords with salt. Thereafter none crosses there in the wet season.
- **12 an Cèitean, VE 9,049** — *The Black Wind remembered at Ceann chiar* (Ceann chiar). The people of Ceann chiar, rebuilding after the Black Wind, set a stone in the midst of their settlement and cut on it a mark for every house lost: twenty-two.
- **7 an Lùnastal, VE 9,094** — *A dry year on the eastern plain* (Muileann bhàn). The rivers of the eastern plain run low for a whole summer, and the households of Dùn ìseal and Muileann bhàn drive their cattle to the warm springs to drink. The shared surplus holds, and no deaths are counted.
- **9 an t-Iuchar, VE 9,140** — *A second wave on the south coast* (Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol). The sea comes in again over the low ground at Cnoc chaol, less far than before. The new houses stand higher on the slope, and none is lost.
- **4 an Dàmhair, VE 9,186** — *The ground shakes at Cill ghlas again* (Scàineadh Cill ghlas). The old crack at Cill ghlas moves again, and the spring shifts back uphill. The line of white stones is broken in two places, and is laid again.
- **5 an t-Sultain, VE 9,231** — *Cnoc bheag under the Carragh* (Cnoc bheag). Households settle on the bank of the Abhainn ìseal at Cnoc bheag, a short walk from Carragh Cnoc bheag. They set their houses so that no door faces the stone.
- **1 an Dùbhlachd, VE 9,278** — *The seal rocks of Inis bhàn* (Inis bhàn). The households of Inis bhàn on the lower Abhainn ìseal take seals from the skerries off the river mouth by agreement, one household to a rock. A rock taken out of turn is the commonest quarrel in their tellings.
- **2 an t-Samhain, VE 9,323** — *Fields at Achadh mhòr* (Achadh mhòr). The wide field at Achadh mhòr, near the warm springs, is cleared and banked, the largest single field of the age. Its bank is laid with the stones of an older wall that no one claims.
- **7 an Cèitean, VE 9,370** — *The harbour at Baile ghlas* (Baile ghlas). The households of the Red Hill draw up their boats at Baile ghlas, along the lake shore from the hill, in sheds of stone and turf. It becomes the fishing harbour of the Red Hill.
- **5 an t-Ògmhios, VE 9,414** — *Achadh naomh's spring-fields* (Achadh naomh). Settlers at Achadh naomh in the north water their fields from a spring they will not build over, and lead the water round it in channels. The spring is fenced before any house is.
- **10 am Màrt, VE 9,451** — *Caol gharbh on the rough strait* (Caol gharbh). Households settle at Caol gharbh on the north-east coast and fish the strait in skin boats. They lay paddles beside their dead.
- **8 an Giblean, VE 9,506** — *Doire chiar* (Doire chiar). A settlement grows up under the dark oaks at Doire chiar in the north. Its people pen pigs in the wood and drive them out to the acorns at the fall of the year.
- **11 am Faoilleach, VE 9,551** — *The river landing at Caol shean* (Caol shean). Caol shean, on the Abhainn ìseal east of the vein, becomes the river landing of the hill households of the east. Salt, fish and seal-skins come up the river to it from the coast, and go on from it into the keepers' country.
- **9 an Gearran, VE 9,597** — *Dùn dhearg raised* (Dùn dhearg). A hill-fort with a double bank is raised at Dùn dhearg, east of the vein, by households who owe nothing to Dùn ìseal. The Stone Kings' list does not name its holders; it says only that Dùn dhearg came not to the gatherings.
- **14 an t-Samhain, VE 9,644** — *Dùn dhearg comes to the ford* (Fèill Muileann òg). In the time of Catrìona Mhòr the households of Dùn dhearg come to the ford gathering for the first time, bringing seal-skins and asking for salt. They are given ground of their own on the far bank.
- **13 an Dùbhlachd, VE 9,648** — *Settlers at Àth fhiadhaich* (Àth fhiadhaich). Households settle at Àth fhiadhaich in the south-eastern hills, by a ford where wild cattle cross. They take the calves and rear them, and their herds become the best in those hills.
- **17 an t-Sultain, VE 9,651** — *Ceann àrsaidh* (Ceann àrsaidh). Households from the Red Hill settle the point at Ceann àrsaidh on the Abhainn fhionn. They find an old river landing there and name the place for it: the ancient headland.
- **19 an t-Sultain, VE 9,651** — *Cnoc thais in the north-west* (Cnoc thais). Households settle on the damp hill at Cnoc thais in the north-west and drain it with ditches. The ditches carry water still.
- **16 an Dàmhair, VE 9,651** — *Inis mhòr* (Inis mhòr). Households settle Inis mhòr on the Abhainn ghorm in the north-east and live by the fish of its sheltered pools. They build their houses in two rows facing each other, the oldest street on Dia-thìr.
- **27 an Giblean, VE 9,670** — *Baile gheal in the south-west* (Baile gheal). Baile gheal is founded on the south-western plain round a house with white-limed walls. The lime is burned from the shells of the old middens along the coast.
- **26 an Cèitean, VE 9,670** — *Àth bheag on the eastern coast* (Àth bheag). Households settle the small ford at Àth bheag on the far eastern coast, the easternmost dwelling of the age on the main island. Their boats go out after the geese on the islands.
- **26 an Cèitean, VE 9,670** — *Catrìona Mhòr* (Dùn ìseal). Catrìona Mhòr, twelfth of the Stone Kings, holds Dùn ìseal; hers is the last name in the spoken list. It is told that she knew every household of the hills by its line seven names back.
- **23 an t-Iuchar, VE 9,670** — *Seumas Òg of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). Seumas Òg holds the Red Hill, and with him the spoken list of the Red Hill ends. In the next age what the reciters kept of it is written down.
- **23 an t-Iuchar, VE 9,670** — *The two lists recited together* (Fèill Muileann òg). At the ford gathering, in the time of Catrìona Mhòr, the list of the Stone Kings and the list of the Red Hill are recited one after the other from the first name to the last. It takes from dusk to dawn. For the first time both are heard whole.
- **29 am Màrt, VE 9,673** — *Lots drawn for the slab* (Tobar dhìreach). The lot for the keeper of the slab is drawn now among households from every part of the hills, not only those near the crack. The keepers' house at Tobar dhìreach becomes a place of pilgrimage.
- **28 an Gearran, VE 9,676** — *The keepers number nine* (Tobar dhìreach). The keepers of the slab are made nine, one drawn by lot for each of nine districts of the hills. They meet at the slab when a keeper dies, and at no other time.
- **9 an Cèitean, VE 9,678** — *Coal in every hearth by the handful*. Every household of the hills burns its handful of the coloured coal, measured in a copy of the stone cup, on one night in the dark of the year, the night later kept as Samhain. All burn at once by agreement, so that the low fires of the handful show on every hillside on the same night.
- **10 an Giblean, VE 9,681** — *A handful refused at Cnoc dhubh* (Cnoc dhubh). The household of the Cnoc dhubh trench, where the two diggers were crushed, refuses its handful of coal for as long as any remembers. No household before it is known to have chosen not to burn at all.
- **4 an Dàmhair, VE 9,684** — *Counting the households* (Dùn ìseal). The people of Catrìona Mhòr count the households of the hills by knots on a cord, a knot to a hearth. The cord of Dùn ìseal is said to have borne some nine hundred knots, the greatest count made on Dia-thìr in this age.
- **2 an t-Samhain, VE 9,687** — *The saying on the column recut* (Calbh Cnoc ghorm). The words on the column at Cnoc ghorm, worn shallow, are recut in their old grooves by a hand from the hill of the Stone Kings. Some later readers hold that the recutting changed a letter; none can prove which.
- **1 an Dùbhlachd, VE 9,690** — *The last Seann-Dhaoine midden disturbed* (Seann Dunn). Households at the eastern Seann Dunn cut into the old midden for a house-floor and find the tally stones. They put them back in the order they lay and build elsewhere.
- **30 an Dùbhlachd, VE 9,693** — *Eilean ìseal given to the dead* (Eilean ìseal). The households of the south-east coast begin to row their dead to Eilean ìseal, after the old manner of the Seann-Dhaoine. Whether they learned it from the Seann Vell graves on Eilean dhearg, or came to it of themselves, is not told.
- **10 an t-Ògmhios, VE 9,696** — *Gilleasbuig Beag's island* (Eilean chrom). Eilean chrom, where Gilleasbuig Beag was left, stays empty and unfished. His fire is seen on it for three nights, the tellings say, and then no more.
- **9 an t-Iuchar, VE 9,699** — *The keepers ask to be named* (Fèill Muileann òg). The nine keepers of the slab ask Catrìona Mhòr to declare their charge before the whole ford gathering, so that no king after her may draw the lot at Dùn ìseal. She neither refuses nor agrees, and the matter is left to the next age.
- **7 an Lùnastal, VE 9,873** — *The eve of the Binding*. So ends the Ancient Age. The handful is kept everywhere in the hills, the keepers are nine, the sharing before the storms is kept on every coast, and the saying is spoken at every gathering. None of it is yet declared, and no oath is yet sworn over the vein. With that swearing the next age begins.

## Age II · An Aois Naomh

*The Holy Age · the Flame Era, FE 1 – 2,960*

- **23 an t-Sultain, FE 1** — *The Binding of the First Flame*. Custody is declared over the vein, and the first flame is bound at Dùn ìseal: the undying flame of Brìde, kept over the stone of Crom Cruaich. Its keepers, Òrd Bhrìde, are the first order on Dia-thìr to govern both rite and people, and they are older by centuries than any king.
- **28 an t-Ògmhios, FE 4** — *Beathag Bhàn keeps the first flame* (Dùn ìseal). At Dùn ìseal under the central mountains the keepers of the slab and the households sworn to the Binding choose Beathag Bhàn to hold the first flame for Brìde and to answer to Crom for what is taken from the vein. The spoken roll of the Keepers begins with her name. Of her life before it nothing is remembered.
- **27 an t-Iuchar, FE 10** — *The nine hearths* (Dùn ìseal). Nine households about the mountain's foot, one for each district of the old keepers of the slab, take the tending of the flame in turn, each sending a son or daughter to sit with it through a season. The later houses of custody all claim descent from one or another of the nine. Not all the claims can be true.
- **19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15** — *Talla na Lasrach raised* (Dùn ìseal). A long hall of dry stone and turf is raised over the flame at Dùn ìseal, with one door toward the vein and none toward the sea. It is rebuilt many times on the same footings, and the footings are all of it that anyone can now swear to.
- **17 am Faoilleach, FE 21** — *Seann Spioradan nan Dia-thìreach established*. At the hearths the eldest of the island's folk-ways takes shape: reverence for the ancestors, for the vein, for the weather that rules the mining season, and for the sìth of the hills and mounds. It keeps no priests, and it has never ceased.
- **22 an Dàmhair, FE 27** — *The weather-cairns of Cnoc ghlas* (Cnoc ghlas). Watchers build cairns on the ridge above Cnoc ghlas and read the cloud on the high passes from them, to tell the Hall when the galleries may be opened for the season. A wrong reading costs the whole mountain its season, and the watchers are chosen with more care than the Keeper.
- **20 an t-Samhain, FE 33** — *The ban on fires in sight of Doire uaine* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). In obedience to the old inscriptions the Keepers forbid any fire, of wood or of coal, to be lit in sight of the Doire uaine hills. Herders who winter on those slopes eat cold for the season. The ban is never lifted, and none is known to have owned to breaking it.
- **5 am Faoilleach, FE 34** — *Làrach an Teampaill left unentered* (Làrach an Teampaill). Beathag Bhàn walks to Làrach an Teampaill, finds its altar already turned toward the mountain, and declares the place not the Hall's to keep. The Keepers set no foot in it for the rest of the age. Whose it was they did not say, and it seems they did not know.
- **3 an Gearran, FE 44** — *Death of Beathag Bhàn* (Dùn ìseal). Beathag Bhàn dies at Dùn ìseal and is laid on the slope facing the vein, with her back to the sea. The nine hearths choose Muireach Liath, her sister's son, to keep the flame after her.
- **15 an Gearran, FE 48** — *Coal by the basket* (Dùn ìseal). Muireach Liath fixes the first common measure for coal carried down from the galleries: a lidded basket of plaited heather, one to a household, filled once a season. Baskets of that weave are made at Dùn ìseal still, for no purpose but the making.
- **17 am Faoilleach, FE 53** — *Allt an Àigh named* (Allt an Àigh). A stream is held to bring good fortune to any who drink of it in a certain quarter of the moon. Pilgrims come to it, and have never wholly ceased to come.
- **14 an Giblean, FE 57** — *The pilgrims' path from Caol shean* (Caol shean). A path is worn from the river landing at Caol shean up the valley to Allt an Àigh. It is walked by night, so that pilgrims reach the water in the right quarter of the moon. Fishermen who walk it are said to lose fewer boats; no count was kept either way.
- **16 am Màrt, FE 59** — *The Hall declines the stream* (Allt an Àigh). Muireach Liath rules that Allt an Àigh belongs to the ancestors and the weather and not to the vein, and that the Hall will not keep it. Here the Keepers' rite and the older folk reverence first plainly part, and each side afterwards cites the ruling as proof that it was right.
- **22 an Dàmhair, FE 66** — *The sick carried to Muileann ruadh* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). The sick are carried up in litters to the warm springs below Muileann ruadh and bathed at dawn. The Keepers allow it, for the heat of the water comes from the mountain and no one breaks the stone for it.
- **23 an t-Sultain, FE 71** — *Muileann chiar founded* (Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid). A seam of silver is found near the great vein but apart from it. It is the first wealth of the island other than the coal.
- **20 an t-Samhain, FE 74** — *Fearchar Airgeadach works the silver* (Muileann chiar). Fearchar Airgeadach, a basket-carrier of the nine hearths, is the first known to smelt the silver of Muileann chiar and hammer it into rings. His furnace burns wood and peat. It is the first fire on the island that answers to no one in the Hall.
- **19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 74** — *Silver is not holy* (Muileann chiar). Asked whether the new seam falls under the flame, Muireach Liath answers that silver shows no colour when it breaks and so is not the mountain's. Muileann chiar is left free to dig as deep as it likes, and it digs. Every later quarrel over the silver begins from these words.
- **28 an t-Ògmhios, FE 84** — *Silver for salt at Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). Carriers take rings of Muileann chiar down to the river quays at Ros fhionn and trade them for salt fish and sealskin, one ring for a boatload. It is the first trade in anything but food, and the first whose price is remembered.
- **30 an Cèitean, FE 89** — *Death of Muireach Liath* (Dùn ìseal). Muireach Liath dies at Dùn ìseal, keeping the flame. The nine hearths pass over three of other lines and choose his daughter Gormshuil nic Mhuirich. After her the Keeper's office stays in the house of Muireach for many generations.
- **11 an t-Sultain, FE 96** — *Sliochd Mhuirich named* (Dùn ìseal). The kin of Gormshuil nic Mhuirich at Dùn ìseal begin to be called Sliochd Mhuirich, the house of Muireach, the first house of custody known by a name and not by a hearth. No account that survives tells of the other eight hearths objecting.
- **10 an Dàmhair, FE 103** — *The first school of the druids founded*. The first of the Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, the druid schools, gathers about one question: why the vein answers some hands and not others. For the first time within the Old Faith the coal is reasoned about, and not only revered.
- **8 an t-Samhain, FE 110** — *Sìleas nic Coinnich in the wood* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). Sìleas nic Coinnich, a cutter from Muileann chiar in the far east, begins to teach in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar. At the galleries she had seen the coal break bright with its colours under some cutters' picks and dull under others, and she will not let the question be.
- **7 an Dùbhlachd, FE 118** — *The stag in the grove* (Muileann chiar). The hearers of Sìleas nic Coinnich at Muileann chiar name themselves the stag's people, for a stag said to have stood in the grove through a whole lesson. The school's later name, the stag's name Camaran, and the telling that it was the white stag of Flidais, lady of the deer, are found first in writings far younger than these days.
- **18 an Cèitean, FE 125** — *The Hall shuts the galleries to the stag's people* (Dùn ìseal). Gormshuil nic Mhuirich forbids the hearers of Sìleas to cut in the galleries of Dùn ìseal, holding that a question asked of the vein is a demand made of it. The stag's people keep their school in the east and send no cutters to the mountain for a long while after.
- **16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 132** — *The smoke at Cnoc dhubh* (Cnoc dhubh). In a hard winter a household at Cnoc dhubh burns its coal by the basketful and not by the handful. The smoke settles in the valley, and three of the household and two neighbours die of it. The Keepers are sent for, and the case is argued at Dùn ìseal for the rest of the season.
- **15 an t-Iuchar, FE 139** — *Fionnlagh Dall and the stone cup* (Dùn ìseal). Fionnlagh Dall, Keeper after Gormshuil, has the old keepers' stone cup cut anew in grey stone to hold just what a cupped pair of hands will hold, and sets it for the measure on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal. He is blind, and fills it by touch before the council, and none can say afterwards that he favoured anyone's hands.
- **13 an Lùnastal, FE 142** — *The Small-Burning Law*. The custom of the handful is made law: no household may burn more than a measured handful of the coal in a season. It becomes the holy law of the Keepers of Brìde's flame and Crom's stone, and it holds for centuries.
- **1 an Cèitean, FE 145** — *The first sentence under the Law* (Seann Tarr). A household of Seann Tarr burns twice its measure in a season and loses its right to the coal for the season after, the first sentence given under the Small-Burning Law. Its name is set on the roll with the offence beside it, and for many centuries its descendants petition to have the offence struck out.
- **30 an Cèitean, FE 148** — *No coal on the beacons* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). The Keepers rule that no coal may feed a beacon, since a beacon burns for strangers. The fire on the headland at Tobar dhearg is kept with driftwood and seal fat, and so are all the sea-lights of the island after it.
- **4 am Màrt, FE 151** — *The carriers' path to Ceann chaol* (Ceann chaol). A carriers' path is cut from the mountain down to the harbour of Ceann chaol, with steps hewn at the steep places. The Hall's baskets go down it to the southern households, and the dried fish of the south comes up.
- **3 an Gearran, FE 154** — *The carriers drowned on the Abhainn dhomhain* (Abhainn dhomhain). The Abhainn dhomhain rises in the night and takes eleven carriers and their baskets at a ford. The Hall mourns the coal with the carriers, and Fionnlagh Dall asks the council for a way across that the river cannot take.
- **5 am Faoilleach, FE 157** — *The first bridges* (Drochaid Cathair dhearg). Stone crossings begin to join the mining paths of the interior to the coast. From them in time come Drochaid Cathair dhearg and Drochaid Ros fhionn.
- **7 an Dùbhlachd, FE 160** — *Ailean Clachair's crossing at Ros fhionn* (Drochaid Ros fhionn). Ailean Clachair and forty masons of the nine hearths bridge the river above Ros fhionn with a single span of fitted stone, from which Drochaid Ros fhionn descends. Ailean sets a hearth-sign in the keystone. Every bridge the masons build after bears one, and a bridge without it is not trusted.
- **8 an t-Samhain, FE 163** — *The masons' custom* (Ros dhomhain). The bridge-masons form a fellowship bound by an oath sworn on the stone cup at Dùn ìseal: no span to be closed in the dark, and none to be paid for in coal. Their lodge is kept near the western crossing, in the country of Ros dhomhain.
- **10 an Dàmhair, FE 166** — *The tavern roads begin* (Am Buabhall Fortanach). The first waypoint houses are raised along the mining roads. From them come in time Am Buabhall Fortanach, An Taigh-òsta Grianach and the others of the circuit.
- **11 an t-Sultain, FE 169** — *Mòr nic Dhùghaill's house* (Am Buabhall Fortanach). Mòr nic Dhùghaill, a widow of Doire shean, keeps the first waypoint house on the site of Am Buabhall Fortanach. She serves the carriers jugged buffalo from her own herd, and the house has served it ever since.
- **13 an Lùnastal, FE 172** — *The house at the middle of the road* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). A second waypoint house is built where the carriers' road from the mountain meets the road to the western harbours, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr. It is a turf longhouse with a hearth at either end, one for carriers going up and one for carriers coming down.
- **22 an Dàmhair, FE 175** — *The road-peace* (An Sligeanach Fad' às). The keepers of the waypoint houses agree that no feud may be pursued under an inn roof or within a spear's throw of its door. The custom is first set down at the house on the site of An Sligeanach Fad' às. It is the oldest law on the island that no Keeper made.
- **23 an t-Sultain, FE 178** — *Seann Mhorn resettled* (Seann Mhorn). Fishers of the nine hearths settle the harbour at Seann Mhorn and keep the name they find there, which is not of their own tongue; the old name came with the stones, they say. It is the first such name known to be taken over and not replaced.
- **20 an Dàmhair, FE 181** — *Seann Warr resettled* (Seann Warr). Families walking the new road from the mountain settle the harbour of Seann Warr on the western shore of Loch chrom in like manner. They find house-footings there already, and build on them, as the carriers' song has it, without asking whose.
- **23 an Lùnastal, FE 184** — *Death of Fionnlagh Dall* (Dùn ìseal). Fionnlagh Dall dies at Dùn ìseal. At his own asking he is not laid on the slope with the Keepers before him, but carried south to the old graves near Cnoc dhìreach, which no living people had yet claimed.
- **18 an t-Samhain, FE 184** — *Fionnlagh Dall carried to the old graves* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). The bearers are eleven days on the road with the body of Fionnlagh Dall, and lay it at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach among graves older than any name. The Keepers after him cannot agree why he asked it; two answers are given, and neither is chosen.
- **21 an t-Sultain, FE 189** — *The mausoleum consecrated*. Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, already ancient, receives its first burial that is set down by name. The burial-ground that no one claimed is claimed.
- **26 an t-Ògmhios, FE 194** — *The grave-keepers of Cnoc dhìreach* (Cnoc dhìreach). A few families settle at Cnoc dhìreach to tend Tuam Cnoc dhìreach after the Keeper's burial. The Hall pays them in coal, a handful each a season, the only payment in coal the Law ever allows.
- **25 an t-Iuchar, FE 381** — *Eilidh nic Ìomhair keeps the flame* (Dùn ìseal). The nine hearths choose a Keeper from outside the house of Muireach for the first time: Eilidh nic Ìomhair, of Dùn dhearg. Sliochd Mhuirich refuses for a season, then yields at Dùn ìseal, on the condition that the stone cup never leaves Talla na Lasrach.
- **29 an Giblean, FE 385** — *The Four Houses sworn* (Dùn ìseal). Under Eilidh nic Ìomhair the office of Keeper is bound to four houses of custody: Sliochd Mhuirich of Dùn ìseal, Sliochd Ìomhair of Dùn dhearg, Sliochd Thormoid of Seann Dunn and Sliochd Raghnaill of Seann Tarr. The other hearths keep their seats on the council, but lose their claim to the flame. Most of the later nobility of the island descends from one of the four, or says it does.
- **28 an Cèitean, FE 389** — *The house of Tormod at Seann Dunn* (Seann Dunn). Sliochd Thormoid raises a hall and a shrine at Seann Dunn, facing the mountain across the river. A lamp of coal burns in the shrine at the Law's measure. The other houses complain that the measure of Seann Dunn is always the fullest.
- **2 am Màrt, FE 393** — *The house of Raghnall at Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). Sliochd Raghnaill takes for its seat Seann Tarr on the north-eastern coast, the town whose household was first sentenced under the Law. The house keeps boats and not galleries, and grows rich on the fishing.
- **31 am Màrt, FE 397** — *Round Eilean dhubh* (Eilean dhubh). Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail round Eilean dhubh and come home, the first voyage made to see a coast and not to fish it. The house's songs name the steersman Tormod Ruadh. He brings back word of rock and birds, and of having gone, and of nothing else.
- **26 an t-Sultain, FE 401** — *The outlaws of the north-west waters* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Households stripped of their right under the Law for a third offence take to boats, live off the north-western waters, and raid the fishing strands. They are called spùinneadairean, plunderers, and the name stays with those waters after them.
- **28 an Lùnastal, FE 405** — *The boat lost off the north-west* (Uilebheist na Mara). A fishing boat out of Baile chrom is lost in calm water off the north-western coast. The two men who swim home say that something rose under it. Each year thereafter the boat's village keeps a wake for it. Of the thing they saw no more is told.
- **23 an t-Samhain, FE 409** — *The fire at Baile chrom relit* (Taigh-solais Baile chrom). After the loss the fishers of Baile chrom light the old beacon on the point again, fed with driftwood as the Law requires. From it comes Taigh-solais Baile chrom.
- **25 an Dàmhair, FE 413** — *Seann Bhrenn resettled* (Seann Bhrenn). Fishers from the north side of the mountain settle the harbour of Seann Bhrenn on the northern coast and keep its old name, as the western settlers kept Seann Warr's. They find a stone quay under the silt and use it.
- **20 am Faoilleach, FE 417** — *The ancestor-cairn at Cathair naomh* (Cathair naomh). The people of Cathair naomh in the north raise a cairn for their dead on the hill above the town, and bring it a stone at every burial. It is the greatest ancestor-cairn in the north, and it grows still.
- **22 an Dùbhlachd, FE 421** — *The panthers let pass* (Imrich nam Pantar). The crossing of the great cats is found to run straight over the carriers' southern road. Eilidh nic Ìomhair rules that no panther may be killed on the road in its season, and the carriers wait in the waypoint houses until the crossing is done. The rule is kept, for it costs the carriers only time.
- **19 am Màrt, FE 434** — *The granaries of Dùn dhearg* (Dùn dhearg). Sliochd Ìomhair builds stone granaries at Dùn dhearg and fills them from the lowland fields, holding grain against the storm season as the old custom of sharing asks. So the house gains what the Hall never had: people who owe it their bread.
- **18 an Gearran, FE 448** — *Baile Mòr dhomhain at the foot of the pass* (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Carriers who take the Hall's baskets north over the high pass settle at its southern foot, where Baile Mòr dhomhain now stands, to rest their beasts before the climb. The town lives by the pass, and by little else.
- **16 an Cèitean, FE 461** — *The reverent centuries*. Generation after generation mines the same small measure and burns the same small measure, and the people neither grow nor dwindle. The rolls call them the reverent centuries.
- **17 an Giblean, FE 475** — *Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid keeps the flame* (Seann Dunn). Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn becomes the first Keeper of Sliochd Thormoid. He keeps the flame longer than any Keeper before him, and changes nothing while he keeps it.
- **5 an t-Sultain, FE 488** — *The shepherds of Achadh chaol* (Achadh chaol). Shepherds settle the upland fields at Achadh chaol in the north-east and send their wool down to the harbours. Their headman sits one season on the council at Dùn ìseal, is found to hold no hearth-right, and goes home.
- **4 an Dàmhair, FE 502** — *The Keepers' count of the old places* (Làrach an Dùin-fhaire). Coinneach Mòr sends walkers to list the ruins of the old people. They bring back Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin, Làrach an Teampaill and the standing stones. The list says who does not own each place, and not who built it; the Keepers rule that it shall not guess.
- **2 an t-Samhain, FE 515** — *The fence round Carragh Cnoc bheag* (Carragh Cnoc bheag). The people of Cnoc bheag set a ring of stakes round the old standing stone above their town, that the cattle may not rub against it. Every generation after renews the ring. The stone is never moved.
- **1 an Dùbhlachd, FE 529** — *The bath-house at Muileann ruadh* (Muileann ruadh). A roofed bath-house is built over the warm springs below Muileann ruadh, with sleeping-places for the sick and their bearers. The Hall appoints a keeper of the springs, who tends them in the name of Dian Cècht, the healer. It is the first office the Hall makes that has nothing to do with the coal.
- **30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 542** — *The silver weights of Muileann chiar* (Muileann chiar). The silversmiths of Muileann chiar cast a set of weights, the least the weight of a barley-corn and the greatest that of a newborn lamb. Every trader on the carriers' roads comes to use them, and for the rest of the age a thing weighed at Muileann chiar is said to be weighed fairly.
- **10 an Dùbhlachd, FE 556** — *The market under the Hall* (Dùn ìseal). A market is held under the walls of the Hall at Dùn ìseal on the four quarter days, Samhain, Là Fhèill Brìde, Bealltainn and Lùnastal, when the households of the eastern hills come up with their dues. Hides, venison, charcoal, honey and the silver of Muileann chiar change hands there on the new weights. The Keepers allow no coal to be sold on their ground, and none is.
- **28 am Faoilleach, FE 565** — *The stag's people at Cnoc bhàn* (Cnoc bhàn). A house of the stag's people is founded at Cnoc bhàn, north of the mountain, and after the long exclusion takes cutters again. Its teachers keep the question of Sìleas nic Coinnich as she left it: why does the coal show its colours for one hand and not another?
- **26 an Gearran, FE 574** — *Seonaid Chiar reopens the galleries to the stag's people* (Dùn ìseal). Seonaid Chiar, Keeper of the house of Muireach, lets cutters trained by the stag's people back into the galleries at Dùn ìseal, sworn to ask nothing of the vein aloud. The Hall's roll calls it a reconciling. The school remembers it as a truce.
- **27 am Màrt, FE 579** — *Cathair mhòr walled* (Cathair mhòr). The people of Cathair mhòr on the southern coast build a wall of fitted stone about their headland town, the first town wall on the island. What they feared no one has told.
- **16 am Faoilleach, FE 584** — *Ceann leathan's fish-market* (Ceann leathan). Ceann leathan becomes the market of the southern fishing and sends dried fish inland along the carriers' paths. Its harbour-master keeps tallies on notched sticks. Several are kept at Muileann chaol, the oldest counted things in its keeping.
- **14 an Gearran, FE 589** — *The shrine at Inis thais* (Inis thais). A shrine to the ancestors lost at sea is raised at Inis thais on the western coast. Its keepers burn their season's handful on the shore and not indoors, so that the drowned, gone west over the sea, may see it.
- **29 an Giblean, FE 594** — *Cuan shean's salt-pans* (Cuan shean). The people of Cuan shean on the western coast dig salt-pans on the flats below the town and boil sea-water over peat. Their salt goes inland along the western road and keeps the fish of half the island.
- **31 am Màrt, FE 599** — *Salt-carriers on the heath above Baile fhiadhaich* (Baile fhiadhaich). Salt-carriers from Cuan shean settle on the western heath above Baile fhiadhaich, by a stream that runs all summer. The heath about it is not worth the plough, and its people keep goats.
- **2 am Màrt, FE 604** — *The sunny house* (An Taigh-òsta Grianach). A waypoint house is built on the eastern road where the carriers from Cnoc leathan meet the southern coast path, on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach. It faces south, and from the first is known for its warmth, which is all its name has ever meant.
- **1 an Gearran, FE 609** — *Cnoc leathan's market* (Cnoc leathan). Cnoc leathan, at the eastern end of the road past the sunny house, becomes the market town of the south-eastern hills. Its carriers' guild holds the right to carry for the Hall on the stretch down to the coast.
- **23 an Lùnastal, FE 614** — *The fall in the high gallery* (Dùn ìseal). A roof falls in the highest gallery at Dùn ìseal and kills four cutters. The gallery is walled up and left. Seonaid Chiar orders props of oak set in every gallery after, and for the first time the Hall spends timber on the mountain.
- **25 an t-Iuchar, FE 634** — *Cathair dhomhain founded* (Cathair dhomhain). Carriers settled at the mouth of the western road raise a town on the rise above the harbour and name it Cathair dhomhain. Its shrine keeps the Law's measure strictly, and its people are proud of it.
- **26 an t-Ògmhios, FE 654** — *A fishing town at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). The old settlement of the Red Hill, shrunk to a small fishing town, grows again at the western bridge-foot on the Abhainn dhomhain, a little above its meeting with the Abhainn gheal below Loch chrom. The ground is afterwards called Cathair dhearg, for its red stone. As yet it is a place carriers pass through on the way to somewhere else.
- **28 an Cèitean, FE 674** — *Goraidh mac Ìomhair called rìgh* (Dùn dhearg). At Dùn dhearg the lowland households who eat from the granaries of Sliochd Ìomhair begin to call its head, Goraidh mac Ìomhair, their rìgh, their king. None before him was ever so called. Goraidh claims nothing over the vein, and is careful to tell the Hall so.
- **9 an t-Sultain, FE 694** — *The division of keeping* (Dùn ìseal). The council at Dùn ìseal and Goraidh mac Ìomhair agree on a division. The Keeper keeps the flame and the galleries; the rìgh keeps the roads, the granaries and the peace of the lowlands. The rìgh may not enter the galleries, and the Keeper may not raise spears. On this division the island is governed for the rest of the age.
- **11 an Lùnastal, FE 714** — *Goraidh Mòr's hall* (Dùn dhearg). Goraidh mac Ìomhair, called Goraidh Mòr, builds a timber hall on the hill at Dùn dhearg, with a granary at each corner. Its post-holes could still be seen when the surveyors of the Library walked the hill, and they measured and drew them.
- **22 an t-Sultain, FE 719** — *The first road-toll* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). Goraidh Mòr sets a toll on the carriers' roads, one fish in twenty or its worth, to pay the road-guards and keep up the bridges. The keepers of the waypoint houses gather it, and keep a share of it, and the rolls say so.
- **21 an Dàmhair, FE 754** — *Mòrag of the Roads* (Dùn dhearg). Mòrag nic Ghoraidh takes the hall at Dùn dhearg after her father Goraidh Mòr. She is called Mòrag nan Rathad, Mòrag of the Roads, for in her first years she walks every carriers' road on the island and orders the bad stretches made anew.
- **26 an t-Iuchar, FE 781** — *The golden house* (An Taigh-seinnse Òir). Mòrag nan Rathad has a waypoint house built on the road north of Seann Dunn, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Òir, to shorten the carriers' stage from the coast to the mountain. It is the first waypoint house raised by a ruler and not by a family.
- **24 an Lùnastal, FE 794** — *The bridge-foot rebuilt* (Drochaid Cathair dhearg). At the bidding of Mòrag nan Rathad the western crossing of the Abhainn dhomhain is rebuilt in wider stone, so that two laden carriers can pass on it. The hearth-sign of Ailean Clachair is cut again in its keystone. From this time the town at the bridge-foot begins to grow.
- **16 am Faoilleach, FE 834** — *Dòmhnall Crùbach* (Dùn dhearg). Dòmhnall Crùbach, Dòmhnall the Lame, follows his mother Mòrag at Dùn dhearg. He cannot walk the roads as she did, and rules through the keepers of the waypoint houses, who grow mighty in his reign.
- **14 an Gearran, FE 863** — *The waypoint-keepers of Ceann mhin* (Ceann mhin). In the reign of Dòmhnall Crùbach the keepers of the waypoint houses about the harbour town of Ceann mhin take the gathering of the road-toll into their own hands and pay the rìgh what they judge fair. Their judgement is generous to themselves, and the rolls keep the sums.
- **19 an t-Samhain, FE 879** — *Baile àrsaidh on the western heath* (Baile àrsaidh). Settlers from Cathair dhomhain take the wet heath of the west coast and found Baile àrsaidh, where the soil is thin and the yellow scorpions thick. They swear their oaths on a scorpion's sting kept in a box, and their neighbours think it a strange custom.
- **18 an Dùbhlachd, FE 879** — *The storm at Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). A storm drives the sea over the harbour at Seann Chwen and takes the boats and a third of the houses. The Keeper sends the Hall's grain from Dùn ìseal, and Dòmhnall Crùbach sends his from Dùn dhearg. The survivors remember that the Hall's came first.
- **15 am Màrt, FE 914** — *The stag-letters* (Muileann chiar). At Muileann chiar in the far east the teachers of the stag's people make the cutters' tally-notches into signs for sounds, so that a teaching may be kept without a teacher. These are the first letters the Dia-thìrich use: the ogham, which the druids call the gift of Ogma. From them come nearly all the later hands of the island.
- **12 an Cèitean, FE 914** — *The letters set against the obelisk* (Carragh Cnoc bheag). Scholars of the stag carry their new letters to Carragh Cnoc bheag and set them beside the marks on the obelisk. They match nothing. The scholars write that the stone's makers were not their teachers, and that is the first thing the Dia-thìrich ever write of the old people.
- **10 an t-Ògmhios, FE 914** — *Sìleas Dhonn* (Dùn dhearg). Sìleas Dhonn, niece of Dòmhnall Crùbach, holds Dùn dhearg after him. In her reign the keepers of the waypoint houses are bidden to render account of the tolls at her hall once a year, and several of them do.
- **14 an Gearran, FE 991** — *The lords of Caol leathan* (Caol leathan). The harbour town of Caol leathan in the south-west grows rich on the western fishing and the southern end of the carriers' road. Its leading family, under Lachlann Ciar, takes the road-toll for itself and sends none of it to Dùn dhearg.
- **12 an Cèitean, FE 994** — *Iain Garbh* (Dùn dhearg). Iain Garbh, Iain the Rough, son of Sìleas Dhonn, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg and demands the western tolls of Caol leathan. Lachlann Ciar sends back a basket of fish-bones.
- **13 an Giblean, FE 999** — *The War of the Roads begins at Muileann òg* (Muileann òg). Iain Garbh marches west with the road-guards and the lowland levies, and burns the toll-house at Muileann òg that the men of Lachlann Ciar had taken. It is the first war of Dia-thìreach against Dia-thìreach. The Hall will bless neither side.
- **19 an t-Samhain, FE 1,000** — *Uisdean mac Ruairidh's refusal* (Dùn ìseal). The Keeper Uisdean mac Ruairidh refuses the messengers of Iain Garbh at Dùn ìseal the Hall's handful for the warband's hearths, saying that the flame does not warm men who go out to kill. The warband winters on peat. Iain Garbh never forgives the Hall, and never enters it.
- **21 an Dàmhair, FE 1,001** — *The fight at Àth fhiadhaich* (Àth fhiadhaich). The men of Caol leathan meet the levies of Iain Garbh at the ford of Àth fhiadhaich and hold it for a day before they give way. Forty lie dead of both sides. Long afterwards the carriers call it the ford of the forty.
- **16 am Faoilleach, FE 1,002** — *Baile ghlas burned* (Baile ghlas). The men of Lachlann Ciar, falling back on Caol leathan, burn Baile ghlas, that the levies of Iain Garbh may find no grain. Its people walk to Cathair dhomhain, and many never return.
- **18 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,003** — *Baile chiar holds* (Baile chiar). Baile chiar, south of the western bridge-foot, shuts its gate on both hosts in the War of the Roads and feeds the burned-out folk of Baile ghlas through the winter. Neither side forgives it, and neither attacks it.
- **2 an t-Samhain, FE 1,005** — *The siege of Caol leathan* (Caol leathan). Iain Garbh shuts Caol leathan in from the land for a season, but its boats bring in fish from the sea, and the harbour he cannot close. His levies begin to go home for the harvest, and the siege ends without an assault.
- **4 an Dàmhair, FE 1,006** — *The peace at Mòr nic Dhùghaill's house* (Am Buabhall Fortanach). Iain Garbh and Lachlann Ciar meet under the roof of the waypoint house that is afterwards Am Buabhall Fortanach, where by the road-peace neither may draw. Caol leathan keeps half its tolls and sends half to Dùn dhearg, and Lachlann Ciar swears to the Law before the Keeper's witness. So the War of the Roads ends in a house built to feed carriers.
- **12 am Faoilleach, FE 1,009** — *The wolf-sworn of Caol leathan* (Caol leathan). Men who fought for Caol leathan become its road-guards and swear their watch on a white stone carved as a wolf, kept at the town gate. They call themselves the wolf-sworn. Later ages read more into the stone than they did, and call it Lia Fàil.
- **14 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,036** — *Caol fhiadhaich rebuilt* (Caol fhiadhaich). Caol fhiadhaich on the south-western shore had sent its boats to feed Caol leathan through the siege. In thanks Lachlann Ciar gives it a share of the western tolls, and with it the town builds a harbour wall.
- **15 an t-Samhain, FE 1,044** — *Death of Iain Garbh* (Dùn dhearg). Iain Garbh dies at Dùn dhearg. His daughter Catrìona buries him in the floor of the hall and not on the slope at Dùn ìseal, and the Hall does not ask for him.
- **17 an Dàmhair, FE 1,046** — *Catrìona Ghlic* (Dùn dhearg). Catrìona Ghlic, Catrìona the Wise, rules from Dùn dhearg. She sends her own son to sit a season with the flame, the first child of the royal house to do so since the division of keeping. By the end of her reign the Hall and the hall are on speaking terms again.
- **8 an Cèitean, FE 1,081** — *The house on the northern road* (An Leòmhann Buidhe). Catrìona Ghlic has a waypoint house built on the northern road above Inis mhòr, on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe. It serves the carriers who take the Hall's baskets to the northern households and bring back wool.
- **9 an Giblean, FE 1,085** — *The house on the cold road* (An Taigh-seinnse Reòta). A stone house is built on the open moor, on the road between Baile Mòr dhomhain and the northern coast, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, for carriers caught by snow. The Hall pays its keepers in grain and the crown in cloth, and they complain of both.
- **11 am Màrt, FE 1,089** — *Inis mhòr grows* (Inis mhòr). The river port of Inis mhòr in the north becomes the gathering-place of the northern wool trade and outgrows every other northern town. Its people ask Catrìona Ghlic for a road-guard of their own, and are given one.
- **22 an t-Samhain, FE 1,122** — *The market at the fords of Baile Mòr dhomhain* (Baile Mòr dhomhain). The lords of the deep river set a market at Baile Mòr dhomhain, where the carriers' road from the south meets the paths down from the hill pastures. Cattle, sheep, horses, hides and the white stone of the hills are sold at the fords on the day after each new moon, and the lords take one fleece in forty from the sellers.
- **10 an Gearran, FE 1,166** — *Muileann shean on the northern road* (Muileann shean). A mill is built at Muileann shean on the northern road, to grind the grain the carriers bring over the pass, and a town grows round it. The Hall pays the miller in grain, and he pays the rìgh's toll in flour.
- **1 an t-Sultain, FE 1,211** — *The unremembered rulers* (Dùn dhearg). Eleven rulers hold Dùn dhearg between Catrìona Ghlic and Ealasaid Chiar. The later king-list gives their names and their order, and nothing more. For the same years the Keepers' roll gives five Keepers, and of them too only the names.
- **3 an Lùnastal, FE 1,255** — *Tormod Scrìobhaiche learns the letters* (Muileann chiar). Tormod mac Iain, a younger son of the house of Tormod, is sent east to Muileann chiar to learn the stag-letters. He is the first of the royal kin to read, and for the rest of his life he is called Tormod Scrìobhaiche, Tormod the Writer.
- **22 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,299** — *Ealasaid Chiar* (Dùn dhearg). Ealasaid Chiar takes the hall at Dùn dhearg and brings Tormod Scrìobhaiche there as her clerk. She bids him set down in order the name of every ruler of the hall that the reciters can give him.
- **20 an Lùnastal, FE 1,299** — *The first written king-list*. Rulers are first set down by name, and no longer only remembered in tales. The rolls of succession in every later age are kept after this pattern.
- **18 an t-Sultain, FE 1,300** — *The contents of Tormod's roll* (Dùn dhearg). Tormod Scrìobhaiche's roll, kept in the hall at Dùn dhearg, runs from Goraidh Mòr to Ealasaid Chiar. The earlier names he has from the reciters and the later from living memory, and he marks which are which. In three places it differs from the Keepers' spoken roll; Tormod writes down both readings and does not choose.
- **17 an Dàmhair, FE 1,320** — *The Keepers' roll written down* (Dùn ìseal). Shamed, in the Hall's own words, by the rìgh's clerk, the Keepers have their spoken roll written in stag-letters at Dùn ìseal. It begins with Beathag Bhàn, and it is longer than Tormod's by several centuries.
- **15 an t-Samhain, FE 1,569** — *The watchers of the dark wood* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). A small company settles at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the wood never cleared, and keeps watch for a black horned beast that they say walks in it. The people of Cathair dhearg call them the wood-watchers. None of their own accounts is older than Òrd Mhacha, the order of Macha, which afterwards claims them and takes the beast for a sign of Dubh Sainglenn, the black horse.
- **14 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,576** — *The wood-watchers in the stag's grove* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). Wood-watchers come east and cut a black-barked tree in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, saying that the beast had shown it to them. The stag's people call it theft from a place of teaching. Both sides send to Dùn dhearg and to Dùn ìseal.
- **12 am Faoilleach, FE 1,581** — *The stag's people claim the dark wood* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). In answer the stag's people send teachers west to hold their lessons in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, saying that the first stag came from there. Now each side claims both woods, and in either wood the two companies meet and do not speak.
- **10 an Gearran, FE 1,589** — *The holy-wood dispute*. Rival rites contend for Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the first such strife that is remembered. It is settled by dividing the keeping of the woods, and no side is judged the victor.
- **11 am Màrt, FE 1,595** — *The boundary stones of the woods* (Dùn dhearg). The woods are divided at Dùn dhearg before Fearchar Òg, rìgh after Ealasaid Chiar, and the Keeper Calum Liath. The stag's people keep the eastern wood and the wood-watchers the western, and each may walk in the other's wood unarmed and without cutting. Boundary stones are set at the edges of both woods with the terms cut on them in stag-letters. Two of the eastern stones remain.
- **9 an Giblean, FE 1,602** — *Calum Liath's surveyors* (Dùn ìseal). The Keeper Calum Liath sends cutters with knotted cords and lamps into every gallery at Dùn ìseal, to follow the vein as far as it can be followed and mark where it thickens and thins. The work keeps the cutters from the coal for three seasons, and the households go short to pay for it.
- **27 an t-Samhain, FE 1,607** — *The measuring of the vein*. For the first time men try to reckon how much coal the mountain holds. Their reckoning proves far too hopeful.
- **26 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,607** — *The reckoning of the cords* (Dùn ìseal). The reckoning of Calum Liath is cut on a slab in the Hall at Dùn ìseal: the mountain can give every household its handful for more generations than there are grains in the granaries of Dùn dhearg. It is read out at the council and heard in silence, and the Hall takes the silence for assent.
- **22 an Gearran, FE 1,621** — *The deaths in the lower gallery* (Dùn ìseal). Two youths of the nine hearths, sent into the lower gallery at Dùn ìseal without a Keeper's cutter to guide them, break the wrong face and are crushed. They had been less than a season in the galleries. Their families ask the council what the Hall owes them, and the council has no answer.
- **24 am Faoilleach, FE 1,628** — *The apprentice-binding custom*. Young Dia-thìrich are first bound for seven years to a master of the vein's custody before they may go near the coal themselves. Every later guild of the mines is shaped on this binding.
- **21 an Giblean, FE 1,634** — *Oighrig Bhàn's first bound* (Dùn ìseal). Oighrig Bhàn, Keeper after Calum Liath, binds the first twelve apprentices under the new custom at Dùn ìseal, each to a master cutter by name. They swear on the stone cup to serve seven years before they touch the vein. Four of the twelve are afterwards Keepers, which is the best that can be said for the custom.
- **23 am Màrt, FE 1,641** — *The stag's people take apprentices* (Cnoc bhàn). The house of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn takes the seven years for its own cutters and adds a rule: an apprentice keeps a written account of every stroke, and the account is read. These strike-books are the school's chief record for the rest of the age.
- **18 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,647** — *The long reign of Fearchar Òg* (Dùn dhearg). Fearchar Òg, who divided the woods, rules long at Dùn dhearg and is remembered chiefly for dying old. He was named Òg, the young, for coming to the hall as a boy, and the name stuck.
- **20 an Cèitean, FE 1,654** — *The silver tokens* (Muileann chiar). The clerks of Fearchar Òg begin to pay the road-guards in small silver rings of the Muileann chiar weight, stamped with the hall's mark. It is the first payment in metal by any ruler on Dia-thìr. The rings travel further than the guards do.
- **8 an Cèitean, FE 1,661** — *The toll-house at Àth ghlas* (Àth ghlas). A toll-house is built on the ford at Àth ghlas, where the southern road crosses the river toward Ceann leathan, and the road-guards are paid there in the new silver rings. Its keeper is the first sent from the rìgh's hall, and not chosen in the place.
- **9 an Giblean, FE 1,665** — *The road-guards' games at Ceann leathan* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). The road-guards of the south begin to meet each year at Ceann leathan and fight with blunted staves for a silver ring. The meeting outlives its purpose, and on its field Còmhrag Ceann leathan is afterwards fought. The first winner whose name is kept is a woman, Mòrag Dhubh of Cnoc mhòr.
- **5 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,665** — *The fair at Muileann òg* (Fèill Muileann òg). Muileann òg, burned in the War of the Roads, is rebuilt as a market town. A fair is held there each harvest at Lùnastal for the trade of the western and southern roads, and from it Fèill Muileann òg descends.
- **3 an Lùnastal, FE 1,665** — *The landing on the Abhainn uaine* (Cidhe Beag). A landing for river-boats is built on the Abhainn uaine at the place since called Cidhe Beag, so that the grain of the lowlands may go upriver by boat and not on carriers' backs. The carriers of the eastern road protest to Fearchar Òg, and lose.
- **11 am Màrt, FE 1,685** — *The river-boats* (Abhainn uaine). Flat river-boats of hide over withy begin to carry grain and salt fish up the Abhainn uaine from the landing at Cidhe Beag. The boatmen form a fellowship of their own, sworn on a paddle, and vie with the carriers for the Hall's baskets.
- **8 an Cèitean, FE 1,685** — *The boatmen of Muileann chrom* (Muileann chrom). Muileann chrom, up the valley from the landing at Cidhe Beag, becomes the home of the river-boatmen and their fellowship. Its yards build the flat hide boats for every river of the island.
- **6 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,685** — *Beathag Mhòr* (Dùn dhearg). Beathag Mhòr, great-granddaughter of Fearchar Òg, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg. The list calls her banrìgh, queen, the first so called, and not rìgh with a woman's name after it; the change of word is the list's own.
- **12 am Faoilleach, FE 1,699** — *The fleece-measure of Baile Mòr fhionn* (Baile Mòr fhionn). The lords of the western plain hold a market at Baile Mòr fhionn and make the fleece of a grown ewe its measure. Grain, wine, cattle and the horses of the plain are all priced in fleeces. The silver rings of Muileann chiar are taken there too, but reckoned in wool.
- **10 an Gearran, FE 1,699** — *The hall moves to Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag Mhòr moves her hall from Dùn dhearg to the town at the western bridge-foot, Cathair dhearg, to sit where the roads, the river and the western harbours meet. Dùn dhearg keeps the old granaries and the graves of the house of Ìomhar. From this reign Cathair dhearg is the seat of rule on Dia-thìr, whatever else changes.
- **22 an Gearran, FE 1,699** — *Dùn dhearg after the move* (Dùn dhearg). Dùn dhearg, left behind, keeps its granaries and its pride. Its people go on calling it the rìgh's hill, and for many generations its reeves will send their accounts to Cathair dhearg in no hand but their own.
- **23 am Màrt, FE 1,699** — *The red hall* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag Mhòr's hall at Cathair dhearg is built on the rise above the harbour, of the red stone that names the town. Its foundations lie under the later citadel. The masons cut the hearth-sign in its lintel as though it were a bridge.
- **9 an Giblean, FE 1,699** — *Cathair dhomhain against Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhomhain). The harbour of Cathair dhomhain, older and larger, grudges the new seat on its doorstep and refuses the queen's toll on its boats. Beathag Mhòr grants it a charter of its own tolls. The two towns, a few miles apart, are rivals for the rest of the age.
- **22 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,699** — *Disputed hands* (Dùn ìseal). The council at Dùn ìseal is asked to judge more quarrels over the right to the handful than over anything else: new households, divided households, households that claim descent from one of the nine hearths without proof. Dùghall mac Raghnaill, Keeper after Oighrig Bhàn, asks the queen for a counting.
- **11 am Faoilleach, FE 1,735** — *Beathag Mhòr orders the count* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag Mhòr and Dùghall mac Raghnaill agree that every household on the island claiming the handful shall be counted, its right proved or refused, and its name written. The clerks at Cathair dhearg are to write, and the Keepers to judge.
- **9 an Gearran, FE 1,735** — *The waypoint houses as counting-houses* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). The counters make their stations at the waypoint houses, for every household on the island lies within a day of one. The keepers of the houses feed the counters at the queen's cost, and in the houses the count is afterwards remembered as a good year.
- **22 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,735** — *The census of hands*. The households that hold the old right to burn the coal are counted across the whole island for the first time. So it is shown that the burning of the coal was already rationed by rule.
- **21 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,735** — *The count of hands* (Cathair dhearg). The rolls of the count, kept at Cathair dhearg, give eleven thousand four hundred households holding the right, and some two thousand whose claims were refused. The refused are written on a roll of their own, and it is that roll later generations search when they would prove an ancestor's standing.
- **19 an Lùnastal, FE 1,735** — *The refused of Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). Most of the refused households of the north-eastern coast are fisher-families about Seann Tarr who had never burned coal at all, and now find they have no right to begin. Sliochd Raghnaill takes up their cause at the council and loses. The fisher-families burn peat and say it is warmer.
- **17 an t-Sultain, FE 1,735** — *The light at Baile ìseal* (Taigh-solais Baile ìseal). The old beacon on the eastern point at Baile ìseal is rebuilt, kept with driftwood and seal fat as the Law requires, to bring the fishing boats of the eastern coast home in the dark. From it comes Taigh-solais Baile ìseal.
- **16 an Dàmhair, FE 1,735** — *The light at Muileann bheag* (Taigh-solais Muileann bheag). The old beacon on the northern headland at Muileann bheag is rebuilt; from it comes Taigh-solais Muileann bheag. Its keepers are fisher-families of the north-west, who pay no toll to Cathair dhearg in return for keeping it.
- **14 an t-Samhain, FE 1,735** — *The light at Àth dhearg* (Taigh-solais Àth dhearg). Sliochd Raghnaill rebuilds the old beacon on the north-eastern cape at Àth dhearg, to mark the way in toward Seann Tarr. From it comes Taigh-solais Àth dhearg.
- **13 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,735** — *Death of Beathag Mhòr* (Dùn dhearg). Beathag Mhòr dies at Cathair dhearg and by her own command is carried back to Dùn dhearg to lie among the house of Ìomhar. No royal journey before it was so long.
- **24 an Cèitean, FE 1,736** — *Ruairidh Liath* (Cathair dhearg). Ruairidh Liath, son of Beathag Mhòr, rules from Cathair dhearg. He is grey already when he takes the hall, and his byname is the list's one jest.
- **19 an Lùnastal, FE 1,745** — *The Silver Feud begins* (Muileann chiar). Ruairidh Liath demands one ring in five of the silver taken at Muileann chiar, saying the tokens that pay his guards should cost him nothing. Sliochd Fhearchair, the silversmiths' house, answers with Muireach Liath's ruling: silver is not holy, and so not the crown's either. They close the workings sooner than pay.
- **17 an t-Sultain, FE 1,746** — *The closing of the silver* (Muileann chiar). For three seasons no silver leaves Muileann chiar. The road-guards go unpaid, the fair at Muileann òg trades in grain again, and the tolls of the eastern road go ungathered. It is called the Silver Feud, though no one is killed in it.
- **16 an Dàmhair, FE 1,749** — *The Keeper's judgment on the silver* (Dùn ìseal). At the asking of both sides the Keeper Dùghall mac Raghnaill rules at Dùn ìseal that the words of Muireach Liath stand, and silver is not the mountain's; but also that the crown keeps the roads the silver travels. Ruairidh Liath takes one ring in ten, Sliochd Fhearchair opens the workings again, and each calls it a victory.
- **14 an t-Samhain, FE 1,750** — *The Muileann chiar weight made law* (Muileann chiar). In the settlement the silver weights of Muileann chiar are declared the only lawful weights on the roads of the island. Copies in bronze are sent to every waypoint house, and the house of Fearchar is paid for each.
- **25 an Giblean, FE 1,781** — *The bronze-casters of Muileann dhearg* (Muileann dhearg). The bronze copies of the Muileann chiar weights are cast at Muileann dhearg, where a family of casters learned the craft from the silversmiths. They go on to cast bells, pins and lamp-bowls, and their lamp-bowls hold the Law's measure exactly.
- **24 an Cèitean, FE 1,781** — *Seonag Chrom* (Cathair dhearg). Seonag Chrom, granddaughter of Ruairidh Liath, rules at Cathair dhearg. She gives the clerks a room of their own in the red hall and a wage in silver, and from her reign the king-list is kept year by year and not reign by reign.
- **22 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,854** — *Inis bheag's school of letters* (Inis bheag). At Inis bheag on the Abhainn bheag in the north a teacher of the stag's people begins to teach letters to fishers' children who will never cut coal. It is the first teaching of letters for their own sake. The Hall's roll notes it, and adds that fish do not need reading.
- **21 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,926** — *Peigi nic Tormoid, clerk of the hall* (Cathair dhearg). Peigi nic Tormoid, of the line of Tormod Scrìobhaiche, is clerk of the hall at Cathair dhearg, the first whose own hand can be told from the others in the copies that survive. Her entries are short, and she never gives a reason where a fact will serve. Much of what is known of the middle of the age is in her hand, or copied from it.
- **30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,999** — *The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). At Seann Skell on the northern coast the fowler families keep a hawk in every household and feed it before the household eats. They burn their season's handful at dawn with the hawk on the wrist, for the flame, they say, is a hunger and should be fed as a hunger is fed. They call the hawk Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, the grey hawk of time, as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, eldest of men, who lived down the ages as a salmon, an eagle and a hawk; between them the two remember all things. From them Òrd an t-Seabhaig counts its beginning.
- **28 am Faoilleach, FE 2,072** — *The hawk-rite spreads up the Abhainn ìseal* (Inis ìseal). The dawn burning with the hawk spreads from Seann Skell on the northern shore up the Abhainn ìseal to Inis ìseal and Cnoc bheag. The Keeper at Dùn ìseal writes that the rite keeps the measure exactly and is therefore no concern of the Hall. Never again does the Hall say so of any rite.
- **1 am Faoilleach, FE 2,145** — *The sting-oath at Ros bheag* (Ros bheag). The swearing on a scorpion's sting spreads from Baile àrsaidh up the western coast to Ros bheag, and the harbour court there takes it for every oath of trade. For the rest of the age a merchant who will not swear on the sting is not trusted in the western harbours.
- **3 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,217** — *The wolf-stone at Inis thais* (Inis thais). The wolf-sworn road-guards of Caol leathan set a second wolf-stone at the shrine of Inis thais, and the keepers of the shrine begin to pray before it as well as to the drowned. The stone is white quartz, dragged from the mountain on a sledge at a cost greater than the shrine's.
- **28 an Gearran, FE 2,290** — *The strike-books compared* (Cnoc bhàn). Donnchadh mac Iain, a teacher of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn, reads through the strike-books of many generations of apprentices. He finds that the coal breaks brighter in its colours for cutters in their later years than in their first, whatever their house, and argues that the vein answers practice. The elders answer that it answers what a cutter was born with, and that practice only shows it.
- **30 am Faoilleach, FE 2,300** — *Donnchadh mac Iain leaves Cnoc bhàn* (Muileann chaol). Donnchadh mac Iain and twenty-two of his hearers leave the house at Cnoc bhàn and settle at Muileann chaol, taking copies of the strike-books with them. The elders of Cnoc bhàn call it theft of the books. Donnchadh calls it copying, which it is.
- **7 an t-Sultain, FE 2,317** — *The founding of the rival druid school*. A school of druids breaks away, holding that the vein answers labour and not birth. Centuries later the Long War is fought over the same question in another shape.
- **9 an Lùnastal, FE 2,330** — *The school at Muileann chaol* (Muileann chaol). The school of Donnchadh mac Iain at Muileann chaol keeps strike-books of its own under a rule the elder school never had: a cutter's parentage is not written in the book at all. The two schools of the stag dispute by letter for the rest of the age, and both keep the letters.
- **4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,366** — *The Hall hears the two schools* (Dùn ìseal). The Keeper Raonaid Dhubh hears both schools of the stag at Dùn ìseal and gives no ruling, saying that the vein has not asked the Hall to decide. The Hall's roll sets down the hearing and the refusal. No refusal of the Hall is more often cited.
- **6 an Dàmhair, FE 2,376** — *What the people of Cnoc ghorm say of their stone* (Calbh Cnoc ghorm). Scholars of the stag from Muileann chaol come to Calbh Cnoc ghorm and cannot read it. The people of Cnoc ghorm tell them the stone says: we did not come; we were here. The scholars write that the people say so. No later hand explains either the stone or the saying.
- **21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,386** — *The digging at Làrach an Dùin* (Làrach an Dùin). Men of Baile ghorm dig under the fallen walls of Làrach an Dùin for the riches the ruin was said to hold, and find ash and nothing else. The Keeper has them sentenced as if they had broken the Law, though no law covered it, and the sentence stands as the rule for all the old places after.
- **23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,391** — *Baile ghorm's penance* (Baile ghorm). The families of the diggers at Baile ghorm do penance by keeping in repair the road from their town to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach. In the southern hills it is called the diggers' road still.
- **16 am Faoilleach, FE 2,406** — *Lachlann Bàn* (Cathair dhearg). Lachlann Bàn takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. He builds granaries in every province seat that will have one, and makes a law about them, and for these he is remembered.
- **14 an Gearran, FE 2,411** — *The shared-meal law written* (Cathair dhearg). Lachlann Bàn and the Keeper Raonaid Dhubh make the old unwritten custom law at Cathair dhearg: a household with grain above its winter's need gives the surplus to the common granary of its district before the storm season, and the granary feeds any household of the district that runs short. The successors of Peigi nic Tormoid write it into the rolls in full. It is the first law made by rìgh and Keeper together.
- **19 an t-Samhain, FE 2,425** — *The granary of Cnoc mhòr* (Cnoc mhòr). Cnoc mhòr builds its common granary under the new law before any other district, and sends word of it to Cathair dhearg. Lachlann Bàn sends back a silver ring for the reeve.
- **18 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,435** — *The common granaries of the mountain* (Muileann chiar). Common granaries are raised under the new law in the mountain districts round Muileann chiar, where the households live by cutting and carrying and grow little of their own. The lowland districts grumble at filling them.
- **12 an Cèitean, FE 2,445** — *The granary at Cathair mhòr* (Cathair mhòr). A common granary is built within the old wall at Cathair mhòr, the first behind a town wall. The southern fishing towns, having no grain, send dried fish to it for their share.
- **10 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,455** — *Raiders in the eastern waters* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Outlaws in boats raid the eastern fishing strands from the islets offshore, taking dried fish and nets. Sliochd Raghnaill arms its boats at Seann Tarr and burns two of the raiders' boats. The rest escape.
- **15 am Màrt, FE 2,461** — *Oighrig nic Lachlainn* (Cathair dhearg). Oighrig nic Lachlainn, daughter of Lachlann Bàn, takes the hall at Cathair dhearg. She has no children, and before her reign is half done the houses begin to count their claims.
- **13 an Giblean, FE 2,472** — *The late snow on the high passes* (Cnoc ghlas). The weather-watchers on the cairns above Cnoc ghlas see snow lying on the high passes long past the opening of the galleries. The Hall keeps the galleries shut for the cutters' safety, and the mountain households wait.
- **5 an t-Sultain, FE 2,472** — *The poor season in the mountain* (Muileann chiar). The galleries open late and close early, and the coal carried down is a third of a common season's. The mountain households of Muileann gheal, Doire uaine and Àth dhìreach, who trade their carrying for grain, have nothing to trade, and by the season's end they are eating their seed.
- **4 an Dàmhair, FE 2,473** — *The first recorded famine averted*. A poor mining season brings three settlements near to starving. The shared-meal law, made a generation before, holds and saves them. It is the first true trial of the custom.
- **15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,473** — *The granaries opened* (Muileann gheal). Under the shared-meal law the common granaries of the mountain districts are opened at Muileann gheal. When they run low the granaries of Dùn dhearg and the southern coast send grain up the carriers' roads without being asked twice, and the carriers bear it for no fee. None in the three settlements is known to die of hunger that winter.
- **18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,474** — *Àth dhìreach after the poor season* (Àth dhìreach). At Àth dhìreach, one of the three settlements the granaries fed, the carriers who brought up the grain are given the right to rest in any house of the town without payment for as long as they live. The last of them dies old, and the right with him.
- **16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,474** — *The reeves of Dùn dhearg send the grain* (Dùn dhearg). The reeves of Dùn dhearg, who had withheld their accounts from Cathair dhearg for generations, open the old granaries of the house of Ìomhar to the mountain without waiting for an order. Oighrig nic Lachlainn writes that she would have given the order had they waited. The successor of Peigi nic Tormoid notes that they did not.
- **19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,511** — *Death of Oighrig nic Lachlainn* (Cathair dhearg). Oighrig nic Lachlainn dies at Cathair dhearg with no heir of her body, and with her ends the line of Goraidh Mòr, as the list reckons it. The red hall is shut, and its clerks keep it.
- **10 an Giblean, FE 2,513** — *The four houses meet* (Dùn ìseal). The Four Houses of custody meet at Dùn ìseal to choose a ruler, for no custom covers a hall without an heir. Sliochd Ìomhair claims it by blood, Sliochd Thormoid by the clerks, Sliochd Raghnaill by its boats. Sliochd Mhuirich, holding the Keeper's office, makes no claim.
- **12 am Màrt, FE 2,516** — *The election of Gilleasbuig Mòr* (Seann Dunn). The houses choose Gilleasbuig Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn, a grandson of the clerks' line, to hold the red hall. The Keeper sets the stone cup in his hands before the council, and so for the first time a ruler is made at Dùn ìseal. Sliochd Ìomhair consents, on condition that its graves at Dùn dhearg remain the burying-place of the kings.
- **11 an Gearran, FE 2,517** — *Gilleasbuig Mòr at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). Gilleasbuig Mòr takes the red hall. He keeps the clerks' office in the hands of his own house and has the king-list copied again from the beginning, with a line drawn beneath Oighrig nic Lachlainn. The line is in every later copy.
- **13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,537** — *The shrine at Seann Dunn enlarged* (Seann Dunn). Gilleasbuig Mòr enlarges his house's shrine at Seann Dunn into a temple with a court for pilgrims. The other houses say still that its coal-lamp burns fuller than the measure, and every season a Keeper's cutter is sent to try it.
- **27 an Giblean, FE 2,541** — *Death of Gilleasbuig Mòr* (Dùn dhearg). Gilleasbuig Mòr dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried among the house of Ìomhar at Dùn dhearg, as was agreed. His son Tormod Òg follows him without a meeting of the houses, and none asks for one.
- **29 am Màrt, FE 2,558** — *The gap in the list* (Cathair dhearg). Nine rulers of the house of Tormod reign between Tormod Òg and Anna Ruadh, and the king-list at Cathair dhearg gives their names and years and little else. The successors of Peigi nic Tormoid were diligent and brief; for these reigns the rolls tell mostly of harvests, tolls and the mending of bridges.
- **24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,571** — *The bridge at Cathair dhearg widened* (Drochaid Cathair dhearg). The bridge at Cathair dhearg is rebuilt a third time, wide enough now for a cart, for carts have come onto the lowland roads. The hearth-sign is cut again in the keystone. The span stands on the piers of Mòrag nan Rathad.
- **24 an Giblean, FE 2,583** — *Riders on the lowland roads* (Dùn dhearg). The road-guards of Dùn dhearg begin to ride the lowland roads on the small horses of the southern grass country, and a guard can now reach a waypoint house before a quarrel there has cooled. They are the first riders whose names are kept, and for long the only ones.
- **23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,598** — *The crossing at Ros fhionn repaired* (Drochaid Ros fhionn). A flood takes the eastern approach of Ailean Clachair's span above Ros fhionn, and it is mended. The masons find their founder's hearth-sign still sharp in the keystone, and leave it untouched.
- **21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,613** — *The bridge at Dùn chrom* (Dùn chrom). The masons' fellowship bridges the river below Dùn chrom, joining the southern road to the western without the long way round by Cathair dhearg. The toll is set at half the road-toll, and Cathair dhearg complains.
- **19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,628** — *The bridge at Ceann àrsaidh* (Ceann àrsaidh). A bridge is built at the river town of Ceann àrsaidh, the fourth stone crossing of the lowlands. The masons' roll names the forty who built it, all of the fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill, who had learned the craft while the boats lay idle.
- **18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,643** — *The bridge at Doire mhin* (Doire mhin). The masons' fellowship builds a small bridge at Doire mhin to carry the southern road over a stream that floods each spring. Beside the hearth-sign in the keystone is cut the name of Beathag Clachair, who cut it: the first mason's mark known.
- **16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,658** — *The far-off house* (An Sligeanach Fad' às). The waypoint house on the site of An Sligeanach Fad' às, the oldest house under the road-peace, is rebuilt in stone. It lies so far from any town that the carriers say one is never nearer to it than halfway, and from the saying it takes its name.
