- **15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,672** — *Fire-water on the northern road* (An Leòmhann Buidhe). The house on the northern road, on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe, begins to serve a spirit distilled from barley that the carriers call fire-water. The Keepers rule that it is not a burning and no concern of theirs. The house's trade doubles.
- **13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,687** — *Caol mhòr in the north-west* (Caol mhòr). The fisher-families of the north-west gather at Caol mhòr under a headman of their own, and send tolls to Cathair dhearg only in the years the road-guard comes to take them. Little is written of the north-west in this age, and most of it is complaint of that.
- **4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,702** — *Seal-oil from Ceann mhòr* (Ceann mhòr). Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast begins to trade seal-oil down the western coast to Ros bheag for silver rings, and its beacons burn it. For many generations the seal-oil lamps of the western harbours are the brightest light on Dia-thìr.
- **3 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,717** — *The high pastures of Muileann leathan* (Muileann leathan). Herding families take the high pastures above Muileann leathan in the north and keep sheep there for the wool of Inis mhòr. They hold no right to the handful, have never held one, and are not counted in the census of hands.
- **30 am Faoilleach, FE 2,732** — *Inis mhin on the northern shore* (Inis mhin). Inis mhin, a fishing harbour on the northern shore, comes into the rolls for the first time when its headman goes to the wool-fair of Inis mhòr to complain of the road-guard's toll. The complaint is written down in full, and it is all that is written of the town in this age.
- **28 an Gearran, FE 2,747** — *The raid on the western strands* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Raiders from the north-western waters take a season's dried fish from the strands of the north-western coast. The sting-sworn merchants of Ros bheag pay for two armed boats to watch the strands, and the raiders move north.
- **29 am Màrt, FE 2,761** — *The second sighting* (Uilebheist na Mara). Two boats of Baile chrom tell of something vast moving beneath them in the north-western water, the second such sighting remembered. One boat does not come home. The wake that Baile chrom keeps for the first loss is kept now for both.
- **27 an Giblean, FE 2,776** — *Round the islands* (Seann Tarr). Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail from Seann Tarr round the offshore islands, Eilean ruadh, Eilean dhearg and Eilean fhada among them, and come home in one season. No crew of the age goes further from the coast than the islands, and none is known to have wished to.
- **26 an Cèitean, FE 2,791** — *Summer herders on Eilean ruadh* (Eilean ruadh). Families from the coast take sheep over to Eilean ruadh for the summer grazing and bring them back before the storms. They build turf shelters there, which later herders use again.
- **24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,806** — *Anna Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). Anna Ruadh of the house of Tormod takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. She walks the whole circuit of the roads, the first ruler to do so since Mòrag nan Rathad, and she walks it twice.
- **23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,809** — *Anna Ruadh at Am Buabhall Fortanach* (Am Buabhall Fortanach). On her first circuit Anna Ruadh stops at the house on the site of Am Buabhall Fortanach, where the War of the Roads was ended, and eats the jugged buffalo like a carrier. The keepers of the house tell of it still.
- **21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,813** — *Anna Ruadh at the sunny house* (An Taigh-òsta Grianach). On the eastern road Anna Ruadh lodges at the house on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach and grants its keepers a toll of their own for the upkeep of the road to Cnoc leathan, Slighe Cnoc leathan. No other waypoint house on the island holds a royal charter.
- **12 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,816** — *Anna Ruadh at Ceann mhin* (Ceann mhin). At Ceann mhin on the south-eastern coast Anna Ruadh hears the quarrel of the fishers and the carriers over who may carry dried fish up to the mountain, and rules that both may. The fish going inland is doubled, and its price at Dùn ìseal halved.
- **11 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,819** — *The contest at Ceann leathan in stone* (Ceann leathan). Anna Ruadh gives the road-guards' contest at Ceann leathan a stone-walled field, and for its prize a silver ring from the red hall. Fighters come to it from all the south, and the losers are fed at the crown's cost.
- **23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,822** — *A wood-watcher in the red hall* (Cathair dhearg). Anna Ruadh keeps a wood-watcher from Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag in her household at Cathair dhearg to read the omens of the hall. So the rite of the wood-watchers, the rite of Macha, goddess of sovereignty and of horses, first comes to the capital. The Keeper sends a protest from Dùn ìseal, and the rolls give no answer.
- **24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,826** — *Cathair dhomhain and the wood-watchers* (Cathair dhomhain). The shrine at Cathair dhomhain, proud of its strict keeping of the Law, will take no wood-watcher, and its people say that the capital has given its omens to folk who sit in trees. From this the rivalry of the two towns takes a turn in matters of faith that it never loses.
- **26 an Cèitean, FE 2,829** — *Death of Anna Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). Anna Ruadh dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Dùn dhearg among the house of Ìomhar and the kings of her own house. Her son Coinneach Bàn takes the hall.
- **27 an Giblean, FE 2,832** — *Coinneach Bàn* (Cathair dhearg). Coinneach Bàn rules long and quietly from Cathair dhearg. In his reign the clerks of the hall begin to copy the rolls for the provinces, so that each province seat has its own copy of the laws. Several of those copies survive where the first writings are lost.
- **16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,835** — *Seumas Bàn keeps the flame* (Dùn ìseal). Seumas Bàn of Sliochd Mhuirich is chosen Keeper. Reading the Hall's roll at Dùn ìseal he finds that more than half the Keepers of the age were of his own house, and has the fact struck from the preface. The unstruck copy survives.
- **18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,838** — *The rites counted at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). Seumas Bàn has the clerks of the Hall list every rite on the island that burns the handful and every one that lays claim to the vein, that the council may know what it keeps. The list holds the Hall's own rite, the ancestor-keeping of the old folk, the dawn-hawk of the north coast, the wood-watchers of the west, the wolf-sworn, the sting-oath, and both schools of the stag. The clerks write that a thousand years before no such list would have been needed.
- **19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,840** — *The hawk-keepers refuse the Hall's cutter* (Seann Skell). The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell turn away the Hall's cutter who comes to try their measure, saying their measure is the hawk's, and the hawk is not the Keeper's. The cutter goes home with the refusal in writing. No rite had refused the trial of the measure outright before.
- **21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,843** — *The wolf-sworn build a hall* (Caol leathan). The wolf-sworn of Caol leathan build a hall of their own about the white wolf-stone at the town gate, and swear oaths there that are no longer road-guards' oaths. The stone, they say, watches the whole island as the guard watches the road, and will cry out beneath the rightful king. From this hall comes Òrd na Cloiche, the order of the Stone, and the wolf-sworn begin to be called the Fianna.
- **3 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,846** — *The sting-oath at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). At Seann Skell in the west the sting-oath of the harbour court becomes a creed. Its keepers hold that one power stings the liar wherever he may be, Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, and that the scorpion is but his sign; theirs is the first teaching on the island to call itself the only true one, and the Hall's roll sets it down as new. Thereafter the oath is sworn over a cup marked with the scorpion, Manannan's Cup of Truth, which is said to break in three at three lies spoken over it and to be made whole by three truths. Òrd Mhanannain dates itself from this court.
- **4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,849** — *Seann Vell swears on the sting* (Seann Vell). Seann Vell, on the western coast below Cuan shean, takes up the sting-oath of its neighbours. Its shrine keeps a scorpion carved in yellow stone, the first image of the creature made for worship and not for swearing on.
- **13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,852** — *The dark wood keeps its own rite* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). The wood-watchers of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag cease to send to the Hall for judgement of their quarrels, and judge them under the trees. They hold that the black beast has two natures, one that keeps and one that devours, and that the vein has the same. The order of Macha afterwards tells of the two horses that drew one chariot, the black Dubh Sainglenn and the grey Liath Macha: two horses, one yoke.
- **11 an Gearran, FE 2,855** — *The common root of the orders*. The one folk-faith of the island begins plainly to divide into the several ways that later ages name apart: the orders of An Creideamh Sean, the Old Faith, and the hearth-keeping of Na Seann Spioradan, the Old Spirits. From this time the belief of the Dia-thìrich is no longer one.
- **16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,858** — *The council divided by rite* (Dùn ìseal). The council at Dùn ìseal, which had sat by hearth and by house, begins to sit in companies by rite. Seumas Bàn complains that he keeps the flame now for eight peoples, each of whom thinks itself its only keeper. The seating holds for the rest of the age.
- **15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,860** — *Allt an Àigh keeps its pilgrims* (Allt an Àigh). Pilgrims of every rite go on walking to Allt an Àigh in the right quarter of the moon; it is the one custom of the island that the Hall's list sets under no company. In one season the path from Caol shean is paved anew by pilgrims of four rites.
- **19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,863** — *The springs at Muileann ruadh common to all* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). The keeper of the springs at Muileann ruadh rules that the sick of every rite shall be bathed without asking which. Her ruling is copied into the rolls of the provinces. It is the last ruling of the age on which every company of the council agrees.
- **18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,866** — *Cnoc dhìreach's weavers* (Cnoc dhìreach). The town of Cnoc dhìreach in the east, on the carriers' road south of the springs, becomes known for a heavy undyed cloth that the carriers wear on the high passes. It is not the grave-keepers' village by the old tombs, and the rolls tell the two Cnoc dhìreachs apart by that cloth.
- **23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,869** — *The dyers of Muileann bhàn* (Muileann bhàn). The dyers of Muileann bhàn in the eastern hills learn to fix a pale blue from a hill plant, and the carriers' cloth of all the mountain country is dyed there. The Keepers wear it undyed, and say so.
- **21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,872** — *Muileann dhomhain's mill* (Muileann dhomhain). A water-mill is built at Muileann dhomhain in the eastern hills to grind the grain of the common granaries of the mountain districts. The miller keeps one measure in sixteen, and the rolls call it fair.
- **26 an Cèitean, FE 2,875** — *The flood at Àth chiar* (Àth chiar). Rain on the eastern hills brings the river over the ford at Àth chiar, and it carries off the carriers' shelter and six of the townsfolk. The common granary of the district stands on a rise, is untouched, and feeds the town through the winter.
- **24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,878** — *The oyster-beds of Seann Bhral* (Seann Bhral). The people of Seann Bhral on the south-eastern coast begin to lay oyster-beds in the shallows, a craft that came, they say, with the name of their town. The Library's copy of the provincial roll sets down the claim and marks it doubtful.
- **20 an Gearran, FE 2,880** — *Seann Vell's harbour* (Seann Vell). Seann Vell on the south-eastern coast grows into a city on the southern fishing and the silver of Muileann chiar brought down the eastern road. Its harbour is the first on the island with a stone quay.
- **22 am Faoilleach, FE 2,883** — *The light at Tobar dhearg rebuilt* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). The old beacon at Tobar dhearg on the southern cape is rebuilt as a stone tower with the fire on its top, the first sea-light raised above the ground. It burns seal-oil of the north-west, carried the whole length of the island.
- **19 an Giblean, FE 2,886** — *Muileann naomh's mill-shrine* (Muileann naomh). At Muileann naomh on the southern coast a mill and a shrine share one roof, and the miller keeps the shrine's handful beside his millstones. The Keeper's cutter who comes to try it finds the measure kept and the flour good.
- **21 am Màrt, FE 2,889** — *Dùn thais walled* (Dùn thais). Dùn thais in the eastern hills is walled, and a temple of the stag's people is raised within it, the first of theirs built in stone and not kept in a grove. The elder school at Cnoc bhàn sends it teachers.
- **16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,892** — *The wool-fair of Inis mhòr* (Inis mhòr). Inis mhòr holds a wool-fair at every shearing, and buyers come to it from all the northern coast and some from Cathair dhearg. Its silver is weighed on the Muileann chiar weights sent to the northern road.
- **18 an Cèitean, FE 2,895** — *Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern coast* (Baile Mòr mhòr). Baile Mòr mhòr, on the northern coast west of Seann Toll, grows great enough on the fishing to send its own member to the council at Dùn ìseal. The Four Houses mislike it, and seat its member at the foot of the hall.
- **13 an Lùnastal, FE 2,898** — *The northern boats at Seann Toll* (Seann Toll). The harbour at Seann Toll becomes the home of the northern fishing fleet. Its boatbuilders make the longest craft on the island, built for a day's run along the coast and never for open water.
- **15 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,900** — *Drought at Achadh shean* (Achadh shean). A dry summer burns the pastures round Achadh shean in the east, and by spring the district's common granary is empty. Grain is sent from Baile chaol and Cuan ruadh under the shared-meal law, and the district repays it over the harvests after.
- **10 an Dàmhair, FE 2,903** — *Baile chaol's repayment* (Baile chaol). The rolls at Baile chaol set down the repayment of the drought grain by Achadh shean, measure by measure, to the last. The clerk adds that no such debt in the rolls was repaid in full before.
- **11 an t-Sultain, FE 2,906** — *The panthers late* (Imrich nam Pantar). The great cats cross the southern road late, and fewer than the carriers remember. The weather-watchers read it for a hard winter, and are right. The Keepers note it without remark.
- **13 an Lùnastal, FE 2,909** — *The watch-tower at Baile ruadh* (Baile ruadh). A timber watch-tower is raised at Baile ruadh on the north-eastern coast to look out for raiders from the islands, manned by turns by the fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill. It is the only tower of war the age builds.
- **11 an t-Sultain, FE 2,912** — *Cuan ruadh's boats* (Cuan ruadh). The fishers of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast give boats and men to the watch against the island raiders. In return Sliochd Raghnaill gives the town a place on the council at Dùn ìseal beside its own seat.
- **10 an Dàmhair, FE 2,915** — *The drowned-feast at Inis chrom* (Inis chrom). At Inis chrom on the western coast the families of the drowned hold a feast on the shore each year and set an empty place for each of the lost. The custom spreads to the harbours northward as far as Seann Warr.
- **8 an t-Samhain, FE 2,918** — *The potters of Baile ghorm* (Baile ghorm). Potters at Baile ghorm on the south-western coast begin to fire a hard red ware of the local clay, and their jars carry the oil and grain of the western road. Sherds of it lie on every waypoint-house site the Library's surveyors have walked.
- **19 an Giblean, FE 2,920** — *Cnoc àrsaidh's kilns* (Cnoc àrsaidh). Potters of Baile ghorm set up new kilns at Cnoc àrsaidh in the south-west, where the clay is better and the wood nearer. There the red ware of the western road is made for the rest of the age.
- **18 an Cèitean, FE 2,923** — *Cathair fhada grows* (Cathair fhada). Families leaving the crowded harbours about Cathair dhearg settle at Cathair fhada on the southern coast and raise its long street along the ridge. They bring a wood-watcher with them, and a copy of the laws.
- **16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,926** — *Cnoc naomh's ancestor-shrine* (Cnoc naomh). The people of Cnoc naomh keep a shrine to the ancestors and to the sìth of the hill in the old folk way, with no hawk, wolf, sting or stag in it. The Hall's list of rites names them among the keepers of the old reverence, which by now is a company of its own.
- **15 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,929** — *Mòr nic Coinnich crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Mòr nic Coinnich, granddaughter of Coinneach Bàn, takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. The Keeper Catrìona nic Mhuirich sets the stone cup in her hands at Dùn ìseal, as the houses had done for Gilleasbuig Mòr. Hers is the last name written in the king-list of the Holy Age.
- **2 an Giblean, FE 2,939** — *The Hall's roll at the close of the age* (Dùn ìseal). At the close of the age the Keepers' roll holds one hundred and forty names, from Beathag Bhàn to Catrìona nic Mhuirich, and the king-list more than ninety, from Goraidh Mòr to Mòr nic Coinnich. The Small-Burning Law is unchanged in any word since the stone cup of Fionnlagh Dall, and the cup stands yet on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal.
- **1 an Cèitean, FE 2,949** — *The last age of even population*. So ends the Holy Age. The chroniclers of after days look back on it with some unease: it is the last time in the history of Dia-thìr that no family's lives ran longer than any other's.

## Age III · An Aois Scaraidh

*The Age of Sundering · the Landfall Era, LE 1 – 1,819*

- **6 am Faoilleach, LE 1** — *Land is found*. Word comes of a land across the open water, where no people like the Dia-thìrich dwell. Who first found it is not told.
- **9 an t-Samhain, LE 1** — *The tidings at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). Three crews from the western harbours bring word of the far land to the hall of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, daughter of Mòr nic Coinnich, at Cathair dhearg. None claims to have been first. The queen's scribe takes down all three tellings; they agree on the coast and on nothing else.
- **8 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *The Choosing*. A vote, or what the later chroniclers call a vote, settles who will go. Only the willing go; no lots are drawn and none are pressed.
- **12 an t-Sultain, LE 2** — *The roll of the willing* (Seann Skell). The harbour scribes of Seann Skell open a roll of those who mean to go, written by household and not by name, on boards in the harbour-house. A later hand notes that names were struck out as often as they were added.
- **11 an Dàmhair, LE 2** — *The queen neither commands nor forbids* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag declares that the crown will send no one across the water and keep no one back. Within the season her younger sister, Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, enters her own household on the roll at Seann Skell.
- **14 an Lùnastal, LE 3** — *The custodians count the cost* (Muileann dhearg). The vein-house above Muileann dhearg, keeper of Crom's stone and heir to the Keepers' Hall at Dùn ìseal where Brìde's flame was first bound, counts the households of the coal-right that have entered the roll. The custody-book makes it nearly one in five, and says the count was made twice, for the first figure was not believed.
- **16 an t-Iuchar, LE 5** — *The ships are built*. The shipwrights of the island, used to small coasting craft, build ships to keep the open sea, the first in the memory of Dia-thìr.
- **14 an Lùnastal, LE 5** — *Alasdair Saor lays the first keel* (Seann Skell). On the river strand below Seann Skell the shipwright Alasdair mac Iain, called Alasdair Saor, lays down the first deep-keeled hull built on Dia-thìr. Until then the island's boats were sewn-plank coasters that never lay a night out of sight of land.
- **26 an Lùnastal, LE 5** — *The oaks of Doire fhionn* (Doire fhionn). The oak grove that named Doire fhionn is felled for the keels of the fleet and drawn to the coast on ox-sleds. It never grew again, and the village kept a name it had no more cause for.
- **24 an t-Sultain, LE 5** — *The shipwrights' fellowship* (Seann Skell). Alasdair Saor gathers the wrights of the Seann Skell strand into one fellowship, and binds each apprentice for seven years after the manner of the vein custodians. The custody-book names it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights.
- **12 an t-Sultain, LE 6** — *The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh* (Inis àrsaidh). The first finished hull is taken down the Abhainn naomh and out past Ros àrsaidh, where the ships of Inis àrsaidh put to sea, for trial in open water. It founders in a following sea and eleven are drowned. Alasdair Saor alters the setting of the keel, and every later hull of the fleet is built to the new pattern.
- **11 an Dàmhair, LE 8** — *The rope-walks of Cuan shean* (Cuan shean). Cuan shean lays out long rope-walks along its harbour front and gives all its hemp fields to cordage for the fleet. Its rope trade lasts some centuries beyond the Sundering.
- **9 an t-Samhain, LE 9** — *The sail-cloth levy* (Baile àrsaidh). Every weaving household in Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh owes a set length of close-woven sail-cloth, scored on tally-sticks at the shire seat. The tallies survive; how many paid is not known.
- **20 an Giblean, LE 13** — *The star-lore of Cuan ruadh* (Cuan ruadh). The old steersmen of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast, the only sailors of the island who had ever held a course by night, teach the pilots of the fleet to steer by the stars. Their lore was written down only in part, and that part is lost.
- **19 an Cèitean, LE 18** — *The willing choose their leaders* (Seann Skell). The households of the roll meet at Seann Skell and choose Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, the queen's sister, and Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a custodian of the vein, to lead them. The custody-book records the choice; how it was made is not told.
- **17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 25** — *The handful for the new hearth* (Muileann dhearg). The vein-house rules that each departing ship may carry one sealed measure of the coal, no more than a single household may burn in a season under the Small-Burning Law. It is the only writing in the custody-book addressed to those who were leaving.
- **16 an t-Iuchar, LE 30** — *The west quay lengthened* (Seann Skell). Masons from the capital lengthen the west quay at Seann Skell with dressed stone, so that the deep hulls may lie alongside at low water. On these stones the later rite was held.
- **20 an Gearran, LE 38** — *The strife over the grain*. Strife over how much of the island's stored grain the ships may take all but ends the venture. Within a season it is settled; how is not recorded.
- **21 am Màrt, LE 38** — *Àth shean shuts its granaries* (Àth shean). In the strife over the fleet's grain Tormod mac Coinnich, reeve of the granaries at Àth shean, bars the store-houses and sets a watch on them until the matter is settled. He holds no office afterward.
- **3 an Giblean, LE 38** — *Grain down Abhainn dhomhain* (Abhainn dhomhain). The strife settled, grain barges go down Abhainn dhomhain to the capital, on by the coast to Ros àrsaidh, and up the Abhainn naomh to Seann Skell. A tally-keeper at Drochaid Cathair dhearg counts forty-one barges passing.
- **2 an Cèitean, LE 38** — *The fleet assembled* (Seann Skell). The fleet lies complete at Seann Skell. The custody-book gives nineteen hulls; a later hand in the margin makes it twenty-one. Which is right has never been settled.
- **18 an Giblean, LE 40** — *The night of lamps* (Seann Skell). On the last night before the sailing every house on the Seann Skell waterfront sets a lamp on its sill and keeps it burning till morning. It is the first custom of the Sundering written down as a custom, and the town kept it long after its cause had become a tale.
- **19 an Giblean, LE 40** — *The Setting-Out*. The willing sail west. The chronicles of the island fall silent on them as the ships clear the harbour; the Dia-thìrich tell that the fleet sailed into Manannan's mist, toward the Otherworld.
- **19 an Giblean, LE 40** — *The sunwise turn* (Seann Skell). Before going down the Abhainn naomh to the open sea the fleet goes once round the river pool of Seann Skell sunwise, diosal, for luck, and the watchers on the quay count the hulls as they pass. The harbour scribe's account ends at the foot of the pool.
- **22 am Faoilleach, LE 44** — *The years counted from the turn* (Muileann dhearg). Donnchadh mac Thormoid, scribe of the vein-house, begins to number the years from the sunwise turn at Seann Skell, and calls them the years of the Diosal. The count is his; the crown's scribes take it up a generation later.
- **27 an Dàmhair, LE 44** — *Tidings reach Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). Tidings of the fleet reach Seann Skell, by what road or whose mouth is not told. The harbour scribe copies them in a shaking hand; the copy came down to later keepers water-stained and lacking its end.
- **24 an Dùbhlachd, LE 44** — *Two landfalls*. Such broken tidings as come back tell of two coasts reached, not one. In this telling lies the seed of the two peoples that came after.
- **1 an Lùnastal, LE 46** — *Mòrag's line struck* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag strikes her sister Mòrag and Mòrag's children from the succession, as no longer on Dia-thìr. The act stands without comment between a grain ruling and the mending of a bridge.
- **3 an t-Iuchar, LE 53** — *The thinning*. Cut off from the vein, the strength the crossing asked of them fades in the children of those who went. By the third generation over the water nothing is left that Dia-thìr would know.
- **28 an t-Sultain, LE 53** — *The custodians' second count* (Muileann dhearg). The vein-house counts again the households of the coal-right and sets the loss at one hand in five. Beside it Donnchadh mac Thormoid writes that the vein answers no differently for those who stayed.
- **1 an Lùnastal, LE 54** — *The Mourning Custom*. Dia-thìr sets in order a rite of mourning for the departed, neither wholly grief nor wholly feast. In a far later age it was used again, uneasily, for a very different leaving.
- **27 an Dàmhair, LE 54** — *The white sorrow first kept at court* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag mourns her sister in undyed wool, with one place left empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast. The court calls it an Tùrsa Geal, the white sorrow, and within a generation it is kept in every harbour town of the island.
- **7 am Faoilleach, LE 55** — *The custodians fewer*. With part of the coal-bound folk gone, the Dia-thìrich order themselves anew about a smaller and closer class of custodians. From this shape every later nobility descends.
- **4 an t-Iuchar, LE 55** — *The seven houses of custody* (Muileann dhearg). The custodian households that remain are gathered into seven houses, each answerable to the vein-house for its share of the coal and of the measured burning: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. Here for the first time the right to the coal passes by house and not by apprenticeship.
- **28 an t-Iuchar, LE 55** — *Death of Queen Beathag* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, the last ruler of Dia-thìr who saw the fleet. Her son Raghnall mac Uilleim is crowned in the same hall.
- **25 an t-Samhain, LE 61** — *The rite of the empty harbour*. A rite grows up about the quay the ships sailed from. It is still kept, lessened, on a day that none can now date truly.
- **24 an Dùbhlachd, LE 64** — *The harbour at half trade* (Seann Skell). The harbour-master of Seann Skell finds his berths at half their old use, for the fishing households that crewed the fleet are gone. The rope-walks of Cuan shean turn off hands for the first time.
- **8 an Gearran, LE 65** — *The second silence*. There is a rumour of a second, smaller crossing, with fewer ships and no word of where they went. Nothing that survives confirms or denies it.
- **5 am Màrt, LE 67** — *The watch at Ceann mhòr* (Ceann mhòr). The fishing families of Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast keep a watch from the headland for returning sails, household by household in turn. The watch lapses within a generation. No sail is seen.
- **13 am Màrt, LE 67** — *The west quay renamed*. The quay the ships sailed from is given a new name, so that common trade might go on under the old one without the memory. It is an early and quiet forgetting, made on purpose.
- **15 an Lùnastal, LE 67** — *Cidhe an Diosail* (Seann Skell). The departure berth is entered in the harbour rolls of Seann Skell as Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn. The name Cidhe an Iar passes to the new fish-wharf at the north end of the strand, and within a few years the fishers use it without a thought.
- **21 an Lùnastal, LE 67** — *Roghnaich takes its narrow sense*. In the custody-book the verb roghnaich, to choose, begins to stand with no object, meaning to have chosen the crossing. The scribes of the next century use it so without explaining it, the surest sign that it had passed into common speech.
- **31 an Lùnastal, LE 67** — *The first generation that never saw the fleet*. Children born soon after the Setting-Out grow up never having seen the harbour with those ships in it. To them the leaving is already history.
- **8 an t-Sultain, LE 67** — *Death of Alasdair Saor* (Seann Skell). Alasdair Saor, who laid the first deep keel, dies at Seann Skell. His last work was a coasting trader of the old sewn-plank kind, built for a fish merchant of Inis àrsaidh.
- **27 an t-Ògmhios, LE 84** — *The shipwrights' fellowship ends*. No more sea-going ships being wanted, the fellowship that built the fleet of the Sundering quietly breaks up. Its craft is half forgotten by the time anyone needs it again.
- **29 an Cèitean, LE 85** — *The keel-moulds burned* (Seann Skell). In a hard season the patterns and moulds of the broken fellowship, kept in a shed on the strand at Seann Skell, are burned for firewood. The harbour-master notes the loss of the shed and not of what was in it.
- **30 an Giblean, LE 109** — *The mountain divided among the houses* (Muileann dhearg). The seven houses draw lots at the vein-house for the galleries each will keep, and the vein-house confirms each its Small-Burning measure. The lot-stones were kept in a bag at Muileann dhearg and shown to visitors for centuries after.
- **14 an t-Iuchar, LE 109** — *The coppice law of Doire fhionn* (Doire fhionn). The great oaks gone to the fleet, the shire of Doire fhionn forbids the felling of any living oak without the reeve's mark and begins to cut its woods by coppice. The law spreads to every shire with a Doire in its name.
- **12 an Lùnastal, LE 109** — *The lamps kept at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). The waterfront of Seann Skell keeps the night of lamps each year on the eve of the rite of the empty harbour. The children are told the lamps are for ships coming home, and the priests do not gainsay it.
- **9 an Dàmhair, LE 109** — *Death of Donnchadh mac Thormoid* (Muileann dhearg). Donnchadh mac Thormoid, the vein-house scribe who began the count of years, dies at Muileann dhearg. His last entry is the season's burning of coal, household by household, in the same hand as his first.
- **7 an t-Samhain, LE 125** — *Raghnall dies; Ìomhar crowned* (Cathair dhearg). King Raghnall mac Uilleim dies at Cathair dhearg after a long and quiet reign, and his son Ìomhar mac Raghnaill is crowned. The custody-book gives Raghnall's reign a single line.
- **6 an Dùbhlachd, LE 149** — *The silversmiths of Muileann chiar* (Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid). Silver of the seam at Muileann chiar, mined since the Holy Age, is wrought into neck-rings for the heads of the seven houses. The smiths' fellowship of the seam, heirs of Sliochd Fhearchair, keeps its craft within four families.
- **4 am Faoilleach, LE 154** — *Inis mhòr's grain fleet* (Inis mhòr). Inis mhòr in the north builds barges to carry grain down the Abhainn ghorm to Caol bheag, and from Ros chiar at the river mouth west along the coast to Cnoc bheag. They are sewn-plank boats of the old kind, and none lies a night out of sight of land.
- **2 an Gearran, LE 156** — *The coughing sickness at Caol fhiadhaich* (Caol fhiadhaich). A coughing sickness runs through Caol fhiadhaich on the south-west coast and kills some two hundred before it burns out. The shared meal is kept throughout, and the reeve holds that it saved the rest.
- **3 am Màrt, LE 164** — *Am Buabhall Fortanach rebuilt in stone* (Am Buabhall Fortanach). The old road-house of Am Buabhall Fortanach burns to its footings, and its keeper, Eilidh nic Chaluim, rebuilds it in stone. It is already known for its jugged buffalo.
- **7 an Dàmhair, LE 179** — *The spirit-house at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). The keepers of the Old Spirits, the faith of the hearths, raise a house for the ancestors at Dùn ìseal, and cut the names of the dead of the eastern shires on wooden posts. The posts are cut anew each generation as the old ones rot.
- **30 an Giblean, LE 180** — *Ìomhar dies without an heir* (Cathair dhearg). King Ìomhar mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg with no living child, and with him ends the line of Beathag. The heads of the seven houses are summoned to the capital to name a king.
- **19 an Gearran, LE 182** — *Fearchar mac Lachlainn chosen* (Cathair dhearg). The heads of the houses choose Fearchar mac Lachlainn of Baile Mòr dhomhain, of Clann Fhearchair, and he is crowned at Cathair dhearg. He is the first king made by the custodian houses and not by descent.
- **20 am Màrt, LE 194** — *A court at Baile Mòr dhomhain* (Baile Mòr dhomhain). King Fearchar keeps his court part of each year at Baile Mòr dhomhain, near the mountain, that he may take counsel of the vein-house without a journey. The double court lasts as long as his house.
- **21 an Gearran, LE 209** — *The fishers of Àth fhiadhaich* (Àth fhiadhaich). After a season of losses the fishing families of Àth fhiadhaich join in one fellowship to share boats and nets. It is the first fishers' fellowship on the east coast.
- **21 an t-Ògmhios, LE 211** — *Fearchar Donn crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Fearchar mac Lachlainn dies, and his son, called Fearchar Donn, is crowned at Cathair dhearg without dispute.
- **20 an Giblean, LE 229** — *Gormshuil of the Hawk* (Cnoc bheag). At Cnoc bheag, where the dawn-hawk rite of the Holy Age is still kept, the priestess Gormshuil nic Artair teaches that the hawk of the rite is Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, eldest of men, and remembering all things with him. The vein, she teaches, is the Hungry Hawk, to be fed the measured handful and no more, for a hawk overfed will not hunt and a hawk starved will turn on the hand. Her followers gather the old rite into the first house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig, the order of the Hawk of Acaill.
- **22 am Màrt, LE 239** — *The hawk-house at Ros gheal* (Ros gheal). Gormshuil's pupils found a second house of the Hawk at Ros gheal. Its priests take charge of the measured burning for all the country between Ros gheal on the coast and Cnoc bheag up the river.
- **17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 244** — *Flood at Seann Vell* (Seann Vell). In a wet spring the river at Seann Vell on the south-east coast breaks its banks and carries away the lower mills. The mill-wrights build them again on the higher bank.
- **5 an t-Ògmhios, LE 251** — *The sayings of Gormshuil written* (Cnoc bheag). After Gormshuil's death her sayings are written at Cnoc bheag as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the Book of the Hawk. The copyist, Ùisdean mac Pàdraig, marks every saying he did not hear from her own mouth, and these are the greater part.
- **23 an t-Samhain, LE 259** — *The storm that took Seann Toll's boats* (Seann Toll). A northern storm, named Am Fuath Mòr in the harbour rolls, breaks the harbour wall of Seann Toll and sinks forty boats at their moorings. Eighteen fishers drown.
- **16 an t-Iuchar, LE 261** — *Seann Toll walls its harbour again* (Seann Toll). Seann Toll builds its harbour wall again, higher and with a hooked end, to a plan the reeve had from the masons of the capital. The wall stands through every storm of this age.
- **12 an t-Sultain, LE 261** — *The walls of Dùn dhearg* (Dùn dhearg). Clann Ìomhair, who hold the land about Dùn dhearg in the eastern hills, wall it in stone. These are the first walls on the island raised by a custodian house and not by the crown.
- **11 an Dàmhair, LE 261** — *Queen Sìleas's measures* (Cathair dhearg). Sìleas nic Fhearchair, crowned after her father Fearchar Donn, fixes one measure for grain across the island, the firlot of Cathair dhearg, so that barter between shires need not begin with a quarrel over the size of a basket. Firlots of oak bound with iron are sent to every shire seat.
- **22 an t-Sultain, LE 284** — *Tally-houses in the royal granaries* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Sìleas sets a tally-house in each royal granary, where every exchange of grain for cloth, salt or labour is cut on paired sticks, one for each party. It is the first reckoning of trade across the whole island, and it runs without coin.
- **17 an t-Samhain, LE 287** — *The market charter of Cathair fhada* (Cathair fhada). Queen Sìleas grants Cathair fhada a market on its ridge at every full moon, with a tally-house for the south; it is the first market right cut on paired sticks. The merchants of the long city carry the honey, hemp, wax and pots of the south to the capital, and begin to go as one company to the harvest fair at Muileann òg.
- **21 an Dàmhair, LE 289** — *Drochaid Cathair dhearg widened* (Drochaid Cathair dhearg). The old stone bridge over Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg is widened for two carts to pass. Queen Sìleas's name is cut on the downstream parapet, and may still be read there.
- **26 an t-Iuchar, LE 304** — *The crossing days of the panthers* (Imrich nam Pantar). In the southern hills near Imrich nam Pantar the herders keep the panther roads clear on the days the great cats cross, and drive their flocks off the paths beforehand. The crossing days are the first thing the southern shires agree on in writing.
- **24 an Lùnastal, LE 304** — *An Leòmhann Buidhe on the north road* (An Leòmhann Buidhe). An Leòmhann Buidhe, a road-house on the northern mining road, serves the coal-carters oatcakes fried in linseed oil, and fire water. Its keeper is fined for watering the fire water.
- **29 an Cèitean, LE 314** — *The house of disputation at Dùn thais* (Dùn thais). Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn, a druid of the schools of Flidais, lady of the deer, founds a house of disputation at Dùn thais, where the old question of the schools, Carson an làmh seo?, why the vein answers some hands and not others, is argued by rule. Pupils come from as far as Caol bheag.
- **1 an Giblean, LE 324** — *Coinneach's question* (Dùn thais). In open disputation Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn asks whether the hands that went with the fleet were those the vein answered best, and whether it now answers fewer. The seven houses forbid the question at their own tables; it is the first time they forbid a question and not a deed.
- **30 an Giblean, LE 324** — *Baile Mòr mhòr grows* (Baile Mòr mhòr). After a run of poor seasons Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern plain takes in families from the upland farms and doubles within a generation. Its reeve divides the common grazing anew.
- **27 an t-Ògmhios, LE 324** — *Death of Queen Sìleas* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Sìleas nic Fhearchair dies at Cathair dhearg after a reign of more than fifty years. Her son Uisdean mac Dhùghaill is crowned.
- **2 an Gearran, LE 344** — *The deep hull that would not float true* (Inis àrsaidh). A merchant of Inis àrsaidh has a deep-keeled hull built for the long coast run eastward. The wrights no longer remember how Alasdair Saor scarfed his keels; the hull lists so badly at launch that it is broken up for timber.
- **3 am Màrt, LE 354** — *Salt pans at Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). The river town of Ros fhionn in the north-east lays out salt pans at the brine springs on its river flats and sends salt inland over Drochaid Ros fhionn. Within a generation Ros fhionn salt is the common measure of worth in the north-eastern shires.
- **18 an t-Sultain, LE 361** — *The wool of Baile gharbh* (Baile gharbh). The weavers of Baile gharbh make a heavy undyed cloth that sheds rain, and it becomes the common cloak of the north-east. In this cloth the white sorrow is kept.
- **20 an Lùnastal, LE 369** — *Salt over Drochaid Ros fhionn* (Drochaid Ros fhionn). So many salt carts cross Drochaid Ros fhionn that the bridge-keeper is granted a handful from each load. His salt-box is said to hold more than some villages' granaries.
- **27 an Cèitean, LE 379** — *The wells crack at Cill ghlas* (Scàineadh Cill ghlas). An earth tremor in the hills about Cill ghlas cracks three wells and brings down a byre. The custodians of the vein-house note it, and note that the galleries were untouched.
- **26 an Giblean, LE 394** — *The Hollow Man spoken of again* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). The shepherds of the Doire uaine hills will light no fires on the high pastures, for the old inscriptions of Marbh-bheò Doire uaine. A reeve sent from Muileann chiar to make them see sense does not stay the night.
- **25 an Cèitean, LE 394** — *Aonghas mac Uisdein crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Uisdean mac Dhùghaill dies, and his son Aonghas mac Uisdein is crowned at Cathair dhearg. Aonghas is the first king to learn his letters as a child.
- **23 an t-Ògmhios, LE 394** — *Àth fhiadhaich salt fish* (Àth fhiadhaich). Àth fhiadhaich begins to salt its catch with Ros fhionn salt and send it inland to the mining towns. From this time the mining shires eat salt fish in the lean season.
- **28 am Màrt, LE 409** — *Clach first preached at Inis thais* (Inis thais). Dòmhnall mac Ailein, a net-maker of Inis thais, where the wolf-sworn's stone Clach stands, preaches that the stone is Lia Fàil, which cries out under the rightful king, and that its sworn guards are the Fianna, who keep the island as a wolf keeps its range. His hearers are the first congregation of Òrd na Cloiche, the order of the Stone.
- **16 an Dùbhlachd, LE 419** — *The wolf-house at Inis thais* (Inis thais). The followers of Dòmhnall mac Ailein raise at Inis thais the first temple on the island to Lia Fàil by name. It is roofed with slate brought by sea from the north.
- **29 am Faoilleach, LE 429** — *Hawk and wolf at Caol leathan* (Caol leathan). The priests of the Hawk and the Fianna of the Stone both claim the harbour shrine at Caol leathan. The king's reeve divides its days between them, as the sacred woods were divided in the Holy Age, and the division holds.
- **28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 435** — *The market inside the new gate* (Seann Skell). Seann Skell on the Hawk bay is walled, and a market is granted inside the new landward gate, where amber, whale-oil, honey and the sheep of the northern moors are sold. The amber-workers of the bay swear to sell no rough amber outside the walls.
- **31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 441** — *Macha at court* (Cathair dhearg). King Aonghas takes up the wood-watchers' rite of Macha, which keeps the two horses of one chariot, foaled on one night, Liath Macha the grey and Dubh Sainglenn the black: two horses, one yoke, light and dark two powers in balance, and the vein belonging to both. The court follows him, and Òrd Mhacha, the order of Macha, becomes the order of Cathair dhearg and the crown.
- **28 am Màrt, LE 446** — *Fire at Tobar dhearg* (Tobar dhearg). Fire runs through the thatch of Tobar dhearg and burns most of the village. It is rebuilt with slate from the quarries nearby, and is known thereafter for its slate roofs.
- **14 am Faoilleach, LE 471** — *Macha's priests in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). The custody of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, shared since the Holy Age, passes by royal grant to the priests of Macha. The other claimants leave the wood without contest. Why is not told.
- **11 an t-Iuchar, LE 479** — *The druid schools keep Coille Naomh Muileann chiar* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). The druids of the schools take the keeping of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, the wood of Flidais's white stag, and walk its bounds each year. The walk becomes the one open rite of the schools.
- **29 am Faoilleach, LE 484** — *The drovers of Àth chiar* (Àth chiar). Drovers of Àth chiar begin to drive cattle each year over the eastern hills to the mining towns. Theirs are the first roads on the island marked with cairns.
- **23 an t-Ògmhios, LE 484** — *Eilidh Dhubh's tracts* (Doire chiar). At Doire chiar Eilidh nic Iain, called Eilidh Dhubh, wakes again the teaching of the rival school of the Holy Age, that the vein answers labour and not birth, and sets it out in tracts that her pupils copy. The tracts are read aloud at harvest gatherings across the north-east.
- **2 an Dùbhlachd, LE 484** — *The tracts burned at Muileann dhearg* (Muileann dhearg). The vein-house commands every copy of Eilidh Dhubh's tracts brought to Muileann dhearg and burned, and some hundred are given up. Eilidh is not punished. She dies at Doire chiar, still teaching.
- **31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 484** — *Death of King Aonghas* (Cathair dhearg). King Aonghas mac Uisdein dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried by the rite of Macha, the first king so buried. His son Iain mac Aonghais is crowned.
- **27 an Gearran, LE 496** — *Tormod Bàn crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Iain mac Aonghais dies after a short reign, and his son Tormod mac Iain, called Tormod Bàn for his white hair, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. The houses swear to him without dispute.
- **8 an Lùnastal, LE 509** — *Winter at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). An Taigh-seinnse Mòr on the central mining road becomes the house where the ox-teams of the mountain wait out the worst of the snow. Its keeper, Iain mac Mhurchaidh, builds them a second byre and keeps a book of the teams that lodged.
- **6 an t-Sultain, LE 514** — *The bell-founders of Muileann naomh* (Muileann naomh). A family of Muileann naomh casts the first bronze bell on Dia-thìr to hang in a hawk-house. It cracks in its first frost; the second holds.
- **5 am Màrt, LE 519** — *An Gàire Dubh* (Cuan dhearg). A storm named in the south-coast rolls An Gàire Dubh, the Black Laugh, drives the sea over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg and spoils the season's salt fish. The town is built again a street further from the shore.
- **13 an t-Sultain, LE 526** — *The hawk-house at Muileann naomh* (Muileann naomh). Muileann naomh in the south becomes the southernmost house of the Hawk, and rings its bell at each measured burning. There the Hawk's teaching holds when it fades elsewhere in the south.
- **18 an t-Ògmhios, LE 534** — *The king's sons drowned in Abhainn fhionn* (Abhainn fhionn). Both sons of King Tormod Bàn drown when a ferry overturns on Abhainn fhionn in spate. The king has no other child.
- **8 an t-Sultain, LE 547** — *Death of Tormod Bàn* (Cathair dhearg). King Tormod Bàn dies at Cathair dhearg without naming an heir, and three claims are laid before the houses at once.
- **21 an Giblean, LE 552** — *The three claimants* (Cathair dhearg). The crown is claimed by Catrìona nic Aonghais of Inis thais, niece of the late king; by Dùghall Garbh of Baile Mòr dhomhain, his half-brother; and by Raghnall Ruadh, head of Clann Raghnaill and master of the vein-house. The seven houses divide among them, and the War of the Three Claimants begins.
- **20 an Cèitean, LE 553** — *Seann Warr shuts its gates* (Seann Warr). Seann Warr, the port nearest the capital on the west, shuts its gates to all three claimants and declares for none. Twice besieged in the war, it is taken by neither.
- **22 an Gearran, LE 554** — *The ford at Àth shean* (Àth shean). The host of Dùghall Garbh meets that of Raghnall Ruadh at the ford of Àth shean and breaks it. The custody-book counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned in the ford.
- **24 an t-Sultain, LE 555** — *The burning of Doire mhin* (Doire mhin). Raghnall Ruadh's men in retreat burn the village of Doire mhin and its granary, to deny them to Dùghall. The villagers winter at Cathair mhòr on the charity of Macha's priests.
- **26 an Dùbhlachd, LE 557** — *The siege of Cathair dhomhain* (Cathair dhomhain). Catrìona nic Aonghais besieges Cathair dhomhain, which had declared for Dùghall, and takes it after forty days, when its wells are fouled by the dead of the siege lines. She lets the garrison go free on their oath.
- **24 am Faoilleach, LE 558** — *The hearths refused* (Muileann dhearg). Raghnall Ruadh, holding the vein-house, denies the measured handful of coal to every hearth and temple in the shires that stand against him. Hearths lit with the coal for generations go cold, and this deed turns more against him than any battle.
- **14 am Faoilleach, LE 560** — *The battle of Muileann chrom* (Muileann chrom). The hosts of Catrìona and Dùghall, joined for the purpose, meet Raghnall Ruadh below Muileann chrom. Raghnall falls on the field, and the next day his own custodians open the vein-house.
- **16 an Dùbhlachd, LE 561** — *Death of Dùghall Garbh* (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Dùghall Garbh dies at Baile Mòr dhomhain of the wounds he took at Muileann chrom. His followers go over to Catrìona without further fighting.
- **13 am Màrt, LE 562** — *Catrìona Bhuadhach crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Catrìona nic Aonghais is crowned at Cathair dhearg, and is known thereafter as Catrìona Bhuadhach. So ends the War of the Three Claimants, after some ten years.
- **12 an Gearran, LE 565** — *The ruling of the hearth* (Muileann dhearg). Catrìona Bhuadhach and the vein-house set down in law that no claimant, house or king may withhold the measured handful from any lawful hearth. It is the first law written to bind the custodians themselves.
- **10 an Cèitean, LE 584** — *Catrìona's road south* (Am Buabhall Fortanach). Queen Catrìona has the road south from the capital by Baile shean and Am Buabhall Fortanach at Doire shean laid with stone, that her own town of Inis thais may be reached in any weather. It is called Rathad na Banrighinn.
- **11 an Giblean, LE 594** — *Seann Warr's gates honoured* (Seann Warr). In memory of its standing aside in the war, Queen Catrìona grants Seann Warr the right to keep its own gates and take its own tolls. The grant is cut over the landward gate.
- **7 an t-Iuchar, LE 604** — *Death of Catrìona Bhuadhach* (Cathair dhearg). Catrìona Bhuadhach dies at Cathair dhearg. Her son Lachlann mac Iain is crowned, and the houses swear to him in a single day, a thing the chroniclers remark on.
- **8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 624** — *The Book of the Three Claimants* (Cathair dhearg). Seònaid nic Coinnich, a clerk of Queen Catrìona's household, writes the story of the war from the custody-book and from the witness of those who fought. It is the oldest history of Dia-thìr that survives written as one tale and not as entries.
- **3 an t-Sultain, LE 624** — *The sickness at Inis chrom* (Inis chrom). A spotted fever kills some three hundred at Inis chrom on the south-west coast. The Fianna of the Stone nurse the sick, and many of them die of it; thereafter the town is the Stone's.
- **5 an Lùnastal, LE 634** — *The oyster beds of Doire shean* (Doire shean). Doire shean, a village on the southern shore, lays out oyster beds in its shallow bay and sends oysters by cart to the capital. The trade makes it rich enough to be a shire seat.
- **26 an Dàmhair, LE 644** — *The feast-market at Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). The crowds that come to the ancestor shrine at Seann Tarr for the great feasts begin to hold a market on the three feast days, chiefly of honey, beeswax for the shrine lights, and the dyes of Baile fhiadhaich. The wax lights of Seann Tarr are soon burned at ancestor shrines all along the north-eastern coast.
- **1 an t-Sultain, LE 654** — *Manannan preached at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). At Seann Skell, where the sting-creed of the Holy Age first called itself the only true one, the preacher Mànas mac Ruairidh proclaims its one power to be Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, whose Cup of Truth bears the yellow scorpion. He teaches that Manannan shut the western sea behind the fleet with his mist, which hides Dia-thìr from every ship beyond it, and that the crossing must not be tried again. His hearers are the first congregation of Òrd Mhanannain, the order of Manannan.
- **30 an t-Sultain, LE 654** — *Death of Lachlann mac Iain* (Cathair dhearg). Lachlann mac Iain, son of Catrìona Bhuadhach, dies at Cathair dhearg, and his daughter Anna is crowned. The chroniclers call his reign quiet, and mean it as praise.
- **29 an Dàmhair, LE 674** — *Manannan's order at Ros bheag and Cuan shean* (Ros bheag). Fishing families carry the teaching of Manannan's order down the west coast to Ros bheag and Cuan shean. At Cuan shean the rope-makers are among the first to turn to it.
- **27 an t-Samhain, LE 694** — *Within sight of land* (Ros bheag). The priests of Manannan at Ros bheag lay down that no boat of the faithful may go out of sight of the headlands. The rule is kept on the west coast for centuries, and steering by the stars, already half lost, is lost there wholly.
- **19 an t-Ògmhios, LE 699** — *The granaries of Àth shean rebuilt* (Àth shean). The royal granaries at Àth shean, standing since before the Sundering, are pulled down and built again in stone on raised floors against the rats. The tally-house is rebuilt with them.
- **24 am Faoilleach, LE 714** — *The rope-walks shortened* (Cuan shean). Cuan shean takes up half its rope-walks and sows the ground with barley. The rope trade had lived on the fleet and then on the fishing, and the fishing no longer needs rope of such length.
- **22 an Gearran, LE 724** — *Wave at Cnoc chaol* (Cnoc chaol). A great swell with no storm behind it runs up the beach at Cnoc chaol on the south coast and carries off the drying racks and two children. The village sets its racks higher up the shore.
- **11 an t-Samhain, LE 731** — *The market of the eastern road* (Baile Mòr dhìreach). Baile Mòr dhìreach, the citadel on the straight eastern road, is granted a market for the east coast. There the fish and sail-cloth of the coast towns meet the furs, hides and dyes of the hills, and the dyers of Baile Mòr ruadh sell their colours nowhere else.
- **23 am Màrt, LE 739** — *The two counts reconciled* (Muileann dhearg). The vein-house and the crown's scribes find that their counts of years since the Setting-Out differ, and settle the difference by agreement. The same agreement fixes the day of the rite of the empty harbour, which each count had placed otherwise; later scribes cease to pretend it was fixed by proof.
- **12 am Faoilleach, LE 769** — *The druid school at Inis mhòr* (Inis mhòr). Pupils of Dùn thais found a house of disputation at Inis mhòr, and the question of the vein is argued in the north for the first time. Its first master, Fionnlagh mac Aonghais, is remembered for refusing every answer offered him.
- **10 an Gearran, LE 769** — *Queen Eilidh Bhàn crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Eilidh Bhàn, fifth ruler of the house of Catrìona, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. The annals of her long reign are almost wholly of harvests.
- **22 an Gearran, LE 769** — *The bath-house at the hot springs* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). Clann Choinnich rebuilds in dressed stone the old bath-house over the hot springs of Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, and admits the sick of any house one day in seven. Its physicians keep a book of cures, afterwards lost.
- **24 am Faoilleach, LE 784** — *The sea-thieves of the north-west* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Boats out of the small islands off the north-west coast begin to rob the coasting traders of fish and grain. The sea-thieves are Dia-thìrich, men of the north-west shore, and the harbour rolls name some of them.
- **26 an Dùbhlachd, LE 789** — *Baile chrom half empty* (Baile chrom). The reeve of Baile chrom on the north-west coast reports half the houses of the town empty, their families gone east before the sea-thieves and the poor harvests. The crown remits the town's grain dues.
- **27 an t-Samhain, LE 801** — *The raid on Eilean dhubh* (Eilean dhubh). A force sent by Queen Eilidh Bhàn lands on Eilean dhubh and burns the sea-thieves' boats on the strand. Their leader, Uilleam Ruadh, is taken to Cathair dhearg and hanged.
- **19 an Giblean, LE 819** — *The dearth on the north-west shore* (Gorta Baile chrom). Harvest after harvest fails along the north-west shore, and the dearth is more than the shared meal can bear. Families leave the coast for the inland shires and the east, and the north-west is thinly held from this time to the end of the age.
- **20 an Cèitean, LE 829** — *The king-list recopied* (Cathair dhearg). The scribes of Queen Eilidh Bhàn copy the king-list of Dia-thìr afresh from its oldest surviving roll, adding the rulers since the Sundering. The new copy begins the present age with the Choosing and not with the fleet.
- **19 an Gearran, LE 835** — *The strand-market at Àth fhionn* (Àth fhionn). Àth fhionn, the ford town where the coast road crosses the clear river, holds a market on the strand for the north coast, of fish, the flesh and oil of stranded whales, wool and barley. The fishers of the north coast no longer carry their catch to Inis mhòr.
- **21 an Giblean, LE 841** — *Eilidh Bhàn dies without an heir* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Eilidh Bhàn dies at Cathair dhearg without a child, and the house of Catrìona ends with her. The seven houses meet at the vein-house and not at the capital.
- **23 am Màrt, LE 846** — *Dòmhnall Ruadh crowned* (Cathair dhearg). The houses name Dòmhnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill, of the line of the claimant slain at Muileann chrom. He is crowned at Cathair dhearg and keeps the mastery of the vein-house with the crown.
- **6 an t-Ògmhios, LE 859** — *The crown and the custody joined* (Muileann dhearg). Dòmhnall Ruadh's reeves write into the custody-book that the ruler of Dia-thìr is also master of the vein-house. Thereafter the heads of the seven houses sit as the king's council, and the custodians and the court are one body.
- **1 an t-Ògmhios, LE 865** — *The custody's seal on the king's letters* (Muileann dhearg). From the joining of the crown and the custody the king's letters bear the vein-house's own seal: a trellis of gold on blue, which the custodians read as the galleries of the mountain, and over it a hollow lozenge for Crom's slab, laid on the first break. The crown adds a white band across the field and nothing more. From this time the seal is the arms of the kingdom.
- **10 an Dùbhlachd, LE 871** — *Death of Dòmhnall Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). Dòmhnall Ruadh, the first to hold both the crown and the vein-house, dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Muileann dhearg. His son Raghnall Òg is crowned.
- **20 an t-Ògmhios, LE 889** — *The schism of the Hawk* (Cnoc bheag). A council of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag divides over whether Mòd's measure may ever be raised. Those who hold it fixed for ever keep the name of the Hungry Hawk and the house at Cnoc bheag; those who hold that a greater flock may be fed a greater handful are called the Fed Hawk.
- **17 an Lùnastal, LE 899** — *The harbour of Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). Seann Chwen builds its harbour mole and becomes the port of the coal-carts coming down from the mountain to the coast towns of the south.
- **23 an Giblean, LE 909** — *The Fed Hawk at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). The priests of the Fed Hawk, driven from Cnoc bheag, settle at Seann Skell on the north coast, not the western river port of that name. The custody-book writes their teaching down as an error, and at length.
- **25 an Lùnastal, LE 919** — *The Fed Hawk's petition* (Seann Skell). From Seann Skell the Fed Hawk asks the king's council to raise the measured handful by a quarter for the hearths of the north coast. The council refuses. It is the first plea on record to alter the Small-Burning Law.
- **14 an Dàmhair, LE 929** — *The gallery at Cill ghlas* (Cill ghlas). A second tremor in the hills of Cill ghlas brings down a gallery of the vein and kills fourteen labourers of the custodians. The vein-house closes the gallery and sets at its mouth a stone with the fourteen names.
- **12 an t-Samhain, LE 939** — *The coal-roads kept by the crown* (Cathair dhearg). The king's council takes the roads from the mountain to the coast into the crown's keeping, that no house may stop the carts bearing the measured coal to the temples. The roads are marked with posts bearing the crown's sign: the carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, An Rathad Tuath over the pass by Muileann fhada, Slighe Muileann dhearg south from the hills by Muileann chrom, and Slighe Baile òg down to the southern Seann Skell.
- **17 an Gearran, LE 944** — *The crown's riders* (Cathair dhearg). Fresh horses are kept for the crown's riders at the waypoint houses on the coal-roads, and a rider changing at every house carries the council's word from Cathair dhearg to the mountain between dawn and dark. The stabling is paid out of the coal-road tolls.
- **17 an Lùnastal, LE 949** — *The high pastures of Doire uaine forsaken* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). The last shepherd families leave the high pastures of the Doire uaine hills for the valley villages. They give the grazing as the reason; every one of them speaks also of the Marbh-bheò.
- **9 an Lùnastal, LE 959** — *The salt fair at Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). Ros fhionn holds its great salt fair, and the reeve counts some four thousand people on the flats in a single day. It is the height of the town, and the chronicle calls it the richest place in the north-east.
- **31 an Dàmhair, LE 969** — *Cathair mhòr the largest town* (Cathair mhòr). Cathair mhòr, its market drawing the trade of all the south, grows greater than the capital. The capital remains the seat of the crown, and the lesser town.
- **18 an t-Sultain, LE 979** — *The stair at Toll-dubh* (Toll-dubh). Quarrymen north of the capital break into Toll-dubh, the shaft of the old tales, long lost, and find a stair cut in the rock going down beyond their lamps. The custodians of the vein-house wall up the entrance. The one quarryman who went down never tells what he saw.
- **11 an Gearran, LE 994** — *The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr* (Cathair mhòr). The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr begin to make cooking pots, which are sold on every road of the island. Each bears its maker's sign, and some are still found in the ground.
- **31 am Faoilleach, LE 999** — *Ailean measures Làrach an Teampaill* (Làrach an Teampaill). Ailean mac Dhùghaill, a scholar of the druid school at Dùn thais, measures the ruin of Làrach an Teampaill and writes that its altar faces the central mountains and not the sea. Who set it so he will not guess.
- **20 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,011** — *Ailean's tables of the old ruins* (Làrach an Dùin-fhaire). Ailean mac Dhùghaill finishes his tables of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin and Làrach an Teampaill, with the measure, stone and lie of each. He cannot say whether one people built all three, and because of his tables no scholar after him could say either.
- **23 am Faoilleach, LE 1,019** — *Queen Mòrag Ruadh crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Mòrag Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill is crowned at Cathair dhearg. Hers are the first household accounts of a ruler that survive whole.
- **18 an Dàmhair, LE 1,034** — *The obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag cleaned* (Carragh Cnoc bheag). The priests of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag clear the moss from the obelisk of Carragh Cnoc bheag and try to read the old letters on it. They cannot, and they write down that they tried.
- **19 an t-Sultain, LE 1,039** — *Caol shean's fishing year* (Caol shean). Caol shean, whose boats fish the east coast from the mouth of the Abhainn chaol, lands the greatest catch in its rolls, so great that the salt runs short and half is dried in the wind. The dried fish sells poorly, and the town goes back to salting.
- **15 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,039** — *The thousandth year* (Seann Skell). The vein-house marks the thousandth year of its count with a single measured burning of the coal on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell, and Queen Mòrag Ruadh is there. It is told that the flame burned the colour of the vein, and that the crowd went home without a word.
- **28 an Giblean, LE 1,051** — *The market above the mill-race* (Cnoc bhàn). The hill-lords of Baile ghorm hold a market for the farms of the south-east at Cnoc bhàn, above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada. Its common goods are grain, clay and honey. Its rare good is pearls, which the women of the shore take from the mussel beds in the shallows, and which no other market sells.
- **16 an t-Samhain, LE 1,064** — *The blue dyers of Baile ghorm* (Baile ghorm). The dyers of Baile ghorm in the south-east make a fast blue from a marsh plant and a mordant of their own. Cloth of Baile ghorm blue becomes the feast-day dress of the seven houses.
- **29 an Lùnastal, LE 1,079** — *The swallowing cough at Muileann dhomhain* (Muileann dhomhain). A sickness that closes the throat breaks out at Muileann dhomhain and moves along the coast road. The town loses near a third of its people.
- **26 an Cèitean, LE 1,081** — *The cough at Seann Bhral* (Seann Bhral). The swallowing cough comes to the port of Seann Bhral. The townsfolk themselves close the harbour, and keep the shared meal by leaving food at the town gate.
- **7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,082** — *Queen Beathag Fhionn closes the roads* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag Fhionn, crowned after her mother Mòrag, closes the coast road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain and sets reeves at the fords to turn travellers back. The cough goes no further west.
- **5 an Lùnastal, LE 1,104** — *Muileann dhomhain resettled* (Muileann dhomhain). Families from the hills about Muileann dhomhain settle the town that the swallowing cough emptied, and take the empty houses by lot. The older families of the town say they never again knew half their neighbours.
- **13 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,119** — *Drochaid Ros fhionn repaired* (Drochaid Ros fhionn). The arches of Drochaid Ros fhionn, worn by seven centuries of salt carts, are built anew at the cost of the salt-masters of Ros fhionn, whose names are cut on the keystones.
- **2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,129** — *Death of Queen Beathag Fhionn* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag Fhionn, who closed the coast road against the cough, dies at Cathair dhearg. Her son Ailean is crowned, first of four kings of that name in the house of Raghnall.
- **13 am Màrt, LE 1,139** — *The Baile ghorm blue fades* (Baile ghorm). The last dyer who knew the Baile ghorm mordant dies without apprentices, having quarrelled with both of hers. The blue that follows is the common blue of the rest of the island.
- **11 an Giblean, LE 1,149** — *The ancestor-posts of Dùn ìseal burned* (Dùn ìseal). Lightning fires the ancestor-posts at Dùn ìseal. The keepers cut the names again from memory and from the custody-book, and own in their roll that some are guesses.
- **29 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,159** — *The silting of Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). A shifting bar below Ros fhionn silts up the Abhainn bheag, and the salt barges can no longer reach the quays. The salt-masters take their trade to Caol gharbh on the coast.
- **8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,169** — *Caol gharbh takes the salt* (Caol gharbh). Caol gharbh, a fishing village, becomes the salt port of the north-east, and its harbour is dug out and walled with the money of the Ros fhionn masters.
- **25 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,169** — *The stone on the neck* (Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich). Caol gharbh and Caol chrom, the two harbours of the strait, send their headmen to a stone on the neck of land between them, and there settle the dues the salt-boats pay to each. Thereafter they meet at that stone over every quarrel of the strait, and it is called Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich, the meeting of the neck.
- **20 an Cèitean, LE 1,179** — *Drochaid Ros fhionn falls quiet* (Drochaid Ros fhionn). The salt going by sea from Caol gharbh, the carts no longer cross Drochaid Ros fhionn. The office of bridge-keeper is done away with, and from this time the bridge is little used.
- **16 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,184** — *The market-court stays at Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). The salt-masters take their ships to Caol gharbh but leave their market-court on the headland at Ros fhionn, where the weights and tally-sticks are kept. The farms and forges of the north-eastern hills still bring their goods there, and the town keeps its market after it has lost its harbour.
- **25 am Màrt, LE 1,189** — *Seòlaid Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). The salt of Ros fhionn now goes by sea: its boats run down the river past Caol gharbh, round the north-east cape, south along the eastern shore past Seann Tarr and Àth bheag, and west again into the bay below Caol shean, where the salt goes inland. The lane is called Seòlaid Ros fhionn after the town whose salt made it, and the eastern boats keep it long after the salt-pans fail.
- **15 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,189** — *The millers of Muileann shean* (Muileann shean). The mills of Muileann shean are fitted with a new gearing, cut in oak, that turns two stones from one wheel. Within a lifetime it spreads to the mills of the north.
- **21 an Giblean, LE 1,199** — *The Sea-Watcher off the north-west* (Uilebheist na Mara). Fishers of the thinned north-west coast see the Sea-Watcher, Uilebheist na Mara, near enough to foul their nets. The few boats still working those waters draw further in.
- **29 an t-Samhain, LE 1,209** — *The table of years at Dùn thais* (Dùn thais). Raghnall mac Chaluim, a scholar of the druid school at Dùn thais, sets out a table showing that the heads of the custodian houses live some years longer, on the whole, than the tenants of their lands. He asks whether the vein answers the hand that holds it. The finding is set down with unease, and no answer.
- **29 an Giblean, LE 1,219** — *The table forbidden* (Muileann dhearg). The king's council forbids the copying of Raghnall mac Chaluim's table of years, and the house of disputation at Dùn thais is shut for a generation. Raghnall's own copy is kept in the vein-house and entered in its inventory.
- **2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,229** — *The great gale at Inis mhòr* (Inis mhòr). Before the autumn grain fleet has sailed, a gale out of the north-east drives the sea up the river at Inis mhòr higher than any then living had seen. Boats are crushed at their moorings, and the grain fleet does not sail until spring.
- **3 an t-Sultain, LE 1,246** — *Baile ruadh's quarrel with Achadh naomh* (Baile ruadh). Baile ruadh and Achadh naomh in the far north-east go to law over the grazing on the hills between them. The case is heard three times at Cathair dhearg, and settled by dividing the hills along a stream.
- **10 an t-Samhain, LE 1,259** — *Pilgrims at Allt an Àigh* (Allt an Àigh). The keepers of the Old Spirits renew the pilgrimage to Allt an Àigh, and a guest-house is built beside the stream for those who come to drink at the right phase of the moon. Its book names pilgrims from every shire.
- **7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,266** — *Death of King Ailean mac Raghnaill* (Cathair dhearg). King Ailean mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, leaving two sons by different mothers, Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, and each has been told he is the heir.
- **8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,270** — *The battle of Cnoc naomh* (Cnoc naomh). Alasdair Bàn's men seize Cnoc naomh and Iain Ciar takes it back. The houses divide four to three, and from this battle Cogadh nam Bràithrean, the Brothers' War, takes its name.
- **17 an Lùnastal, LE 1,272** — *The fire at Ceann mhin* (Ceann mhin). Alasdair Bàn's ships burn the waterfront of Ceann mhin, which held for his brother. The fire takes the rope stores and the granary, and the town begs its bread of Cathair mhòr.
- **19 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,274** — *The battle of Muileann ghlas* (Muileann ghlas). Iain Ciar defeats Alasdair Bàn below Muileann ghlas. Alasdair is taken alive; his captains are let go home.
- **12 an t-Sultain, LE 1,276** — *The brothers' peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). The brothers make peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on neutral ground between their lands. Alasdair Bàn gives up his claim and has the lordship of Seann Chwen for life. Iain Ciar is crowned.
- **8 an Dàmhair, LE 1,291** — *Death of Alasdair Bàn* (Seann Chwen). Alasdair Bàn dies at Seann Chwen, having kept the peace he made. His lordship returns to the crown.
- **29 an Dàmhair, LE 1,295** — *White stone from Baile Mòr dhomhain* (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Masons of Ceann leathan buy a veined white stone from the hills above Baile Mòr dhomhain for the new front of their temple. From this time the quarry is worked, and its marble goes south by the carriers' road to every town that can pay for it.
- **20 an Giblean, LE 1,299** — *Iain Ciar's grain law* (Cathair dhearg). Having seen Ceann mhin beg its bread, King Iain Ciar commands that every shire seat keep a year's grain in store against the next war. The law is kept as long as he lives.
- **14 an Lùnastal, LE 1,304** — *The account of the Brothers' War* (Cathair dhearg). Pàdraig mac Ruairidh, a clerk of King Iain Ciar, writes the story of the Brothers' War. It praises the king at every turn, and it is the only account that survives, to the vexation of later readers.
- **28 an Giblean, LE 1,319** — *The inns of the mining roads chartered* (An Sligeanach Fad' às). The crown grants a charter to the seven great road-houses of the mining circuit, An Sligeanach Fad' às among them, and makes their keepers answerable for the roads between them. The keepers meet once a year at An Sligeanach Fad' às to settle their accounts.
- **17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,326** — *Death of Iain Ciar* (Cathair dhearg). King Iain Ciar dies at Cathair dhearg. His grain law lapses within a few years, as he had foreseen in a note in his own hand.
- **22 am Màrt, LE 1,339** — *An Taigh-seinnse Òir's beef* (An Taigh-seinnse Òir). An Taigh-seinnse Òir, at the eastern end of the circuit, is written into the charter-roll as keeping syrupped beef for the custodians' reeves on their rounds. It is the first dish of that house on record; the rest of the entry is a complaint about the price.
- **20 an Giblean, LE 1,349** — *An Taigh-seinnse Reòta* (An Taigh-seinnse Reòta). An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, the road-house on the bare northern road, is snowed in for a whole season with a party of custodians' reeves within. They live on its pickled spinach and fire milk, and their complaint stands in full in the charter-roll.
- **11 am Màrt, LE 1,359** — *The hull that sank at launch* (Seann Skell). Seumas mac Iain, a boat-builder of Seann Skell, tries to build a deep-keeled hull again from the scraps of the Sundering fellowship's lore still remembered on the strand. At its launch it fills and sinks, and Manannan's priests preach on it for a year.
- **31 an Cèitean, LE 1,369** — *The Caol ìseal fishers go east* (Caol ìseal). Their own harbour silted, the fishing families of Caol ìseal on the north coast move east to Caol bheag. Caol ìseal becomes a farming town.
- **4 an Gearran, LE 1,389** — *The southern lane* (Caol fhiadhaich). The fishers of Caol fhiadhaich, on the wild strait of the west coast, take their boats round into the southern sea, along the whole south coast to the mouth of the Abhainn uaine, and up it to the landing of Cidhe Beag below Baile thais, where they sell dried fish for grain. The older harbours of the south coast, which had never sailed beyond their own capes, begin to follow. The lane is named for its first sailors: Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich.
- **5 am Màrt, LE 1,389** — *The keel-song of Cuan shean* (Cuan shean). Iseabail nic Lachlainn, a gatherer of songs for the royal household, takes down a work-song of the rope-makers of Cuan shean that names the parts of a deep keel. Half its words mean nothing to those who sing it. It is all that survives, in any form, of the craft of the Sundering fleet.
- **25 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,389** — *The Stone's schism at Inis thais* (Inis thais). The Stone's congregation at Inis thais divides over whether the dead may be prayed for at Clach. Those who say no keep the temple; the others build a second house at Baile gheal.
- **3 an Gearran, LE 1,399** — *The grey storm at Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). A storm named Gailleann Ghlas comes out of the east and destroys the harbour of Seann Tarr. The village is rebuilt and the harbour is not; its boats go to Cuan ruadh.
- **8 an Lùnastal, LE 1,399** — *The second wolf-house at Baile gheal* (Baile gheal). The dissenters from Inis thais raise their house at Baile gheal and pray there for the dead by name. The two houses of the Stone are not reconciled in this age.
- **29 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,409** — *Cuan ruadh's new harbour* (Cuan ruadh). Cuan ruadh builds a second harbour arm for the boats from Seann Tarr, and thrives on the east-coast fishing for the rest of the age.
- **31 an Cèitean, LE 1,429** — *Queen Catrìona Bheag crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Catrìona Bheag of Clann Raghnaill is crowned at Cathair dhearg, the first queen in more than three centuries. It is written that she was small, and that no one said so twice.
- **26 an Lùnastal, LE 1,439** — *The grey glaze of Muileann gheal* (Muileann gheal). The potters of Muileann gheal make a grey-green glaze that no other kiln on the island can match, and the custodian houses buy it for their tables. The secret is kept within one family, Clann Mhic Phàil.
- **28 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,449** — *The oath of the seven* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Catrìona Bheag has the heads of the seven houses swear to the ruling of the hearth before her, the first renewal of the oath since Catrìona Bhuadhach. Clann Choinnich swears last.
- **14 am Màrt, LE 1,459** — *Macha's great house at Cathair mhòr* (Cathair mhòr). The priests of Macha raise their great house at Cathair mhòr, the largest roofed building on Dia-thìr in this age. Its floor of black and white was eleven years in the laying.
- **17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,469** — *The eastern Toll-dubh* (Toll-dubh). Charcoal-burners in the east find again the eastern Toll-dubh of the old tales, with the same cut stair as the one walled up in the west. The custodians wall this one too, and the scribe binds the two entries of the custody-book each to the other.
- **2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,479** — *The dry years at Achadh shean* (Tiormachd Achadh shean). Three dry seasons one after another empty the wells of the eastern shires about Achadh shean. The shared meal holds, and the crown carts grain in from the south.
- **2 an t-Samhain, LE 1,489** — *The water-rights of Achadh shean* (Achadh shean). The reeves of Achadh shean share the deep wells among the households by lot and by turn, and write the sharing on a board at the well-head. The board is renewed each generation; the lots are never drawn again.
- **24 an t-Sultain, LE 1,499** — *The firlot of Àth shean* (Àth shean). The granary of Àth shean finds that its firlot has worn smaller than the standard of Cathair dhearg, and has been so for generations. The reeve's accounts are put right as far back as anyone can reckon.
- **30 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,509** — *The grey glaze lost* (Muileann gheal). The last of Clann Mhic Phàil dies at Muileann gheal without passing on the glaze. For a generation the potters of the town try to match it, and fail.
