- **6 an t-Sultain, AE 107** — *The cattle of Baile chaol* (Baile chaol). At Baile chaol the herds are slaughtered in the second summer of the drought, rather than watched as they die. The salt meat is sold to the Company for the camps, at a price the Company names.
- **5 an Dàmhair, AE 107** — *Doire fhionn walks for water* (Doire fhionn). At Doire fhionn in the east the women walk each day to the spring at Àth ruadh and back for water, half a day's journey. The custodians record it for the three dry years, and then cease.
- **1 an Cèitean, AE 108** — *Pilgrims at Allt an Àigh* (Allt an Àigh). The spring of Allt an Àigh, said never to have failed, runs on through all three dry years. Pilgrims who keep Na Seann Spioradan come to it from all the east, the first of them at Bealltainn, and the Administration sets a watchman to charge them for the water. He is called back after one season.
- **30 an Cèitean, AE 108** — *The pilgrims' road at Inis uaine* (Inis uaine). Pilgrims bound for Allt an Àigh gather at Inis uaine, and the townsfolk feed them freely, as the Old Spirits require. The town's own wells are low, and it gives away more water than it keeps.
- **25 an Giblean, AE 109** — *Drought-fever at Baile Mòr ruadh* (Baile Mòr ruadh). A fever of foul water follows the drought into the towns, worst at Baile Mòr ruadh, where the wells had been deepened into the old middens. Two hundred and sixty die. The Mission's report is the first to name the cause rightly.
- **3 an Cèitean, AE 109** — *The fever at Cnoc shean* (Cnoc shean). The drought-fever spreads to Cnoc shean, whose one well is found tainted. The custodians close it, and for a year the town drinks from carts.
- **29 an Dàmhair, AE 109** — *The Mission's wells* (Achadh shean). The Mission sinks deep wells at Achadh shean and Àth chrom with a boring-rig brought from an Tìr Thall, and they hold. The custodians of the east set down the Mission's wells and the Company's tallies on facing pages, without comment.
- **16 am Màrt, AE 110** — *Achadh chaol goes to the pits* (Achadh chaol). Their fields burned out by the drought, the people of Achadh chaol in the north-east go to the pits for wages, the first villagers of the eastern farm country to do so. Their custodian writes it down as the end of the village, not a flitting.
- **25 an Lùnastal, AE 110** — *The tally not lowered* (Baile Mòr dhìreach). The coal tally is not lowered in the drought. The custodians of the east, their joint petition unanswered, each write to Haskins alone; to each he answers that the matter is under consideration.
- **3 an Gearran, AE 111** — *The petition of Àth mhòr* (Àth mhòr). Iseabail nic Leòid, custodian of Àth mhòr, writes the longest of the single petitions, forty pages listing her town's dead beasts. Haskins answers in two lines. Both survive, bound together by a later clerk.
- **15 an Gearran, AE 111** — *The first inheritance of mixed blood*. A suit over whether a child of one Dia-thìrich and one human parent may inherit the customary rights of mining is decided, and the Administration makes the ruling wholly to its own gain.
- **4 am Màrt, AE 111** — *The case of Thomas Hale* (Ros dhomhain). The child was Thomas Hale, grandson of the marriage at Baile dhìreach of Eilidh nic Ruairidh and Samuel Hale, who claimed a share in a customary cutting through his Dia-thìrich grandmother. Oliver Dunstan, magistrate at Ros dhomhain, ruled that customary rights descend only through the line the Administration owns, and that it owns only its own.
- **2 an Giblean, AE 112** — *Dunstan's rule applied* (Ros dhomhain). Within a few years Dunstan's ruling is used to pass eleven customary cuttings to the Company, each because some holder in the line had married a human or been born of one. The custodians stop entering such marriages in the roll.
- **25 an t-Ògmhios, AE 113** — *A cutting at Cnoc dhubh taken* (Cnoc dhubh). Among the cuttings taken under Dunstan's rule is the old customary working at Cnoc dhubh, held by one family since the Holy Age. A great-grandmother of the line had married a human sailor; that is enough.
- **29 an Dùbhlachd, AE 113** — *The Lamp-Watch* (Baile thais). A fellowship of pit crews calling itself the Lamp-Watch begins to meet at Baile thais and Cnoc chaol under cover of a burial club. Its first known deed is to pay for the burying of an old breaker who had died in the Company's lock-up.
- **28 an t-Ògmhios, AE 114** — *Edward Vane Commissioner* (Ros dhomhain). Robert Haskins is called home after a quarrel with the Company over the price of steamship berths, and Edward Vane follows him. Vane is the first Commissioner born on Dia-thìr, at the Residency, and he speaks Dia-thìris, badly, but he speaks it.
- **27 an t-Iuchar, AE 115** — *The tram-road to Ros dhìreach* (Ros dhìreach). Vane lays an iron tram-road, drawn by mules, from the southern workings down to the coal port at Ros dhìreach. It halves the cost of shipping coal, and ends the carting trade of the villages on the old road.
- **25 an Lùnastal, AE 116** — *The night-shift order*. For the first time the digging is made to run without ceasing, day and night, and the mountain is given no season of rest at all.
- **23 an t-Sultain, AE 116** — *The night crews at Cnoc chaol* (Cnoc chaol). The order falls first on Cnoc chaol, where the Company's newest galleries are opened to crews working by coal-lamp in two shifts. The custodians' roll writes that the hill was given no silence at all, and leaves the rest of the page blank.
- **3 an Lùnastal, AE 117** — *The night-shift strike* (Cnoc chaol). The crews at Cnoc chaol refuse the night shift, and within a week are replaced by crews brought from the coast under the Company's new contracts. The Lamp-Watch keeps the strikers' families for a season, and then its money is gone.
- **5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 117** — *The strikebreakers of Muileann dhomhain* (Muileann dhomhain). The crews that replace the strikers at Cnoc chaol are brought through Muileann dhomhain, where the townsfolk turn them from every door. They sleep in the Company's barns, and several go home the next season.
- **17 an t-Ògmhios, AE 118** — *Matthew Dunne's sermon* (Ros dhomhain). Matthew Dunne, the Mission's minister at Ros dhomhain, preaches against the night-shift order from the chapel pulpit, saying the Dia-thìrich are right that even the ground must rest. The Company complains to the Mission, and Dunne is called back to an Tìr Thall. The Lamp-Watch copies the sermon and reads it in the camps.
- **14 an Lùnastal, AE 119** — *The lung-rot at Cnoc chaol* (Cnoc chaol). A wasting sickness of the lungs spreads among the night crews at Cnoc chaol and Baile thais. Unlike the Green Death it kills slowly. The Company pays the widows a pension for a year, then stops.
- **12 an t-Sultain, AE 119** — *Iain Maor and the night shift* (Muileann chrom). Iain Maor, overseer at Muileann chrom, writes to the Company that the night shift is killing his crews faster than it is paying for them. The letter survives because the Company filed it with his dismissal, which was undone a month later for want of anyone else.
- **22 am Màrt, AE 120** — *The coal line* (Muileann chrom). The Company opens its railway from the pits at Muileann chrom down by Cathair dhearg to the deep-water quay at Ros dhomhain. Its engines burn the island's own coal, as the steamships do, and the tram-road to Ros dhìreach is left to the mules. Within a year the carters' guild of Doire chaol, which had hauled the coal on Rathad na Mèinne for eighty years, loses the long haul. From the first day the Dia-thìrich call the engine carbad-iarainn, the iron chariot, and the railway the coal line.
- **18 an Giblean, AE 120** — *Coal-lamps from Baile ghorm* (Baile ghorm). The potteries of Baile ghorm take a contract for clay lamp-bodies for the night crews, thousands in a year. The potters' own book notes that they are the first lamps made on the island for work in the dark by command.
- **21 an Gearran, AE 121** — *Fionnan born*. A second child is born bound to the coal as Aisling was, half a century after her. So it is known that the thing is no chance of one birth: it comes of the digging, and it will go on.
- **19 an Cèitean, AE 122** — *The Administration's count of the people* (Ros dhomhain). The Administration counts the people of Dia-thìr by district for the first time. Its figures for the humans are true to the household; for the Dia-thìrich they are rounded to the hundred, and in the hill districts to the thousand.
- **20 an Giblean, AE 123** — *The district of the outer coasts* (Seann Vell). The Administration makes the outer coasts one district and rules it from the harbour office at Seann Vell on Eilean ruadh, where its revenue cutters lie: the islands of the west and south, Eilean bhàn with Cuan dhearg and Cnoc chaol, and the southern edge of the windy coast in the far north-west. Its surveyors walk to the edge of the great moss there, which no chain can cross, and go no farther. Beyond it the district map is left blank.
- **6 an Lùnastal, AE 123** — *Seònaid nic Dhùghaill, last of the druid masters* (Dùn thais). Seònaid nic Dhùghaill, the last master of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean to teach openly in the Age of Strangers, dies at Dùn thais. No one is named after her, and the school's register ends with her death. It is taken up again only long after the humans are gone.
- **5 am Màrt, AE 124** — *The custodians' rolls at Muileann chaol* (Muileann chaol). The custodians of the east begin to send copies of their rolls for safe keeping to the town of Muileann chaol, which still kept Beathag nic Thòmais's loft of papers, beyond the Residency's reach. The copying is done in the houses of three families, and the copies kept in a cellar.
- **5 am Faoilleach, AE 125** — *The second Muileann chaol* (Muileann chaol). Some of the copies bound for Muileann chaol go by mistake to the smaller town of that name further north, and are kept there for years before the mistake is found. The custodians note that they were kept just as well.
- **23 am Faoilleach, AE 126** — *The word found at last*. With two children now known, the custodians agree on a word for what is befalling them: fuil-ghuail, "coal-blood", rendered in the humans' tongue as coal-touched. It is meant as a physician's word. It outlives that meaning.
- **21 an Gearran, AE 126** — *The custodians who named it* (Cill ghlas). The word was agreed at a meeting of custodians at the shrine of Cill ghlas, where the oldest cutting still stood open. They chose a plain word, fit for the physician's book. The roll gives the vote; who first put the word forward it does not say.
- **26 an t-Samhain, AE 127** — *The Administration's register* (Ros dhomhain). The Residency, hearing of the word, orders that any Dia-thìrich child showing the change be reported to the Commissioner's office. The custodians obey by reporting none.
- **7 an Giblean, AE 129** — *The third change of coin*. The old barter of the Dia-thìrich is struck down as lawful payment altogether. Every bargain on the island now goes by the humans' coin.
- **17 an t-Sultain, AE 129** — *The barter houses closed* (Ros dhomhain). The barter houses at Ros dhomhain and Cathair dhearg, where cloth and fish had changed hands without coin since before the Crossing, are shut by order. A clerk of the Residency writes that the ledgers are now "complete for the first time."
- **22 am Màrt, AE 130** — *The fishwives of Inis mhòr* (Inis mhòr). The fishwives of Inis mhòr, who had sold by barter at the river steps since before the Crossing, will take no coin for a week, in protest at the shutting of the barter houses, and give their fish away. The Company's clerks record it as a glut.
- **17 an t-Ògmhios, AE 130** — *Marks borrowed at interest* (Cathair dhearg). Barter being struck down, the hill villages borrow marks at interest from the Company's stores to buy seed. Within a few years most of the villages of Muileann chrom owe the Company more than a year's crops.
- **20 an Giblean, AE 131** — *The old market at Muileann òg* (Muileann òg). The old barter market at Muileann òg, where hill and coast had met to trade since the Holy Age, closes after its last season. The ground stands empty until, long after, it is used for a fair.
- **12 an t-Sultain, AE 131** — *Mòrag nic Iain Maor* (Muileann chrom). Iain Maor dies, and his daughter Mòrag takes the overseer's staff at Muileann chrom, the first woman to hold it. The Company approves her in a letter that calls her "a safe pair of hands."
- **24 an Lùnastal, AE 132** — *Charles Merriman Commissioner* (Ros dhomhain). Edward Vane dies at the Residency. Charles Merriman comes after him with a small company of armed constables, the first standing force the Administration has kept on Dia-thìr.
- **11 an Dàmhair, AE 132** — *The constable post at Muileann shean* (Muileann shean). Merriman's first constable post is built at Muileann shean on the northern coal road, a stone house with a yard for horses. The townsfolk call it the humans' second Residency, and do not mean it kindly.
- **25 an Giblean, AE 133** — *A barracks at Tobar ghorm* (Tobar ghorm). A second post is raised at Tobar ghorm, near the northern workings. The village's custodian is paid rent for the ground, and with it buys the village out of its debts to the Company store.
- **28 an Lùnastal, AE 133** — *A grey-night vigil at Baile chrom* (Baile chrom). The Mission at Cathair gheal reports that human labourers near Baile chrom keep vigil by night in the fields, praying in silence under the sign of a grey goose, which they call the wild goose of the Spirit. The Mission cannot find whence the practice came, and calls it irregular, a superstition learned of the Dia-thìrich. The Dia-thìrich of Baile chrom disown it.
- **21 an Dàmhair, AE 133** — *Manannan's priests on the grey night* (Ceann mhòr). The priests of Òrd Mhanannain at Ceann mhòr answer the Mission's report of the grey-night vigils. The practice owes something to the Dia-thìrich, they say, but to their own harbours and not to Baile chrom: the human fishing families of Ceann mhòr learned from them the night prayer to keep the sea shut, and the labourers inland keep it as a vigil of their Church, a night of silence under the wild goose of the Spirit in place of a prayer to Manannan. The priests call it Manannan's prayer gone astray, and do not admit its keepers to their house.
- **1 an Giblean, AE 134** — *The dockers' strike at Ros dhomhain* (Ros dhomhain). The dockers of Ros dhomhain, Dia-thìrich and human alike, refuse to load coal for nine days over the new berth charges. It is the only strike of the age in which human workers stand with Dia-thìrich. Merriman's constables break it, and the human dockers are shipped west.
- **30 an Giblean, AE 134** — *Seann Vell's dockers stay out* (Seann Vell). The dockers of Seann Vell, the harbour next to Ros dhomhain, refuse to load the coal sent to them during the strike. When it ends they are not shipped west, for there are no humans among them; but they are not hired again either.
- **29 an Cèitean, AE 134** — *Lorccan born*. A third such child is born, in a mining town and not a camp; the thing is no longer bound to any one place.
- **3 am Màrt, AE 135** — *Cian born*. A fourth is born within a year of the third. Never again do the children of the undying generation come so close together.
- **4 am Faoilleach, AE 136** — *Blasting-powder at Cill ghlas* (Cill ghlas). The Company begins to drive galleries under the hills about Cill ghlas with blasting-powder shipped from an Tìr Thall. The custodians of the shrine ask that no charge be set within sight of the old cutting. The Company's engineer marks their asking on his plan, and sets the charges below it.
- **2 an Gearran, AE 136** — *Powder landed at Caol ìseal* (Caol ìseal). The blasting-powder for the new galleries is landed at Caol ìseal on the northern coast, away from the crowded southern harbours, and carted inland under guard. The town's custodians ask what is in the barrels and are told it is lamp-oil.
- **9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 137** — *Scàineadh Cill ghlas*. The Rending: in the hills east of the capital, about Cill ghlas, the earth tears open along a fault beneath a common working. Dozens are killed, and a whole mining district is shut for a generation.
- **17 an t-Ògmhios, AE 137** — *The first open fight*. A mining death, which the Dia-thìrich workers lay at the door of the humans' carelessness, leads to the first bloodshed between the two peoples.
- **3 an t-Iuchar, AE 137** — *The shrine at Cill ghlas lost* (Cill ghlas). The Rending swallows the old cutting at Cill ghlas, where the custodians had kept the rites through all the age, and its shrine with it. The custodians' roll sets down the loss of the shrine before the loss of the dead; a later copyist has put them in the other order.
- **13 an t-Samhain, AE 137** — *The district closed* (Scàineadh Cill ghlas). The Company shuts the whole district of the Rending and fences it, leaving Cill ghlas, Àth chaol and their hamlets in the shires of Muileann dhearg and Muileann chiar without work. The villages empty toward Baile thais and Muileann dhearg, and the closed district is left to the thorn.
- **22 an t-Samhain, AE 137** — *The meeting on the moor road* (Coinneachadh an Fhearainn). The folk turned out of the closed district send their eldest to the custodians of Muileann dhomhain, who meet them at a standing stone on the moor road below the town, lest the Company's clerks see them in the town hall. At the stone the custodians lend them the land at the edge of the fenced ground. The place is called Coinneachadh an Fhearainn, the meeting of the land.
- **5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 137** — *Achadh chaol raised by the dispossessed* (Achadh chaol). Folk of the closed district build a new village at Achadh chaol, at the edge of the fenced ground, on land lent by the custodians of Muileann dhomhain. It is the only settlement of the age founded by Dia-thìrich for Dia-thìrich with no Company surveyor's hand in it.
- **13 an Dùbhlachd, AE 137** — *The fight at Muileann chrom* (Muileann chrom). The death that began it was a flooded gallery at Muileann chrom, where seven died after the pumps were stopped to save fuel. When the Company's agent came to the pithead the crews stoned him and his constables, and the constables fired. Four Dia-thìrich and one constable were killed.
- **4 am Faoilleach, AE 138** — *Mòrag Maor at the inquiry* (Muileann chrom). At the Administration's inquiry into the fight the overseer Mòrag nic Iain Maor bears witness that the pumps were stopped on the agent's order. Her words are struck out. The Lamp-Watch gets a copy of them all the same.
- **2 an Gearran, AE 138** — *The grey fever* (Baile thais). A fever of the chest comes in on the ships and runs over the whole island, from the capital to the eastern farms. It kills the young and strong more than the old, the Mission notes in alarm. The camps, already hungry, bury more than the towns.
- **14 an t-Iuchar, AE 138** — *The grey fever at Cathair mhòr* (Cathair mhòr). At Cathair mhòr the grey fever shuts the market for the first time in the town's memory. The custodians' roll gives the dead by street, and the longest list is of the street where the carters lived.
- **6 an Dùbhlachd, AE 138** — *The grey fever at Dùn thais* (Dùn thais). At Dùn thais the fever takes the physician the Administration sent to treat it, and two of the Mission's nurses. The old houses of the druid masters are opened as sick-rooms.
- **27 am Faoilleach, AE 139** — *The second petition*. This one carries a threat beneath its words, not a plea. It is the first writing of the Dia-thìrich the Administration troubles to answer, and it answers with more guards, not with concessions.
- **12 an Lùnastal, AE 139** — *The signatories of Cnoc dhìreach* (Cnoc dhìreach). Coinneach Ruadh, custodian of Cnoc dhìreach, signs the second petition, and in the same week is turned out of his post as clerk to the Company store. He is one of eleven who sign and lose Company work for it.
- **29 an Dùbhlachd, AE 139** — *Eilidh nic Raghnaill* (Baile thais). The second petition was drawn up by Eilidh nic Raghnaill, a crew-leader of Baile thais and one of the Lamp-Watch, and signed by custodians and crew-leaders of thirty-one settlements. It ends with a sentence the Residency underlined: that the hill would not be worked by people who were not asked.
- **25 an Gearran, AE 140** — *The constables tripled* (Ros dhomhain). Merriman answers by tripling the constables and posting companies at Muileann chrom, Baile thais, Ceann fhada and Cnoc chaol, each with a walled store. The constables are paid from the tithe.
- **26 am Màrt, AE 140** — *Barracks at Dùn chrom* (Dùn chrom). A barracks for the constables is built at Dùn chrom, on the capital side of the hills, with room for two hundred men. For most of its first year it stands empty, for want of constables to fill it.
- **24 an Giblean, AE 140** — *Ìomhar Seabhag* (Seann Skell). At Seann Skell the hawk-priest Ìomhar Seabhag preaches that Mòd's hunger has turned on those who have eaten the hill. The hawk-shrines of the west begin to serve as meeting-houses for the Lamp-Watch, and the constables do not yet know it.
- **23 an Cèitean, AE 140** — *The hawk-faithful of Ros gheal* (Ros gheal). At Ros gheal the hawk-faithful fishing families, who had chased out the Company's customs officers a century before, raise a shrine to Mòd on the harbour wall. The constables order it down. It is built again three times in a single season.
- **21 an t-Ògmhios, AE 140** — *The hawk and the druids at Inis bhàn* (Inis bhàn). At Inis bhàn the priests of the hawk and a few who still keep the questions of the druid school in private meet for a disputation, the first between them in living memory. It is written that it settled nothing, and that both sides afterwards signed the petition.
- **20 an t-Iuchar, AE 140** — *The grey fever in the north-west* (Baile chrom). The grey fever returns and settles in the north-west, about Baile chrom and the towns of the concession, where it kills humans as readily as Dia-thìrich. The Mission's hospital at Cathair gheal overflows, and for the first time Dia-thìrich and human sick lie in the same wards.
- **6 am Màrt, AE 141** — *Muileann fhionn shut in* (Muileann fhionn). Muileann fhionn, a Dia-thìrich mill town in the north-west, shuts its roads against the fever and keeps them shut for a season. Human carters of the concession are turned back with their loads at the town's edge.
- **18 an Giblean, AE 141** — *The fever at Tobar fhiadhaich* (Tobar fhiadhaich). At Tobar fhiadhaich in the north the fever takes one household in three. The custodians of the village burn no huts; they had heard of Àth ghlas in their grandparents' time, but judge it too late.
- **9 an t-Sultain, AE 141** — *The road-houses make ready* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). The road-houses along the old mining roads begin to serve as waystations for bands of armed men. The roads make ready for a war not yet declared.
- **17 an t-Sultain, AE 141** — *An Taigh-seinnse Òir* (An Taigh-seinnse Òir). An Taigh-seinnse Òir, the great house on the eastern road beyond Dùn dhearg, digs a well in its yard and builds a wall round the well. The keeper tells the Company's carters it is against thieves.
- **14 an Dàmhair, AE 141** — *An Leòmhann Buidhe* (An Leòmhann Buidhe). An Leòmhann Buidhe, the road-house on the northern road through the druid country, takes on six new ostlers in a single season, none of whom know anything of horses.
- **22 am Faoilleach, AE 142** — *An Taigh-òsta Grianach walled* (An Taigh-òsta Grianach). An Taigh-òsta Grianach, called the singing house since the songs of Fearchar Bàrd, raises a wall round its yard and sets a watch on its gate.
- **3 an t-Iuchar, AE 142** — *Am Buabhall Fortanach barred* (Am Buabhall Fortanach). Am Buabhall Fortanach, the great road-house on the south-western road, bars its gates at dusk and keeps a watch on the roof. Its keeper, Tormod Buabhall, keeps a list of travellers and sends it up the road each week, to whom is not told.
- **30 an Lùnastal, AE 142** — *The harbour of Doire shean* (Doire shean). The little harbour of Doire shean, below Am Buabhall Fortanach, becomes the landing for the goods the house cannot take by road. The fishermen of Doire shean are paid in silver from the east.
- **28 an t-Sultain, AE 142** — *An Taigh-seinnse Reòta* (An Taigh-seinnse Reòta). At An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the northern road the stables are rebuilt with a loft for sleeping men. The Company's carters mark that the loft is never empty, and never holds the same men twice.
- **27 an Dàmhair, AE 142** — *An Sligeanach Fad' às* (An Sligeanach Fad' às). An Sligeanach Fad' às, on the eastern road near the silver country, becomes the post-house through which the Lamp-Watch sends word from the camps to Muileann chiar. The silver guild pays its keeper's rent.
- **25 an t-Samhain, AE 142** — *The runners of Àth fhiadhaich* (Àth fhiadhaich). Runners from Àth fhiadhaich carry the Lamp-Watch's letters from An Sligeanach Fad' às to the silver town. They are boys of twelve and thirteen, too young for the constables to stop.
- **28 am Faoilleach, AE 143** — *Achadh mhòr keeps the ledgers* (Achadh mhòr). The Lamp-Watch's ledgers of the money it has from the silver guild are kept at Achadh mhòr, a village near the house on the eastern road, in the roof of the village shrine.
- **26 an Gearran, AE 143** — *Seònaid's house* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, the carters' house on the coal road that Seònaid Bhàn opened again in the early years of the digging, is kept now by her great-grandson Aonghas. It is the busiest of the walled houses, the one the constables search most often and find least in.
- **27 am Màrt, AE 143** — *The first stoppage together*. For the first time the mining country stops work on one day in many places at once. Scattered as it is, the resistance of the Dia-thìrich can act as one when it chooses.
- **27 am Màrt, AE 143** — *Muileann bheag in the north-east* (Muileann bheag). The workings at Muileann bheag in the north-east, among the druid villages, stop with the rest. The town's custodian writes that it is the first thing the town has done with the hills in a hundred years.
- **27 am Màrt, AE 143** — *The northern pits at Àth dhomhain* (Àth dhomhain). The pits north of the hills at Àth dhomhain stop with the rest on the day of the stoppage, the word brought by a runner and not by the beacon. Their crew-leaders are among those shipped west.
- **27 am Màrt, AE 143** — *Ceann bheag stops* (Ceann bheag). The coal stage at Ceann bheag on the northern coast stops loading the same day. Its dockers had not been told; they stop because the coal stops coming.
- **27 am Màrt, AE 143** — *The quarrymen of Cnoc gheal* (Cnoc gheal). The quarrymen of Cnoc gheal in the north-east, who cut stone for the Company's buildings, lay down their tools on the day of the stoppage unasked. Why, no one says.
- **27 am Màrt, AE 143** — *The day the pits stopped* (Muileann chrom). On the day of the stoppage every working in the Muileann chrom district halted at once, and with them Baile thais, Cnoc chaol, the silver town and the eastern pits at Ros fhionn. The sign was a beacon fire lit on the hills above Doire mhòr, which the Company took for a heath fire.
- **27 am Màrt, AE 143** — *The coal ships wait* (Ros dhomhain). The Company's steamships lie six days at Ros dhomhain with empty holds. The agents at the quay write that they have never seen the harbour so quiet, and that it frightened them more than the crowds.
- **30 an Dùbhlachd, AE 143** — *The stoppage broken* (Ros dhomhain). The stoppage ends when the constables shut the Company stores in every district at once. Forty crew-leaders are taken; thirty-two are let go without charge, and eight are shipped west to an Tìr Thall for trial and never heard of again.
- **28 am Faoilleach, AE 144** — *Beacon hill at Doire mhòr* (Doire mhòr). Doire mhòr, which refused the first contract and then lost its water, has by now but a few households. The beacon of the stoppage was lit on its hill by the children's children of Beathag Dhubh's people, and the constables burn the heather of the hill to deny it to them.
- **25 an Giblean, AE 144** — *Fewer ships from the west* (Muir Mhanannain). The keepers' daybooks at the five beacons show fewer ships from an Tìr Thall each year, and the ships that come are older. The Company's letters speak of troubles at home and do not say what they are.
- **13 an Giblean, AE 145** — *Caol leathan's idle harbour* (Caol leathan). At Caol leathan the wool for the humans' market waits for room in ships that do not come. The merchants of the town begin to sell their wool inland again by barter, against the law.
- **9 an Dàmhair, AE 145** — *Caol bheag's empty quay* (Caol bheag). The Company's quay at Caol bheag on the northern coast, built for the eastern trade, sees one ship in a season. The Company's agent there writes that he has been forgotten.
- **24 an Cèitean, AE 146** — *Leave no longer asked*. The humans' Administration begins to give commands without seeking the counsel of the Dia-thìrich at all. The pretence of leave asked and given is dropped.
- **2 an t-Samhain, AE 146** — *Lionel Strake Commissioner* (Ros dhomhain). Charles Merriman leaves Dia-thìr in ill health, and Lionel Strake, a soldier, comes after him. His commission, read aloud at the Residency, makes no mention of the Council of Custodians, and he does not call on it.
- **26 an Gearran, AE 147** — *The council locked out* (Cathair dhearg). Strake has the council hall at Cathair dhearg locked and its keys lodged at the Residency. The custodians meet instead in Macha's temple, whose priests, who had blessed the humans' coin, now shelter those who petitioned against it.
- **27 am Màrt, AE 147** — *The iron bird* (Ros dhomhain). Strake brings a flying machine from an Tìr Thall in the hold of a Company steamship and has it flown from a field above the Residency over the coal country, to count the workings from the air. The Dia-thìrich call it eun-iarainn, the iron bird. The custodians enter it in the roll as the first thing seen over Dia-thìr that flew and was not alive.
- **25 an Giblean, AE 147** — *The edict of seizure*. The humans' Administration claims the right to take any dwelling of the Dia-thìrich it deems needful for the widening of the workings. Of all the grievances it is the one most often named in every surviving account of what followed.
- **17 an t-Sultain, AE 147** — *The seizure of Doire mhòr* (Doire mhòr). The first dwellings taken under the edict are those of Doire mhòr, for a new shaft beneath the hill, and constables carry out the last households. The village that refused the first contract is the first emptied by the last.
- **19 an Dàmhair, AE 147** — *Evictions at Baile dhomhain* (Baile dhomhain). At Baile dhomhain, the first camp laid out on paper, two streets are pulled down for a spoil-tip. The families are offered huts at Àth ìseal and marks for their timber; most go to kin in the hill villages instead.
- **24 an Cèitean, AE 148** — *Mòrag Maor lays down the staff* (Muileann chrom). Mòrag nic Iain Maor, fourth of her line to hold the overseer's staff at Muileann chrom, will not carry out evictions in her district, and breaks the staff at the Company's door. Three other overseers give up their places in the same month, and the Company puts humans in them.
- **21 an t-Iuchar, AE 148** — *The silver guild arms* (Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid). The silver guild of Muileann chiar, still holding its seam under the compact of a century before, begins to buy rifles through the eastern pirates. Its ledger enters them as refining tools.
- **19 an Lùnastal, AE 148** — *Rifles by way of the pirates* (Spùinneadairean-mara). The silver guild's rifles come ashore from the raiders' boats in the eastern waters, where no Company gunboat has sailed for years. The raiders take their pay in bar silver, by weight.
- **20 an Lùnastal, AE 148** — *The council in the forest of Cnoc bheag* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). Custodians, crew-leaders of the Lamp-Watch and the dissenting priests of Macha meet in the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag and make one council for the mining country, and choose Eilidh nic Raghnaill to speak for it. No human writing records the meeting.
- **3 am Faoilleach, AE 149** — *The order to seize* (Ros dhomhain). Strake orders the taking of Eilidh nic Raghnaill and the members of the forest council. The constables go to Baile thais and find the house empty and the town silent.
- **20 an Gearran, AE 149** — *War*. The Dia-thìrich, acting together across the whole mining country for the first time, pass from grievance to open war.
- **28 an Gearran, AE 149** — *The stores taken at Muileann chrom* (Muileann chrom). The war opens in the hills. At Muileann chrom crews under Mòrag nic Iain rush the walled store at first light, and its eleven constables yield without a shot. The rifles and the grain of the store are carried off before noon.
- **24 an Cèitean, AE 149** — *The quay at Ceann fhada seized* (Ceann fhada). Crews from the camps take the Company's coal quay at Ceann fhada and sink two barges across its mouth. No coal leaves the hills by water again in this age.
- **1 an t-Ògmhios, AE 149** — *The siege of the store at Baile thais* (Baile thais). At Baile thais the constables hold their walled pithead against the town for eleven days, as long as the first strike a lifetime before, and yield on the twelfth when their water fails. Eilidh nic Raghnaill sends them under guard to the coast unharmed. The Residency did not look for such mercy, and did not return it.
- **9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 149** — *The crews meet on the moor* (Coinneachadh a' Mhonaidh). Crew-leaders of Baile gharbh and the other northern pits meet by night on the moor above Cnoc naomh and fix the week of their rising. Each brings a stone of spoil from his own pit, and the stones are left in a cairn. The place is called Coinneachadh a' Mhonaidh, the meeting of the moor.
- **30 an t-Ògmhios, AE 149** — *The northern pits rise* (Baile gharbh). The crews at Baile gharbh and the northern pits rise in the same week, take the constable posts at Muileann shean and Tobar ghorm, and send the constables south on foot.
- **9 an Lùnastal, AE 149** — *The coal road cut* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). Aonghas, keeper of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, shuts the gates of the house across the coal road, and the men in its loft come down armed. The road between the capital and the hills is cut at its half-way stage, and stays cut.
- **17 an Lùnastal, AE 149** — *Uilleam Gobha's forge* (Muileann dhearg). At Muileann dhearg the smith Uilleam Gobha makes the Company's own blasting-powder into grenades cased in tin from the coal sheds, and forges pike-heads from rails torn up in the galleries. The rebels' council writes that without him it could not have fought its first season.
- **18 an Lùnastal, AE 149** — *The capital rises* (Cathair dhearg). At Cathair dhearg the custodians break the Residency's locks on their council hall and sit in it again. The townsfolk hold Drochaid Cathair dhearg against the constables sent up from the harbour, and barricade the bridge built for the coal-carts with the carts themselves.
- **25 an Lùnastal, AE 149** — *Cathair dhomhain joins* (Cathair dhomhain). At Cathair dhomhain the townsfolk break open the Company's warehouse, the first building on Dia-thìr the Company ever owned, and carry off its tools for the council's companies.
- **19 an t-Samhain, AE 149** — *Muileann mhin takes sides* (Muileann mhin). At Muileann mhin, a river port just east of the capital, the townsfolk argue for three days, and then send boats to the council. Through the winter the boats carry food down the Abhainn fhionn to the capital.
- **27 an t-Samhain, AE 149** — *The Residency fortified* (Ros dhomhain). Lionel Strake draws the Administration back into the Residency above Ros dhomhain and fortifies the Company's quarter of the harbour. The city below, Dia-thìrich almost to a man, neither joins the rising nor withstands it, and the constables do not trust it enough to leave the walls.
- **5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 149** — *The fight at the ford of Àth chiar* (Àth chiar). A column of constables and Company guards under Major Peter Ashdown marches up the coal road to relieve the hills, and is met at the ford of Àth chiar, where the rebels hold the far bank. Ashdown loses forty men and his baggage and turns back. The rebels lose nineteen, and the council's roll names them all.
- **3 am Faoilleach, AE 150** — *Ashdown's retreat through Dùn chrom* (Dùn chrom). Ashdown's column falls back through Dùn chrom and lies a night at the barracks there. In the morning the town has shut its gates behind them, and the column goes on to the coast without its wounded, whom the townsfolk keep and nurse.
- **15 am Faoilleach, AE 150** — *The silver town rises* (Muileann chiar). The silver guild of Muileann chiar declares for the council and opens its armoury, and the Company's agents in the town are escorted to the coast with their papers. The guild's ledger notes that here alone the rising took nothing, for the humans had never held anything there to take.
- **17 am Faoilleach, AE 150** — *The surrender at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). The small constable post at Dùn ìseal, cut off by the rising at the silver town, yields to the silver guild's riflemen after a single exchange of fire. The east of the island is clear of human arms.
- **27 am Faoilleach, AE 150** — *Dùn dhearg declares* (Dùn dhearg). The custodians of Dùn dhearg declare for the council and send it grain. Theirs is the town whose custodian wrote the only surviving defence of the Small-Burning Law, and their declaration quotes it.
- **1 an Gearran, AE 150** — *Cnoc leathan's riflemen* (Cnoc leathan). Riflemen raised at Cnoc leathan in the east join the silver guild's companies and hold the eastern road. The Company's carters on the road are let go home with their carts.
- **13 an Gearran, AE 150** — *The eastern pits at Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). The crews of the eastern workings about Ros fhionn stop the pumps and walk out, and the lower galleries flood. The Company's engineers there go down the Abhainn chaol and take ship at Seann Mhorn for Ros dhomhain. The bridge on the eastern coal road falls silent.
- **15 an Gearran, AE 150** — *Seann Toll shelled* (Seann Toll). A Company steamship comes up the Abhainn uaine and shells the coal stage at Seann Toll to deny it to the rebels, and sets the fishing town behind it burning. Twenty-three townsfolk die. For the first time the humans turn the island's own coal, burning in their boilers, against a town of the Dia-thìrich.
- **17 an Giblean, AE 150** — *The Leaden Hawk company* (Cuan dhearg). At An Cupa Dàna, the inn at Cuan dhearg, seven hawk-faithful crewmen of the river towns wait nine hours for the council's letters to the Hawk coast, and leave with them at dark. Each wears a hawk cast in lead from the cartridges taken at the store at Muileann chrom, and they are called Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, the Leaden Hawk company.
- **20 an Giblean, AE 150** — *The Leaden Hawk walks to the Hawk coast* (Cnoc bheag). The company goes on foot and lightly laden: past the burned stage at Seann Toll, through Baile thais, over the hills by Achadh dhomhain and Cuan bheag, down the Abhainn ìseal by Ceann òg and Inis ìseal to Cnoc bheag, and along the Hawk coast by Inis bhàn, Ros gheal and Seann Skell to Inis mhin, some eighty miles in a little over three days. At every hawk-house on the way they read the council's letter aloud, and at Seann Skell they leave it with Ìomhar Seabhag.
- **21 an Giblean, AE 150** — *Rumours at Inis mhin* (Inis mhin). At Inis mhin, the northern landing the humans had walled, the company lies twelve hours in a boat-shed and hears that Strake's constables ride the western roads out of Ros bheag every day. They hire a carriage of a carter of the town and leave the roads altogether.
- **23 an Giblean, AE 150** — *The watch in the grasslands* (Tobar dhomhain). Two days by carriage across country, off every road, bring the company to the grasslands above Tobar dhomhain in the western hills. They lie eleven hours in the long grass above the road from Ros bheag to the northern concession and count the constables' riders who pass. Their own list gives forty-one riders, none of them going north.
- **25 an Giblean, AE 150** — *The Leaden Hawk at Inis thais* (Inis thais). Two days more by carriage, still off the roads, bring the company down to Inis thais, eight days after it left Cuan dhearg. The priests of Òrd na Cloiche hear the council's letter in the temple of the Stone. They will send no men, but they shut the harbour of Inis thais to the Company's ships and give the hawk-faithful the use of the Fianna's roads. There the Leaden Hawk's road ends, and its seven join the hawk company when it is mustered at the western Seann Skell.
- **29 an Giblean, AE 150** — *Coaling from Inis mhòr* (Inis mhòr). The Company's steamships take their fuel from the coal stacked on the quays of Inis mhòr, the river port just east of the capital, whose barges carry it down the Abhainn fhionn to the ships at Cathair dhomhain. The townsfolk set the stacks alight. The ships put in at Ros dhomhain instead, and burn their own stores.
- **10 an Cèitean, AE 150** — *The fishermen of Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). Fishing boats of Seann Chwen and Ros ruadh, sailing by night along the south coast, board a Company coaster at anchor and burn her. The Company draws its coastal shipping back to the harbours of Ros dhomhain and Ros bheag.
- **11 an Cèitean, AE 150** — *The other Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). The fishermen of the other Seann Chwen, further west on the south coast, join the raids along the shore. The rolls tell the two towns apart by the names of their boats.
- **24 an Cèitean, AE 150** — *Cathair gheal behind its walls* (Cathair gheal). The human town of Cathair gheal in the northern concession shuts its gates and raises a militia, but sends none of it south to the Residency. Its magistrate writes to both sides asking to be left alone. The council grants it; Strake does not answer.
- **28 an Cèitean, AE 150** — *Muileann àrsaidh closes its road* (Muileann àrsaidh). Muileann àrsaidh, a town of the concession, blocks its road with carts and keeps a watch on it against both sides. No one attacks it. The watch is kept to the end of the war.
- **5 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150** — *The hawk-shrines open* (Seann Skell). From the shrine at Seann Skell Ìomhar Seabhag declares that the war is Mòd's own hunger turned back on those who fed it. The hawk-shrines of the west become mustering houses, and a company of the hawk-faithful marches south to join the council.
- **8 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150** — *The hawk company at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). The company of the hawk-faithful is mustered at Seann Skell, the western city, a short march north-east of the human port of Ros bheag. It holds the road between Ros bheag and the north-west for the rest of the war.
- **9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150** — *The southern beacon dark* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). The keepers at Tobar dhearg put out the beacon, and the keepers at Àth dhearg and Baile ìseal do the same. Company ships feeling their way along the coast by night run on the reefs the beacons were built to light, and two are lost.
- **10 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150** — *No relief from the west* (Muir Mhanannain). The Administration's letter-books ask again and again for troops and ships from an Tìr Thall. In the whole first year of the war one ship comes, with dispatches and a few crates of cartridges, and sails again within the week.
- **26 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150** — *The winter lines* (Ros dhomhain). Through the first winter of the war the council holds the hills, the east and the capital; Strake holds the Residency, the harbour quarter below it, and the western ports. Neither side has the strength to attack the other.
- **4 an t-Iuchar, AE 150** — *Grain from Seann Warr* (Seann Warr). Seann Warr, the farming town in the south-east and not the salt port of that name in the west, sends grain to the hills through the winter by the eastern roads. The council's roll lists the carts.
- **8 an t-Iuchar, AE 150** — *Hunger in the capital* (Cathair dhearg). Its harbour held by the Residency, Cathair dhearg goes short through the winter. The custodians share out the grain by household, and the roll records that they took the same share as everyone else.
- **9 an t-Iuchar, AE 150** — *The burning of the tithe-books*. In three raids the rebels destroy the tithe ledgers of the humans' Administration. Later chroniclers make much of it; it did little.
- **5 an Lùnastal, AE 150** — *The counting-house at Ros dhomhain* (Ros dhomhain). The first raid was on the Company's counting-house at the Ros dhomhain quay, within the lines. Men of the harbour quarter under Dùghall Dubh came in over the roofs, carried the tithe books into the yard and burned them.
- **6 an Lùnastal, AE 150** — *The tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh* (Ceann àrsaidh). The second raid burned the Administration's tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh, where the share owed by every settlement in the hills had been entered since the first schedule. The clerks were let go. The custodians of Ceann àrsaidh asked that one ledger be spared for the record, and their own people refused them.
- **7 an Lùnastal, AE 150** — *The weigh-house at Muileann chrom* (Muileann chrom). The third raid burned the Company's weigh-house at Muileann chrom with its steelyard ledgers, where the coal of the hills had been entered by the ton since the first contract. The rebels' own chronicler writes that the fire burned green.
- **25 an Lùnastal, AE 150** — *The fight at Cnoc ghorm* (Cnoc ghorm). Company guards and constables sallying from the capital's harbour to win back the eastern road are driven back at Cnoc ghorm, in the hills beyond the capital. It is the Administration's last attempt in the war to reach the mining district.
- **4 an t-Sultain, AE 150** — *The harbour quarter changes sides* (Ros dhomhain). After the raid on the counting-house the Dia-thìrich of the Ros dhomhain harbour quarter open the lower gates to the council's companies, and Strake is left holding only the Residency and the Company's quays. The same night men of the quarter burn the Company's flying machine in its shed above the town. It had not flown since the war began, for want of the spirit its engine burned, and nothing has flown over Dia-thìr since that was not a bird.
- **5 an t-Sultain, AE 150** — *Cuan uaine opens its quays* (Cuan uaine). The river quays of Cuan uaine, east of the capital, open to the council's boats. With them and the harbour quarter of Ros dhomhain both lost, the Residency can be fed only by water, up the Abhainn gheal from the sea.
- **21 an t-Sultain, AE 150** — *Strake forsakes the Residency* (Ros dhomhain). Lionel Strake leaves the Residency by water, down the Abhainn gheal, with his officers, the Mission's clergy and the Company's agents, and takes the Administration to Ros bheag. The council's companies enter the Residency the next morning and find it stripped of all but its furniture.
- **23 an t-Sultain, AE 150** — *Ros bheag the last seat* (Ros bheag). At Ros bheag, the western port the humans had used since the early years, Strake sets up what is left of the Administration. The human families of the west and south, a few thousand in all, gather behind its walls.
- **3 an Dàmhair, AE 150** — *Outposts at Ros àrsaidh* (Ros àrsaidh). Strake posts constables at Ros àrsaidh, north of Ros bheag, to hold the coast road, Ceum Ros àrsaidh. The townsfolk bring them food and news, and the news is always a day old.
- **4 an Dàmhair, AE 150** — *Hunger in Ros bheag* (Ros bheag). The roads cut and no ships coming from the west, Ros bheag runs short of food within months. By Strake's order the Company's stores are opened to the human families and the Dia-thìrich townsfolk alike, the one deed of his the Dia-thìrich rolls give him credit for.
- **20 an Dàmhair, AE 150** — *Cuan shean refuses the humans* (Cuan shean). The custodians of Cuan shean, where the first humans came ashore, shut its harbour to Company ships. The council's roll sets it down and says no more.
- **31 an Dàmhair, AE 150** — *The families of Baile dhìreach* (Baile dhìreach). At Baile dhìreach each side asks the children of the old joint council, many of them of both peoples, which they are. Most of them, it is written, would not answer, and neither side made them.
- **1 an t-Samhain, AE 150** — *The last ship from the west* (Muir Mhanannain). The last ship known to come from an Tìr Thall anchors at Ros bheag at Samhain. She brings no troops and no grain, only a sealed letter for the Commissioner, and sails again on the next tide with as many passengers as she can hold.
- **2 an t-Samhain, AE 150** — *The truce of Àth àrsaidh* (Àth àrsaidh). Envoys of the council and of the Administration meet at Àth àrsaidh, on the edge of the northern concession, and agree a truce: the humans left on Dia-thìr shall withdraw into the north-west under the council's safe-conduct, and the council shall leave the towns of the concession standing.
- **20 an t-Samhain, AE 150** — *Baile Mòr ruadh receives the columns* (Baile Mòr ruadh). The truce names Baile Mòr ruadh, the greatest town of the north-west, as the place where the columns will be received. Its Dia-thìrich folk are given the choice of staying or going south. The roll gives the numbers of each, and they are close.
- **29 an t-Samhain, AE 150** — *The columns go north* (Cuan shean). The human families of Ros bheag, Cuan shean, Baile dhìreach and the south-west march north along the western roads under guard of the council's companies. Few of them had ever lived in the north. The roll records that no column was attacked, and none was helped.
- **30 an t-Samhain, AE 150** — *The columns at Àth chrom* (Àth chrom). The columns cross the ford at Àth chrom on their way north. The custodians of the town stand at the ford and count them over, and it is the last count the Dia-thìrich make of the humans on Dia-thìr in this age.
- **1 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *Àth leathan* (Àth leathan). At Àth leathan, the last stage before the northern country, the columns camp for a night. The custodians of the town write that the humans asked the name of the place, and that several of them wrote it down.
- **5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The ship that sailed west* (Cuan shean). Lionel Strake, the last Commissioner, sails west from Cuan shean with his officers in the last ship on the island able to make the crossing. The keeper at Taigh-solais Baile chrom sets down her passing in his daybook. Nothing on Dia-thìr tells of her coming anywhere.
- **19 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The beacons relit* (Taigh-solais Baile chrom). The council orders the five beacons lit again, from Baile chrom round to Tobar dhearg. The keepers' daybooks, which had counted human ships since the ring was finished, are still kept, with nothing in them.
- **29 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The rolls sent to Muileann chaol* (Muileann chaol). The custodians send what survives of the rolls of the age, their copies of the petitions, the book of Baile thais and the letter-books left in the Residency, to the cellars at Muileann chaol. What the Administration's own clerks carried west with Strake is not known.
- **1 am Faoilleach, AE 151** — *The Severance*. The war ends, and the crossing itself is shut: whatever way let the humans reach Dia-thìr closes. The humans still on the island are led into the northern country that their children's children hold to this day. Cian and Lorccan, not yet twenty, grow up in the wake of it.

## Age V · An Aois Rìoghachd

*The Age of the Kingdom · the Severance Era, SE 1 – 71*

- **22 am Màrt, SE 1** — *The Tuathaich homeland fixed*. The descendants of the humans stranded by the Severance are settled by law in the north of the island and held there. It is a confinement; yet their children's children call it home.
- **3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 1** — *The Severance companies stood down* (Cathair dhearg). The war-companies of the last campaign against the human administration are disbanded at Cathair dhearg. Their rolls go to the council unburned, and the companies are never abolished; they live on as names on a list.
- **31 an t-Iuchar, SE 1** — *The boundary stones set* (Caol mhòr). Stones are set on the north roads where the Tuathaich country begins. No wall follows them. Many stand by the roadside yet, and no one has been paid to move them.
- **9 an Dùbhlachd, SE 1** — *The hungry year at Doire ghlas* (Doire ghlas). The stores that came over the water from an Tìr Thall come no more, and in their first year alone the northern settlements go short of grain. Tuathaich memory, taken down long after, puts the dead at Doire ghlas above two hundred. The Dia-thìrich made no count.
- **11 an t-Ògmhios, SE 2** — *The human counting-houses emptied* (Ros dhomhain). Clerks of the council enter the human administration's counting-houses at Cathair dhearg, Ros dhomhain and Seann Skell and carry off every written thing. What the raids of the war have left of the tithe ledgers is boxed with the rest, unread, for few of the clerks can read the humans' hand.
- **10 an t-Iuchar, SE 2** — *The north-west ports without a master* (Inis àrsaidh). At Ceann mhòr, Cathair gheal and Inis àrsaidh the humans' harbour officers sail with the last ships before the crossing closes, and take their keys with them. The Tuathaich fishermen break the locks of the harbour stores and share out what they find, house by house.
- **27 an t-Iuchar, SE 2** — *Rìoghachd Dia-thìris declared* (Cathair dhearg). The state names itself a kingdom, though it is ruled as before. Its own records carry the same contradiction to this day.
- **25 an Lùnastal, SE 2** — *The Moot at Caol mhòr* (Caol mhòr). Tuathaich householders of the northern towns meet at Caol mhòr and choose for their speaker Walter Hale, once a harbour clerk. The Moot has no standing in Dia-thìrich law. It meets all the same and keeps its own minutes, which run unbroken from that day to this.
- **23 an t-Sultain, SE 2** — *The council of the kingdom seated* (Cathair dhearg). A royal council of twelve is seated at Cathair dhearg, drawn from the custodian families and the captains of the Severance war. Its minute-books are the oldest unbroken record of the state in this age.
- **8 an t-Ògmhios, SE 3** — *The harbour-houses of Ros dhomhain taken over* (Ros dhomhain). The customs sheds that the humans built at Ros dhomhain, the greatest port of the kingdom, pass to Dia-thìrich harbour-masters. The first of them, Dùghall mac Iain, keeps the humans' tariff for want of another, and in the years after puts it into Dia-thìris line by line.
- **11 an t-Ògmhios, SE 3** — *The ship sent west* (Muir Mhanannain). The council sends a ship out past the western capes to seek the crossing the humans used. She returns after a month of open water with nothing to tell: no land, no ship, no sign of the passage. No second ship is sent. The priests of Manannan at Seann Skell say that the lord of the sea has shut the western sea again, as they have prayed him to since the Crossing.
- **19 an t-Ògmhios, SE 3** — *Niall crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Niall, first ruler of the restored kingdom, takes the throne at Cathair dhearg by Macha's rite. His is the first name in the line that the state's chronicles keep unbroken from this year on.
- **7 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3** — *A saying enters speech* (Cathair dhearg). The crowning passes with so little dispute that 'mar a thàinig Niall', the way Niall came, becomes a saying for any smooth handing-on of power. It is first found written in a tavern ledger at Cathair dhearg, against a debt settled without argument.
- **12 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3** — *The shires drawn* (Cathair dhearg). The council divides the kingdom into siorrachdan, each named for its seat, and keeps most of the human administration's district lines under the new names. The humans' surveys are the only whole ones on the island; the kingdom uses them and says nothing of it.
- **15 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3** — *The windy coast left out* (Seann Vell). The shire lines stop where the humans' survey stopped, at the edge of the great moss of the far north-west. The windy coast beyond, an Oirthir Ghaothach, with its sealers and fowlers, is set in no shire and given no maor. The council's minute says only that it 'is not in the survey'.
- **20 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3** — *The island shires* (Eilean dhìreach). Two rocks that each kept a customs station of the Administration, Eilean dhìreach off the Tuathaich coast and Eilean ìseal off the east coast, are kept as shires of their own, for the council has no rule for folding one district into its neighbour. Neither has a town to name it, and each shire takes the name of its island.
- **23 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3** — *The market of Ceann mhòr* (Ceann mhòr). At the drawing of the shires the Tuathaich of Ceann mhòr are granted a market right for the north-west coast. Its court sits in the harbour store whose locks the fishermen broke. Fish, whale-oil, seal-oil, amber, dyes and the tobacco of the concession farms are sold there.
- **4 am Faoilleach, SE 4** — *The maoir appointed* (Ceann mhòr). A maor is set over each shire to gather the Crown's dues and keep its peace. In the Tuathaich shires the maoir are Dia-thìrich, lodged in the seat towns. At Ceann mhòr the maor lives in the old human magistrate's house, and the townsfolk call it by its old name.
- **21 am Faoilleach, SE 4** — *The Crown's dues set* (Cathair dhearg). The council sets the dues the maoir shall gather: a head-due, cìs-cinn, on every household by the number of its heads, and a market-due, cìs-margaidh, on every sale made by a seller of the kingdom. The humans' harbour tariff at Ros dhomhain stands until the kingdom has a coin of its own to take the market-due in.
- **2 an Gearran, SE 4** — *The roll of arms* (Cathair dhearg). The council's clerks make Clàr nan Suaicheantas, a roll of arms, so that each maor may seal the letters of his court. The kingdom's arms are cut anew from the old seal of the custody, and every shire is given arms of its own. Many charges are copied from a book of arms left at the Residency, and so lions, parrots and crocodiles stand on the seals of shires where none was ever seen. The Dia-thìrich shires bear the pointed shield of the custody's seal; the Tuathaich shires keep the rounded shield of the humans' district seals. At Seann Skell in the west the house of Òrd Mhanannain asks for its badge, the yellow scorpion of Manannan's cup, and that shire alone of all the roll bears a scorpion.
- **8 am Màrt, SE 4** — *The maor of Baile Mòr mhòr* (Baile Mòr mhòr). Coinneach mac Ailein, first maor of Siorrachd Baile Mòr mhòr, holds his court under the market roof of the town, for the humans' courthouse has burned. He keeps it there after the new courthouse is built, and so do those who follow him.
- **3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 4** — *Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol*. The Great Wave falls without warning on the southern coast and lays waste Cnoc chaol, Cuan dhearg and Achadh mhin in a single night. It is the first disaster the new state meets by its own means.
- **24 an t-Samhain, SE 4** — *The dead of the Great Wave counted* (Cuan dhearg). Relief parties from Cathair dhearg come to Cuan dhearg on the southern coast and count the dead of the three settlements at a little over nine hundred. The harbour of Cuan dhearg is gone, and its boats are found in the fields behind the town. The wave has run on up the gulf as far as Ros gharbh, the seat of its shire, broken its quays and cast the gulf's fishing fleet on the headland. The town stands high and loses few of its people, but nearly every boat.
- **6 an Dùbhlachd, SE 4** — *Achadh mhin under salt* (Achadh mhin). The fields of Achadh mhin lie under salt and will not bear. The council moves the survivors to higher ground and pays for their seed from the treasury. It is the first relief the restored kingdom grants.
- **23 an Dùbhlachd, SE 4** — *Cnoc chaol rebuilt on the hill* (Cnoc chaol). Cnoc chaol is built again on the slope behind the old town, beyond the wave's reach. The old site is left as the water left it. The townsfolk call it an Tràigh Bhàthte, the drowned strand, and do not build there.
- **4 am Faoilleach, SE 5** — *Tonn* (Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol). In the survivors' accounts gathered by the relief parties, 'tonn', wave, is used of anything sudden and overwhelming. Within a generation the sense is heard across the south: 'tha e san tonn', he is in the wave of it.
- **1 an Giblean, SE 5** — *The wave's reach on Eilean mhin* (Eilean mhin). The Great Wave passes also over the low island of Eilean mhin off the southern coast, where none then lived the year round. The shepherds who summered there do not go back.
- **30 an Giblean, SE 5** — *The old human coinage withdrawn*. All the humans' coin still in hand is cried down and ceases to be money. Within a year a new coinage of the Rìoghachd takes its place, minted with ink of coal dust in its seal.
- **9 an Dàmhair, SE 5** — *The mint at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). A mint is set up in the old human counting-house at Cathair dhearg under Fearchar mac Dhòmhnaill, called Fearchar Bonn. The seal of each coin is pressed with an ink ground from coal dust, so that a clipped coin shows the colour at its edge.
- **7 an t-Samhain, SE 5** — *The northern savings voided* (Caol mhòr). The Tuathaich households kept what savings they had in the humans' coin. Now it is withdrawn, and their savings are worth their weight in metal and no more. The Moot at Caol mhòr petitions the council for an exchange. The petition is received and filed.
- **2 an Gearran, SE 6** — *Joseph Marlow's ploughshares* (Doire mhin). At Doire mhin in the north the smith Joseph Marlow melts down his neighbours' withdrawn coin and casts it into ploughshares, and sells them back at the cost of the charcoal. The Tuathaich songs name him yet.
- **3 am Màrt, SE 6** — *The coin at Inis thais* (Inis thais). At Inis thais on the south-west coast the new coin is scarce for most of the year, and the merchants trade in chits written on the paper of the house of the Stone. When the coin comes the chits are redeemed at the house's door, and the house keeps a tenth.
- **18 an Giblean, SE 6** — *Òrd Bhrìde given its doctrine*. The Coal Rite, Òrd Bhrìde, the order that keeps Brìde's flame and Crom's stone, is given a settled doctrine within the Old Faith. Until now it was a scattered folk reverence; now it is built upon the leyline and the unbroken line of the coal-touched.
- **17 an Cèitean, SE 6** — *The first high custodian of the Rite* (Seann Skell). Dòmhnall mac Thormoid is named Àrd-choimheadaiche of Òrd Bhrìde and seated at Seann Skell on the southern coast, where the order's greatest house stands. His first charge is to write an order of worship. There had never been one.
- **23 an Cèitean, SE 6** — *The Hawk houses refuse* (Cnoc bheag). The houses of Òrd an t-Seabhaig about Cnoc bheag refuse the new order of worship, holding that the older form of the Old Faith needs no custodian above the local altar. They are not compelled. Here begins the long quarrel of the Hawk and the Rite.
- **29 an Cèitean, SE 6** — *The hawk-house at Muileann naomh takes the order* (Muileann naomh). The hawk-house at Muileann naomh, southernmost of the Hawk's houses and farthest from Cnoc bheag, takes the Rite's written order of worship and becomes a house of Òrd Bhrìde. Its bell, the first hung in any hawk-house, now rings at the Rite's measured burnings. No other house of the Hawk follows.
- **2 an Gearran, SE 7** — *The houses of the Stone stand aside* (Baile Mòr fhionn). The houses of Òrd na Cloiche in the south-west, whose Clach, the Lia Fàil, is not Crom's stone, are bidden to send witnesses to the settling of the Rite at Seann Skell. They send none, and a letter wishing it well.
- **10 an Gearran, SE 7** — *The Moot's schoolhouse petition* (Caol mhòr). Walter Hale asks the council for leave to open schools in the north that teach in the humans' tongue. The council answers that the kingdom's schools teach in Dia-thìris and it has no others. The Moot's minute calls the answer 'clear, at least'.
- **26 an Gearran, SE 7** — *The crown's order and the court* (Cathair dhearg). The house of Òrd Mhacha at Cathair dhearg, the order of the capital and the crown, is given the keeping of the coronation regalia, as it had before the humans came. The Rite's high custodian asks a share in the keeping and is refused.
- **29 an t-Ògmhios, SE 7** — *The first census after the Severance*. The state counts its own people for the first time since it took back the island. The roll notes, and says no more of it, how few the coal-touched are.
- **30 an t-Iuchar, SE 7** — *The census of the faiths* (Baile chrom). The first census of the restored kingdom enters every town under the faith its people keep, the Old Faith, the Old Spirits or the Church. It is the first such roll since Seumas Bàn's clerks counted the rites at Dùn ìseal. On the far north-western cape beyond Baile chrom, where there is no town, the clerks find scattered families with no house of any faith, and on Eilean ghorm and the smallest islets no one to ask. All these they enter as *gun chreideamh*, without a faith.
- **15 an Lùnastal, SE 7** — *The count taken from the road* (Doire ghlas). Dia-thìrich census clerks count the Tuathaich towns of Siorrachd Doire ghlas from the road and enter few of the houses. That same year the Moot keeps its own tally. The two totals differ by nearly a fifth, and each side holds to its own.
- **23 an Lùnastal, SE 7** — *The circuit justices* (Cathair dhomhain). Justices are appointed to ride circuit among the shires, and the first of them is Eilidh nic Leòid of Cathair dhomhain. Her circuit takes in eleven shires of the south-west and is most of a year in the riding.
- **27 an t-Sultain, SE 7** — *The head-due first collected* (Cathair dhearg). The maoir gather the head-due for the first time, on the households the census counted, at eighteen purses on every hundred thousand heads, and take it with the harbour dues.
- **3 am Màrt, SE 8** — *Muileann bhàn's waterworks* (Muileann bhàn). Muileann bhàn on the southern plain builds the first public waterworks of the restored kingdom: a stone tank on the hill, fed by the mill-race, with lead pipes to four street wells. The Guild of Hewers sends its surveyors to learn the making of it.
- **10 an t-Sultain, SE 8** — *The Leòid ruling* (Seann Bhral). Sitting at Seann Bhral, Eilidh nic Leòid rules that land held by Tuathaich under human title passes to the Crown, and that the right to work it stays with the holders and their heirs. The ruling is cited in nearly every land case of the age after.
- **9 an Dàmhair, SE 8** — *The coal line repaired* (Muileann chrom). The railway the humans built from the central mountains to the sea, broken in three places in the Severance war, is mended as far as Muileann chrom. A Rail Board is formed at Cathair dhearg to run it, with a clerk, two engineers and the humans' timetable.
- **17 an Dùbhlachd, SE 8** — *The bridge at Cathair dhearg re-dedicated* (Drochaid Cathair dhearg). The stone bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain below the capital, rebuilt in the humans' day, is hallowed anew with a name-stone in Dia-thìris. The humans' stone is left in its place and turned to face the river.
- **15 am Faoilleach, SE 9** — *The necropolis at Cnoc dhìreach* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). The shire of Ceann mhin closes the old burial ground at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach to new graves, for the vines have broken so many stones that no room can be found. Families of the town still tend the old graves, and some say the place is not empty after dark.
- **13 an Gearran, SE 9** — *Eaglais nan Tuathach persists*. The Tuathaich communities keep their Church alive in the north. Quietly they keep also the telling of the First Canoe, the voyage of Naomh Breandan to the Isle of the Blessed, which the Dia-thìrich priesthood calls superstition still.
- **14 am Màrt, SE 9** — *The Grey Night kept openly* (Baile chrom). At Baile chrom in the far north-west the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane holds the vigil of Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise in the open, for the first time since the Severance. The sect keeps one night of silence in the year under Sìne, the Peaceful Goose, its name for the wild goose of the Holy Spirit. The bishops of the Church call the vigil irregular. Outsiders are not told which night it is.
- **30 am Màrt, SE 9** — *The churches of the north* (Cnoc ghorm). Most Tuathaich towns keep An Eaglais, the Church their forebears brought at the Crossing; the Dia-thìrich of the west coast beside them keep Manannan's order. A church is built at Cnoc ghorm, the greatest in the north.
- **12 an Giblean, SE 9** — *The cattle-market at Muileann fhionn* (Muileann fhionn). Muileann fhionn, the mill-town the humans built to guard the northern landing, is granted a market right for the north-western inland country. The Tuathaich drovers bring their cattle and sheep to it, and from it the droves go south to Ceann leathan and the farms of the south-east. It grows to be the greatest cattle-market on the island.
- **29 an Giblean, SE 10** — *The church school at Cnoc ghorm* (Cnoc ghorm). The church at Cnoc ghorm opens a school for its priests. It teaches in the humans' tongue and reads the Bible in the Dia-thìris text its preachers use on the west coast. In all the north, both are taught there only.
- **11 an Cèitean, SE 10** — *The border wall proposed*. A fixed boundary between the Dia-thìrich and the Tuathaich country is proposed for the first time. It is refused as needless, for the two peoples already keep apart of their own will.
- **9 an t-Ògmhios, SE 10** — *The minute on the wall* (Cathair dhearg). The council minute that refuses the boundary wall runs to four lines. The fourth reads: 'They do not come south.' Five of the twelve councillors initial it; the other seven do not sign against it.
- **8 an t-Iuchar, SE 10** — *The Allt an Àigh walk* (Allt an Àigh). The followers of Na Seann Spioradan keep their yearly walk to the holy well called Allt an Àigh in the east, whose water, the old tales say, brings fortune. The custodians of the Rite speak against the walk and do not forbid it.
- **11 an Gearran, SE 11** — *The walkers at Achadh gharbh* (Achadh gharbh). The walkers to Allt an Àigh lodge at Achadh gharbh on the way, and the village builds a long hall for them. The hall's keeper writes each walker's shire in a book, and by the end of the decade it holds names from fifty shires.
- **15 an Cèitean, SE 11** — *The mine worked to the full again*. The mine's yield after the Severance comes up to what it gave under the humans, and then passes it. The working is the same as before. Only the profit goes to other hands.
- **23 an Cèitean, SE 11** — *The Sloc Mòr concession* (Achadh dhomhain). The Crown grants the working of the Sloc Mòr, the great shaft at Achadh dhomhain, to Uisdean mac Ùisdein of Cathair mhòr, whose house held an overseer's post under the humans. The Crown takes a fifth of the yield. The terms are the humans' terms with the names changed.
- **18 an t-Samhain, SE 11** — *The night-shift kept* (Cnoc fhiadhaich). The council will not end the working of the vein by day and night that the humans ordered two generations before. The mountain is still given no season of rest. The custodians of the Rite enter a protest, and then bless the shafts.
- **14 am Màrt, SE 12** — *The pit towns fill* (Muileann dhearg). Dia-thìrich families from the hungry east go to the vein-towns for wages. Muileann dhearg doubles in size within three years. Its hall of the druid school, shut since the humans' time, is taken for a hewers' lodging and twice enlarged in those same years.
- **6 an Lùnastal, SE 12** — *Baile thais grows on the coal road* (Baile thais). At Baile thais the coal road from the central mountains comes down to the Abhainn uaine above the gulf, and the town takes in carters, inns and a ropewalk. Its people double in a decade, and it is given a shire court.
- **4 an t-Sultain, SE 12** — *Raiders off Cathair gheal* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Ships that fly no flag, some manned by men who once served the human administration, begin to raid the coast off Cathair gheal in the north-west. The Tuathaich towns suffer first, and no one defends them.
- **3 an Dàmhair, SE 12** — *The coal line reaches the Sloc Mòr* (Achadh dhomhain). The mended railway is carried up the valley to the pithead at Achadh dhomhain. The first coal train runs from the Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg in the kingdom's name, on the humans' rails.
- **25 an Cèitean, SE 13** — *The quarry at Achadh dhomhain* (Achadh dhomhain). The spoil of the Sloc Mòr, a grey stone veined with black, is cut and sold for building under the quarry-mark of the house of Mac Ùisdein. For forty years after it is used in public buildings across the south.
- **8 an t-Iuchar, SE 13** — *The shunting yards at Muileann chrom* (Muileann chrom). The Rail Board lays new sidings at Muileann chrom, where the coal trains from the Sloc Mòr are broken up and made up again for the ports. The families of the yard, who work the small engines that move the wagons, are counted apart by the Board and live apart in rows beside the lines.
- **21 an t-Sultain, SE 13** — *The western branch* (Seann Bhral). The Rail Board carries a branch of the coal line west from Cathair dhearg to the port of Seann Bhral, with a spur north to the pits at Àth leathan, so that the western workings may send their coal east by rail.
- **20 an Dàmhair, SE 13** — *The guilds restored*. The old custom of binding apprentices, from the Holy Age, is taken up again in a changed form. It is now kept for Dia-thìrich alone.
- **6 an t-Samhain, SE 13** — *The Guild of Hewers chartered* (Achadh dhomhain). The first guild under the restored custom, the Guild of Hewers, is chartered at Achadh dhomhain. Its oath is sworn with a hand on a piece of coal. By the charter its rolls are open to Dia-thìrich only.
- **29 am Faoilleach, SE 14** — *The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain* (Ros dhomhain). The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain take a guild charter of their own and bind their first thirty apprentices in a single day on the slipway.
- **28 am Màrt, SE 14** — *The indentures broken* (Cuan shean). At Cuan shean and Seann Bhral the Tuathaich boys already bound to Dia-thìrich masters are loosed from their indentures under the charter rule. Some go north. Most stay on as day-labourers, outside the guilds and their wages.
- **26 an Giblean, SE 14** — *The chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh* (Ceann àrsaidh). The ship-chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh, on the Abhainn fhionn east of the capital, take a guild charter and the sole right to supply the Crown's patrol boats. The right outlasts the boats.
- **23 an t-Ògmhios, SE 14** — *The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin* (Muileann mhin). The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin, who make the coal lamps of every shaft on the island, are chartered as a guild. Their mark, a flame over a hammer, is stamped on every lamp. Of all the guild marks, the humans' traders copied this one only.
- **6 am Faoilleach, SE 15** — *The weavers of Baile chiar* (Baile chiar). The weavers of Baile chiar are chartered as a guild. Their cloth of southern wool undersells the northern cloth at the fair, until the mills of Doire ghlas are built.
- **14 am Faoilleach, SE 15** — *Agnes Pike's school* (Doire ghlas). Agnes Pike, a Tuathaich teacher, opens a school at Doire ghlas that teaches in the humans' tongue, with the Moot's money and without the council's leave. Within ten years there are nine such schools in the north. The council never licenses them and never shuts them.
- **19 an t-Iuchar, SE 15** — *The Cill ghlas district reopened* (Scàineadh Cill ghlas). The mining district shut since the Rending is surveyed and declared safe to work. On the surveyors' word the first new shafts are cut well back from the old fault line.
- **27 an t-Iuchar, SE 15** — *The Leòid circuit in the north* (Ceann mhòr). Eilidh nic Leòid rides the northern circuit for the first time and holds court at Ceann mhòr. Of the nineteen cases brought before her, seventeen are Tuathaich suits over land. In fifteen she finds for the Crown, citing her own ruling.
- **2 an Giblean, SE 16** — *Eilidh nic Leòid dies* (Cathair dhomhain). Eilidh nic Leòid dies at Cathair dhomhain. Her rulings are bound in one book, the first law-book of the restored kingdom, and every circuit justice after her carries a copy.
- **1 an Cèitean, SE 16** — *Leabharlann Muileann chaol founded* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). A great library is founded at Muileann chaol. In time it holds the fullest record of the island's past that has come down.
- **28 an t-Ògmhios, SE 16** — *Ailean Leabhar, first keeper* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Ailean mac Iain, called Ailean Leabhar, is made the first keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol. He brings with him the council's minute-books and what is left of the humans' tithe ledgers, takes in the custodians' rolls kept in the town's cellars since the Severance war, and spends his first years having them read.
- **3 an t-Samhain, SE 16** — *A chur san Leabharlann* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Within a few years 'a chur san Leabharlann', to put it in the Library, is said of anything settled beyond dispute. Ailean Leabhar is said to have disliked the phrase, for the library settles nothing, he said, and only keeps.
- **30 an Cèitean, SE 17** — *The first readers* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The library's first reading room is opened to any who can show a letter from a shire maor. The first reader written in its book is a shipwright of Ros dhomhain, who asks for the humans' plans of their hulls.
- **27 an t-Iuchar, SE 17** — *The bath-house at the hot springs* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). A new bath-house is built over the hot springs near Muileann ruadh, paid for by the Guild of Hewers for miners sick with the dust. The guild's sick-roll for its first year names four hundred men by name and shift.
- **25 an Lùnastal, SE 17** — *The keepers of the five lights* (Taigh-solais Baile chrom). The five lighthouses built under the humans are given Dia-thìrich keepers by royal warrant. At Taigh-solais Baile chrom on the Tuathaich coast the keeper is a Dia-thìrich man lodged in a Tuathaich town, and his warrant bids him report what he sees on land as well as at sea.
- **22 an Dàmhair, SE 17** — *The Muileann chaol town grows* (Muileann chaol). Copyists, binders and paper-makers settle at Muileann chaol about the library. The town is granted a market charter, and its first market day is held in the library's yard.
- **23 an t-Sultain, SE 18** — *The paper-mill at Tobar dhìreach* (Tobar dhìreach). A paper-mill is built at Tobar dhìreach, a few miles from the library, on the stream below the village. For half a century nearly every page of the royal chronicle is written on its paper.
- **20 an t-Samhain, SE 18** — *The first royal chronicler appointed* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). An office is made to keep the records of the kingdom. From it comes the archive whence these annals are drawn.
- **20 an t-Samhain, SE 18** — *The years counted by the ages* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol).
