The Dia-thìrich had rested by the moon, on the nights of the full and the dark, and the Mission made a great deal of the difference. The custodians made little of it. It was the Mission's own minister Matthew Dunne who told the Company, against the night-shift order, that the Dia-thìrich were right that even the ground must rest (17 an t-Ògmhios, AE 118), and the Mission recalled him for it.

### IX. The Three Faiths and the Two Reckonings

The kingdom lives by the civil calendar; but the moon was never put away, and it runs on beside the civil months as the reckoning of the Old Faith.

*An Creideamh Sean*, the Old Faith, keeps its feasts by the moon. Its four fire-feasts fall on the first nights of Samhnas, Gearras, Bealltach and Lùghnas, and its orders reckon the moons as the druid schools declare them, between-moon and all. Òrd Bhrìde lights its first lamp of the year on the first night of Gearras and not on the civil day, and in a year when the moon runs late its lamp is lit nearly a fortnight after the Church's candles.

*Na Seann Spioradan*, the Old Spirits, keep the night-count at the hearth. They count a journey, a mourning or a guest's stay in nights, and their dead are waked for three nights and not three days. They keep the feasts with the Old Faith, by the moon, at the hearth and at the mounds.

*An Eaglais*, the Church, keeps the civil calendar and the week it brought, with its day of rest, its two fasts and its own feasts on their civil days. The kingdom keeps the quarter-days on the first day of their civil months (section X), and the council, the courts and the markets follow the kingdom.

So a feast of the Old Faith and the same feast in the kingdom's calendar may fall a fortnight apart, and no one on Dia-thìr thinks it strange.

### X. The Quarter-Days

Four feasts divide the year into quarters. They are the great feasts of the Old Faith and older than any order now on the island, and all three faiths keep them in some fashion, though each for its own reasons (Appendix B). The kingdom keeps them on the first day of their civil months. The Old Faith keeps them on the first night of their moons (section IV).

**Là Fhèill Brìde**, 1 an Gearran, also called Imbolc, is the feast of Brìde, whose flame was bound at Dùn ìseal. Every hearth is swept and relit and the year's first work in the fields begins. The followers of Na Seann Spioradan set a sheaf by the door. Òrd Bhrìde and the Hawk order, the two forms of her rite, light their first lamp of the year from the altar-flame. The Church keeps the day as the feast of a saint of the same name.

**Bealltainn**, 1 an Cèitean, takes its name from a bright fire, and it is the feast of summer's beginning, when the Otherworld stands near. Cattle go up to the high pastures between two fires. In the Holy Age this was the day the Hall asked the cairn-watchers of Cnoc ghlas whether the galleries might open. The first sentence under the Small-Burning Law is dated 1 an Cèitean, FE 145, on Bealltainn itself. Whether the day was chosen for the sentence the roll does not say.

**Lùnastal**, 1 an Lùnastal, is Lugh's feast of first-fruits and gathering, which he made in memory of his foster-mother Tailtiu, and the month is named for it. Markets open, contests are held, and oaths are taken before witnesses. Cathal was crowned on the feast itself, 1 an Lùnastal, DE 3.

**Samhain**, 1 an t-Samhain, marks summer's end, when the Otherworld stands open, the sìth of the mounds are abroad, and the Old Faith names Donn and the dead of the year. Before the humans came it was also the beginning of the Dia-thìrich year. The Hall filled the baskets of the Small-Burning Law at Samhain, the galleries closed, and the dead were thought nearest. The Tuathaich, whose calendar came to them from an Tìr Thall, keep the day with the rest of the island, in the Church's way, as the feast of all the saints and the day of the dead. They have never counted the year from it.

### XI. Feasts and Days Particular to Dia-thìr

Beside the quarter-days Dia-thìr keeps days that spring from its own history. Those that the chronicles bear witness to are given below, on their civil days; under "since" stands the day on which the custom is first found.

| Day | Where | What is kept | Since |
|---|---|---|---|
| 24 an t-Samhain, at night | Seann Skell waterfront | The night of lamps: a lamp on every sill until morning. Children are told the lamps are for ships coming home. | 18 an Giblean, LE 40; kept each year from 12 an Lùnastal, LE 109 |
| 25 an t-Samhain | Cidhe an Diosail, Seann Skell | The empty-harbour rite, on the day the old counts agreed; in the harbour towns called Là an Diosail | 25 an t-Samhain, LE 61; the day fixed 23 am Màrt, LE 739 |
| no fixed day | the harbour towns, the court | *An Tùrsa Geal*, the white sorrow: undyed wool and one place set empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast | 27 an Dàmhair, LE 54 |
| yearly, on the shore | Inis chrom and the harbours north to Seann Warr | The drowned-feast, an empty place for each of the lost | 10 an Dàmhair, FE 2,915 |
| yearly | Baile chrom | The wake for the boat lost off the north-west | 28 an Lùnastal, FE 405 |
| the crossing days | the southern hills, Imrich nam Pantar | The panther roads kept clear, flocks driven off the paths | 26 an t-Iuchar, LE 304 |
| yearly | Coille Naomh Muileann chiar | The druid schools walk the bounds of Flidais's wood | 11 an t-Iuchar, LE 479 |
| harvest | Fèill Muileann òg | The great fair, with its northern day | 5 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,665; the fair established 16 an Dàmhair, SE 21 |
| yearly | Còmhrag Ceann leathan | The contest with staves, since edged tools were banned | 9 an Giblean, FE 1,665; established 4 am Màrt, SE 23 |
| yearly, at its quarter of the moon | Allt an Àigh | The walk of the Old Spirits to the healing water | 8 an t-Iuchar, SE 10 |
| yearly | Seann Dunn | The ancestors of forty families named aloud by their living heads | 28 an Dàmhair, SE 22 |
| yearly | Cnoc ghorm | The northern feast of the sea, kept at the church as a blessing of the boats | 11 an Gearran, SE 26 |
| one night, undisclosed | Baile chrom and the north | The vigil of the Grey Night under Sìne, the Peaceful Goose, the wild goose of the Spirit; outsiders are not told which night | 14 am Màrt, SE 9 |

The days of the older customs are given as the Library turned them (section XII). The night of lamps and the empty-harbour rite were fixed by the moon, and since the civil calendar came in the harbour towns have kept them on the civil days that the Library's tables give.

The day of the Setting-Out has never been kept as a feast. The chronicles say nothing more of the departed once the ships clear the harbour, and the island has kept its remembrance of them there, at the harbour where the rolls fall silent, on the day the custody-book gives for the turn and not on the day they sailed. Since 23 am Màrt, LE 739, the empty-harbour rite has fallen on that day, though the harbour scribe, whose count the island followed, sets the turn on the day of the sailing. The Library does not forget that the custody-book may have taken its day from the rite, and not the rite from the book. By the last entry of the Age of Sundering the rite was kept by eleven people (25 an t-Samhain, LE 1,803). How many keep it now the chronicles of the later ages do not say.

**The Severance**, 1 am Faoilleach, AE 151, is kept at Cathair dhearg by the council as the day on which the latter history of the kingdom begins, and the era named for it bore its memory in every date for seventy-one years. The Mourning Custom of the Sundering, first made for a parting that was chosen, was used again, uneasily, for this parting that was not, and the council's keeping of this day is the use most often meant. In the north the day is not kept. It is worked through like any other, and the Tuathaich say that this is their way of keeping it.

**The Long War** left two days. The Battle of Àth leathan, 11 an Giblean, DE 21, opened *An Cogadh Fada*. Tuathaich families have raised a cairn without leave on the field at Àraich Àth leathan, and it grows by a stone or two whenever the patrols pass; whether they come on the day of the battle nobody has written down. The Battle of Muileann ghlas, 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22, ended the war, and the regiments raised in the campaign keep that day at their stations. So the two days are kept by two peoples; and the Library, whose record of the war is sealed (14 am Faoilleach, DE 24), holds what it can of both.

### XII. How the Library Turned the Old Dates

Every date in these annals is given in the civil calendar, with a day of the civil month and a year of the era, though for most of the island's history nobody who lived it counted so. The Library made it so, and the labour took three generations.

It began with Beathag nic Thòmais, the mill-owner's widow who bought up old copies of the custody-book and the harbour rolls and kept them in a loft over her mill at Muileann chaol (21 an Cèitean, LE 1,659). She did not reckon years. But she set copies that disagreed side by side and declined to choose between them (27 an Giblean, LE 1,679), and that became the way of all who worked in Muileann chaol after her. She left her loft to the town on condition that nothing in it be burned (24 an Lùnastal, LE 1,699).

The joining of the counts was done in the cellar. From 5 am Màrt, AE 124, the custodians of the east sent copies of their rolls to Muileann chaol for safekeeping, away from the Residency's reach, and three families did the copying. While they copied, they laid the counts against each other. Where the king-list gave a ruler's years and the Hall's roll gave the burnings of the same reign, the two could be made to meet, and each meeting fixed a stretch of the older count against the newer. The copyists called the result *Clàr nan Aoisean*, the table of the ages. It is the first writing that runs one numbered line of years from the Binding to the copyists' own day, in the years of the Diosal. It is also the first to divide the island's past into ages, and to set before the Holy Age an older age whose length, the table owns, it cannot measure. When the custodians sent what survived of the Age of Strangers to the same cellars (29 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150), the table was carried through to the Severance, and in that form it gave the ages down to the Severance the bounds that historians of Dia-thìr still use.

Leabharlann Muileann chaol, founded 1 an Cèitean, SE 16, took the table as one of its first possessions. The council's clerks had emptied the humans' counting-houses (11 an t-Ògmhios, SE 2) and boxed the ledgers unread, because few of them could read the humans' hand. Ailean Leabhar, the Library's first keeper, spent his first years having them read (28 an t-Ògmhios, SE 16), and he had every date in them, and in the custodians' rolls, turned into the civil calendar. For the Age of Strangers the double-dated pages of the custodians' clerks were his guide, since they set the humans' day above the night of the moon. For the ages before the Crossing he had only the moons, and he turned them by the Hall's roll of the between-moons, reckoning moon by moon back from the first double-dated page to the Binding. Each date so turned he set in the era of its age, as the council afterwards ordered for all the kingdom's records (section III). When the Library absorbed the provincial archives (26 an t-Iuchar, SE 67), the table was checked against them and corrected where the archives knew better. When the sixth era was proclaimed, the Library re-headed the years since the first working dubhan as the chronicler had done.

So a reader of these annals who finds a Holy Age deed set on 3 an t-Samhain should remember that those who did it knew no such day. They knew a night of the moon Samhnas, and they began their year at Samhain and counted it by nights. The Library's day is the civil day on which that night would have fallen, as near as the roll of the between-moons allows. Where the roll has gaps, the day may be a half-moon out, and the Library says so. Ailean Leabhar disliked the saying *a chur san Leabharlann*, "to put it in the Library," on the ground that the Library settles nothing and only keeps it (3 an t-Samhain, SE 16). The turned dates should be read in the same spirit.

**Where the dates come from.** For the Age of Dubhan, the Age of the Kingdom and the Age of Strangers the days are remembered: they come from rolls, ledgers, letter-books and the chroniclers' own entries, and from the Crossing on they were written in the civil calendar or beside it. For the Age of Sundering they are remembered more thinly, from the custody-book, the harbour rolls and the crown's king-list, all dated by the moon, and a good many were settled by agreement, as the day of the empty-harbour rite was. For the Holy Age the years come from the Keepers' roll, the king-lists and the Hall's count of burnings, which do not always agree, and the days mostly from the feasts and moons the rolls name. For the Ancient Age all rests on the tellings, the king-lists without lengths of reign, the tally walls and the tide-count. The tellings keep the order of things well and the distance between them poorly. Where they agree, the date is as sure as they are; where they disagree or fall silent it is not, and such a date should be trusted for the order it keeps rather than for its year.


## Appendix E — Words Born from History

Here are gathered the words, names and sayings of Dia-thìris that the island's history made, or bent to a new sense. They are set out in the manner of a historical dictionary. Each entry gives the headword and its part of speech, what it says word for word, what it has come to mean, the event that gave it that meaning, and a line from the annals or the six books.

At the heart of it stands the chronicle's own list of *Words Born from History*, and every word on that list is entered here with the meaning the chronicle gives it. The rest are taken from the annals and the books: titles and offices, laws and customs, the names of storms, places and quarrels, and the sayings that the annals quote. A few are the words that Dia-thìris made for the strangers' things. Dia-thìris took few words from the humans, and most of those late (Appendix F). Where the humans said *train*, *engine* or *strike*, the island made a name out of old roots, and some of those names are entered here under the years in which the annals first had need of them.

### How to Read an Entry

The headword is given in full. An article (*an*, *am*, *a'*) is written with it but not counted in the order, which is the island's order of eighteen letters, *a b c d e f g h i l m n o p r s t u*, the grave accent being ignored. Dates are given in the era of each age (Appendix D). Where no annal marks the first use of a word, the entry says so and gives only the event from which the word comes. Citations are given as the sources give them: the annals as this history renders their prose, the verses in Dia-thìris (Appendix F, *Of Translation*).

*n.* noun · *m.*, *f.* masculine, feminine · *pl.* plural · *v.* verb · *v.n.* verbal noun · *adj.* adjective · *phr.* phrase or saying · *lit.* literally

### The Glossary

#### A

**a chur san Leabharlann** *phr.* · lit. "to put it in the Library"
To make a thing official and past dispute. From the founding of Leabharlann Muileann chaol (1 an Cèitean, SE 16); within a few years it was said of anything settled (3 an t-Samhain, SE 16).
> "Ailean Leabhar is said to have disliked the phrase, for the library settles nothing, he said, and only keeps." — annals, SE 16

**Aisling-aois** *n. f.* · lit. "Aisling-age"
An unnaturally long youth in anyone; said half in jest of ordinary people who look young for their years. From the first of the immortal generation, born in the mining camps (7 am Màrt, AE 69). No annal marks its first use. Of all the words on the chronicle's list, in this one alone the jest and the legend are the same.
> "…and she does not age as the folk about her age. Her name is Aisling." — annals, AE 69

**Àrd-choimheadaiche** *n. m.* · lit. "high watcher"
The high custodian of Òrd Bhrìde, the order of Brìde's flame, seated at Seann Skell. The office came when the Rite was set in order (18 an Giblean, SE 6), and Dòmhnall mac Thormoid was the first to hold it (17 an Cèitean, SE 6). It is not the "high custodian" of the Age of Strangers, who headed the Council of Custodians; the two share a name in translation, and nothing more.
> "The Àrd-choimheadaiche at Seann Skell writes to every house of the Rite that the new fuel is not forbidden, since it is not coal, and not blessed, since it is not coal." — annals, DE 4

#### B

**Binnean a' Chlachair** *n. m.* · lit. "the Mason's point"
The highest summit of the island. When the gold coal had woken in the sea, the Mason's children carried the coals that were left to the highest point they knew and dropped them from it, and the snowflake coal took fire in the falling; from that day the height has borne their name. The tellers say that Lugh stood on it with Caoran on the first evening and named the winds. See *Seachd Guail, na*.
> "It was Lugh who stood with Caoran on the highest summit of the island on the first evening and named the winds for him, and so the snowflake coal is his in honour." — the Telling of the Making

**bonn-rìoghachd** *n. m.* · lit. "realm-coin"
Currency. Under the humans the coin was the mark, and barter was driven out in three reforms (13 an Gearran, AE 17, 2 an Dàmhair, AE 86, 7 an Giblean, AE 129). The Dia-thìris word belongs to the coinage struck when the humans' coin was withdrawn (30 an Giblean, SE 5). Its first mint-master was called Fearchar Bonn from his work (9 an Dàmhair, SE 5). After the re-pegging to dubhan (5 an Cèitean, DE 15) the realm-coin no longer rested on the vein.
> "Within a year a new coinage of the Rìoghachd takes its place, minted with ink of coal dust in its seal." — annals, SE 5

#### C

**Caoran** *n. m.* · lit. "ember"
The Young God, *an Dia Òg*, youngest son of an Dagda and Danu. Each god of his line made a world of the thing dearest to him when he came of age; Caoran chose coal, and out of coal he made all that is, the earth last of all and the island after it, and in the island's coal he hid the elements. He is the maker of this world and the god of the coal. The Old Faith still honours an Dagda first, as father of the gods (Appendix B). The name is the word for an ember such as lies in the ash of a spent fire, for it was from such an ember, under his father's cauldron, that he took the first coal.
> "He looked at the coal in his son's hand for a long time, and then he said, 'It will do.' It is said that no word of his was ever dearer to Caoran." — the Telling of the Making

**carbad-iarainn** *n. m.* · lit. "iron-chariot"
A train; the first of the *iarainn* words Dia-thìris made for machines. The kingdom mended the humans' coal line (9 an Dàmhair, SE 8) and ran its own first train on 3 an Dàmhair, SE 12.
> "The first coal train runs from the Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg in the kingdom's name, on the humans' rails." — annals, SE 12

**Cha do chaill sinn blàr, ach chaill sinn an teine** *phr.* · lit. "we did not lose a battle, but we lost the fire"
A defeat without fighting. An unsigned verse of the cold shires, from the day Raghnall Ruadh refused the measured handful to every hearth that stood against him (24 am Faoilleach, LE 558).
> "…this deed turns more against him than any battle." — annals, LE 558

**Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann** *phr.* · lit. "we did not come; we were here"
The doctrine of the Ancient Age, complete on Calbh Cnoc ghorm (6 an t-Samhain, VE 4,851). Who cut it is not known.
> "Here, it may be, the belief was first spoken." — annals, VE 4,851

**Cha loisc clach na beinne do choigrich** *phr.* · lit. "the mountain's stone will not burn for strangers"
The Keepers' ruling that no coal might feed a beacon (30 an Cèitean, FE 148). It held until the humans' towers were lit with a coal flame (22 an t-Sultain, AE 91).
> "The Keepers rule that no coal may feed a beacon, since a beacon burns for strangers." — annals, FE 148

**Cha tàinig long** *phr.* · lit. "no ship came"
The entry in the beacon-keepers' daybooks from the Severance on, after the council had the five beacons relit (19 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150).
> "The keepers' daybooks, which had counted human ships since the ring was finished, are still kept, with nothing in them." — annals, AE 150

**Chaidh an gual dhachaigh** *phr.* · lit. "the coal went home"
The tellings' words for the coal taken by Gilleasbuig Beag (2 an Lùnastal, VE 7,732), which was neither burned nor kept but laid back under the slab (4 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,734).
> "The tellings make much of it: the coal went home." — annals, VE 7,734

**Cidhe an Diosail** *n. m.* · lit. "the quay of the sunwise turn"
The berth at Seann Skell from which the fleet of the Sundering sailed. Its old name, Cidhe an Iar, passed to a new fish-wharf so that trade could go on without the memory (13 am Màrt, LE 67, 15 an Lùnastal, LE 67).
> "The departure berth is entered in the harbour rolls of Seann Skell as Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn." — annals, LE 67

**Clann a' Chlachair** *n. pl.* · lit. "the Mason's children"
The line of the mason who broke into the coal vein and carried home the first fire (20 am Faoilleach, VE 1). It is recited from the mason down, each son of each father, in the manner of the old begats (Appendix A, *The Line of the Mason*). To one of this line the Keeper of the Kin gave the Telling of the Making, and in this line the seven coals were woken, one by one, over many generations. By the waking of the fire coal its people were known as *Luchd-ceasnachaidh a' Ghuail Dhìomhair*.
> "The mason's children kept the telling after, father to son and mother to daughter, and said it over at the dark of the year word for word, and long afterward it was written down." — the Telling of the Making

**Clann na Ceiste** *n. pl.* · lit. "the children of the question"
The short name of *Luchd-ceasnachaidh a' Ghuail Dhìomhair*, the name the recited lists use. The question is the one their forebear put to the Keeper in the grove of Doire ghlas: why the coal has colours in it. Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings, was of them (9 an Lùnastal, VE 5,324).
> "…who had asked it why the coal of Dia-thìr has colours in it when the coal of the common earth has none." — the Telling of the Making

**Clann nan Dè** *n. pl.* · lit. "the children of the gods"
The godkin: the people of the island, descended from the godfolk, *an Dia-shluagh*. The name is kept in the Old Faith and in the style of the first king, *Rìgh Chlann nan Dè*. Only the eyes of the godkin see the colours of the coal; the humans, when they came, saw black coal and nothing more (23 an Giblean, AE 3).
> "And the Young God set the colours so that only the eyes of the godfolk and their children should see them." — the Telling of the Making

**Cogadh nam Bràithrean** *n. m.* · lit. "the war of the brothers"
The war between Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, named from its first battle (8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,270).
> "The houses divide four to three, and from this battle Cogadh nam Bràithrean, the Brothers' War, takes its name." — annals, LE 1,270

**Coimhdeach na Fine** *n. m.* · lit. "the keeper of the kin"
The spirit that watches over the island's people for Caoran. It is neither god nor ghost; it has no feast and no house, and when it shows itself it comes as a figure of smoke. It came to one of the Mason's line in the grove of Doire ghlas, told him the Telling of the Making and gave him the riddle (see *Luchd-ceasnachaidh a' Ghuail Dhìomhair*); generations later it came again to the grove, lit the rainbow coal, and bade Ailean Mòr keep watch over the coals until they were cold (9 an Lùnastal, VE 5,324). The Keepers of Brìde's flame in the Holy Age share its name in the common tongue and nothing else.
> "It is neither a god nor a ghost." — the Telling of the Making

**Comann nan Saor-luinge** *n. m.* · lit. "the fellowship of the ship-wrights"
The guild that built the fleet of the Sundering (24 an t-Sultain, LE 5). It melted away when no more ocean-going hulls were wanted (27 an t-Ògmhios, LE 84).
> "The custody-book names it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights." — annals, LE 5

**Còmhrag** *n. f.* · lit. "combat"
With the article, the yearly melee at Ceann leathan (4 am Màrt, SE 23), fought on the field of the Holy Age road-guards' games (9 an Giblean, FE 1,665).
> "Two men die in the melee he wins." — annals, of the first champion, SE 23

**cridhe-iarainn** *n. m.* · lit. "iron-heart"
An engine. The annals first have need of it for the shunting engines at Muileann chrom (8 an t-Iuchar, SE 13), and again when the Shipwrights' Guild court ruled that fitting one to a boat was not shipwrighting (23 an Giblean, DE 6).
> "The families of the yard, who work the small engines that move the wagons, are counted apart by the Board and live apart in rows beside the lines." — annals, SE 13

**cuimhne-coinneimh** *n. f.* · lit. "meeting-memory"
Minutes. Above all, those of the Moot at Caol mhòr, which has no standing in Dia-thìreach law and has kept its minutes since its first sitting (25 an Lùnastal, SE 2). See *Tha e scrìobhte a-nis*.
> "It meets all the same and keeps its own minutes, which run unbroken from that day to this." — annals, SE 2

#### D

**Dia Òg, an** *n. m.* · lit. "the young god"
Caoran, youngest of the Tuath Dè. The making of the world was his coming of age, for in his line a god was a child until he had made a thing and kept it. See *Caoran*.
> "He is called an Dia Òg, the Young God, and he is young still, as the gods reckon it." — the Telling of the Making

**Dia-shluagh, an** *n. m.* · lit. "the god-host"
The godfolk, the first people of the earth, whom Caoran woke out of the island itself and gave the island to keep. They found the coloured coal in their first days, did not understand it and let it lie. Their children are *Clann nan Dè*. The doctrine *Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann* is theirs in its oldest sense.
> "'This is yours,' the Young God said to them. 'Keep it, and it will keep you.'" — the Telling of the Making

**diosal** *adv.*, *n. m.* · lit. "sunwise"
The sunwise turn. The fleet went once round the river pool of Seann Skell sunwise (19 an Giblean, LE 40), and the years were counted from that turn (22 am Faoilleach, LE 44).
> "Before going down the Abhainn naomh to open water the fleet went once round the river pool of Seann Skell sunwise, *diosal*, for luck." — the Third Book

**dòrlach** *n. m.* · lit. "a handful"
The sealed measure of coal. The vein-house allowed one to each departing ship (17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 25). See *Làn na glaice*.
> *Dòrlach airson an teallaich ùir, / is an seann teallach fhathast blàth.* "A handful for the new hearth, and the old hearth still warm." — the Third Book

**Dubh an gual, 's dubh an dubhan** *phr.* · lit. "black the coal, and black the dubhan"
A rhyme of the north, heard in both tongues, from the years when the coinage was pegged to the new fuel (5 an Cèitean, DE 15).
> *Dubh an gual, 's dubh an dubhan, / ach cò leis an teine?* "Black the coal, and black the dubhan; but whose is the fire?" — the Sixth Book

**dubhan** *n. m.* · lit. "the black one" (*dubh* + *-an*)
The made fuel, written with a small letter. From the name of Dubhan, born SE 29, whose first working fuel came on 19 an t-Ògmhios, DE 1. So a man's name wore down into a common noun.
> "…for the fuel itself, as well as for the man who made it, years before the trade built upon it is whole." — annals, DE 11

**dubhan-tùsail** *n. m.* · lit. "dubhan of the beginning"
A rough first attempt that looked like a dead end and later mattered; used in any field. From Dubhan's failed experiments (1 an t-Iuchar, SE 61). First recorded in a letter of the druid school at Caol shean, of the school's own revival (22 an Dàmhair, DE 11).
> "It is used of a first attempt that seemed a dead end and proved otherwise…" — annals, DE 11

#### F

**fadachadh** *v.n. m.* · lit. "lengthening", from *fadaich*, *fada*
To be crushed after holding out too long; *am fadachadh*, a total and final defeat. Narrowed by An Cogadh Fada, from Àth leathan (11 an Giblean, DE 21) to Muileann ghlas (10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22), and first heard among Tuathaich speakers of their own defeat (10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22).
> "…'chaidh am fadachadh', they got long-warred… It is said as a jest, and those who say it do not laugh." — annals, DE 22

**faire-obrach** *n. f.* · lit. "work-watch"
A shift. The annals first have need of it for the humans' night-shift order (25 an Lùnastal, AE 116), which the kingdom kept (18 an t-Samhain, SE 11).
> *Cha d' fhuair a' bheinn fois a-riamh, / is cha d' fhuair sinne.* "The mountain never got its rest, and neither did we." — the hewers' saying, the Fifth Book

**Fèill** *n. f.* · lit. "feast-day, fair"
With a town's name, a fair; above all Fèill Muileann òg (16 an Dàmhair, SE 21), heir to the harvest fair held there after the War of the Roads (5 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,665).
> "A fair is held each year at Muileann òg, and it becomes the greatest gathering on the island." — annals, SE 21

**Fo mhullach an taighe, chan eil nàmh ann** *phr.* · lit. "under the roof of the house there is no enemy"
The road-peace, the oldest law on the island that no Keeper made (22 an Dàmhair, FE 175). The War of the Roads ended under such a roof (4 an Dàmhair, FE 1,006).
> "…no feud may be pursued under an inn roof or within a spear's throw of its door." — annals, FE 175

**fuil-ghuail** *n. f.* · lit. "coal-blood"
The condition of those who bond with the vein and do not age as others do, and the people who have it. For half a century it had no name (13 am Faoilleach, AE 71), until the custodians made this one (23 am Faoilleach, AE 126). The humans rendered it *coal-touched*.
> "It is meant as a physician's word. It outlives that meaning." — annals, AE 126

#### G

**Gaoth Dhubh, A'** *n. f.* · lit. "the black wind"
The oldest storm whose name is kept (1 an Gearran, VE 7,740); the first named storm lost its name (30 am Faoilleach, VE 5,470). The harbour rolls went on naming storms: Am Fuath Mòr, "the great hate" (23 an t-Samhain, LE 259), and An Gàire Dubh, "the black laugh" (5 am Màrt, LE 519).
> "Of all storms it is the eldest whose name is kept." — annals, VE 7,740

**gual dathach, an** *n. m.* · lit. "the coloured coal"
The coal of Dia-thìr, in which Caoran hid the elements, each in its own colour; there is none anywhere else in the world. Its seven kinds are *na Seachd Guail*. Only the godkin see its colours: to the humans it was black coal and no more (23 an Giblean, AE 3), where Gormshuil nic Fhearchair had forty words for the colours of it broken (13 an Dùbhlachd, AE 2). *Gual* alone is coal of any kind, and the Library writes *an gual dathach* where it must be plain which is meant.
> "Together they are called an gual dathach, the coloured coal. There is no coloured coal anywhere in the world but on Dia-thìr, for the gift was for Dia-thìr alone." — the Telling of the Making

**gun chreideamh** *adj. phr.* · lit. "without a faith"
Of land or people that keep none of the three faiths. The first census of the restored kingdom so entered the far north-western cape beyond Baile chrom, Eilean ghorm and the smallest islets (30 an t-Iuchar, SE 7); the phrase has stood on the map for that land since.
> "All these they enter as *gun chreideamh*, without a faith." — annals, SE 7

#### I

**Ithidh Mòd an neach a dh'itheas an cnoc** *phr.* · lit. "Mòd will eat whoever eats the hill"
The saying of the feathered doors, from the years when the hawk-priests were barred and the crews carried the Hawk order's sermons themselves (10 an Cèitean, AE 76). Mòd is the Hawk of Acaill, as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, and the hill is the vein.
> "The overseers' reports of these years list hawk-feathers nailed above hut doors as a matter for punishment." — annals, AE 76

#### L

**Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig** *n. m.* · lit. "the law of the small burning"
The Small-Burning Law: no household might burn more than a measured handful of coal in a season (13 an Lùnastal, FE 142). The ruling of the hearth bound the custodians never to withhold that handful (12 an Gearran, LE 565). The Law was never repealed; it lapsed (2 an Dùbhlachd, AE 21).
> "The Law is never repealed; once its keeping no longer pays, it is no longer kept." — annals, AE 21

**Làn na glaice, 's gun tuilleadh** *phr.* · lit. "the fill of the hollow hand, and no more"
The measure of the Ancient Age (5 an Lùnastal, VE 6,334). When Fionnlagh Dall re-cut the stone cup to hold two palms (15 an t-Iuchar, FE 139), the saying became *Làn an dà bhois, agus gun tuilleadh*.
> "It is nowhere written and everywhere kept." — annals, VE 6,334

**Loisc iad an leabhar, ach cha do loisc iad an cnoc** *phr.* · lit. "they burned the book, but they did not burn the hill"
Said of the raids on the tithe ledgers (9 an t-Iuchar, AE 150).
> "Later chroniclers make much of it; it did little." — annals, AE 150

**Luchd-ceasnachaidh a' Ghuail Dhìomhair** *n. pl.* · lit. "the questioners of the hidden coal"
The Inquisitors of the Mystic Coal: the name that *Clann a' Chlachair* bore by the time the fire coal was woken, from the generations they had spent in asking what the Keeper's riddle meant. *Dìomhair* is hidden, secret, holy in the way of things not told. The recited lists shorten it to *Clann na Ceiste*.
> *Tha spiorad fa leth san speur, san talamh agus sa mhuir. Meascaich na spioradan agus bidh iad uile-chumhachdach.* "The sky, the earth and the sea each carry their own spirit. Merge the spirits, and they become almighty." — the Keeper's riddle, the Telling of the Making

#### M

**maor** *n. m.*, *pl.* **maoir** · lit. "steward"
Under the humans, an overseer: a Dia-thìreach set over Dia-thìrich for the Company. Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill took his byname from the office (19 an Cèitean, AE 36, 17 an t-Ògmhios, AE 36). The kingdom gave the word to the Crown's officer in each shire (4 am Faoilleach, SE 4). The kenning *maor-obrach*, "work-steward", is a manager.
> "…from the office the Dia-thìrich give him his byname: Raghnall Maor, Raghnall the steward." — annals, AE 36

**mar a thàinig Niall** *phr.* · lit. "the way Niall came"
Any passing of power that goes uncommonly smoothly. From Niall's crowning (19 an t-Ògmhios, SE 3), which passed without dispute (7 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3).
> "It is first found written in a tavern ledger at Cathair dhearg, against a debt settled without argument." — annals, SE 3

**Marbh-bheò** *n. m.* · lit. "dead-alive"
The Hollow Man of the Doire uaine hills, which attacked anyone who lit a fire in its sight (9 an Giblean, VE 3,251). The rule against open fires after dark came from it (26 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,783), and shepherds still named it when they left the high pastures (17 an Lùnastal, LE 949).
> *Na las teine far am faic e thu.* "Light no fire where it can see you." — the First Book

#### O

**ogham** *n. m.* · lit. "Ogma's letters"
The letters of Dia-thìr. The teachers of the stag's people made them from the cutters' tally-notches (15 am Màrt, FE 914), and the druids name them for Ogma, god of letters. Nearly every later hand on the island descends from them (Appendix F).
> "These are the first letters the Dia-thìrich use: the ogham, which the druids call the gift of Ogma." — annals, FE 914

#### R

**rìgh** *n. m.* · lit. "king"
A ruler of the lowlands, as against the Keeper of the flame. Goraidh mac Ìomhair was the first so called (28 an Cèitean, FE 674); under the division of keeping the rìgh had the roads and the granaries, the Keeper the flame (9 an t-Sultain, FE 694).
> "None before him was ever so called." — annals, FE 674

**Rìgh Chlann nan Dè** *n. m.* · lit. "king of the children of the gods"
The style of the first king of the island's people. After the seven coals had burned together and the seven-night vigil was kept, Caoran came with the Tuath Dè, named Ailean Mòr so, and put into him the power that had been in the coals. Ailean told no one of it, all his life; with it he took the hill of Dùn ìseal and made the first kingdom (9 an Lùnastal, VE 5,324).
> "When the godfolk woke, Macha looked them over, one by one, and said that there was no king among them yet." — the Telling of the Making

**Rìghrean na Cloiche** *n. pl.* · lit. "the kings of the stone"
The oldest oral king-list, opening with Ailean Mòr (9 an Lùnastal, VE 5,324). The name was given to it later.
> "…it gives no lengths of reign, and it is older than the name Dia-thìrich." — annals, VE 5,324

**roghnaich** *v.* · lit. "choose"
With no object: to have chosen the crossing, to choose exile for good. From the Choosing (8 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1); the narrow sense is in the custody-book from 21 an Lùnastal, LE 67. The plain sense was never lost.
> *Roghnaich iadsan, agus dh'fhuirich sinne.* "They chose, and we stayed." — the Third Book

#### S

**scàinte** *adj.* · lit. "rent, split"
Reeling, shaken, of a person as well as a building. From Scàineadh Cill ghlas, the Rending (9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 137). No annal marks its first use.
> "Dozens are killed, and a whole mining district is shut for a generation." — annals, AE 137

**Scaradh, a'** *n. m.* · lit. "the parting"
The Sundering (19 an Giblean, LE 40); loosely, any lasting parting, chosen, between people who belonged together. Later it was used also of the Severance (1 am Faoilleach, AE 151), which was not chosen, and the one word now serves for both.
> "The chronicles of the island fall silent on them as the ships clear the harbour…" — annals, LE 40

**Seachd Guail, na** *n. pl.* · lit. "the seven coals"
The seven kinds of the coloured coal, each holding one element and each woken by its own element and by nothing else. The Mason's line learned to wake them over many generations, the gold coal first and the rainbow coal last; that is why the Ancient Age is so long.

| Coal | Colour | Holds | How it was woken |
|---|---|---|---|
| *gual dubh* | black | the earth | buried deep; warm on the next day |
| *gual teine* | the colour of fire | fire | dust on the hands, at the snap of the fingers |
| *gual sneachda* | snowflake | the air | dropped from Binnean a' Chlachair |
| *gual òir* | gold sheen | the sea | thrown into the sea |
| *gual airgid* | silver sheen | river water | thrown into a river |
| *gual donn-ruadh* | mahogany | life | the blood of a misstrike, in the grove |
| *gual bogha-froise* | rainbow | the spirit | lit by the Keeper when the six were brought together |

The first king kept watch over them seven nights, one for each coal, and on the eighth they were cold (9 an Lùnastal, VE 5,324).
> "These are na Seachd Guail, the Seven Coals, and this is what each holds." — the Telling of the Making

**seann-chunntas** *n. m.* · lit. "old account"
A grievance nobody in power acts on and nobody cancels. Tuathaich speakers coined it (18 an Giblean, DE 26) for the tabled archive request (15 an Gearran, DE 17) and the reparations motion left to die (10 an t-Ògmhios, DE 25).
> "The Dia-thìrich in office do not take up the word." — annals, DE 26

**Seann-Dhaoine** *n. pl.* · lit. "old people"
The Old Ones, the people before the Dia-thìrich. The name is a plain Dia-thìris description, and no annal dates it. Their first sure trace is the midden at Seann Dunn (28 an Lùnastal, VE 751).
> "The Seann-Dhaoine, whoever they were, who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin…" — annals, VE 5,671

**siorrachd** *n. f.*, *pl.* **siorrachdan** · lit. "shire"
Named in the annals from the Age of Sundering (9 an t-Samhain, LE 9). The kingdom redrew the shires on the humans' district lines (12 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3), and has had a hundred and twenty-three since SE 38 (Appendix H).
> "…the kingdom uses them and says nothing of it." — annals, SE 3

**sliochd** *n. m.* · lit. "seed, offspring"
A house of custody known by a founder's name, not a hearth. Sliochd Mhuirich was the first (11 an t-Sultain, FE 96); four were bound to the Keepers' office (29 an Giblean, FE 385).
> "…the first house of custody known by a name and not by a hearth." — annals, FE 96

**stad-oibre** *n. m.* · lit. "work-halt"
A strike. The first lasted eleven days (13 an Dàmhair, AE 77); the first held in several regions on one day came in AE 143.
> "The strike ends when the food, which the humans' Administration holds, runs out." — annals, AE 77

#### T

**Tha an long ag ithe a' chnuic** *phr.* · lit. "the ship is eating the hill"
Fearchar Bàrd's most quoted song, made when the Company's steamships began to burn the island's coal to carry it away (15 an Gearran, AE 103).
> *Tha an long ag ithe a' chnuic / gus an cnoc a ghiùlan air falbh.* "The ship is eating the hill to carry the hill away." — the Fourth Book

**Tha e scrìobhte a-nis** *phr.* · lit. "it is written now"
The Moot's whole minute on the day the census figures were read at Caol mhòr (6 an t-Samhain, SE 64). The Fifth Book takes it for its epigraph.
> "The Moot's minute says only: 'Now written.'" — annals, SE 64

**Tìr Thall, an** *n. f.* · lit. "the land beyond"
The humans' homeland, whose own name no Dia-thìreach scribe set down (26 an Gearran, AE 2).
> "From the first season the scribes call it an Tìr Thall, the land beyond, and its people simply the humans." — annals, AE 2

**tonn** *n. m.* · lit. "wave"
A sudden, overwhelming change: *tha e san tonn*, "he is in the wave of it". From Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol (3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 4), by way of the survivors' accounts (4 am Faoilleach, SE 5).
> "Within a generation the sense is heard across the south." — annals, SE 5

**Tràigh Bhàthte, an** *n. f.* · lit. "the drowned strand"
The old site of Cnoc chaol, left as the Great Wave left it (23 an Dùbhlachd, SE 4).
> "The townsfolk call it an Tràigh Bhàthte, the drowned strand, and do not build there." — annals, SE 4

**Tùrsa Geal, an** *n. m.* · lit. "the white sorrow"
The mourning for the departed, neither wholly grief nor wholly rejoicing (1 an Lùnastal, LE 54), first kept at court by Queen Beathag for her sister (27 an Dàmhair, LE 54). In a much later age it was used again, uneasily, for a departure of a very different kind.
> "…with one place left empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast." — annals, LE 54

#### U

**uaine** *adj.* · lit. "green"
Beside its plain sense, sickly, plague-marked. From A' Phlàigh Uaine (9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 73), first seen as a greenish pallor at Achadh dhomhain (5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 73).
> "…in a field beyond the spoil-heaps still called the green acre." — annals, AE 73

### Of What Is Not Known

Fewer first uses can be proved than a reader might wish. *Scàinte*, *Aisling-aois* and the loose sense of *a' Scaradh* stand on the chronicle's list, but no annal marks the day any of them was first said. The rope-makers of Cuan shean sing a keel-song whose words have lost their sense (5 am Màrt, LE 1,389). The Tuathaich's own memory of the Long War is filed as folklore, and the northern towns' own accounts are among the things the royal record says it does not hold (25 an Giblean, SE 43). Where the history of a word is lost, the gap is left as it is.


## Appendix F — The Tongues and Peoples of Dia-thìr

Here is gathered what the rolls and chronicles hold of the peoples who have lived on Dia-thìr and of the
speech they used. It is drawn from the royal chronicles, from the rolls and custody-books copied into
Leabharlann Muileann chaol, from the map of the kingdom, and from the word-lists that survive from the Age
of Strangers. Where the sources are silent, that is said, and the silence is left as it was found.

### I. The Peoples

Five peoples, or kinds of people, stand in the island's history. Two of them are gone. One, the
*fuil-ghuail*, is hardly a people in the common sense of the word; yet the chronicles have come to speak
of it as one, and so it is set down here with the rest.

| People | Dia-thìris name | In the chronicles | On the map today |
|---|---|---|---|
| The Old Ones | *na Seann-Dhaoine* | Age I; their works end before the Holy Age | no town; thirty towns and thirteen shires bear their names |
| The people of Dia-thìr | *na Dia-thìrich* (sg. *Dia-thìreach*) | every age | 441 of 505 towns; the capital and the sea |
| The humans | the chronicles' plain name for them | Age IV | none by that name; their descendants are the Tuathaich |
| The northerners | *na Tuathaich* (sg. *Tuathach*) | Age V | 64 towns in the north and north-west |
| The coal-blooded | *an fhuil-ghuail*; in the humans' tongue, *coal-touched* | from Age IV | not counted on the map; counted, briefly, in the censuses |

#### The Seann-Dhaoine

The Dia-thìrich call the people before them *na Seann-Dhaoine*, the Old Ones. The name is a Dia-thìris
one, given from outside. What the Old Ones called themselves is not known, and cannot now be
known.

**What survives of them** is stone, shell and names. The oldest sure trace is the midden at
Seann Dunn (28 an Lùnastal, VE 751): limpet shell, seal bone and burnt weed, laid down over many
lifetimes, with no tool in it shaped the way any later Dia-thìreach shaped tools. After it come the
notched net-weights of Seann Chwen, every stone cut with the same three strokes
(26 an t-Sultain, VE 820); the unmortared mole at Seann Skell on which every later quay wall there
stands (1 an t-Iuchar, VE 951); the two hundred and twelve steps of Seann Bhral (30 an t-Iuchar, VE 1,027); the
stone boxes on Eilean dhearg to which the dead of Seann Vell were rowed (4 an Cèitean, VE 1,096); the
fish-channel of Seann Toll (2 an t-Ògmhios, VE 1,170); the shell causeway of Seann Warr, the first made road
on the island that can still be walked (7 am Màrt, VE 1,233); the fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn
(17 an Giblean, VE 1,443); and the slipways of Seann Bhrenn, wide enough for hulls bigger than any hide
boat; the hulls are gone, and so is any telling of where they went (16 an Cèitean, VE 1,515).

At their widest reach (8 an Cèitean, VE 3,872) they held every coast of the island: the ten places whose
names begin with *Seann*, and the islands off them. Their largest landing was at the place now
called Seann Skell, on the Abhainn naomh.

**The ruins inland** are theirs by the oldest tellings. The telling of the counting of the
dead (29 an Lùnastal, VE 5,671) names the Seann-Dhaoine as "the people who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and
Làrach an Dùin". Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, the walled outpost on the spur above the ground where
Cathair mhòr now stands, has a single gate, and it faces inland, away from the sea
(19 an Cèitean, VE 2,524); Làrach an Dùin, near Ceann mhin, had three rings of wall and room inside for
some four hundred people with their beasts (17 an t-Ògmhios, VE 2,576); and Làrach an Teampaill, in the
eastern hills, has its altar set square to the central mountains (14 an Lùnastal, VE 2,679), toward the
vein and away from the sea. All three were already ruined when the first reliable chronicles begin
(27 an t-Samhain, VE 4,023, 6 am Màrt, VE 4,124, 7 am Faoilleach, VE 4,275). Whether the builders of the outpost built the
fortress too has never been settled. After the high places were left, every new work of the
Seann-Dhaoine lies within sight of salt water (9 an Dùbhlachd, VE 4,325).

**The standing stones** are harder. Carragh Cnoc bheag, Colbh Cnoc chiar and Calbh Cnoc ghorm were
raised in the Ancient Age (17 an t-Iuchar, VE 4,672, 9 an t-Sultain, VE 4,770, 6 an t-Samhain, VE 4,851), and no telling
says by whom. The upper face of Carragh Cnoc bheag bears a line of the unread script; the
four Dia-thìris words, *Bha teine sa chloich*, "there was fire in the stone", lie lower down, cut with
a narrower tool by another hand, and "when that second hand came is not known"
(11 an Lùnastal, VE 4,718). On these stones, and nowhere else, the marks of two peoples lie on
the same face. The wind-stone at the central Seann Chwen is another: a Dia-thìris wind-name cut over an
older mark of the Seann-Dhaoine (13 an Gearran, VE 7,770).

**Their counting.** Late in their time the Seann-Dhaoine began cutting single strokes on flat
stones at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household (31 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,631). At the eastern
Seann Warr the counting stones were built into a wall of some three thousand strokes
(3 an t-Ògmhios, VE 5,712); at Seann Tarr in the north-east they were cut in fives and set in the floor of a
house (2 an t-Iuchar, VE 5,751). At the Seann Chwen near Cuan dhearg the last tally stone was left
half-cut: two strokes finished, a third begun and abandoned (5 an Cèitean, VE 5,833).

**Their end.** After the half-cut stone no new work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their
middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and their script is not cut again
(7 an Gearran, VE 5,874). How they ended no telling knows, and no guess is offered here.
The chronicles do not say that they were driven out, or that they died, or that their blood ran on in
some later people; nor do they say otherwise.

**The hill-folk.** Alongside, or after, the Seann-Dhaoine the tellings set a second people: the
hill-folk of the high valleys around the crack (10 an t-Samhain, VE 4,425), who buried their dead in the
ground rather than on islands, and cut no script. They burned the coal, though sparingly: one sliver,
one fire, at Àth gharbh (12 an Dàmhair, VE 4,475). Whether they shared the island with the Old Ones or
came after them no telling knows. Their own answer, given later, is that they were always
there, and it is the answer the Dia-thìrich give of themselves in the doctrine carried on Calbh Cnoc
ghorm: *Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann*, "we did not come; we were here." When
stag-scholars came to Calbh Cnoc ghorm in the Holy Age and could not read it, the people of Cnoc
ghorm told them what it said, and "the scholars write that the people say so"
(6 an Dàmhair, FE 2,376).

#### The Dia-thìrich

The Dia-thìrich are the people of Dia-thìr: the majority in every age of the island's history, the holders of the
capital, Cathair dhearg, and of the sea. Their name is the island's name with the
people-ending *-aich*; a single person is a *Dia-thìreach*. Writers of the humans' tongue called them
*Dia-thìrian*, and that word is kept in this history for the adjective.

**Custodians.** The Dia-thìrich enter history as custodians. In the Ancient Age a custom set in across
the hill settlements that no fire should take more of the coal than one cupped hand could hold. The
Binding of the First Flame (23 an t-Sultain, FE 1) made the custodianship of the vein a formal order,
"older by centuries than any king", and the Small-Burning Law (13 an Lùnastal, FE 142) made the
custom into rule. The first man in any roll to be called *rìgh* was Goraidh mac Ìomhair at Dùn
dhearg (28 an Cèitean, FE 674), and he claimed nothing over the vein. For the whole of the Holy Age the
kings ruled the roads and the granaries, and the Keepers at Dùn ìseal ruled the mountain. The
Holy Age closes on the last age of even population (1 an Cèitean, FE 2,949). After it, the chroniclers
note with some unease, there was never again a time on Dia-thìr when no family held more years of life
than any other.

**The kingdom.** After the Severance the state restyled itself Rìoghachd Dia-thìris, the Kingdom of
Dia-thìr (27 an t-Iuchar, SE 2), and Niall was crowned at Cathair dhearg (19 an t-Ògmhios, SE 3). The rulers since
are set down in Appendix A. Here it is enough to say that the kingdom is a Dia-thìreach kingdom: its schools
teach in Dia-thìris "and it has no others" (10 an Gearran, SE 7), and the old apprentice-binding custom,
when it was revived, was reserved for Dia-thìrich applicants only (20 an Dàmhair, SE 13).

**The sea.** The Dia-thìrich have always been a people of the coast as much as of the mountain. The largest
towns on the map today stand on the sea or on the rivers that run down to it, and the two largest bear a name older than Dia-thìris:

| Town | Shire | Faith (order) | Population |
|---|---|---|---|
| Seann Skell | Seann Skell | An Creideamh Sean (Òrd Mhanannain) | 74,120 |
| Seann Skell | Seann Skell | An Creideamh Sean (Òrd Bhrìde) | 57,907 |
| Ros dhomhain | Ros dhomhain | An Creideamh Sean (Òrd Mhacha) | 51,589 |
| Seann Bhral | Seann Bhral | Na Seann Spioradan | 49,681 |
| Cnoc bheag | Cnoc bheag | An Creideamh Sean (Òrd an t-Seabhaig) | 49,661 |
| Cathair mhòr | Cathair mhòr | An Creideamh Sean (Òrd Mhacha) | 49,298 |
| Caol bheag | Caol bheag | An Creideamh Sean (Scoiltean nan Draoidhean) | 42,649 |
| Achadh mhòr | Achadh mhòr | Na Seann Spioradan | 42,136 |

The capital itself is not among them. Cathair dhearg is counted at 10,274; its harbour, Ros
dhomhain, is five times its size.

**The departed.** Part of the Dia-thìrich people is not on Dia-thìr. Land was found across the water
(6 am Faoilleach, LE 1); volunteers chose to go, by "a vote, or what the later chroniclers call a
vote" (8 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1); the fleet set out, turning sunwise round the river pool at Seann Skell, in the year
from which the old count of the Diosal ran (19 an Giblean, LE 40). A broken report told of two landfalls
(24 an Dùbhlachd, LE 44), and of the thinning: cut off from the vein, "by the third generation over the water
nothing is left that Dia-thìr would know" (3 an t-Iuchar, LE 53). The departed stand in the
chronicles only as a gap. The island kept them in rites (the empty-harbour rite,
25 an t-Samhain, LE 61; the white sorrow, *an Tùrsa Geal*, 27 an Dàmhair, LE 54) and in words, of which more
below. When the humans came, old sailors at Cuan shean remarked that the strangers had come in from
the same quarter of sea the Sundering fleet once sailed into. The council forbade the remark in its
hall; it was written down all the same, and never answered (9 an Gearran, AE 2). Whether the humans
descend from the departed, no one on Dia-thìr knows.

#### The humans of an Tìr Thall

**The Crossing.** Humans made landfall on Dia-thìr and were granted leave to stay
(5 am Faoilleach, AE 1): the first contact since the Sundering. Three ships out of the west anchored off
Cuan shean, and their master, whom the chronicles call Edmund Harrow, came ashore unarmed and asked by
signs for water (5 an Gearran, AE 1). So the first dealing between the two peoples was made without
words.

**Their homeland.** The strangers named their homeland in their own tongue, but no Dia-thìreach scribe
set the word down. From the first season the chronicles call it *an Tìr Thall*, the land beyond, and
its people simply the humans (26 an Gearran, AE 2). Their own name for their country is written on
Dia-thìr in no hand, and it cannot now be recovered.

**What they called things.** The humans' names for the island's things were few, plain and, to
Dia-thìreach ears, careless. They had a single word for the coloured coal, and it was the word for the black fuel
they burned at home; Gormshuil nic Fhearchair's copyist noted that no Dia-thìris word answered to it,
and that the humans did not ask for one (23 an Giblean, AE 3). So *an gual dathach*, the coloured coal of the vein, became in their tongue plain
*coal*, and the custodians of the vein became, in Samuel Wren's otherwise careful grammar, "keepers
of the coal" (21 an Lùnastal, AE 12). Their offices and bodies came with names in the humans' tongue and kept them (they are given here in English): the
Company, the Administration, the Mission, the Residency above Ros dhomhain (10 an Cèitean, AE 9), the
Commissioner, the Levy, the constable posts. Their faith was the Church, which the Dia-thìrich call *an
Eaglais*, and the Mission was its house on Dia-thìr. Their coin was the *mark*. The townsfolk of Muileann
shean called the constable post there "the humans' second Residency", and did not mean it kindly
(11 an Dàmhair, AE 132).

**The camps.** What the humans built for themselves on Dia-thìr they built for the pit. The camp of
timber huts at Àth ìseal was the first settlement on the island raised for the pit and for nothing else
(6 an Dàmhair, AE 29); Baile dhomhain was laid out on a grid by a Company surveyor, the first Dia-thìreach
town drawn on paper before it was built (10 am Faoilleach, AE 34); the camp at Achadh dhomhain was built
of spoil (1 am Faoilleach, AE 68). Dia-thìreach hands worked the camps and human officers ruled them, and the
record of them is kept in two tongues that seldom agree: the Mission counts four hundred and six
dead of the spotted pox, and the custodians count more, and write the difference in the margin of
the Mission's list (11 an Dàmhair, AE 39). Human families lived on Dia-thìr as well as human officers:
upland pasture in the north-west, around Muileann àrsaidh, was granted for human families who would
not work in the pits (3 an t-Samhain, AE 20). This was the first human settlement in the north; and to
the north, in the end, their descendants were sent.

**Mixing.** The first mixed settlement (22 an Giblean, AE 5) was Baile dhìreach on the south-west
coast, under a council of three Dia-thìrich and three humans, whose founding compact was written twice,
once in each tongue, the only such compact on record in the age (10 an Dàmhair, AE 5). There the
net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh married the human cooper Samuel Hale, and the council entered the
marriage in both its books (26 an Cèitean, AE 7). It was not tried again, and the
first inheritance case of mixed blood (15 an Gearran, AE 111) the Administration decided wholly in
its own favour.

**The going north.** War was declared in AE 149. Before the end, the human families of
Ros bheag, Cuan shean, Baile dhìreach and the south-west marched north along the western roads under
guard of the council's companies; few of them had ever lived in the north; no column was attacked,
and none was helped (29 an t-Samhain, AE 150). The war ended with the crossing itself closed
(1 am Faoilleach, AE 151). Whatever way had let the humans reach Dia-thìr was shut, and those still on the island were
herded to the northern country their descendants hold today.

#### The Tuathaich

From the Severance the chronicles stop calling them humans. The descendants of those left on Dia-thìr are
*na Tuathaich*, the northerners, from *tuath*, north, with the same *-aich* that makes *Dia-thìrich*;
on the page the two names stand like brothers, though the two peoples' fortunes have been far apart. Their
homeland in the north was fixed formally (22 am Màrt, SE 1): "It is a confinement;
yet their children's children call it home." A formal wall between the two peoples was
proposed and rejected as unnecessary, because the two were already keeping apart on their own
(11 an Cèitean, SE 10).

What the Tuathaich call themselves in their own speech the chronicles do not say. The name used here
is the kingdom's name for them.

**Their towns.** The kingdom's map counts sixty-four Tuathaich towns, all in the north and north-west, with
some 543,000 people in them. The Dia-thìrich hold the other 441. The Tuathaich country is some fifteen parts in a hundred of the island's land, the windy coast of the far north-west among it, and the Dia-thìrich country the other eighty-five (Appendix H). The largest Tuathaich towns are these:

| Town | Shire | Faith | Population |
|---|---|---|---|
| Caol mhòr | Caol mhòr | An Eaglais | 42,002 |
| Doire ghlas | Doire ghlas | An Eaglais (Eaglais nan Tuathach) | 40,740 |
| Ceann mhòr | Ceann mhòr | An Eaglais | 32,420 |
| Baile chrom | Baile chrom | An Eaglais (the vigil of the Grey Night) | 27,319 |
| Cnoc ghorm | Cnoc ghorm | An Eaglais | 25,112 |

Every Tuathaich town but one bears a Dia-thìris name, and most of them were Dia-thìreach towns before the
Severance; the north-west had been thinly held since the dearth on that shore in the Age of
Sundering (19 an Giblean, LE 819). One of them, Seann Skell in the shire of
Muileann àrsaidh, bears an Old One's name. The Tuathaich have added no names of their own to the
map.

**Their assembly.** Tuathaich householders from the northern towns met at Caol mhòr and chose a
speaker, Walter Hale, a former harbour clerk (25 an Lùnastal, SE 2). The Moot has no standing in
Dia-thìreach law; it meets anyway, and its minutes run unbroken from that meeting to the present.

**Their faith.** All sixty-four Tuathaich towns keep An Eaglais, the Church, which their forebears
brought over the sea at the Crossing; no Dia-thìreach town keeps it. Fifty-one keep it in the line the
Mission left, and their largest church is at Cnoc ghorm. Twelve are the old congregations of the
north coast, Eaglais nan Tuathach, whose towns lie together in the shires of Doire ghlas,
Muileann leathan, Inis mhin and Àth àrsaidh. One, Baile chrom, keeps the vigil of the Grey Night,
Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise, which the Church's bishops call irregular. The old congregations
keep, quietly, the First Canoe fragment (13 an Gearran, SE 9): among coastal Tuathaich families, "a
named steersman, a first crossing", which their church tells as the voyage of Naomh Breandan to
the Isle of the Blessed, and which the druids of the Old Faith dismiss as superstition
(9 an t-Samhain, VE 2,833). The fragment is set at the head of the Ancient Age, for there its
tellers place it.
The Library has neither upheld it nor struck it out. It is one of the two suppressed histories
that stand at either end of the island's story, and it is left here as it was found.

#### The fuil-ghuail

This section holds to what the rolls and chronicles say.

A child born into the mining camps was exposed to more raw coal across her lifetime than any Dia-thìrian
in living memory, and did not age the way the people around her did. Her name is Aisling
(7 am Màrt, AE 69). What was happening to her had no word, in any language spoken on the island
(13 am Faoilleach, AE 71). A second, Fionnan, was born half a century later (21 an Gearran, AE 121), and
it became plain that this was no single mischance: it came of the working of the pits, and would come
again while they were worked. With two sure cases before them, the Dia-thìreach custodians settled on a word
(23 am Faoilleach, AE 126): *fuil-ghuail*, "coal-blood", rendered in the humans' tongue as *coal-touched*.
It was meant as a physician's word. It was agreed at a meeting of custodians at the shrine of Cill ghlas, and the roll records the vote but not
who proposed it (21 an Gearran, AE 126). The Residency ordered every Dia-thìreach child showing the condition to
be reported; the custodians complied by reporting none (26 an t-Samhain, AE 127). A third case, Lorccan,
was born in a mining town (29 an Cèitean, AE 134), and a fourth, Cian, within a year of him
(3 am Màrt, AE 135).

After the Severance the Coal Rite, Òrd Bhrìde, was set in order within the Old Faith, built around the
leyline and "the unbroken line of the coal-touched" (18 an Giblean, SE 6). The first census of the
kingdom noted, without further comment, exactly how few such people exist (29 an t-Ògmhios, SE 7), and
the published census of a later generation gave a number and nothing else (8 am Faoilleach, SE 65). The
number is printed nowhere else, and it is not printed here.

Whether the *fuil-ghuail* are a people is a question of words. They are born to Dia-thìreach families;
in Dia-thìreach speech the word names the gift that sets the Dia-thìrich apart from the Tuathaich; and the druid schools have asked since the Holy Age why the vein answers some hands and
not others. The chronicles do not settle it.

### II. The Tongues

#### Dia-thìris

Dia-thìris is the tongue of Dia-thìr, spoken by the Dia-thìrich in every age. Three
things mark it at once on the page:

| Feature | Dia-thìris | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Long vowels | **grave accent only**: *à è ì ò ù* | *mòr, sìth, Dia-thìris* |
| The cluster /sk/ | written **sc**, never *sg* | *uisce, scoil, sceul, Scàineadh* |
| "City" | *cathair* | *Cathair dhearg* |

Its greeting of thanks is *gu robh math agad*. Its verbs come first in the sentence
(*Chunnaic Cian an long*, "Cian saw the ship"); it has no word for "a", no words for yes and no,
and two initial mutations.

**Lenition.** After many words an initial consonant softens, and the change is written with *h*:
*b > bh, c > ch, d > dh, f > fh, g > gh, m > mh, p > ph, s > sh, t > th*. The possessives, the past
tense, a feminine noun after the article, an adjective after a feminine noun, most simple
prepositions and the second element of a name all cause it. It does not touch vowels, nor *l, n,
r* in writing, nor the clusters *sc, sp, st, sm*; and after a word ending in *n* it spares *d, t*
and *s*, which is why the map has *Seann Dunn* and *Seann Toll* but *Seann Bhral*.

**Broad and slender.** Vowels are broad (*a o u à ò ù*) or slender (*e i è ì*), and within one
word a consonant takes vowels of the same class on both sides: *caol le caol, leathan le
leathan*, slender with slender, broad with broad. That is why so many endings come in pairs, and why
the small rivers are *Ciaras* but *Àrsaidheas*.

**Sounds.** For the reader who would say these names aloud:

| written | said | example |
|---|---|---|
| bh, mh | v | *Seann Bhral* |
| ch | as in *loch* | *Seann Chwen* |
| dh, gh | a voiced *ch* before broad vowels; *y* before slender | *Cathair dhearg* |
| fh | silent | *Àth fhada* |
| sh, th | h | *Dùn thais* |
| sc | sk | *Scàineadh* |

The stress falls on the first syllable.

**How Dia-thìris names new things.** Dia-thìris was long spoken on an island that few new things reached, and
it was slow to borrow. The humans brought many new things, and the kingdom after them more. In the first
generations after the Crossing the Dia-thìrich named nearly all of them from old roots, calling the thing by
what it does or what it is like: head first, the describer after, hyphenated, two elements and seldom
three. Many of these kennings are still the common words. The loans Dia-thìris did take came mostly later:
*bus*, the bus; *tacsaidh*, the taxi; *rèidio*, the radio; and many words of the sciences, such as
*ogsaidean*, oxygen, and the names of the elements. Some of the kennings, with their literal sense:

| English | Dia-thìris | literally |
|---|---|---|
| train | *carbad-iarainn* | iron-chariot |
| engine | *cridhe-iarainn* | iron-heart |
| computer | *inntinn-iarainn* | iron-mind |
| aeroplane | *eun-iarainn* | iron-bird |
| telephone | *guth-sreinge* | string-voice |
| cable | *sreang-theine* | fire-string |
| socket | *tobar-dealanaich* | lightning-well |
| battery | *ciste-spionnaidh* | strength-chest |
| heater | *teine-gun-lasair* | flameless-fire |
| camera | *cìste-scàile* | shadow-chest |
| film | *sceul-scàile* | shadow-tale |
| novel | *leabhar-sceòil* | tale-book |
| documentary | *sceul-fìrinne* | truth-tale |
| plastic | *cèir-chruaidh* | hard-wax |
| inflation | *lobhadh-airgid* | money-rot |
| internet | *lìon-fiosa* | tidings-net |
| crossing (street) | *àth-coise* | foot-ford |
| tyre | *bròg-cuibhle* | wheel-shoe |

The kennings fall into families: machines are *iarainn*, of iron; screens and pictures are *scàil* and
*scàthan*, shadow and mirror; electricity is *dealan*, spark, and *dealanach*, lightning. A
crossing for feet is a ford, *àth*, the same word the map uses for a town at a river.

**Words born of the island's history.** Old words have also taken new senses from what the island lived
through. The royal chroniclers keep a list of these, and the rolls date the first use of most.

| Word | Plain sense | Sense given by history | First recorded |
|---|---|---|---|
| *roghnaich* | to choose | to have chosen the crossing; to choose exile | 21 an Lùnastal, LE 67 |
| *a' Scaradh* | the Sundering | any chosen, permanent parting; later used of the Severance | Age of Sundering |
| *uaine* | green | sickly, plague-marked, after A' Phlàigh Uaine (9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 73) | Age of Strangers |
| *scàinte* | rent, cracked | shaken, of a person, after Scàineadh Cill ghlas (9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 137) | Age of Strangers |
| *Aisling-aois* | Aisling's age | an unnaturally long youth in anyone, said half in jest | Age of Strangers |
| *mar a thàinig Niall* | the way Niall came | any smooth handing-over of power | 7 an Dùbhlachd, SE 3 |
| *tonn* | wave | a sudden, overwhelming change: *tha e san tonn* | 4 am Faoilleach, SE 5 |
| *a chur san Leabharlann* | to put it in the Library | to make a thing settled and official | 3 an t-Samhain, SE 16 |
| *dubhan* | a man's name | the synthetic fuel | 23 an t-Sultain, DE 11 |
| *dubhan-tùsail* | dubhan of the beginning | a first attempt that seemed a dead end and proved otherwise | 22 an Dàmhair, DE 11 |
| *fadachadh* | lengthening | to be crushed after holding out too long: *chaidh am fadachadh* | 10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22 |
| *seann-chunntas* | old account | a grievance nobody in power acts on and nobody cancels | 18 an Giblean, DE 26 |

Of the Sundering the language also keeps one strange relic. A work-song of the rope-makers of Cuan
shean names the parts of a deep keel, and half its words have no meaning to anyone who sings it
(5 am Màrt, LE 1,389). Nothing else of the fleet's craft survives in any form. Whether the lost words
are old Dia-thìris, or the cant of the wrights, or something else, no one has shown.

#### The tongue of the Seann-Dhaoine

Of the Old Ones' speech nothing survives but names. Ten roots are known, each standing after the
Dia-thìris word *seann*, "old", which lenites it where Dia-thìris lenites:

| Root | As written on the map | Towns bearing it | Shires named from it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dunn | Seann Dunn | 3 | yes |
| Cwen | Seann Chwen | 3 | yes |
| Skell | Seann Skell | 4 | yes (three) |
| Bral | Seann Bhral | 3 | yes |
| Tarr | Seann Tarr | 3 | yes |
| Vell | Seann Vell | 5 | yes (three) |
| Morn | Seann Mhorn | 2 | — |
| Brenn | Seann Bhrenn | 2 | yes |
| Toll | Seann Toll | 3 | yes |
| Warr | Seann Warr | 2 | yes |

Thirty towns on the map bear these names, and thirteen shires are named from them.

The Dia-thìrich did not translate these names; they took them over. The fishers who resettled Seann
Mhorn in the Holy Age kept "the name they find there, which is not of their own tongue", and said
the old name came with the stones (23 an t-Sultain, FE 178). It is the first such taking-over on
record. So the harbour-names of an older people outlived them inside a newer tongue, kept whole and
hard like shells in a stone, and never put into Dia-thìris.

**What can be said.** The roots are single syllables. Seven of the ten end in a doubled consonant
(*-nn, -ll, -rr*). Three of them hold letters that Dia-thìris writes nowhere else: *k* in *Skell*, *v* in
*Vell*, *w* in *Cwen* and *Warr*. Everywhere else Dia-thìris writes the sound *sk* as *sc*, yet no scribe
has ever written Seann Scell; they kept the foreign *k* as they found it, and the grammarians count
*sk-* among the clusters that do not lenite.

**What cannot be known.** What any root meant. Whether *seann* was ever the Old Ones' own element,
or only the Dia-thìrich's word for places they found already named (the second is the common
reading, and the likelier; but it is no more than a reading). Whether the roots come from one tongue or several.
Two of them look like Dia-thìris words, *toll*, a hole, and *dunn* beside *dùn*, a fort. The
likeness has tempted scholars in every age and proves nothing, and the Library takes no side.

**The script.** The Seann-Dhaoine also cut signs. Rows of them stand on the cliff above Seann Tarr
(5 an Giblean, VE 1,301), in the script that is found again on the standing stones. It is not Dia-thìris. It
has never been read, and not one sign of it has an agreed meaning. The stag-scholars of the Holy Age
set their own new letters against the obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag and found that they matched
nothing, and wrote down that the stone's writers were not their teachers (12 an Cèitean, FE 914).
Samuel Wren copied the obelisk and sent it west to the scholars of an Tìr Thall; no reply is
recorded (5 an Gearran, AE 17). Edwin Lowe copied the pillar near Cnoc chiar, compared it with Wren's
copy, and decided that the two were not the same script and that neither was Dia-thìreach; his notes stop
there (9 an Lùnastal, AE 65). The strokes on the midden stones are a count, and have nothing to do with
this script. Whether the script records the Old Ones' tongue, or some other, or no tongue at all, is
not known.

#### The humans' tongue

The humans spoke a plain tongue, and this history renders it in English (see *Of Translation*
below). The names they carried were names of that tongue: Edmund Harrow, Thomas Pike, Samuel Wren,
Josiah Pell, Henry Maddox, Arthur Lisle, Samuel Hale, Edwin Lowe.

**The season of translation.** Human clerics and Dia-thìreach custodians spent a full season trying to
build a shared vocabulary, and neither side's account of what was agreed survives intact
(27 am Màrt, AE 2). Samuel Wren and the custodian Gormshuil nic Fhearchair kept parallel
word-lists. Wren's survives in the Administration's letter-books; Gormshuil's was lost, and only its
first leaf is known from a copy: forty words for the colours of broken coal (13 an Dùbhlachd, AE 2).
Against those forty the humans had one word, and it was *coal*.

**The tongue of rule.** The humans wrote their agreements in their own tongue only. The first
written treaty (27 an Giblean, AE 8) was signed at Cathair dhearg by Tormod mac Ailein, who could not
read the tongue it was written in; who read it to him, no roll says (7 an Cèitean, AE 8).
The Harbour Articles were written the same way, and that time two custodians refused to sign
(16 an t-Samhain, AE 19). The Mission's school at Ros dhomhain taught Dia-thìreach children in the humans'
tongue (9 an Cèitean, AE 51); a generation later Iain Maor, the first overseer schooled there, kept his
reports in the humans' tongue and his household in Dia-thìris (23 an Giblean, AE 87). The Levy's officers
read the names of the chosen at Caol mhòr from a list in the humans' tongue, and the custodians took
the names down again in Dia-thìris, "that they may know whom to look for" (3 am Màrt, AE 88).

**Loanwords.** Few crossed, and most of those late. In the first generations Dia-thìris took the
humans' goods and named them in its own way, as told above, and kept few of the humans' words for them.
The humans for their part, so far as the rolls show, used the Dia-thìris names of places as they found them;
*fuil-ghuail* they did not borrow but turned into their own tongue, *coal-touched*, and that word,
rather than the Dia-thìris, is the one the kingdom's own later entries use of the Rite's "unbroken line".
What passed the other way, into the humans' speech, is best seen after the Severance, in the north.

The Dia-thìris word for the humans' country, *an Tìr Thall*, is the only name the island has for it.

#### Tuathaich speech

The speech of the north is a mixed speech, and the chronicles speak of it only in passing. This much
they say.

The Tuathaich kept the humans' tongue. Walter Hale asked the council for leave to open schools in
the north teaching in it, and was refused (10 an Gearran, SE 7); Agnes Pike opened one at Doire ghlas
anyway, with Moot money and without the council's leave, and within a decade there were nine
(14 am Faoilleach, SE 15). The Moot later counted eleven such schools, and three that had begun to teach
Dia-thìris as well, at the parents' asking (7 an t-Ògmhios, SE 29). The church at Cnoc ghorm taught its
priests in the humans' tongue while reading the Bible in the Dia-thìris text its preachers use on the
west coast: the only place in the north where both are taught (29 an Giblean, SE 10).

The Tuathaich live among Dia-thìris names and use Dia-thìris words. The words the north has added to the
island's speech in the present age are Dia-thìris in form: *fadachadh*, from *fada*, long, the name of
the war they lost (10 an Dùbhlachd, DE 22), and *seann-chunntas*, an old reckoning, which official Dia-thìreach
usage pointedly does not take up (18 an Giblean, DE 26). The word *dubhan* for the fuel came out of the
north, from the name of Dubhan, a Tuathach, and it spread before the fuel did (23 an t-Sultain, DE 11);
the royal chronicler who first set it down spelled it three ways in two lines (21 an t-Samhain, DE 1).

Beyond this the chronicles do not go. The northern towns' own accounts are among the things the royal
chroniclers say they do not hold (25 an Giblean, SE 43). How far the humans' tongue has drifted in the north
since the crossing closed, how much Dia-thìris is spoken at a Tuathach hearth, and in which tongue the
First Canoe is told, the Library cannot say.

#### Names and naming

**Personal names.** Dia-thìreach names are the old given names of the island: Ailean, Beathag, Catrìona, Dòmhnall,
Eilidh, Fearchar, Gormshuil, Iain, Mòrag, Raghnall, Sìleas, Tormod. A person is further named from
the father, with *mac*, son, or *nic*, daughter, and the father's name in the genitive, lenited
where Dia-thìris lenites: Tormod mac Iain; Eilidh nic Iain; Gormshuil nic Fhearchair; Donnchadh mac
Thormoid; Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill; Oighrig nic Lachlainn.

**Bynames** are as common as patronymics and often outlast them. They name a colour, a trade, a
size or a deed. After a woman's name the byname is lenited, after a man's it is not: Seònaid Mhòr,
Eilidh Dhubh, Beathag Bhàn, but Ailean Mòr, Calum Liath, Dùghall Garbh. Trade-names are nouns and
stand as they are: Alasdair Saor, the wright; Iain Maor, the overseer. Some bynames are earned:
Tormod mac Iain, the first of the royal kin to read, was called Tormod Scrìobhaiche, Tormod the
Writer, for the rest of his life (3 an Lùnastal, FE 1,255).

**Kindreds** take *Sliochd*, the seed or line, or *Clann*, the children, with a founder's name in the
genitive: Sliochd Ìomhair, Sliochd Mhuirich, Clann Choinnich.

**Human and Tuathaich names** are of the humans' tongue and are kept in their own spelling: Walter
Hale, Agnes Pike. The humans' names for the island's things were lost at the Severance; their names
for themselves lived through it.

**Place names.** Dia-thìreach places are named by a generic noun and a describing word after it. On the
map the describer is always lenited, whatever the gender of the generic (*Baile ghorm, Cnoc bheag,
Dùn thais*). In speech it would not be lenited after a masculine noun; the names keep an old fixed
usage, as old compounds are kept. The generics are these:

| Generic | Sense | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| *Cathair* | stone fort; city | capital, city |
| *Dùn* | fortified hill | capital, city |
| *Baile Mòr* | great settlement | city |
| *Baile* | settlement, town | town |
| *Àth* | ford | town |
| *Cnoc* | hill | town |
| *Muileann* | mill | town |
| *Cill* | holy cell, shrine | village, hamlet |
| *Tobar* | well | village, hamlet |
| *Achadh* | field | village |
| *Doire* | oak grove | village |
| *Carraig* | rock | hamlet |
| *Ros* | headland | port |
| *Ceann* | head, point | port |
| *Cuan* | harbour | port |
| *Caol* | strait | port |
| *Inis* | island | port |

The describers are colour, size and character words: *mòr, beag, dubh, geal, bàn, dearg, ruadh,
uaine, glas, fada, domhain, ìseal, fiadhaich, naomh, fionn, ciar, gorm, sean, òg, garbh, min, caol,
leathan, crom, dìreach, àrsaidh*. The great rivers are *Abhainn* with a describer; the small ones
take a root and the ending *-as* or *-eas* by broad and slender. A shire, *siorrachd*, takes the name
of its seat, or, where it has no town, of its island (Appendix H). Names repeat freely: there are four Baile chrom and four Seann Skell, and the rolls
tell them apart by where they lie.

Beside these stand the Old Ones' names, which follow none of the rules above except that the Dia-thìrich
