It stands on the edge of the fenced ground, on land the custodians of Muileann dhomhain lent them at Coinneachadh an Fhearainn, the standing stone on the moor road, and it is the only settlement of that age founded by Dia-thìrich for Dia-thìrich with no Company surveyor's hand in it. It is a village of narrow fields, and it sends its grain to the mills around it. Known for its narrow fields on the edge of the fenced ground.

**Achadh chaol** (Achadh chaol). Founded 27 an Gearran, VE 7,798 by field-clearing households of the east. Achadh chaol is a large village of narrow barley fields and the seat of its province. Its grain goes to the mills of Muileann dhìreach, and the two places have kept the same bargain since the Holy Age. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its narrow barley fields.

**Achadh dhìreach** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 16 an Cèitean, VE 303 by hill-folk of the high valleys. Achadh dhìreach holds the oldest hearths of the high valleys, and it was laid out anew in straight fields by the restored kingdom, when the diggings were worked to the full again and the towns of the plain needed feeding. It is small, fewer than eight hundred people. It feeds Baile Mòr àrsaidh. Known for its straight fields of the restored kingdom.

**Achadh dhomhain** (Muileann chrom). Founded 10 an t-Ògmhios, FE 272 by farmers of Muileann chrom. Achadh dhomhain of Muileann chrom is a large farming village in deep fields, founded in the Holy Age. Its granaries fed the mining camps in the Age of Strangers and were requisitioned in the war of the Severance. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its deep-field granaries of the camps.

**Achadh dhomhain** (Caol shean). Founded 27 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,871 by hosts of the Allt an Àigh pilgrims. Achadh dhomhain of Caol shean is a large village beside Allt an Àigh, the stream of fortune. Pilgrims have come to drink from it since the Holy Age, and the village lives on them. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its lodging of the Allt an Àigh pilgrims.

**Achadh fhada** (Baile chiar). Founded 30 an Dùbhlachd, LE 916 by barley-farmers of the south-west. Achadh fhada, the long field, is a village of barley farms in the capital's southern country. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and has changed little since. It keeps the order of the Stone, unlike most of its neighbours. Known for its long field of barley.

**Achadh fhada** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 31 an Cèitean, LE 664 by druids of the Hungry Hawk. A long field village in the wooded middle west, one of the few settlements where Òrd an t-Seabhaig, the Hawk order, whose rite is the older form of Òrd Bhrìde's, still holds. A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death, struck it in the Age of Strangers. Its fields feed the Hawk-order mill at Muileann uaine. Known for the Hawk-order fields.

**Achadh fhiadhaich** (Ceann bheag). Founded 10 an t-Ògmhios, LE 765 by horse-breeders of the north. Achadh fhiadhaich is a village of the north-east, founded in the long quiet centuries on wild pasture that no earlier people had fenced. It breeds horses and grows hay for the coast, and the carters of Ceann bheag have bought its horses for generations. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its wild-field hay and horses.

**Achadh fhiadhaich** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 19 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,512 by Dia-thìrich fishers of the west coast. A wild field village on the far western shore with a small harbour, kept in Dia-thìrich hands when the Tuathaich homeland was fixed to the north. It faces the waters where the Sea-Watcher is said to live, and pirates are still seen off the coast. Its people follow the order of Manannan. Known for its fishing within sight of the Sea-Watcher's waters.

**Achadh fhiadhaich** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 21 an t-Sultain, LE 1,813 by Dia-thìrich farmers who reclaimed the wild field. A village of fields reclaimed from wild ground in the Age of Sundering, when the island had fewer mouths and more hands to spare. It feeds the towns of Ceann àrsaidh and sends its surplus to Muileann chrom to be ground. It is a large village now, of nearly ten thousand. Known for its reclaimed wild fields.

**Achadh fhionn** (Baile ghorm). Founded 23 an Lùnastal, FE 1,069 by farmers of the south-east. Achadh fhionn is a village of the south-east, founded in the Holy Age in a fair field under Làrach an Dùin. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits and leaves the ruin alone. Its people say the ruin was old when the first Dia-thìrich came. Known for its fair field under Làrach an Dùin.

**Achadh fhionn** (Cnoc shean). Founded 9 an t-Samhain, LE 530 by farmers of Cnoc shean. A fair field village in the south-east, with meadows between the hill-towns of Cnoc shean and Cnoc fhada. It keeps the Old Spirits and is known for its hay. Known for its hay from the fair fields.

**Achadh fhionn** (Ceann mhin). Founded 15 an Dùbhlachd, LE 60 by Dia-thìrich barley farmers. A farming village of fair barley fields between Baile mhin and Àth ghlas. In the Age of Strangers its pastures were taken for the horses of the administration, and they have served as remount grounds for the soldiers of the district ever since. It is a quiet place, larger in fields than in people. Known for its barley fields and remount pastures.

**Achadh gharbh** (Inis bheag). Founded 7 an Dàmhair, LE 205 by farmers from Inis bheag. Rough ground behind the river port of Inis bheag, broken to the plough in the long centuries after the Sundering fleet had gone. It feeds the river port and its fishing boats, and it has grown larger than many towns while keeping the name and customs of a village. The druid schools have a strong following among its farmers, who are said to argue the schools' questions over the furrow. Known for its stony fields that feed Inis bheag.

**Achadh gharbh** (Inis bheag). Founded 3 am Faoilleach, LE 1,104 by farmers of Muileann chaol. A rough field village beside the older Muileann chaol, breaking stony ground for the mill. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and shares its name with two other Achadh gharbhs of the east, which the library's clerks tell apart only by their shires. Known for its stony fields for the old mill.

**Achadh gharbh** (Caol shean). Founded 13 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,597 by the keepers of Allt an Àigh. A rough field village beside Allt an Àigh, the stream said to grant fortune to those who drink at the right phase of the moon. Pilgrims have come since the Holy Age, and the keepers' citadel was built to guard the stream from anyone who would bottle and sell it. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith, whose druids have never agreed whether the stream's luck is real. Known for Allt an Àigh, the stream of fortune.

**Achadh gharbh** (Tobar fhiadhaich). Founded 21 an Giblean, LE 565 by Dia-thìrich peat-cutters of the northern uplands. A village no bigger than a hamlet, of rough moor fields and peat banks above Tobar fhiadhaich. Its peat warmed the northern towns when the Small-Burning Law still held and the coloured coal was not burned freely. Fewer than a thousand people live there now. Known for its rough moor fields and peat.

**Achadh gheal** (Seann Skell). Founded 23 an t-Samhain, FE 2,040 by Dia-thìrich flax-growers of Seann Skell. The white field is the flax country that feeds the linen-weavers of Seann Skell, and in the drying season the whole plain is laid with bleaching cloth. The village is large and prosperous for its kind, and it follows the order of Manannan as the river port does. Its growers' guild has sold to the same Seann Skell houses for longer than either side can prove. Known for its flax fields and bleached linen.

**Achadh ghlas** (Seann Skell). Founded 26 an Lùnastal, FE 1,341 by Dia-thìrich farmers of Seann Skell. A village of grey-green fields on the road north from Seann Skell, whose barley and oats feed the great river port. It lies just south of the Tuathaich line, and since the Severance its farmers have ploughed with one eye on the boundary. In the Long War its barns quartered soldiers of the seventh regiment on the way to Àth leathan. Known for its grey fields on the Seann Skell road.

**Achadh ìseal** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 27 an t-Sultain, LE 1,184 by farmers from Muileann dhomhain. A low field village in the south-east, farming for the mill town of Muileann dhomhain and the port of Ceann chaol. It keeps the Old Spirits. Of its history nothing is written but its harvests. Known for its harvests for the southern mills.

**Achadh mhin** (Cnoc naomh). Founded 1 an Lùnastal, FE 738 by farmers of the southern coast. Achadh mhin is a farming village of the south, founded in the Holy Age. Tonn Mhòr struck it in the first years of the restored kingdom and destroyed it in a single night. It was rebuilt and keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its rebuilding after the Great Wave.

**Achadh mhin** (Baile gharbh). Founded 19 an Lùnastal, LE 1,801 by Dia-thìrich farmers of Baile gharbh. A village of smooth, well-drained fields that feeds the harbour at Ceann dhubh. It is not the Achadh mhin of the southern coast that the Great Wave struck. It has had few recorded troubles and is mentioned in the older rolls chiefly for its tithe. Known for its smooth fields of Baile gharbh.

**Achadh mhòr** (Achadh mhòr). Founded 2 an t-Samhain, VE 9,323 by field-clearing households of the warm springs. Achadh mhòr is still called a field village, though it is one of the largest settlements on the island and the seat of its province. It is the granary of the east, and the shared-meal custom of the Holy Age is said to have been kept here most faithfully. Travellers on the road stop at An Sligeanach Fad' às nearby. Known for the great granary fields.

**Achadh mhòr** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 28 an Gearran, FE 2,856 by Dia-thìrich farmers of Cnoc bheag. A farming village of six thousand just south of the Tuathaich line. It follows the order of Manannan, like its neighbours across the line. It trades with both sides and has been watched by both. Known for its border fields south of the Tuathaich line.

**Achadh naomh** (Achadh naomh). Founded 5 an t-Ògmhios, VE 9,414 by settlers of the spring-fields. Achadh naomh is a large village and the seat of its province in the north-central country, settled in the Ancient Age beside a spring held sacred. Colbh Cnoc chiar stands to its east, carved 'remember the fire'. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Known for its holy field by Colbh Cnoc chiar.

**Achadh naomh** (Achadh naomh). Founded 28 an t-Sultain, FE 2,324 by Dia-thìrich households of the ancestor feasts. The holy field was a meeting ground for the ancestor feasts of the Old Spirits before any house stood on it, and the houses were built around its edge rather than upon it. It is now a village of twenty-five thousand and the seat of its province, yet the field at its heart is still left unploughed. The feasts are kept there as they were in the Holy Age. Known for the ancestor feasts on the unploughed field.

**Achadh shean** (Achadh shean). Founded 21 an Giblean, VE 8,448 by Dia-thìrich farming households. Achadh shean, the old field, is a village of twenty-five thousand and the seat of its province. It gave its name to Tiormachd Achadh shean, the Long Drought, which settled over the island's dry season for three years running in the Age of Strangers. Its granaries were emptied in those years and rebuilt larger afterward, and they are the largest on the eastern coast. Known for the old fields and the Long Drought.

**Àth àrsaidh** (Dùn dhearg). Founded 19 am Màrt, FE 1,894 by the ford-keepers of Dùn dhearg. An ancient ford in the east, between the mill town of Muileann leathan and Seann Mhorn on the coast. It keeps the Old Spirits and a ford-stone where travellers leave a pebble, and it has been a small crossing town since the Holy Age. Known for the pebble-cairn at the ford-stone.

**Àth àrsaidh** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 12 an t-Samhain, VE 8,781 by quarrying households of the north-west; resettled by the Tuathaich. An ancient ford in the north-west, the seat of Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It is a large town of the Church and the market of the Tuathaich southern country. Known for the ancient ford of the Tuathaich.

**Àth bheag** (Baile fhiadhaich). Founded 14 an t-Samhain, LE 224 by the ford-keepers of Baile fhiadhaich. A small ford in the west on the road between Baile fhiadhaich and Cnoc ìseal. It follows the order of Manannan and has never been much more than a crossing, though crown regiments marched through it to Àth leathan in the Long War. Known for a small western crossing.

**Àth bheag** (Baile ìseal). Founded 14 an Giblean, SE 9 by Tuathaich families sent north at the Severance. A small ford settlement founded by Tuathaich families who came north at the Severance. It has fewer than a thousand people. It trades with Baile ìseal and Baile òg, the other Tuathaich towns of its province. Known for a ford settled after the Severance.

**Àth bheag** (Àth bheag). Founded 26 an Cèitean, VE 9,670 by Dia-thìrich ford-keepers of the east coast. Àth bheag is a town of twenty thousand at a ford of the Abhainn dhubh on the east coast, the seat of its province. Pirate ships have been seen offshore, and the town keeps watchers on the dunes. The lighthouse of Baile ìseal lies a short way south. Its salt-pans supply the whole eastern seaboard. Known for its east-coast ford under pirate watch.

**Àth chaol** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 5 an t-Sultain, LE 519 by the ford-wardens of Baile Mòr dhomhain. One of the island's many narrow fords, this one a walled post on the north road into Baile Mòr dhomhain. The city built its walls to hold the crossing in the troubles before the Severance, and it is still garrisoned in name. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its walled ford on the city's north road.

**Àth chaol** (Achadh naomh). Founded 20 an t-Sultain, FE 2,379 by the ford-keepers of Achadh naomh. A narrow ford in the east where the road to the harbour at Inis mhin crosses a stream. It keeps the Old Spirits of the Dia-thìrich, and its ford runs low in the dry months. It is a small market town for the holy field of Achadh naomh. Known for its narrow ford on the Inis mhin road.

**Àth chaol** (Seann Tarr). Founded 6 an Gearran, LE 809 by harbour-folk of Seann Tarr. A narrow harbour ford in the far east, close to the old Seann-Dhaoine harbour of Seann Tarr. It keeps the Old Spirits and sends its fishing to the market at Cnoc uaine. Known for its fishing in the eastern narrows.

**Àth chaol** (Muileann chiar). Founded 30 an Dùbhlachd, AE 66 by miners of the central diggings. A narrow ford-town in the central hills, grown in the Age of Strangers around the camp-roads to the diggings near Cill ghlas. The Rending, Scàineadh Cill ghlas, killed miners of this town in the collapse, and the people here still use scàinte of a man who is shaken. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its miners, who died in the Rending.

**Àth chaol** (Dùn thais). Founded 12 an Lùnastal, LE 1,401 by carters of Dùn thais. A small town at a narrow ford on the Dùn thais road, living on the carts that pass through it. Since the library was founded at Muileann chaol many of its young people have gone to work there as porters and copyists. It has never been walled or fought over. Known for its narrow ford on the Dùn thais road.

**Àth chiar** (Àth shean). Founded 21 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,362 by ford-keepers of the east road. Àth chiar is a ford town east of the capital, founded in the long quiet centuries. The field of Muileann ghlas lies to its south-west, and the town was a supply post in the last battle of An Cogadh Fada. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. The ford carries Rathad na Mèinne, the mine road from the capital to the hills. Known for its dusky ford near Muileann ghlas field.

**Àth chiar** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 30 an Lùnastal, LE 1,347 by the ford-guards of Baile Mòr dhomhain. A dusky ford on the west road out of Baile Mòr dhomhain, walled against the roads' thieves in the Age of Strangers. It is a carriers' town, and the road-house An Taigh-seinnse Reòta at Muileann fhada lies a short way down the road. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its carriers of the west road.

**Àth chiar** (Àth chiar). Founded 18 an Giblean, FE 2,769 by the drovers of the south-east. A dusky ford in the south-east with a citadel, the seat of Siorrachd Àth chiar and a large market town. Its keep was held by Dia-thìrich rebels in the war before the Severance and is still garrisoned. It keeps the Old Spirits and trades with the coast at Seann Mhorn and Muileann chiar to the south. Known for the rebels' keep and southern cattle-market.

**Àth chrom** (Seann Skell). Founded 21 am Màrt, LE 1,271 by fishers of the west. Àth chrom, the bent ford, is a river town at a bend of the Abhainn naomh in the west, below Seann Skell, whose boats go down to the sea at Ros àrsaidh. It was founded in the long quiet centuries. Since An Cogadh Fada, troops of the regiment named for Seann Skell have been quartered close by. Known for its bent ford on the lower Abhainn naomh.

**Àth chrom** (Seann Chwen). Founded 19 an t-Samhain, LE 701 by ford-keepers of the Seann Chwen country. A small ford on a bent stream south of Cill ghlas, where the Rending opened. It follows the order of Macha. Known for its bent ford south of Cill ghlas.

**Àth chrom** (Muileann naomh). Founded 3 an t-Iuchar, LE 989 by Dia-thìrich drovers; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. A drovers' town at the bent ford, Dia-thìrich until the Severance and Tuathaich since. It lies a short way from the field of Àth leathan, and its people carried the dead from that battle. It follows the faith of the Church. Known for its Tuathaich drovers at the bent ford.

**Àth chrom** (Achadh shean). Founded 9 an Giblean, LE 264 by carters of Achadh shean. A small town at a bent ford on the road from Achadh shean to the coast. It lives on the road and has never been more than a crossing. Known for its bent ford on the Achadh shean road.

**Àth dhearg** (Cnoc shean). Founded 26 an Giblean, AE 22 by Dia-thìrich miners bound by the strangers' contracts. Àth dhearg of Cnoc shean began as a mining camp at a ford in the Age of Strangers, and its red water is said to come from the spoil. It is neither the Àth dhearg whose name the northern lighthouse bears nor the western ford that the Great Hunger struck. Known for its red ford of the mining camps.

**Àth dhearg** (Cnoc gheal). Founded 19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 364 by ford-keepers of the north-east coast. A red ford-town near the north-east coast, whose name was given to Taigh-solais Àth dhearg, one of the five lighthouses built in the Age of Strangers at the request of human navigators. The beacon burned the coloured coal for more than a century and was among the first things on the island converted to dubhan. The town keeps the Old Spirits and lives by the coast road and the lighthouse. Known for Taigh-solais Àth dhearg, the north-east beacon.

**Àth dhearg** (Baile chaol). Founded 25 am Faoilleach, FE 1,464 by Dia-thìrich keepers of the holy wood. Àth dhearg stands at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, and its people have acted as keepers of the wood's western paths since the Holy Age. Walls were raised in the Age of Strangers to keep timber-cutters out of the forest as much as to keep raiders out of the town. It is not the Àth dhearg of the lighthouse in the north. Known for its ford at the edge of the holy wood.

**Àth dhearg** (Ceann mhòr). Founded 15 an Giblean, FE 1,909 by Dia-thìrich ford-keepers; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. A red ford on the western coast below the lighthouse of Baile chrom, struck by Gorta Baile chrom in the Age of Strangers and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. Its people keep the faith of the Church, as most of this coast does. It is not the Àth dhearg of the north-eastern lighthouse. Known for its red ford under the Baile chrom light.

**Àth dhìreach** (Achadh chaol). Founded 8 am Màrt, AE 90 by Dia-thìrich carters of the mining road. A straight ford with a citadel in the north-east, built as a waystation on the coal road in the Age of Strangers and fortified in the war before the Severance. Since the Long War it has been the station of An dàrna rèisimeid, the second regiment. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for the second regiment's garrison.

**Àth dhìreach** (Muileann chiar). Founded 20 an Giblean, FE 2,404 by carriers of the mountain country. Àth dhìreach, high in the mountain country, was a carriers' settlement of the Holy Age that the shared-meal law fed through the poor season, and in the Age of Strangers the coal carts crossed at its ford. It is a town of three thousand in the eastern mining district. Its ford is paved with spoil from the diggings. Known for its straight ford of the coal carts.

**Àth dhomhain** (Àth dhomhain). Founded 19 an Lùnastal, LE 1,611 by Raghnall Àthach and his kin. The deep ford here could only be crossed on horseback, and a family of ferrymen became a family of lords by owning the one safe path over it. The citadel on the near bank was fought for in the troubles before the Severance and has been the seat of Siorrachd Àth dhomhain since. The town is large and orderly, a house of the druid schools stands by the gate, and Cnoc mhòr and Baile gheal send it their grain. Known for the horseman's ford and shire citadel.

**Àth dhomhain** (Caol shean). Founded 22 an t-Samhain, LE 1,637 by ford-keepers of Caol shean. A deep ford on the road from Caol shean inland, where goods from the river port are loaded from boats to carts. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for the inland ford of Caol shean.

**Àth dhomhain** (Dùn thais). Founded 6 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,930 by Dia-thìrich ford-keepers of Dùn thais. The deep ford lies below Muileann chaol, and every reader bound for the library crosses it. It is a town of eleven thousand. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its deep ford below Muileann chaol.

**Àth dhubh** (Dùn chrom). Founded 1 an t-Sultain, LE 777 by Dia-thìrich ferrymen of Dùn chrom. The black ford takes its name from the dark water over the crossing. Walls were raised in the Age of Strangers, when the crossing carried much of the capital's traffic eastward. The Battle of Muileann ghlas, the last of An Cogadh Fada, was fought within sight of its walls. Known for the black ford and its walls.

**Àth fhada** (Baile gharbh). Founded 12 an t-Sultain, FE 2,509 by ford-keepers of the north-east road. Àth fhada, the long ford, is a town on the north-east road, founded in the Holy Age. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Its ford is long and shallow, and carts cross it only at low water. Known for its long ford of the north-east road.

**Àth fhada** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 18 am Màrt, LE 908 by Dia-thìrich ford-wardens, resettled by the Tuathaich. A long ford on the north-western roads, held by a Dia-thìrich warden-family through the quiet centuries of the Sundering. After the Severance its houses were emptied and given to Tuathaich families shepherded north, who raised the present walls and made it one of the chief towns of their homeland. The Tuathaich here keep the faith of the Church, and their church stands among the shrines the Dia-thìrich left behind; the ford is still paid for in toll. Its dubhan works, the largest in the north-west, are now its chief trade, and it binds books, a craft the Tuathaich learned at Muileann leathan. Known for the long ford and its toll.

**Àth fhiadhaich** (Àth fhiadhaich). Founded 13 an Dùbhlachd, VE 9,648 by Dia-thìrich herders of the wild cattle. Àth fhiadhaich stands in the south-eastern hills at the ford where the eastern road crosses the meeting of the Abhainn gheal and the Abhainn bhàn, and it has been a river landing since the Holy Age. The traffic of the vein country made it great in the Age of Strangers, and the far-famed road-house An Sligeanach Fad' às stands at Ceann bhàn, a short way down the road. The town keeps the Old Spirits, the oldest folk rite, and its river fishers still bless their nets at the ford. Copper is mined in the hills behind it, and the town's new street is named for the Sloc Mòr. Known for its wild ford of the eastern road.

**Àth fhiadhaich** (Baile gheal). Founded 6 an Cèitean, LE 20 by ford-keepers of the road to Inis thais. Àth fhiadhaich of the south-west is a ford on the pilgrimage road from Caol leathan to the temple of Lia Fàil at Inis thais. It grew from a single house of the long quiet centuries into a small town that lives on the pilgrims. It keeps the order of the Stone. Known for its ford on the pilgrims' road to Lia Fàil.

**Àth fhiadhaich** (Doire chaol). Founded 14 an t-Sultain, FE 995 by Dia-thìrich ford-keepers of the capital. Àth fhiadhaich is the wild ford on the south road out of Cathair dhearg, a town of ten thousand that grew as the capital grew. Its crossing was paved in the Holy Age, and the road over it carries the capital's trade toward the southern coast. It follows the capital's order, the order of Macha, and its shrine keepers take part in the rites at Cathair dhearg. Known for its wild ford on the capital's south road.

**Àth fhionn** (Àth fhionn). Founded 26 an Giblean, FE 900 by drovers of the southern roads. Àth fhionn, the fair ford, is a large inland town at the crossing of the southern drove road. It has been a resting place for herds and drovers since the Holy Age. Its people keep the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits and hold the drove-road fair at the ford. Known for its fording place of the southern drove road.

**Àth fhionn** (Seann Skell). Founded 13 an t-Samhain, LE 1,782 by farmers of the south-east. Àth fhionn of Seann Skell is a ford town of the south-east. It was founded in the long quiet centuries. Since An Cogadh Fada it has billeted soldiers of the regiments stationed at Seann Skell nearby. It keeps the orthodox rite of Òrd Bhrìde. Known for its billets for the Seann Skell garrisons.

**Àth fhionn** (Muileann shean). Founded 30 an Dùbhlachd, LE 697 by fishers of the north coast. Àth fhionn of Muileann shean is a ford town of the north coast, founded in the long quiet centuries where the coast road crosses a clear stream. It shares the watch-fire of Cnoc gheal and trades with the harbour of Cill leathan. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and is the market town of the north coast. Fish, whale-oil and wool come to its strand-market, and its whale-boats go out every summer. Known for its fair ford of the north coast.

**Àth fhionn** (Seann Bhrenn). Founded 8 am Màrt, FE 238 by the ford-keepers of Seann Bhrenn. A fair ford in the north below the city of Dùn thais, on the road from the Seann-Dhaoine harbour at Seann Bhrenn. It keeps the Old Spirits of the Dia-thìrich and remains a small crossing town. Known for the fair ford.

**Àth fhionn** (Caol mhòr). Founded 25 an Cèitean, AE 14 by human traders, as a waystation. Àth fhionn was a waystation of human traders on the road north, built in the Age of Strangers at a fair ford. The Tuathaich kept it after the Severance. It is small, fewer than a thousand people, and its inn is still built in the humans' manner. Known for a human waystation at the fair ford.

**Àth fhionn** (Ceann mhòr). Founded 14 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,775 by Dia-thìrich ford-keepers; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. A fair ford on the western coast road below the lighthouse of Baile chrom, struck by Gorta Baile chrom in the Age of Strangers and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It is a town of nearly nine thousand and the market for Doire chaol's charcoal. Its people follow the faith of the Church, as most of this coast does. Known for its fair ford of the western coast.

**Àth gharbh** (Doire shean). Founded 28 an t-Sultain, FE 1,855 by drovers of the western road. Àth gharbh, the rough ford, is a walled town of the south-west, a short walk from Doire shean and its great roadside tavern, Am Buabhall Fortanach. That tavern fortified with the others of the old mining circuit before the war of the Severance. Since An Cogadh Fada, A' chiad chabhlach has been stationed here and carries the town's name; its hulls lie in the harbour of Doire shean below. Known for the first fleet's walled ford town.

**Àth gharbh** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 13 an Gearran, VE 4,424 by hill-folk of the high valleys. A rough ford on the hill road near Baile Mòr uaine, where the drovers rest their beasts. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and is a very small place. In a hearth of peat ash here lies the oldest burning of the coloured coal by any household outside the Mason's line, one sliver burnt to a bead. Coinneachadh nan Cupan, the spring where the keeper's stone cup was first checked against its copies, lies on the moor between the ford and Tobar dhìreach. Known for a drovers' ford in the hills.

**Àth gheal** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 29 an t-Sultain, LE 682 by Dia-thìrich ferrymen; resettled by the Tuathaich. Àth gheal was a Dia-thìrich ford-and-harbour town of the long quiet centuries, walled in the Age of Strangers and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. When dubhan came into use it was among the northern towns that went on working the last coal seams. It was one of the holdouts broken in An Cogadh Fada, and its people still speak bitterly of that year. Known for a walled town of the coal-holdouts.

**Àth gheal** (Muileann bheag). Founded 20 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,021 by farmers of Muileann bheag. Àth gheal of Muileann bheag is a ford town near Seann Tarr, founded in the long quiet centuries. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. At the great feasts it lodges the pilgrims bound for the shrine at Seann Tarr. Known for its white ford near Seann Tarr.

**Àth ghlas** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 16 an Giblean, LE 149 by the grey-stone quarrymen. A ford over grey water on the road between Baile Mòr dhomhain and the south, it grew up around a quarry whose pale-grey stone faces half the city's houses. The quarry is now worked out, and the town has shrunk to a waystation for carriers. Its people keep to the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for the worked-out grey quarry.

**Àth ghlas** (Àth ghlas). Founded 12 an t-Iuchar, FE 373 by Dia-thìrich ford-keepers of the central country. The grey ford is the seat of its province, a large town beside Cathair mhòr and a short way from the ruin of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire. The ruin is older than any other dwelling-place known on the island, and the town has kept its people out of it by custom. It lives on trade between Cathair mhòr and the eastern towns. Known for its grey ford below the ruined outpost.

**Àth ghlas** (Ceann mhin). Founded 7 am Màrt, LE 392 by Dia-thìrich ford-keepers. A small town at a grey ford upstream of Drochaid Ros fhionn. It took the traffic when the old bridge fell out of use, and grew as the bridge-villages shrank. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its grey ford that replaced the old bridge.

**Àth ghlas** (Inis thais). Founded 31 am Faoilleach, FE 1,413 by Dia-thìrich traders of Inis thais. Àth ghlas is a large ford-market of the west, near Seann Warr. It follows the order of Manannan. It is one of three places named Àth ghlas and the largest. Known for its grey ford market of the west.

**Àth ghorm** (Seann Dunn). Founded 28 an Giblean, LE 1,403 by ford-keepers of Seann Dunn. A blue ford with a small citadel on the road inland from Seann Dunn, built to hold the crossing for the harbour. It follows the order of Macha and is a small town of carters and toll-keepers. Known for the toll-ford of Seann Dunn.

**Àth ghorm** (Cnoc leathan). Founded 27 an Lùnastal, LE 429 by Dia-thìrich innkeepers of Cnoc leathan. A small town at a blue ford a short way from An Taigh-òsta Grianach, the great roadside inn of the eastern circuit. Its people keep stables and sell to travellers. It fortified its inns before the war, as the tavern road did everywhere. Known for its blue ford by An Taigh-òsta Grianach.

**Àth ìseal** (Muileann chrom). Founded 7 an t-Iuchar, LE 324 by Dia-thìrich ferrymen of Muileann chrom. The low ford floods each wet season, and for part of every year the crossing is made by ferry. The town is small and has always been poor. It sends its surplus down to the quays at Inis ìseal and Ceann fhada. Known for the low ford and its ferry.

**Àth leathan** (Seann Skell). Founded 8 am Màrt, LE 1,303 by Dia-thìrich drovers; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. A Dia-thìrich drovers' village at the wide ford, emptied at the Severance and resettled by Tuathaich families sent north. In the years before the Long War it became a gathering place for the coal-holdouts of the north-west. The Battle of Àth leathan, the first great battle of An Cogadh Fada, was fought on the meadows just west of the ford, and the town has never regained its numbers. Known for the first battlefield of the Long War.

**Àth leathan** (Caol mhòr). Founded 24 am Faoilleach, LE 925 by Dia-thìrich drovers; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. The northern Àth leathan is a drovers' ford resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It is not the battlefield of the Long War, which lies far to the south-west, and its people have spent a generation correcting travellers. It follows the faith of the Church. Known for a drovers' ford in the north.

**Àth mhin** (Dùn chrom). Founded 7 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,064 by wardens of the Dùn chrom crossings. A walled town with a citadel at the smooth ford, one of a chain of crossings east of the capital. It was a quartering place for soldiers in the Age of Strangers and again in the Long War, when it held the kingdom's stores for the campaign that ended at Muileann ghlas. Its people are mostly carters and stable-keepers. Known for the smooth ford and its citadel.

**Àth mhòr** (Baile chaol). Founded 12 an t-Samhain, FE 2,418 by Dia-thìrich road-keepers of Baile chaol. The great ford carries the road from Seann Dunn inland, and for most of its history it has been the busiest crossing in the province. A path leaves the town southward to Làrach an Teampaill, and the folk of Àth mhòr have kept that path cleared for as long as there are accounts of it, though they will not say why. It is a large, plain town of carters, smiths and innkeepers. Known for the great ford and the temple-ruin path.

**Àth mhòr** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 26 an Cèitean, FE 1,598 by Dia-thìrich ford-keepers of the northern plain. One of several towns of this name, this Àth mhòr carries the tavern road across the river near An Taigh-seinnse Reòta. It was a waypoint on the mining roads in the Holy Age and a militia halt in the years before the war. It trades oak from Doire dhìreach down the road to the towns of the plain. Known for its ford on the northern tavern road.

**Àth mhòr** (Àth mhòr). Founded 1 an t-Ògmhios, VE 7,170 by households of the northern ford. Àth mhòr is the walled great ford of the north and the seat of its province, a town of twelve thousand. Its walls were raised in the Age of Strangers, when the northern road carried coal to the coast and the ford was worth holding. Baile bheag lies across the river and handles the traffic after the gates are shut. Known for its walled great ford of the north.

**Àth naomh** (Cuan shean). Founded 26 an Giblean, LE 900 by druids of the order of Manannan. A holy ford near Cuan shean, where the druids of Manannan bless the carts that go down to the harbour. It follows the order of Manannan and is a small town of shrine-keepers and carters. Bog-iron is dug in the moss behind the town, and its forges have made arms and field-guns for the regiments since An Cogadh Fada. Known for its blessing of the harbour carts.

**Àth naomh** (Cnoc thais). Founded 26 an t-Sultain, FE 2,780 by Dia-thìrich druids of the holy ford; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. The holy ford was a Dia-thìrich shrine and crossing, and a citadel was raised over it in the Holy Age. At the Severance the Dia-thìrich left and Tuathaich families took the town, which is now one of the largest they hold. They keep the citadel manned and the old shrine open as their church. Known for its citadel over the holy ford.

**Àth ruadh** (Doire fhionn). Founded 25 an t-Sultain, FE 2,335 by cattle-drovers of the eastern hills. A red-banked ford where the drovers' road crosses a stream in the east, it has been a cattle-market since the Holy Age. It keeps the Old Spirits of the Dia-thìrich, and the drovers still pour a cup into the ford before driving a herd across. The town trades beasts to Seann Dunn on the coast and hides to Baile shean. Furs and hides from the eastern hills are sold at its fair. Known for the drovers' ford and cattle fair.

**Àth shean** (Àth shean). Founded 9 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,684 by farming households of the ford. The northern of the two Àth shean holds the old ford where the road east from the capital crosses its river. It was walled in the Holy Age to guard that crossing and has grown into a large town. An Taigh-seinnse Mòr stands a short way up the road toward Seann Vell. The dark wine pressed on its slopes is sold along the eastern road. Known for its old ford of the eastern road.

**Àth shean** (Àth shean). Founded 15 an Dàmhair, FE 1,963 by ford-wardens of the south. The southern Àth shean is the larger of the two, a great ford town near the south coast. It has been a market since the Holy Age and has never needed walls. Its harbour is the old site of Seann Chwen, a short way east. Known for the great southern ford market.

**Àth shean** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 8 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,486 by boatmen of the Baile Mòr dhomhain river. The old ford and landing that served Baile Mòr dhomhain before the city had quays of its own. Barges from the landing carry the city's goods to the coast, and the boatmen's guild here is older than the city's walls. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith like its great neighbour and is counted, for most purposes, as the city's river-port. Known for the river landing of Baile Mòr dhomhain.

**Àth shean** (Tobar ghorm). Founded 15 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,659 by the ford-lords of Tobar ghorm. An old walled ford with a citadel in the north, holding the road between Tobar ghorm and Cnoc dhubh. Its keep was fought for in the war before the Severance. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for the old walled ford.

**Àth shean** (Seann Skell). Founded 9 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,926 by Dia-thìrich keepers of the northern ford. An old ford on the road north out of the Dia-thìrich country, walled in the Age of Strangers and strengthened again after the Severance, when the Tuathaich country began a short way to the west. It is a town of the Hawk order, Òrd an t-Seabhaig, and its temple is one of the oldest of the order, whose rite is the older form of Òrd Bhrìde's. It trades with Inis bhàn to the south and, warily, with the Tuathaich villages over the line. Known for its old ford on the northern march.

**Àth uaine** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 18 an t-Samhain, FE 2,176 by Dia-thìrich weavers; resettled by the Tuathaich. Àth uaine of Cnoc ghorm is a green ford of the north-west, founded by Dia-thìrich flax-weavers in the Holy Age. It was resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance and still weaves. It keeps the faith of the Church. Known for its green ford and flax-weaving.

**Àth uaine** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 6 an Cèitean, AE 63 by Dia-thìrich miners bound by the strangers' contracts. Àth uaine of Cnoc dhubh began as a mining camp at a ford in the Age of Strangers. Its camp graves lie in the field by the ford, tended by the keepers of the Old Spirits' ancestor rite. The camp outlived its working and became a small farm town. Known for its camp graves by the green ford.

**Àth uaine** (Seann Skell). Founded 3 an Giblean, FE 141 by ford-keepers of Seann Skell. Àth uaine of Seann Skell is a ford town inland of the Hawk bay, founded in the Holy Age. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. It is the market for the three quarrelling harbours of the bay. Known for its green ford inland of Seann Skell.

**Àth uaine** (Doire fhionn). Founded 25 an Giblean, LE 1,715 by the wardens of the Achadh shean road. A small garrison town at the green ford on the road between Doire fhionn and Achadh shean. Its citadel is larger than the town needs, for the ford was once fought over, though by whom is not remembered. Tiormachd Achadh shean, the Long Drought, struck it in the Age of Strangers, and it lives now on toll and on the soldiers who still keep the tower. Known for its garrisoned green ford.

#### B

**Baile àrsaidh** (Baile chiar). Founded 1 an Gearran, FE 476 by custodians of the capital's south. Baile àrsaidh, the ancient town, is a citadel town of the capital's southern country, founded in the Holy Age. Its citadel guards the market at Baile chiar. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its old citadel of the southern country.

**Baile àrsaidh** (Caol mhòr). Founded 15 am Màrt, FE 1,651 by Dia-thìrich shore-lords, resettled by the Tuathaich. An ancient walled town near the harbour of Caol mhòr, one of the Dia-thìrich towns resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. The walls are older than any Dia-thìrich memory of them, and the Tuathaich have kept them. It follows the faith of the Church. Known for its old walls in the Tuathaich north.

**Baile àrsaidh** (Baile àrsaidh). Founded 19 an t-Samhain, FE 879 by settlers from Cathair dhomhain. Baile àrsaidh is the ancient town of the west, the seat of its province and the place where the druids of the order of Manannan have kept their school since the orders divided. It is a large town of twenty thousand. It trades with Seann Skell to the north and with the fleet at Cuan shean to the south. Known for the school of Manannan's druids.

**Baile bhàn** (Caol bheag). Founded 21 an Giblean, LE 1,634 by fullers of the northern coast. A town of fulling-mills and white cloth between the port-city of Ros chiar and the city of Baile Mòr dhìreach. Its fullers bleached wool for the harbours of the north coast and still do, though in smaller measure since the trade moved to Inis mhòr. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its bleached cloth from the fulling-mills.

**Baile bhàn** (Cill dhìreach). Founded 30 an t-Sultain, LE 1,268 by a custodian house of Cill dhìreach. Baile bhàn is a white town with a citadel above Cill dhìreach, built to guard the temple-town and its treasuries. It is a town of five thousand. Its garrison keeps order at Còmhrag Ceann leathan. Known for its citadel above Cill dhìreach.

**Baile bhàn** (Doire mhin). Founded 19 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,238 by Dia-thìrich traders of Doire mhin. Baile bhàn is a white town of nine thousand near Cathair mhòr, on the road toward Muileann ghlas. Before the last battle of the Long War the kingdom's columns marched through it. It follows the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its white walls on the Muileann ghlas road.

**Baile bheag** (Àth mhòr). Founded 20 an Dùbhlachd, LE 180 by carters across the ford from Àth mhòr. A small town across the ford from Àth mhòr, grown up to serve the traffic that the walled town would not let in after dark. It is a town of stables, carters and cheap lodging. It has always hung on Àth mhòr and has never been allowed a market of its own. Known for its carters at the ford.

**Baile bheag** (Muileann bheag). Founded 3 an t-Samhain, LE 1,046 by toll-keepers of Muileann bheag. A small town on the road to Muileann bheag, walled to collect tolls rather than to keep enemies out. It still collects them, and has outlived every attempt to take the right away. It is one of several places named Baile bheag. Known for a walled town of tolls.

**Baile chaol** (Baile chaol). Founded 30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,339 by the valley-folk of the eastern narrows. A town squeezed into a narrow valley in the east and the seat of Siorrachd Baile chaol. Its houses climb the valley sides in rows, and the one road through it has been tolled since the Holy Age. It keeps the Old Spirits and trades with the city of Baile Mòr dhìreach and the market at Cnoc uaine; the sacred forest of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar lies on its western edge. Known for its terraced houses and the valley toll.

**Baile chiar** (Baile chiar). Founded 1 an Gearran, FE 869 by farmers of the capital's southern country. Baile chiar, the dusky town, is the market and provincial seat of the capital's southern country. It has been a farm market since the Holy Age and has never been walled; the citadel at Baile àrsaidh stands close by. Grain from Achadh fhada and the southern farms comes to its market. Its chartered weavers make cloth from southern wool. Known for its market of the capital's southern country.

**Baile chrom** (Doire mhin). Founded 24 am Faoilleach, LE 270 by the tithe-reeves of Cathair mhòr. A walled town on a bend of the road below Cathair mhòr, raised to store and guard the tithe-grain of the Doire mhin country. Its walls were strengthened when the human administration raised the tithe, and it is remembered that the grain was guarded but not shared. It keeps the order of Macha and serves Cill fhada and Muileann ruadh as their market. The dubhan works under its walls supply the forges of the gulf, and the town boils soap. Known for the walled tithe-granaries.

**Baile chrom** (Dùn chrom). Founded 5 am Màrt, LE 682 by herders from Dùn chrom. The lesser of the two Baile chroms in the central midlands, this one lies under the citadel of Dùn chrom and grew as its stockyard. The fighting at Muileann ghlas in the last year of the Long War passed close enough that the town housed wounded for a season. It keeps the order of Macha. Known for Dùn chrom's stockyards.

**Baile chrom** (Baile chrom). Founded 2 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,787 by households from Cnoc ghorm; resettled by the Tuathaich. A bent town on the far north-west coast, the seat of Siorrachd Baile chrom, beside Taigh-solais Baile chrom, the first of the five lighthouses as the ring is counted round the coast to Tobar dhearg. Since the Severance it has been Tuathaich, and it is the one town where Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise, the Church's vigil of the Grey Night, holds the majority; its one night of silence is kept for an Gèadh Fiadhaich, the wild goose of the Holy Spirit. Gorta Baile chrom, the Great Hunger, takes its name from this town, which it struck in the Age of Strangers. Manannan's priests at Ceann mhòr hold that the Grey Night grew out of their own harbour prayer to keep the sea shut, and call it their prayer gone astray; the Church's bishops call it irregular. Known for the Grey Night vigil and the lighthouse.

**Baile chrom** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 16 an Lùnastal, LE 736 by Dia-thìrich market families of Ceann àrsaidh. Baile chrom is named for its bending main street, which follows an old stream-bed. It is a market town between the capital and the northern plain, serving Baile fhiadhaich and Cuan chrom. It shares its name with three other places on the island, and it is named with its province to tell it from them. Known for the bent-street market.

**Baile dhearg** (Achadh chaol). Founded 10 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,076 by farmers of Achadh chaol. A red town in the east on the road to the harbour at Seann Toll. It keeps the Old Spirits. Known for its red walls on the harbour road.

**Baile dhìreach** (Inis thais). Founded 14 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,392 by traders of the order of Manannan from the west. Baile dhìreach, the straight town, is a harbour on the west coast built around one long street to the quay. It was founded in the long quiet centuries by traders of the order of Manannan, among neighbours of the order of the Stone. The two orders have shared its market without any trouble the rolls have thought fit to set down. Known for its straight-street harbour of the order of Manannan.

**Baile dhìreach** (Cnoc gheal). Founded 6 am Màrt, LE 1,154 by road-builders of Cnoc gheal. A straight town on the road from Cnoc gheal to Seann Bhrenn, named for the road that made it. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and is a carters' stop on the way to the coast. Known for the straight road to Seann Bhrenn.

**Baile dhìreach** (Caol shean). Founded 16 an Giblean, FE 875 by Dia-thìrich pilgrims to Allt an Àigh. Baile dhìreach is the nearest town to Allt an Àigh, and the straight road that gives it its name runs from its square down to the stream. It grew up in the Holy Age to serve the pilgrims and still does, alongside Cnoc ìseal further up the road. Its people are wary of strangers who come at the wrong phase of the moon. Gold is washed from the stream below the town, and its refiners make blanks for the mint. Known for the nearest town to Allt an Àigh.

**Baile dhìreach** (Muileann naomh). Founded 3 an Gearran, LE 1,075 by Dia-thìrich traders of Muileann naomh. A small town of one straight street on the far west, twinned with Cnoc gheal a short walk away. It lies close to the Tuathaich line and trades with the villages beyond it. It follows the order of Manannan. Known for its straight street, the twin of Cnoc gheal's.

**Baile dhìreach** (Doire fhionn). Founded 1 an t-Samhain, LE 251 by carters of the Seann Dunn road. A town of one straight road running down to Seann Dunn, whose carters take the dyed cloth of Baile ghorm to the harbour. It is a town of nearly ten thousand. It keeps the Old Spirits. Known for its straight road to Seann Dunn.

**Baile dhomhain** (Muileann chrom). Founded 10 am Faoilleach, AE 34 by a Company surveyor, as a camp for the pits. Baile dhomhain was laid out on a grid by a Company surveyor in the Age of Strangers, a camp for the deep workings and the first town of the Dia-thìrich drawn on paper before a stone of it was set; two of its streets were pulled down for a spoil-tip before the Severance. It is a small town in a deep valley now, farming for the house of Macha's order at Cnoc bhàn, whose tithe-rolls record its harvests without a gap since the kingdom was restored. Known for its tithe-fields of the Cnoc bhàn druids.

**Baile dhomhain** (Baile ghorm). Founded 7 an t-Samhain, VE 7,711 by households of the panther country. The deep town a short walk inland of Baile ghorm, a settlement of the Ancient Age to which the harbour's rope-walks and timber-yards were later moved to be clear of storms. The panthers' migration road, Imrich nam Pantar, crosses its fields, and the townsfolk shut their stock in when the cats pass. It follows the order of the Stone and works almost entirely for the harbour and its fleet. Known for its rope-walks and the panthers' road.

**Baile dhomhain** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 2 an t-Samhain, LE 1,140 by Dia-thìrich followers of the Hawk order. Baile dhomhain is a walled town in a deep valley near Cnoc bheag, one of the towns of the Hawk order. Its walls were raised in the Age of Strangers and strengthened after the Severance, when the Tuathaich line was drawn close by. A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death, struck it in the Age of Strangers. Its trade goes down to the quay at Ceann òg. Known for its walls and its Hawk-order houses in the deep valley.

**Baile dhubh** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 22 an Dàmhair, LE 1,142 by Dia-thìrich herders of the black-soil fields. Named for the dark earth of its fields, Baile dhubh was an ordinary Dia-thìrich farm town until the Severance drew the northern border around it. It kept its people when the province of Cnoc ghorm passed to the Tuathaich, and has lived since by trading with neighbours who have never wholly trusted it, nor it them. Its folk keep the Old Faith in the order of Manannan, whose sea-feasts their neighbours of the Church to the north have always kept beside their own; it is thought that this is why they were left in peace. Known for its standing as a Dia-thìrich enclave on the Tuathaich border.

**Baile dhubh** (Caol mhòr). Founded 4 an t-Samhain, AE 86 by human colliers of the northern seams. Baile dhubh, "the black town", was built by human colliers in the Age of Strangers on one of the northern seams of common coal, which the humans worked alongside the vein in the south. After the Severance it passed to the Tuathaich with the rest of the north. Before the Long War it was one of the towns that refused the new fuel and kept working the last seams that would still yield. Known for its coal pits of the northern holdouts.

**Baile dhubh** (Baile ghlas). Founded 1 an Giblean, AE 69 by human administrators near Seann Warr. Baile dhubh was built in the Age of Strangers as a clerks' town for the human administration near Seann Warr, where the fifth regiment is now stationed. After the Severance its Dia-thìrich people took up the order of the Stone, the Old Faith of the country around it. It has fewer than seven hundred people and lives on the garrison. Known for the old clerks' town by Seann Warr.

**Baile fhada** (Seann Dunn). Founded 27 an Dùbhlachd, LE 720 by Dia-thìrich soldiers of the capital's south. A town of one long street with a citadel at its end, south-east of the capital. It was a garrison town in the Age of Strangers and has kept its citadel manned since. Its people are soldiers' families and carters, and its street is the last stage of the road from the southern coast to Cathair dhearg. Known for its long street and citadel south of the capital.

**Baile fhiadhaich** (Cnoc gheal). Founded 6 am Faoilleach, LE 602 by farmers of the north-east. Baile fhiadhaich of Cnoc gheal is a walled farm town of the north-east. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and walled in the Age of Strangers against raiders from the sea. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Its fields grow the dye-plants of the north-east, and its colours go to the feast-market at Seann Tarr. Known for its walls and its farms.

**Baile fhiadhaich** (Baile fhiadhaich). Founded 17 an t-Iuchar, VE 8,032 by settlers of the western coast. Baile fhiadhaich of the west is a large harbour town and the seat of its province, settled in the Ancient Age. It lies near the field of Àth leathan, and its people remember the first battle of An Cogadh Fada. It keeps the order of Manannan. Known for its west-coast market harbour.

**Baile fhiadhaich** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 7 an Dàmhair, LE 407 by Dia-thìrich hunters of Ceann àrsaidh. The wild town was a hunters' camp in the Age of Sundering, when the forests of Ceann àrsaidh were larger. It still lives on hides and game, and its curing-sheds can be smelled from the road. Its people trade at Baile chrom. Known for its hunters and hide-curers.

**Baile fhionn** (Muileann leathan). Founded 31 an Dàmhair, LE 1,772 by Dia-thìrich farmers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A small fair town in the north-west, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It follows the Tuathaich Church and trades across the line with the Dia-thìrich town of Baile ruadh. Known for its trade across the line with Baile ruadh.

**Baile gharbh** (Baile gharbh). Founded 15 an Lùnastal, VE 7,985 by sheep-keeping households of the north-east. Baile gharbh is a large market town of the north-east and the seat of its province. It has been a wool market since the Holy Age, and the moor towns of Cnoc chaol and Àth fhada bring their flocks and cheese to it. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and has no walls, trusting to Baile Mòr dhìreach close by. Known for its wool market.

**Baile gharbh** (Tobar dhearg). Founded 1 an t-Ògmhios, LE 700 by the carters of Seann Vell. A rough town on the south coast road between Seann Vell and the lighthouse village of Tobar dhearg. It is one of the few towns where Òrd Bhrìde holds the majority, its orthodox druids having come from the pilgrim harbour at Caol naomh. It trades with Muileann naomh and the great port of Seann Skell. Known for an orthodox town of Brìde's flame on the coast road.

**Baile gheal** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 27 an Giblean, FE 715 by Dia-thìrich salt-boilers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A white-washed Dia-thìrich village of the Holy Age, it was one of the settlements emptied and handed to the Tuathaich after the Severance. The newcomers made it a town and a market, trading with the harbour at Caol naomh a short distance away. Its church stands in the shell of the older Dia-thìrich shrine of Manannan, and the two sets of carvings can still be told apart. Known for the church in the old shrine.

**Baile gheal** (Tobar ghorm). Founded 2 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,101 by the lime-burners of Tobar ghorm. A white town named for the lime-kilns that whitened it, walled in the Age of Strangers after raids on the road to the harbour at Inis naomh. It is paired with Cnoc mhòr on the hill above, and the two share a market and a quarrel over which is older. Its people follow the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its lime-kilns and whitewashed walls.

**Baile gheal** (Baile gheal). Founded 27 an Giblean, VE 9,670 by households round a white-limed house. A large white town of the western plain and the seat of Siorrachd Baile gheal. It is a city of the order of the Stone in all but name, and it trades cloth with Baile Mòr fhionn and the harbour of Inis thais. Known for its white cloth of the western plain.

**Baile gheal** (Ceann leathan). Founded 11 an t-Samhain, LE 282 by lime-burners of Ceann leathan. A small town of lime kilns whose white dust gives it its name. It supplies lime to the builders of the eastern coast and the fields around Ceann leathan. It keeps the Old Spirits. Known for its lime kilns of the east.

**Baile ghlas** (Baile ghlas). Founded 7 an Cèitean, VE 9,370 by boat-households of the Red Hill. Baile ghlas is a great harbour town on the capital shore and the seat of its province. Its rope-walks and sail-lofts have fitted ships for the capital since the Holy Age, and it claims, with no record to prove it, to have rigged the Sundering fleet. It has never been walled; the capital's walls stand close by. Known for its rope-walks and sail-lofts.

**Baile ghlas** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 13 an t-Samhain, LE 318 by Dia-thìrich green-dyers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A green-grey town of dyers, emptied at the Severance and resettled by the Tuathaich. It keeps the Tuathaich Church and is a market for Baile Mòr ruadh and Cnoc ghlas. Known for its green dyes and Tuathaich church feasts.

**Baile ghlas** (Cuan ruadh). Founded 4 an Gearran, LE 372 by Dia-thìrich slate-quarriers of Cuan ruadh. A small town of grey slate on the eastern coast, quarrying for the roofs of Achadh shean and Cnoc uaine. Its people keep the Old Spirits. Known for its grey slate of the east coast.

**Baile ghorm** (Baile ghorm). Founded 22 an Gearran, FE 837 by farming kindreds of the south-eastern downs. Baile ghorm is the market of its shire, a large open town without walls where the south-eastern farms bring their grain and wool. Its people keep the Old Spirits, the oldest folk rite of the island, and household shrines to the ancestors outnumber its spirit-houses. Achadh fhionn is its nearest field-village, and the ruin of Làrach an Dùin stands in its hinterland, left alone by custom. Known for its south-eastern grain and wool market.

**Baile ghorm** (Baile ghorm). Founded 7 an t-Ògmhios, VE 5,945 by salt-makers of the southern shore. A landing of drying-racks and boat-sheds on the southern coast, Baile ghorm grew through the Holy Age into the largest harbour between the capital and the eastern capes. Its people keep the order of the Stone, whose stone is Clach, and its quays are lined with the wolf-head posts, for the wolf of the Fianna, that mark a harbour of that order. Since the Long War it has been the station of An treas cabhlach, the third fleet, and its yards now do more work on the crown's hulls than on the town's own boats. Its smaller twin, Baile dhomhain, lies a short walk inland and sends it timber and rope. Known for the third fleet's anchorage and wolf-post quays.

**Baile ghorm** (Doire fhionn). Founded 22 an Lùnastal, LE 309 by Dia-thìrich dyers from Achadh shean. Baile ghorm grew up around woad pits and dye-houses, and its houses were long washed blue from the vats. It sent cloth to Seann Dunn for shipping and yarn to Achadh shean for weaving. The Old Spirits, the old rite of the ancestors, are strong here, and the dyers still leave a first skein at the hearth-stone each season. Known for its woad dyers and blue-washed houses.

**Baile ghorm** (Àth dhomhain). Founded 7 am Màrt, LE 1,757 by slate-quarriers of Àth dhomhain. Baile ghorm is a quarry town whose blue slate roofs half the northern plain. It sends slate to Inis mhòr and takes grain in return. It shares its name with a dyers' town far to the east, and the two are told apart by their provinces. Known for its blue slate quarries.

**Baile ìseal** (Seann Chwen). Founded 5 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,312 by farmers of the Seann Chwen country. A low town in the middle east, a short way south of Cill ghlas and the ground the Rending tore open. It follows the order of Macha and sends its grain to the harbour at Seann Chwen. Known for its grain, south of Cill ghlas.

**Baile ìseal** (Àth bheag). Founded 14 an t-Samhain, LE 197 by fishers of the far east coast. A small low town on the far east coast, beside Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, one of the five lighthouses completed in the Age of Strangers. Pirates are still seen off this coast, and the keepers of the light are also the town's watch. It keeps the Old Spirits. Known for Taigh-solais Baile ìseal and the pirate watch.

**Baile ìseal** (Baile ìseal). Founded 16 an t-Sultain, LE 1,567 by Dia-thìrich farmers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A low walled town in the north-west, the seat of Siorrachd Baile ìseal, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It follows the faith of the Church and is one of the larger Tuathaich towns. Known for the low walled town of the north-west.

**Baile ìseal** (Cill thais). Founded 1 an t-Sultain, LE 827 by farmers of Cill thais. A small walled town near Cill thais and Baile chiar, west of the capital. The walls were raised in the war before the Severance. It follows the order of Macha and has little trade of its own. Known for its small walls near the capital.

**Baile leathan** (Muileann leathan). Founded 21 an t-Iuchar, AE 23 by human settlers from an Tìr Thall. Baile leathan was built by human settlers in the Age of Strangers on the northern coast, one of the few places the strangers founded rather than took. After the Severance it became a Tuathaich town. It keeps the faith of the Church and its oldest families still count their descent from the Crossing. Known for an old strangers' settlement of the north.

**Baile leathan** (Dùn thais). Founded 21 am Faoilleach, FE 2,093 by Dia-thìrich scribes of Dùn thais. Baile leathan is one of the towns nearest Leabharlann Muileann chaol, and many of its people are copyists, binders and parchment-makers for the library. It was a market town of the broad valley long before the library was founded, and it grew quickly after. It keeps the druid schools' habit of reading aloud in the evenings. Known for its copyists and binders for the library.

**Baile mhin** (Baile mhin). Founded 17 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,685 by Dia-thìrich river-folk of the north-east. Baile mhin is a river town on the Abhainn bheag in the north-east and the seat of its province, founded in the Holy Age. Its quays are sheltered and its trade steady, and its barges go down to Caol chrom at the river mouth. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith, and the old landing of Seann Vell lies within its province. Known for its sheltered river quays of the north-east.

**Baile mhin** (Achadh chaol). Founded 23 an Dàmhair, LE 1,175 by carters of the Achadh chaol road. Baile mhin grew where the road from Achadh chaol to the coast levels out, a stopping place for carts. It is a small town of wheelwrights and stables. Its people send their grain to the mills at Muileann dhìreach. Known for its wheelwrights on the Achadh chaol road.

**Baile mhòr** (Tobar fhiadhaich). Founded 17 an t-Iuchar, FE 126 by herders of the northern moor. The name means the great town, and it has never been one; it was great, men suppose, only beside the shielings round it when it was named. It is a quiet market for the wool of the moor, and looks to Cnoc dhubh for its road and to Tobar fhiadhaich for its law. Its folk follow the druid schools of the Old Faith and keep a small reading-house where the druid schools' questions are argued on winter nights. Known for its moorland wool and its ill-fitting name.

**Baile mhòr** (Seann Tarr). Founded 15 an t-Samhain, LE 1,253 by craftsmen outside the walls of Baile Mòr ruadh. Baile mhòr grew outside the walls of Baile Mòr ruadh, a suburb of tanners, dyers and other trades the city would not have within its gates. It has never been walled itself. In the Age of Strangers it was burned once in a quarrel between the city and the administration, and rebuilt in stone. Known for its trade outside the walls of Baile Mòr ruadh.

**Baile Mòr àrsaidh** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 16 an t-Samhain, FE 1,337 by Dia-thìrich traders of the northern plain. Baile Mòr àrsaidh is an ancient market city of the northern plain, ranked a city for its age rather than its size. Its market was old in the Holy Age. It takes oak from Doire dhìreach and grain from Achadh dhìreach. Known for its ancient market of the northern plain.

**Baile Mòr dhìreach** (Caol bheag). Founded 8 an Gearran, FE 1,732 by custodians of the north-eastern road. Baile Mòr dhìreach of Caol bheag is a walled town with a citadel, built by Holy Age custodians where the north-eastern road runs straight. It is small for a city, but it holds the road and the market between Inis mhòr and Baile gharbh. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its walls on the straight road.

**Baile Mòr dhìreach** (Baile chaol). Founded 7 an Gearran, FE 2,051 by custodians of the eastern road. Baile Mòr dhìreach of Baile chaol is a citadel city on the eastern straight road, founded in the Holy Age to hold the road between the vein country and the coast. It was a tithe station in the Age of Strangers, and the ledgers kept there were among those burned in the raids before the Severance. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits and is the market town of the east coast. The first glass-house on Dia-thìr was built here and still works, and the town also makes cheese, boots and sail-cloth. Known for its citadel on the eastern road.

**Baile Mòr dhomhain** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 24 an t-Samhain, FE 101 by the lords of the deep river. A walled city with a citadel on a deep river in the north, the seat of Siorrachd Baile Mòr dhomhain. It was one of the great market cities of the north through the Holy Age and the Sundering and a centre of the human administration in the Age of Strangers. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and holds its four fords and its river landing at Àth shean. It is the market town of the northern hills and the second cattle-market of the island. The white marble of its hills is quarried nearby, and the town is known for its books. Known for the deep-river city and its fords.

**Baile Mòr fhionn** (Caol leathan). Founded 6 an t-Samhain, FE 584 by the lords of the western plain. A great fair walled city of the west, seat of lords before the kingdom and a fortress since. Its citadel was held by Dia-thìrich forces through the war that ended in the Severance, and it is a city of the order of the Stone. It is the chief market of the plain between the capital and the western harbours. Its own vineyards give the plain's wine, and the town salts meat, makes boots and dips candles. Known for the fair citadel of the western plain.

**Baile Mòr mhòr** (Baile Mòr mhòr). Founded 13 an t-Sultain, VE 7,939 by households of the northern plain. Baile Mòr mhòr is the great city of the north, walled and crowned by a citadel, and the seat of its province. It held one of the royal granaries in the Holy Age and was a centre of the human administration in the Age of Strangers. Since the Severance it has stood close to the Tuathaich country to the west, the largest Dia-thìrich city on that frontier. Known for the great walled city of the north.

**Baile Mòr ruadh** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 3 an Gearran, FE 2,252 by Dia-thìrich lords, resettled by the Tuathaich. A red walled city in the north-west, held by Dia-thìrich lords from the Holy Age to the Severance, and since then one of the principal Tuathaich cities. It follows the faith of the Church and governs the Àth àrsaidh country with its fords and towns. Known for the red city of the Tuathaich.

**Baile Mòr ruadh** (Seann Tarr). Founded 15 an Lùnastal, VE 8,634 by settlers on the empty land by Seann Dunn. Baile Mòr ruadh is a walled city of red stone, crowned by a citadel, and the strongest place of its province, though the seat of the shire is the old harbour of Seann Tarr. It was fought over in the Age of Strangers, when the human administration made it a district seat, and when the shires were drawn the seat went back to Seann Tarr. Its walls show repairs of every age. Travellers on the eastern road break their journey at An Taigh-seinnse Òir just west of the city. Its dyers make the reds and blues of the east, and it is one of the chief towns of the east for books and ink. Known for its red-stone walls of the east.

**Baile Mòr uaine** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 22 am Màrt, FE 982 by custodians of Cuan ghlas. Baile Mòr uaine is a walled city with a citadel in the north-eastern hills, founded in the Holy Age. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and is among their strongholds. Its walls were repaired in the Age of Strangers. Its forges are the chief armoury of the north-eastern hills. Known for its walls and its houses of the druid schools.

**Baile naomh** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 1 an Gearran, FE 319 by custodians of the holy wells. Baile naomh, the holy town, grew around wells in the vein country that the Holy Age custodians held sacred. The hot springs of Muileann ruadh lie to the west and the silver workings of Muileann chiar to the north-west. It is a small town of shrines and lodging houses, keeping the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Known for its holy wells of the vein country.

**Baile òg** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 7 an Dàmhair, LE 518 by stone-gatherers of the temple hills. A young town in the eastern hills close by the ruins of Làrach an Teampaill, whose altar faces the vein. Its early houses were built of stones carried off the ruins, a use the elders of the Old Spirits later forbade. It keeps the Old Spirits and serves travellers who come to look at the ruins. Known for its houses of stone from Làrach an Teampaill.

**Baile òg** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 25 am Màrt, LE 110 by carters of Baile Mòr dhomhain. A small young town on the road between Baile Mòr dhomhain and Baile Mòr àrsaidh, grown from a carters' stable. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and lives by changing horses. Known for a carters' stop between two cities.

**Baile òg** (Baile ìseal). Founded 5 an t-Samhain, SE 4 by Tuathaich families sent north at the Severance. Baile òg, "the young town", was built by Tuathaich families who arrived after the Severance and found no empty village to take. It stands a short way from the larger Tuathaich town of Baile ìseal and has always leaned on it. Its houses are the first the Tuathaich built for themselves on the island rather than inherited. Known for the first Tuathaich-built houses.

**Baile òg** (Seann Chwen). Founded 6 an Dàmhair, AE 40 by a mining crew under the human administration. Baile òg, "the young town", was a camp of the diggings east of the capital, raised in the Age of Strangers near Cill ghlas. It emptied when Scàineadh Cill ghlas closed the district for a generation. It was reopened after the Severance, and its people now follow the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its camp houses of the Cill ghlas diggings.

**Baile ruadh** (Seann Tarr). Founded 25 an t-Samhain, LE 72 by herders of Seann Tarr. Baile ruadh is a farm town near the eastern coast, founded in the long quiet centuries. Since the lighthouses were built its people have supplied the keepers of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal on the coast beyond. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Known for its supplies for Taigh-solais Baile ìseal.

**Baile ruadh** (Baile ruadh). Founded 3 an Dàmhair, FE 971 by red-earth farmers of the east. A red town of the east and the seat of Siorrachd Baile ruadh. It keeps the Old Spirits and trades grain with Achadh naomh. Known for its red-earth fields of the east.

**Baile ruadh** (Cuan shean). Founded 9 am Màrt, LE 1,793 by red-clay potters of the Cuan shean country. A red town of potters and brick-makers behind the harbour of Cuan shean, whose kilns have fired the roof-tiles of the western coast since the centuries after the Sundering. It follows the order of Manannan, and its potters mark each jar with a small scorpion, the order's badge, under the base. Most of what it makes goes out through Cuan shean. Known for its red roof-tiles and scorpion-marked jars.

**Baile ruadh** (Inis mhin). Founded 9 an t-Iuchar, FE 957 by Dia-thìrich farmers of the red ground. A red town in the north-west that stayed Dia-thìrich when the Tuathaich homeland was fixed around it, and the line of the border wall that was proposed and never built would have run past its gate. It keeps the Old Spirits of the Dia-thìrich, and its market is used by Tuathaich from Baile fhionn and Dia-thìrich from Àth uaine alike. Known for a shared market on the border.

**Baile shean** (Doire fhionn). Founded 5 an Dàmhair, FE 1,655 by keepers of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar. An old town beside Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, the forest marked sacred before any faith claimed it. Its people have kept the forest's edge since the Holy Age and keep the Old Spirits, though the forest is now held by the druid schools. Known for the keepers of the sacred forest's edge.

**Baile shean** (Cnoc thais). Founded 27 an Cèitean, FE 557 by Dia-thìrich founders; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. An old Dia-thìrich town with walls and a citadel, emptied at the Severance and taken over by Tuathaich families. In the years before An Cogadh Fada it was counted among the northern towns that refused dubhan. Its walls still stand, and the Tuathaich guard them as the Dia-thìrich once did. Known for its old walls held by the Tuathaich.

**Baile shean** (Inis chrom). Founded 18 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,185 by road-guards of Caol leathan. An old walled town of Òrd na Cloiche, the order of the Stone, beside the fort of Muileann bheag. Its walls are older than the fort, and for most of its history it was the stronger of the two. It is small now, and lives on the fort's custom. Known for its old walls and its house of the Stone.

**Baile shean** (Caol ìseal). Founded 13 an Dùbhlachd, FE 727 by Dia-thìrich fishers of the northern shore. Baile shean is an old quay on the northern shore and the port of its province. The inn An Taigh-seinnse Reòta lies inland on the road south, and its pickled spinach goes out through the quay. It is one of several places named Baile shean. Known for its old quay of the northern shore.

**Baile thais** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 5 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,086 by river-boatmen of the Abhainn uaine. Baile thais stands on the Abhainn uaine where the river leaves the hills for its run down to the gulf, and the river landing of Cidhe Beag lies just downstream. Boats have been launched here since the Holy Age to carry goods inland and coal down. It is a busy, unwalled town of boatmen and warehouses. Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich, the southern sea-lane, ends at the landing of Cidhe Beag below the town. Known for the Cidhe Beag landing on the Abhainn uaine.

**Baile thais** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 28 an Cèitean, FE 2,183 by Dia-thìrich eel-fishers of the water-meadows. Baile thais stands on damp ground where the meadows flood each wet season, and its people have always fished the ditches for eels. It is a large town now, and it supplies Cnoc bhàn with hay and fish. The river works that keep the meadows are older than the town's charter. Known for its water-meadows and eel traps.

**Baile uaine** (Àth shean). Founded 5 an Gearran, LE 1,132 by market gardeners of Àth shean. Baile uaine is a small town of market gardens, sending green stuff to Dùn gheal and on to the capital each market day. It has never been walled or fought over. Its people follow the capital's order, the order of Macha, and pay their dues at Dùn gheal. Known for its market gardens for the capital.

#### C

**Caol bheag** (Caol bheag). Founded 15 am Màrt, FE 477 by fishers of the north coast. A small harbour on the northern strait, older than its far larger namesake inland and the one that gave that town its name. It keeps the Old Spirits and is a quiet fishing town, though An ceathramh rèisimeid, stationed at the larger Caol bheag, sends its patrols here. It stands on Eilean fhada, the long island off the north coast, and the strait it is named for is the sound between that island and Dia-thìr. Known for the elder Caol bheag on the strait.

**Caol bheag** (Caol bheag). Founded 14 an Lùnastal, VE 7,737 by fishing households of the north coast. Caol bheag is a river port of more than forty thousand on the narrows of the Abhainn ghorm, crowned by a citadel and the seat of its province; its barges run down to Ros chiar at the river mouth. The fourth regiment, raised in the Long War, is stationed here. The mills of Muileann bheag and the wool of Cnoc chiar pass through its quays. Known for its river port, where the fourth regiment lies.

**Caol chrom** (Caol gharbh). Founded 13 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,275 by the garrison of the bent strait. Caol chrom is a fortified harbour on a bent strait of the north-east, walled and given a citadel in the long quiet centuries. It is a city by rank but small in people, and its garrison has always outnumbered its fishermen. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Its few townsmen boil soap and blow glass for the hill towns. Its headmen and Caol gharbh's meet at Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich, the stone on the neck of land between the two harbours, to settle the dues of the strait. Known for its fortified bent strait.

**Caol dhomhain** (Ceann mhin). Founded 8 an Gearran, LE 1,229 by the watch of the deep strait. Caol dhomhain is a harbour village on a deep strait of the south-east, with a citadel raised in the long quiet centuries to watch it. The village is small, and it lives by the citadel. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Known for the deep strait's watch-tower.

**Caol fhiadhaich** (Inis thais). Founded 13 an t-Iuchar, LE 739 by fishers of the wild strait. Caol fhiadhaich is a harbour on a rough strait of the west coast, within the province of Inis thais. It was founded in the long quiet centuries by fishers who braved waters the older harbours avoided. Its people keep the Old Faith in the order of the Stone. Its women distil scent-waters, the town's second trade after the fishing. The southern sea-lane, Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich, is named for its fishers, who first sailed it round the south coast in the long quiet centuries. Known for its fishing in the wild strait.

**Caol fhiadhaich** (Caol fhiadhaich). Founded 12 an t-Iuchar, VE 6,870 by salmon-trappers of the south-west. A harbour on a wild strait whose pilots earned their living guiding ships through the rocks.
