It is the seat of Siorrachd Caol fhiadhaich and a large town of the order of the Stone, trading with the great tavern-village of Doire shean on its road. The strait pilots still take no ship through without an offering to Clach, the Stone, at the harbour wolf-stone. Known for its strait-pilots and the harbour wolf-stone.

**Caol gharbh** (Caol gharbh). Founded 10 am Màrt, VE 9,451 by Dia-thìrich seafarers of the rough strait. Caol gharbh is a walled harbour on the rough strait and the seat of its province, a village in name but a town of twenty-seven thousand in fact. Its boatyards take oak from Doire chaol and build the heavy boats the strait demands. Its quarrel with Seann Bhrenn next door is as old as the rolls. Its headmen and Caol chrom's meet at Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich, the stone on the neck of land between the two harbours, to settle the dues of the strait. Known for its boatyards on the rough strait.

**Caol ìseal** (Caol ìseal). Founded 21 am Màrt, FE 1,450 by salt-makers of the northern coast. Caol ìseal is a harbour town on a low strait of the north coast and the seat of its province. Its salt pans have supplied the northern fisheries since the Holy Age. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Bog-iron dug behind the pans feeds its forges, which cast field-guns for the regiments. Known for its salt pans of the low strait.

**Caol ìseal** (Baile Mòr mhòr). Founded 25 am Faoilleach, FE 1,428 by the strait-watchers of the north coast. A small harbour-village on the northern strait, with a citadel built to watch the channel. It served Baile Mòr mhòr as a signal-station and watch-post, and it has never been more. It keeps the Old Spirits of the Dia-thìrich, and the watch-fire on its citadel is still lit on the old feast nights. Known for the strait watch-fire.

**Caol leathan** (Caol leathan). Founded 12 am Faoilleach, VE 6,883 by seal-hunting households of the western shore. Caol leathan grew on the wide strait that gives it its name, where the western pilots of the Holy Age took a toll from every boat bound for the capital's waters. Its walls and citadel were raised in the Age of Sundering to hold the strait, and were manned again when the strangers' ships began to use it after the Crossing. It is the northern anchor of the country of the Stone, and its druids look south to the temple of Lia Fàil at Inis thais for their rite. Known for its strait tolls and the western pilots' guild.

**Caol mhin** (Caol mhin). Founded 17 am Màrt, FE 1,345 by Dia-thìrich seafarers of Baile Mòr mhòr. Caol mhin is the harbour of Baile Mòr mhòr on the calm strait, and its fortunes have always followed the city's. It is walled against raiders from the sea. Its quays, which stand on Eilean chrom across the calm strait from the city, load wool and hides from the northern uplands. Known for its calm-strait harbour of Baile Mòr mhòr.

**Caol mhòr** (Caol mhòr). Founded 31 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,785 by Dia-thìrich harbour-folk; resettled by the Tuathaich. Caol mhòr, the great strait, was a Dia-thìrich harbour from the Ancient Age. After the Severance it became the chief port of the Tuathaich, and it is now their largest town. Its yards take timber from Doire mhin, and its people keep the faith of the Church. Known for its place as the chief harbour of the Tuathaich.

**Caol naomh** (Caol mhòr). Founded 9 an Dàmhair, FE 2,043 by Dia-thìrich ferrymen; resettled by the Tuathaich. Caol naomh, the holy strait, is a harbour of the north-west founded by Dia-thìrich ferrymen in the Holy Age, who held the crossing sacred and blessed each boat before it put out. It was resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance, and the new ferrymen kept the blessing without the old words. It keeps the faith of the Church. Known for the holy strait's ferry.

**Caol naomh** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 17 an Giblean, LE 481 by druids of Òrd Bhrìde. A holy strait-harbour near the ruins of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, where the orthodox order of Brìde's flame built a landing for pilgrims coming to the mountain of Crom's stone. It is one of the few towns where Òrd Bhrìde holds the majority, and its druids were among those who set down the order's rite in the first years of the new kingdom. It is a small town and quiet outside the pilgrim season. Pilgrims' boats from the southern Seann Skell come round to its landing by Slighe-mhara chritheanach, the shaking sea-way, named for the swell off the south cape. Known for its pilgrim landing of Òrd Bhrìde.

**Caol ruadh** (Muileann naomh). Founded 14 an Giblean, VE 7,893 by Dia-thìrich fishers of the red strait. Caol ruadh takes its name from the red rock of the strait it watches on the southern coast. It was a quiet fishing town for most of its history, and was among the first to take up the orthodox rite of Brìde's flame and Crom's stone when Òrd Bhrìde was first ordered. Since An Cogadh Fada its harbour has victualled the garrisons and the fleet at Seann Skell close by, and after that war it was chartered for the purpose as the sixteenth market town. Known for its red strait and the orthodox rite of Brìde's flame.

**Caol shean** (Caol shean). Founded 21 an Lùnastal, VE 9,519 by river households of the east. An old river port on the narrows of the Abhainn ìseal, above its meeting with the Abhainn chaol, and one of the great river ports of the island, seat of Siorrachd Caol shean. It sent the coal of the central mountains down the river to Seann Mhorn when the mountain was worked hardest, and now sends dubhan and grain the same way. The spring of Allt an Àigh lies in its hinterland, and pilgrims to it come up the river and land here; the town follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for the great eastern river port, pilgrims' landing.

**Cathair dhearg** (Cathair dhearg). Founded 6 an Dàmhair, VE 5,341 by the holders of the Red Hill. Cathair dhearg, the red city, stands on the Red Hill, whose holders are named in the oldest king-lists; the old settlement shrank to a fishing town and grew again in the Holy Age where the mining roads came down to the water on the Abhainn dhomhain, just above Loch chrom, and Beathag Mhòr made it the seat of rule; Drochaid Cathair dhearg, heir of the first bridges, still carries the road across the river. It kept its walls, citadel and temple through the Sundering and the Age of Strangers, and after the Severance Rìoghachd Dia-thìris was declared here and Niall was crowned in it, first of the restored line. The royal precinct is small for a capital, ringed by the great harbours of Ros dhomhain, Cathair dhomhain and Baile ghlas, and its temple is the first house of Macha, where kings are made by her rite and the two horses of her rite, Liath Macha the grey and Dubh Sainglenn the black, are honoured. The royal quays build seagoing hulls for the Crown. Known for its royal seat and temple of Macha.

**Cathair dhomhain** (Cathair dhomhain). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar, FE 634 by carriers settled at the mouth of the western road. Cathair dhomhain, the deep city, stands beside the capital on the deep-water side of the river mouth, and takes the ships whose draught the royal quays cannot. It was walled and given a citadel in the Holy Age, and its temple of Macha is second only to the capital's. Its harbour carried much of the coal trade in the Age of Strangers and most of the dubhan trade since. It is the market town of the capital shore, and its own workshops bind books and put up salted food for the ships. Its quays stand where the Abhainn fhionn runs into Loch chrom, and the sea-going ships that lie at them come up from the west coast by the Abhainn gheal. Known for its deep-water harbour beside the capital.

**Cathair fhada** (Cathair fhada). Founded 13 an Cèitean, VE 7,846 by households of the south coast. A long walled city in the south, strung along a ridge between the capital's country and the coast, and the seat of Siorrachd Cathair fhada. It follows the order of Macha and has always been one of the capital's chief supports. The Fèill Muileann òg is held a short way north, and the city's merchants rule it. Its market right is among the oldest on the island, and its own trade is in cheese, honey and garments. Known for its merchants of the Fèill Muileann òg.

**Cathair gheal** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 5 am Màrt, VE 6,701 by builders of the western coast; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. Cathair gheal is a walled city of white stone on the far western coast, built by the Dia-thìrich and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. Its walls face the sea, where pirate ships have been seen offshore. It is the market for the Tuathaich villages of Muileann àrsaidh province. Its smiths make the tools of the north-west. Known for its white walls against the pirate coast.

**Cathair mhòr** (Cathair mhòr). Founded 9 an Dùbhlachd, VE 8,170 by Dia-thìrich households of the hills. Cathair mhòr, the great city, grew from households of the Ancient Age who settled below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, a Seann-Dhaoine outpost already in ruins, and it was walled in the Holy Age, the first walled town on the island. It commands the roads between the gulf and the vein country, and it was a counting-house of the tithe in the Age of Strangers and a mustering place in the war that ended it. An treas rèisimeid, raised in An Cogadh Fada, is stationed here and bears its name. Its honey and its salted meat are sold in every market of the south, and its soap-boilers and weavers are the busiest in the gulf. Known for the great city beside the old outpost.

**Cathair mhòr** (Doire mhin). Founded 28 an Cèitean, FE 2,147 by the lords of Doire mhin. A hill-city with a citadel close to the capital, raised by lords of the Doire mhin country who held the roads north of Cathair dhearg. It has always been a garrison town and was one of the strongholds from which the war before the Severance was fought. It follows the order of Macha and draws on the tithe-granaries of Baile chrom and the great village of Doire mhin. It is not the Cathair mhòr of the third regiment, which lies further east. Its glass-house is the largest on the island. Known for the citadel on the capital's north road.

**Cathair naomh** (Seann Toll). Founded 22 an Dùbhlachd, VE 8,485 by unknown builders, later the Dia-thìrich keepers of the Old Spirits. The holy city of the north grew around a ring of stones older than the Dia-thìrich, and who raised them is not known. The Dia-thìrich made it a place of the Old Spirits in the Holy Age and it has never had walls, since the ancestors' ground was held to need none. It is a city of pilgrims and hostels, and the spirit-house keepers of Cnoc chiar and Inis bheag answer to its elders. Dubhan from the works below the town and books copied in its hostels are its trades; the elders have never blessed the works, since dubhan is not of the vein. Known for the unwalled ring of the ancestors.

**Cathair naomh** (Seann Chwen). Founded 1 an Gearran, FE 2,841 by wood-watchers of the western wood. A holy city near the ruins of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, built in the last years of the Holy Age as a seat of learning by the wood-watchers, whose rite became the order of Macha. The ruins are said to have been older than any Dia-thìrich memory when the city was founded, and the druids left them as they were. It is unwalled and trades with the harbour of Seann Chwen and with Ceann leathan. Known for the druids' city by the old outpost.

**Ceann àrsaidh** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 17 an t-Sultain, VE 9,651 by households from the Red Hill. Ceann àrsaidh is a walled river city on an ancient headland over the Abhainn fhionn, east of the capital. It has been a river port since the Holy Age, and its barges run down to Cathair dhomhain where the river runs into Loch chrom and the barges meet the ships that come up from the sea. An Taigh-seinnse Mòr stands on the road to the west. Known for its ancient headland on the capital's river road to the east.

**Ceann bhàn** (Achadh mhòr). Founded 29 an t-Samhain, LE 1,063 by the tavern-keepers of the white headland. A walled river port on a pale headland where the Abhainn gheal meets the Abhainn bhàn, with the famous tavern An Sligeanach Fad' às at its gate, where travellers eat dried venison. It grew around the tavern road, and its walls went up in the troubles, when the roadside houses became militia posts. It keeps the Old Spirits, trades with the great village of Achadh mhòr close by, and sends its goods down the Abhainn bhàn to Seann Warr on the coast. Known for An Sligeanach Fad' às and dried venison.

**Ceann bheag** (Ceann bheag). Founded 15 an t-Iuchar, FE 311 by Dia-thìrich harbour-folk of the north-east. Ceann bheag is a citadel harbour of the north-east, a Holy Age landing that grew with the coastal trade. Its citadel was raised in the Age of Strangers to guard the anchorage the human ships used. The villages of Ceann thais and Achadh fhiadhaich lie within its province and send their goods through its quays. Known for its citadel harbour of the north-east.

**Ceann chaol** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 23 an Giblean, FE 145 by Dia-thìrich seafarers of the narrow point. Ceann chaol is a port city on the narrow point, and the old rival of Ceann mhin along the same shore. Its ships carry the flour of Muileann dhomhain and the grain of the eastern plain. The two harbours have disputed fishing grounds in every age, and the rolls of their disputes are long. Known for its narrow-point harbour, rival of Ceann mhin.

**Ceann chiar** (Seann Tarr). Founded 10 an Dùbhlachd, VE 7,727 by Dia-thìrich fishers of the eastern coast. Ceann chiar is a walled harbour on the eastern coast, walled against the pirate ships that have been seen in these waters in every age. It keeps a watch-fire on its headland. It is the port of Seann Tarr province. Known for its walled harbour against pirates.

**Ceann dhomhain** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 7 am Màrt, FE 1,742 by custodians of the eastern headland. A small city on a headland over a deep reach of the Abhainn naomh, with a citadel that looks down the river toward the sea and back toward the mountain roads. River boats put in here with the cargoes landed at Ceann mhin, at the river mouth, for the library town of Muileann chaol, and the library's scholars and copyists pass through its gate. Its quay-masters have long kept a copy of every cargo-list for the Leabharlann. The druid schools hold the city, and its scholars are counted among the library's oldest correspondents. Known for the library's river landing and cargo registers.

**Ceann dhubh** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 25 an Cèitean, FE 1,742 by Dia-thìrich headland-fishers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A black headland harbour on the north-west coast, all but joined to the city of Inis àrsaidh. It was a Dia-thìrich fishing town until the Severance and has been a Tuathaich harbour since. It follows the faith of the Church, and its boats sail with Inis àrsaidh's. Known for the black headland beside Inis àrsaidh.

**Ceann dhubh** (Baile gharbh). Founded 26 an Cèitean, LE 1,359 by Dia-thìrich fishers of the black headland. Ceann dhubh is a harbour under a dark headland, the port of Baile gharbh province, whose boats work the cold waters of the northern coast. Travellers on the coast road break their journey at An Leòmhann Buidhe a short way west, and the inn buys most of the harbour's catch. The harbour was deepened in the Age of Strangers to take the humans' coal ships, and has been too large for its trade ever since. Known for its harbour under the black headland.

**Ceann fhada** (Muileann chrom). Founded 27 an Cèitean, LE 1,359 by Dia-thìrich river pilots. A long spit of land made Ceann fhada a landing for river craft, and its pilots have guided boats on the Abhainn uaine for centuries. It is the old rival of Inis ìseal, a short way downstream, and the two quays have quarrelled over tolls in every age the rolls cover. It prospered in the Age of Strangers carrying coal-cart loads by water and has held its trade since by carrying grain. Known for its long quay and river pilots.

**Ceann gheal** (Cathair dhomhain). Founded 8 an Gearran, LE 1,328 by fishers of the white headland. Ceann gheal is a harbour town north of the capital, founded in the long quiet centuries. The shaft called Toll-dubh lies in the hills behind it. Quarrymen broke into it in the Age of Sundering and found a stair cut in the rock going down beyond their lamps, and the custodians walled it up; the town's people do not go near it. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its white headland and the Toll-dubh hollow.

**Ceann ghorm** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 29 an Giblean, LE 395 by river pilots of the east. Ceann ghorm, the blue headland, is a river town on the Abhainn chaol in the east whose pilots have long guided boats up from Seann Mhorn on the coast to the landings of Seann Dunn and Ros fhionn. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and grew in the Age of Strangers. Its people follow the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its river pilots of the Abhainn chaol.

**Ceann leathan** (Seann Chwen). Founded 19 an t-Samhain, VE 7,384 by sailing households of the gulf. Ceann leathan, the broad headland, is a walled temple city on the gulf, older than most of the harbours around it. Its temple of Macha is the chief house of her order in the gulf towns. Since the early years of the restored kingdom it has held Còmhrag Ceann leathan, the brutal annual melee, which draws fighters and crowds from every province. It is the market town of the gulf and the old vein country, fifty-two towns in all, and the dearest market on Dia-thìr. Its own trade is in cheese and salted food, and its yards build seagoing hulls. Known for Còmhrag Ceann leathan, the annual melee.

**Ceann leathan** (Ceann leathan). Founded 27 am Màrt, FE 1,810 by Dia-thìrich harbour-folk of the east. Ceann leathan of the east is a harbour town and the seat of its province, founded in the Holy Age on a broad headland facing the open sea. It is not the gulf city of the melee, and its people resent the confusion. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits and a fishing fleet that works as far south as the waters off Seann Bhral. Known for its broad headland harbour of the east.

**Ceann mhin** (Ceann mhin). Founded 18 an Lùnastal, FE 745 by shipwrights of the smooth headland. Ceann mhin is a citadel harbour on the southern gulf shore, long the chief shipyard of the east. When Tonn Mhòr struck in the first years of the restored kingdom, its yards were spared and it took in the survivors of Achadh mhin. It has since grown into one of the great cities of the south. The hemp for its yards grows in its own fields, and its copyists bind books for the south. Known for its shipyards of the smooth headland.

**Ceann mhin** (Ceann mhin). Founded 12 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,663 by harbour-lords of the smooth headland. A smooth headland port, walled, and the seat of Siorrachd Ceann mhin. It was a trading harbour for the northern mines in the Age of Strangers and follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Slighe Ceann mhin, the long road down the east of the island to Seann Dunn, begins at its gate. Known for the northern coal harbour.

**Ceann mhin** (Ceann mhin). Founded 26 an Dùbhlachd, VE 8,351 by Dia-thìrich fishers of the south-eastern shore. Ceann mhin stands below Làrach an Dùin, the ruined fortress of the old builders, and its harbour lies under the fallen walls. The Dia-thìrich fishers who settled there in the Ancient Age would not go up to the ruin, and took no stone from it; who built the fortress is not known. It is now a walled port town of nearly twenty thousand, the seat of its province, and the rival of Ceann chaol along the same coast. Known for its harbour beneath Làrach an Dùin.

**Ceann mhòr** (Ceann mhòr). Founded 6 an Cèitean, FE 163 by Dia-thìrich fishers; resettled by the Tuathaich. Ceann mhòr is a great harbour on a headland of the north-west, under the beacon of Taigh-solais Baile chrom. It was a Dia-thìrich port of the Holy Age, struck by Gorta Baile chrom in the Age of Strangers and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It keeps the faith of the Church. Its first human fishing families learned the harbour prayers of Manannan's priests here, and those priests say the Grey Night vigil of Baile chrom began from them. It has been the market town of the north-west coast since the shires were drawn, and it sends fish, whale-oil, seal-oil, amber, dyes and tobacco south. Glass is blown from the white sand of its beaches. Known for its great headland harbour under the Baile chrom light.

**Ceann òg** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 19 an t-Sultain, AE 8 by Dia-thìrich and human traders together. Ceann òg, "the young headland", was built as a river trading quay on the Abhainn ìseal in the first years after the Crossing, when trade with the humans still ran both ways. It stands near Carragh Cnoc bheag, the stone carved Bha teine sa chloich. The Green Death, A' Phlàigh Uaine, struck it in the Age of Strangers. It follows the Hawk order, and its quay was rebuilt after the Severance for Dia-thìrich boats alone. Seòlaid Ceann òg, the western lane round the capes to the capital's water, is named for its quay. Known for its young river quay near Carragh Cnoc bheag.

**Ceann thais** (Ceann bheag). Founded 30 an Giblean, LE 334 by fishers of the north-east. Ceann thais is a harbour village of the north-east, best known for An Leòmhann Buidhe, one of the great taverns of the old mining circuit, which stands at its edge. It was founded in the long quiet centuries. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for An Leòmhann Buidhe, the Yellow Lion.

**Cill àrsaidh** (Doire fhionn). Founded 19 an Giblean, FE 2,448 by keepers of the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Cill àrsaidh of the north is an old cell of the ancestor rite, founded in the Holy Age and never much more than a village around its shrine. It lies inland of the Hawk bay and has kept to the Old Spirits while its neighbours took up the Hawk order and the rite of Mòd. The shrine keepers are hereditary. Its people gather amber on the strands of the Hawk bay. Known for its ancient cell of the ancestor rite.

**Cill àrsaidh** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 29 an Cèitean, FE 673 by teachers of the druid schools. Cill àrsaidh of Cuan ghlas is an old cell that the teachers of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, the druid schools, took as a retreat early in the schools' history. It became a large village of students and farmers. Through the Age of Strangers the teachers of the schools lay quiet here and kept it alive, and it filled again at the revival. Known for its retreat of the druid teachers.

**Cill àrsaidh** (Muileann bheag). Founded 25 an t-Sultain, FE 2,924 by keepers of the Old Spirits. An ancient cell-site village in the north-east, older than the druid schools that now hold it. The founding shrine is said to have been of the Old Spirits, and its foundations lie under the present meeting-house. It is a large village supplying Muileann bheag. Known for a druids' house on an old shrine.

**Cill bhàn** (Dùn dhearg). Founded 20 am Màrt, FE 276 by keepers of the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Cill bhàn, the white cell, is a village of the Old Spirits' ancestor rite in the east, founded in the Holy Age. It lies near the hot springs and the silver workings of the vein country. It has kept its spirit-house through every age and every change of master. Known for its white cell of the ancestor rite.

**Cill chaol** (Muileann leathan). Founded 10 am Màrt, FE 2,014 by Dia-thìrich druids; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. Cill chaol was a narrow Dia-thìrich chapel village near the northern coast, emptied at the Severance and taken by Tuathaich families. They made its chapel a church of the Tuathaich, and the Dia-thìrich carvings on its doorposts were left in place beside theirs. It is a small place near the lighthouse of Muileann bheag. Known for a Tuathaich church in a Dia-thìrich chapel.

**Cill chiar** (Baile chiar). Founded 16 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,283 by druids of Macha. A small temple-site village at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the forest no one has settled or wholly charted. Its temple-house was built to watch the forest rather than enter it. It follows the order of Macha. Known for the temple-house watching the unclaimed forest.

**Cill dhearg** (Doire chiar). Founded 7 an t-Samhain, FE 549 by druids of the schools. A temple village of red stone near Drochaid Ros fhionn, whose house of the druid schools gave shelter to travellers crossing the old bridge when the river trade was busy. As the trade failed and the bridge fell out of use, the village shrank to its temple-house and a few farms. Its druids still keep a lamp at the bridge-end. Known for its red temple-house by the old bridge.

**Cill dhìreach** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 6 am Màrt, FE 2,650 by druids of the schools for the silver-miners. A temple village a short way from the silver seam at Muileann chiar, whose house of the druid schools has served the silver-miners since the seam was first worked. In the Age of Strangers its druids kept a record of the miners killed underground, one of the few such records to survive. It is not the Cill dhìreach of the central country. Known for its miners' temple by the silver seam.

**Cill dhìreach** (Cill dhìreach). Founded 12 am Màrt, FE 2,599 by wood-watchers of the western wood. Cill dhìreach is a temple village of Macha of twenty-four thousand and the seat of its province. It lies beside Ceann leathan, where Còmhrag Ceann leathan is held each year. Its druids tend the wounded of the melee and bury its dead. Known for its temple-town of the Ceann leathan melee.

**Cill fhada** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 17 an Dùbhlachd, LE 96 by wood-watchers of the western wood. A temple-site village strung along a long ridge near Baile chrom, whose temple of Macha is the longest building in the district. It farms for the market at Baile chrom and sends its grain to the tithe-granaries there. Known for the long temple of Macha.

**Cill gharbh** (Muileann naomh). Founded 27 an Lùnastal, FE 1,926 by Dia-thìrich druids of the western coast. A village around a rough stone shrine on the far western coast of the Dia-thìrich country. Its shrine is older than any of its houses, and Manannan was worshipped there before the orders divided. It is a small village of fewer than two thousand. Known for its rough stone shrine of the west.

**Cill ghlas** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 4 am Faoilleach, FE 1,814 by a house of the druid schools. Cill ghlas, the grey cell, was a quiet village of the druid schools in the hills east of the capital until in the Age of Strangers the workings were driven under it. Late in that age a common cutting tore open a fault around the village; dozens were killed and the working was closed. From the Rending the island has the word 'scàinte'. The village was rebuilt on the far side of the crack, and its people still mark the day of the dead. Known for Scàineadh Cill ghlas, the Rending.

**Cill ghorm** (Cathair dhomhain). Founded 13 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,633 by wood-watchers of the western wood. A temple site on the ridge above the road north from Cathair dhearg, fortified in the Holy Age to guard the approach to the capital. The citadel dwarfs the village, which has never numbered more than a thousand or so, most of them in the service of the garrison and the shrine. Pilgrims of Òrd Mhacha, the order of Macha, stop here before entering the capital. Known for its fortified temple above the capital road.

**Cill ìseal** (Ceann mhòr). Founded 14 an t-Iuchar, LE 935 by Dia-thìrich shrine-keepers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A low church-site village of the Dia-thìrich, emptied at the Severance and resettled by Tuathaich families. It has grown larger than any village, with its church at its heart, and it farms for the harbour of Ros ruadh. The Tuathaich here call it by its Dia-thìrich name and no other. Known for the church of the north-west.

**Cill leathan** (Muileann shean). Founded 27 am Màrt, FE 1,689 by keepers of the north-coast cell. Cill leathan is a large harbour village of the north coast, founded as a cell in the Holy Age. A citadel was raised over its harbour in the Age of Strangers to guard the human ships that used it. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its broad cell and its sea citadel.

**Cill thais** (Cill thais). Founded 15 an t-Samhain, FE 1,933 by wardens of the sacred wood. Cill thais, the damp cell, is a large village and the seat of its province, founded in the Holy Age beside Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag. The forest is sacred to Macha and her black horse and has never been settled or felled, nor ever wholly charted, and the village's wardens keep others out of it under the division of custody that settled the holy-wood dispute. In the Age of Strangers the wardens refused the timber contracts, and how they were let refuse is not told. Known for its wardens of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag.

**Cill thais** (Cuan shean). Founded 22 an Giblean, FE 2,877 by watch-keepers of the western coast. Cill thais is a shrine village on damp ground above the anchorage of Cuan shean, fortified with a citadel in the Holy Age to watch the western sea. The fourth fleet, raised in the Long War, is stationed at Cuan shean below, and the village's druids bless each ship in Manannan's name before it first puts out. It is a small place whose citadel is larger than its village. Known for its fortified shrine of Manannan over the fleet anchorage.

**Cnoc àrsaidh** (Caol mhòr). Founded 19 am Màrt, FE 420 by Dia-thìrich shepherds; resettled by the Tuathaich. Cnoc àrsaidh is a small hill town of the Holy Age on the Abhainn mhòr, crowned by a cairn older than its name. Its Dia-thìrich families went south at the Severance and Tuathaich households took their holdings. It is a small place of hill pasture, looking down on the harbour of Caol mhòr. Known for its hill pasture and the old cairn.

**Cnoc àrsaidh** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 5 an t-Sultain, FE 777 by shepherds of the eastern hills. Cnoc àrsaidh of Dùn ìseal is a hill town crowned by old cairns, above Baile naomh. It has been a shepherding place since the Holy Age. Its people keep the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits and tend the cairns at the turning of the seasons. Known for its cairn hill and its shepherds.

**Cnoc àrsaidh** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 20 an t-Iuchar, LE 410 by hill-farmers from Cnoc dhubh. The 'ancient hill' of the eastern cluster of Cnocs is in fact among the younger of them; it is thought that the name was taken from the old cairn on its summit, and not from the town. It is a small farming town of the druid schools that sells its barley in Cnoc dhubh and Àth dhomhain. Known for the summit cairn and eastern barley.

**Cnoc àrsaidh** (Caol mhòr). Founded 9 an t-Samhain, FE 2,013 by Dia-thìrich hill-lords, resettled by the Tuathaich. A tiny ancient hill with a citadel, far larger than the handful of people who now live in it. It was a Dia-thìrich keep until the Severance and has been a Tuathaich watch-post since. It follows the faith of the Church. Known for an empty citadel on the southern march.

**Cnoc àrsaidh** (Cnoc àrsaidh). Founded 11 am Màrt, VE 7,728 by households of the panther road. Cnoc àrsaidh is a walled town of Òrd na Cloiche and the seat of its province, holding the oldest shrines of the order of the Stone. The panther roads pass close by, and the town keeps a watch on them in the season of crossing. Its walls were raised in the Age of Strangers and have not been needed since. Known for its shrines of the Stone and the panther watch.

**Cnoc bhàn** (Caol ìseal). Founded 21 am Màrt, LE 35 by fishers of Caol ìseal. Cnoc bhàn grew as an overflow of the harbour at Caol ìseal, a white hill with a landing at its foot. Its boats work the kelp beds and the herring of the northern shore. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits and has never needed walls. Known for its white-hill kelp and herring.

**Cnoc bhàn** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 30 an Dùbhlachd, LE 62 by Dia-thìrich fishers; resettled by the Tuathaich. Cnoc bhàn of the north-west is a harbour facing the pirate waters. It was founded by Dia-thìrich fishers in the long quiet centuries and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. Its boats avoid the waters where old sailors place the Sea-Watcher. Known for its harbour facing the pirate waters.

**Cnoc bhàn** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 5 an t-Samhain, LE 1,264 by druids of Macha. A pale hill in the midlands, crowned by a house of Òrd Mhacha, the order of the capital. The town grew around the druids' farms and remains a quiet place of tithe-barns and schools that train acolytes for the capital's temples of Macha. Baile dhomhain and Àth ghlas send it their tithes and their sons. Known for its training of Macha's acolytes.

**Cnoc bhàn** (Caol mhòr). Founded 11 an Lùnastal, FE 1,193 by Dia-thìrich hill-lords, resettled by the Tuathaich. A pale hill with a citadel built by a Dia-thìrich family in the Holy Age, taken over by the Tuathaich when their homeland was fixed. The Tuathaich garrison it as a guard-post on their southern marches, and it follows the faith of the Church. The town sells cattle and hides to Cnoc àrsaidh. Known for the Tuathaich southern guard-post.

**Cnoc bhàn** (Baile ghorm). Founded 23 an Dùbhlachd, LE 250 by the hill-lords of Baile ghorm. A walled pale hill in the south-east above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada, which grinds its grain. The walls were raised when the road from Làrach an Dùin became unsafe. It keeps the Old Spirits and is the market of the south-eastern farms. It sends the pearls of the south-eastern shallows and the clay of its fields to other markets. Known for the market above the mill-race.

**Cnoc bhàn** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 12 am Màrt, FE 282 by a custodian house of the Binding. The white hill was fortified early by a custodian house, and its citadel of pale stone is the oldest standing work in the province that bears its name. In the Age of Strangers it served as a district seat of the human administration, and the ledgers kept in its strong-room were among those later lost in the war. It is now a large town of scholars and advocates: the disputations of the druid schools are held in its hall, and its readers walk daily to the library at Muileann chaol. Known for its white citadel and the druid schools' disputations.

**Cnoc bheag** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 5 an t-Sultain, VE 9,231 by hill kindreds of the north-central country. Cnoc bheag is the small hill only in name: it is the largest town of the north-central country, a river port on the Abhainn ìseal whose barges run down to Ros gheal on the coast, and the heart of the Hawk order of the Old Faith, whose temple here is the chief house of the Hawk of Acaill. The standing stone Carragh Cnoc bheag, carved 'there was fire in the stone', stands a short walk to the south, and the town's older families say their fathers' fathers found it there. A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death, struck the town in the Age of Strangers. Since the Severance it has faced the Tuathaich border, and An siathamh rèisimeid, raised in An Cogadh Fada, is stationed here under the town's name. Known for the carved stone and the sixth regiment.

**Cnoc bheag** (Muileann shean). Founded 8 an Lùnastal, LE 779 by farmers of the north coast. Cnoc bheag of Muileann shean is a small town of hill farms on the north coast, founded in the long quiet centuries. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Its people send their sons to the druid teachers at Cill àrsaidh. Known for its north-coast hill farms.

**Cnoc bheag** (Achadh naomh). Founded 9 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,100 by the herders of Achadh naomh. A small walled hill in the east, raised as a refuge for the herds of Achadh naomh in the troubled years. Its pastures are thin, and the town has always kept fewer herds than its walls could shelter. It keeps the Old Spirits. Known for its hilltop refuge for eastern herds.

**Cnoc bheag** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 5 an Dàmhair, LE 1,027 by shepherds of Cnoc dhubh. A small hill town below Cnoc dhubh, holding the shepherds' market for the province. It has always lived in the shadow of the larger town. It is one of several places named Cnoc bheag and is not the fort of the holy wood near the capital. Known for its shepherds' market below Cnoc dhubh.

**Cnoc bheag** (Cill thais). Founded 8 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,776 by settlers from the Red Hill. Cnoc bheag is a fort with a citadel at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the forest that has never been settled or felled. Settlers from the Red Hill first built here in the Ancient Age, and the fort was raised after the holy-wood dispute of the Holy Age, when the keeping of the wood was divided and given whole to none, to house the custodians of the share that went to the order now called Òrd Mhacha, the order of Macha. It stands outside the trees, never within them, and its twelve thousand people guard the capital's south as well as the wood. Known for its fort at the edge of the holy wood.

**Cnoc chaol** (Baile gharbh). Founded 16 an t-Ògmhios, LE 807 by goatherds of the northern hills. Cnoc chaol, the narrow hill, is a small herding town of the north. It is not the southern Cnoc chaol that gave Tonn Mhòr its name. Its people keep the druid schools of the Old Faith and send their cheese and kids to the market at Baile gharbh. Known for its goat cheese for Baile gharbh.

**Cnoc chaol** (Seann Vell). Founded 23 am Faoilleach, LE 167 by Dia-thìrich shore farmers of Seann Vell. Cnoc chaol is the town the Great Wave is named after. Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol came on the southern coast without warning in a single night and laid it waste, with Cuan dhearg and Achadh mhin. The town was rebuilt higher up the narrow hill, and its people still leave the lowest street empty. Cnoc chaol and Cuan dhearg share Eilean bhàn, off the south coast. Known for the town the Great Wave named.

**Cnoc chaol** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 22 an Cèitean, VE 7,727 by hill-folk of the vein country. Cnoc chaol, on the narrow hill, was a hill settlement of the Ancient Age, where one of the first copies of the keeper's stone cup was ground, and in the Age of Strangers it was a mining camp worked by the ton. It emptied after Scàineadh Cill ghlas closed the district and never recovered. Fewer than seven hundred people live there now, among the spoil heaps. Known for a spent camp on the narrow hill.

**Cnoc chiar** (Seann Toll). Founded 12 an Giblean, FE 596 by spirit-house keepers of Cathair naomh. A dusky hill beside the harbour of Seann Toll, settled by keepers of the Old Spirits who tended waymarks on the pilgrim road to Cathair naomh. It remains a small town of hostels and way-shrines, busy in the feast seasons and empty between them. Known for its way-shrines on the pilgrim road.

**Cnoc chiar** (Achadh naomh). Founded 24 an Lùnastal, FE 10 by keepers of the Colbh. A dusky hill near the standing stone Colbh Cnoc chiar, which carries only the words Cuimhnich an teine, 'remember the fire'. The stone was old when the town was founded, and the town grew around the families who tended it. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith, whose druids still come to argue over a bidding that no one has explained. Known for the stone of 'remember the fire'.

**Cnoc chiar** (Doire mhin). Founded 10 an t-Samhain, LE 1,603 by herders of Doire mhin. A small dusky hill between Doire mhin and Muileann ruadh, pastured by herders of the great village. It follows the order of Macha. Known for its hill pastures of Doire mhin.

**Cnoc chiar** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 24 am Faoilleach, FE 416 by Dia-thìrich shepherds of Cuan ghlas. A large town on the dusky hill, living on the sheep walks above it and on the wool trade with Caol bheag. It was a mustering place for fleeces in the Age of Strangers, when the humans bought wool as eagerly as coal. Its market is the busiest in the province. Known for its sheep walks and wool market.

**Cnoc chrom** (Cnoc mhòr). Founded 23 an Lùnastal, AE 144 by the coal-carriers of the interior. Cnoc chrom was built in the Age of Strangers as a depot on the coal road from the interior to the gulf. It was walled in the years before the war of the Severance, when the mining roads began to arm themselves. It is a small town now and keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its walled depot of the coal road.

**Cnoc chrom** (Caol shean). Founded 26 an Cèitean, AE 35 by Dia-thìrich miners under contract. A crooked hill-town raised when the diggings of the strangers' contracts spread out from the central mountains toward the coast. Its walls were thrown up against the raids of the troubles before the war, and the shafts beneath it gave out before the Severance. It is now a small town of the druid schools that sends its young to the river port at Ros fhionn. Known for the abandoned shafts beneath its walled hill.

**Cnoc dhearg** (Muileann naomh). Founded 31 an Lùnastal, LE 644 by potters of the west. Cnoc dhearg of Muileann naomh is a small town of the west, founded in the long quiet centuries on a hill of red clay. Its potteries supply jars and tiles to the western harbours, and the Age of Strangers brought it a brief trade in crucibles for the assayers. It keeps the order of Manannan. Known for its red-clay potteries of the west.

**Cnoc dhìreach** (Cnoc leathan). Founded 18 an Dàmhair, LE 1,239 by tavern-keepers of the eastern road. A straight hill on the mining road in the south-east, home of An Taigh-òsta Grianach, a famous roadside inn that serves pan-fried spinach with black wine. The inn was fortified as a militia post in the troubles before the Severance and took dubhan lamps with the rest of the tavern circuit. It keeps the Old Spirits and lies close by the ruins of Làrach an Dùin. Known for An Taigh-òsta Grianach.

**Cnoc dhìreach** (Caol fhiadhaich). Founded 4 am Màrt, LE 1,118 by carters of Caol fhiadhaich. A small town on a straight hill road between Caol fhiadhaich and the great mill-town of Muileann bheag. It follows the order of the Stone and is a stop for carters. Known for its carters' stop on the south-west road.

**Cnoc dhìreach** (Ceann mhin). Founded 20 an Lùnastal, FE 22 by Dia-thìrich keepers of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach. A small town on the Sìtheas beside Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, the necropolis whose oldest graves are older than its oldest legible names. Its families have kept the necropolis since the Holy Age, when the first burial there was written down. It lives on the burials of the eastern coast and on the masons who cut the stones. Known for its keepers of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach.

**Cnoc dhìreach** (Cnoc dhìreach). Founded 21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,845 by weavers of the carriers' road. Cnoc dhìreach is the walled seat of the eastern mining district, a town of nearly nineteen thousand. It was walled in the Age of Strangers, when the strikes in the district made the administration uneasy. It is not the small town of the necropolis on the south-east coast. Known for its walled seat of the mining district.

**Cnoc dhubh** (Achadh àrsaidh). Founded 20 an Giblean, FE 2,263 by custodians of the capital's south. Cnoc dhubh of Achadh àrsaidh is a black hill with a citadel, south-east of the capital, founded in the Holy Age. Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag lies to its west and the field of Muileann ghlas to its east. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its black-hill citadel south of the capital.

**Cnoc dhubh** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 10 an t-Iuchar, FE 93 by charcoal-burners of the black hill. A black hill where charcoal burners worked through the long centuries of the Sundering, the Small-Burning Law forbidding them the coloured coal. It is the largest of the cluster of Cnocs in the eastern hills and their common market. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith, and its charcoal is still sold to smiths who will not work with dubhan. Known for its charcoal for the smithies.

**Cnoc dhubh** (Tobar fhiadhaich). Founded 22 an t-Sultain, LE 1,517 by the peat-cutters of the northern moor. A black hill of peat in the north, cut for fuel since the Small-Burning Law left the coloured coal to the custodians and ordinary hearths to turf. It is the road-town for Baile mhòr and Àth shean and follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. The peat-banks are now nearly as worked out as the vein. Known for its peat cut from the black hill.

**Cnoc dhubh** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 2 am Faoilleach, FE 265 by a custodian house that quarried the black hill. The black hill is an outcrop of dark stone that the early custodians hoped was the vein; it was not, and the quarry that tested it became a town. Cnoc dhubh is a walled market for the herders and quarrymen of the hills near Làrach an Teampaill; the seat of the shire is the other Cnoc dhubh, the charcoal-burners' town. Prospectors dug here again in the Age of Strangers and found only rock, which the town remembers with some satisfaction. Known for its black-stone quarries and walled market.

**Cnoc dhubh** (Caol mhòr). Founded 5 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,722 by Dia-thìrich founders; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. Cnoc dhubh is a black hill with coal seams in its flank, first dug by the Dia-thìrich for building-stone and later by the humans for coal. The Tuathaich who resettled it kept the pits open. It was among the northern towns that refused dubhan, and its pits were the last in the north to close after the Long War. Known for the last coal pits of the north.

**Cnoc fhada** (Cnoc shean). Founded 18 am Màrt, LE 1,361 by hill-farmers of Cnoc shean. A long hill in the south-east farmed in terraces since the centuries after the Sundering. It keeps the Old Spirits and trades with Muileann dhomhain. Known for its terraced farms on the long hill.

**Cnoc fhiadhaich** (Ceann mhin). Founded 2 an t-Samhain, LE 1,808 by hunters of the north-east hills. A wild hill above Ceann mhin, settled by hunters and later by carters on the harbour road. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and sends game and hides down to the port. Known for its game and hides for Ceann mhin.

**Cnoc fhiadhaich** (Muileann chrom). Founded 17 am Màrt, LE 488 by hunters of the Muileann chrom country. A wild walled hill in the middle country, near the canoe-landing of Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine. Its walls were raised in the troubled years when the river road carried coal. It follows the order of Macha and trades with Muileann chrom and Inis ìseal. Known for a walled hill by the river road.

**Cnoc fhionn** (Baile ruadh). Founded 25 an t-Samhain, VE 3,715 by hill households of the east. Cnoc fhionn, the fair hill, is a large town of sheltered farms in the north-east. It has been settled since the Ancient Age and keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Its barley and ale go down to the harbour at Seann Tarr. Known for its fair-hill barley and ale.

**Cnoc gharbh** (Ros gharbh). Founded 5 an Giblean, LE 1,014 by quarriers of Ros gharbh. Cnoc gharbh is a rough hill of quarries near Seann Bhral, whose walls were built of its stone. It is a town of nearly five thousand, of quarrymen and carters. The standing column at Cnoc ghorm is not of its stone, a fact its masons have checked more than once. Known for its quarries on the rough hill.

**Cnoc gheal** (Muileann shean). Founded 20 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,177 by watchmen of the north. Cnoc gheal is a white hill with a small citadel, raised as a watchtower in the long quiet centuries to give warning of ships on the northern coast. Its fire could be seen from Cill leathan and Àth fhionn, and the three kept a common watch. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith, and its garrison is now a handful of old soldiers and their families. Known for its white-hill watchtower of the north coast.

**Cnoc gheal** (Cnoc gheal). Founded 5 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,928 by hill-farmers of the north-east. A white hill in the north-east, seat of Siorrachd Cnoc gheal, looking down on the Seann-Dhaoine harbour of Seann Bhrenn. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and is the market for Baile dhìreach and Àth dhearg. Known for the white hill market of the north-east.

**Cnoc gheal** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 16 an Cèitean, LE 555 by Dia-thìrich shepherds; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. A white hill of sheepfolds, Dia-thìrich until the Severance and Tuathaich since. The Dia-thìrich Cnoc gheal lies a short walk south-west, over the line. The two villages share a name and very little else: the one has its church, the other its shrine of Manannan. Known for its white hill sheepfolds on the line.

**Cnoc gheal** (Muileann naomh). Founded 16 am Màrt, LE 784 by Dia-thìrich druids of the order of Manannan. The Dia-thìrich Cnoc gheal is a white hill with a shrine of Manannan mac Lir, twinned with Baile dhìreach. A second Cnoc gheal, held by the Tuathaich, lies a short walk north-east over the line. The two villages share a name and very little else, not even a faith. Known for its white hill shrine of Manannan.

**Cnoc ghlas** (Tobar fhiadhaich). Founded 3 an Cèitean, FE 2,596 by hill shepherds of the northern coast. Cnoc ghlas is a hill town of the northern coast, a sheepwalk settlement of the Holy Age that later opened quarries in the grey slate of its hill. Its slate roofs much of the province of Tobar fhiadhaich. Its people follow the druid schools of the Old Faith, and the town sent more than its share of students to the schools' revival. Known for its grey slate and northern sheepwalks.

**Cnoc ghlas** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 13 an Cèitean, AE 22 by human settlers from an Tìr Thall. Cnoc ghlas of Àth àrsaidh was settled by humans in the Age of Strangers and became a Tuathaich town after the Severance. It keeps the faith of the Church, and its singers are among the keepers of the voyage of Naomh Breandan. Known for its strangers' settlement on the grey hill.

**Cnoc ghlas** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 12 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,275 by Dia-thìrich herders, resettled by the Tuathaich. A small green-grey hill town of the north-west, emptied and resettled at the Severance. It follows the faith of the Church and trades with the Dia-thìrich mill at Muileann chrom over the line. Known for its trade across the line at Muileann chrom.

**Cnoc ghlas** (Dùn dhearg). Founded 21 an Dùbhlachd, FE 8 by quarriers for Dùn dhearg. Cnoc ghlas is the grey hill whose stone built much of Dùn dhearg. It is a quarry town and lives by the city. Its quarrymen keep the Old Spirits' rites of the ancestors and will not open a new face without them. Known for its grey stone for Dùn dhearg.

**Cnoc ghorm** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 15 an Dàmhair, VE 6,685 by farming households; resettled by the Tuathaich. Cnoc ghorm of the north-west is the inland seat of its province and one of the largest Tuathaich towns. It was a Dia-thìrich farm town from the Ancient Age, resettled after the Severance. It is not the place of the stone Calbh Cnoc ghorm, which lies far to the south-east. Its dye-fields and smithies are the busiest in the Tuathaich north. Known for its place as the inland seat of the Tuathaich.

**Cnoc ghorm** (Doire fhionn). Founded 22 an Dàmhair, FE 734 by bee-keepers of the north. Cnoc ghorm of Doire fhionn is a town of the north-central country, founded in the Holy Age. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits and its bees, whose wax lit the shrines at Cill àrsaidh before dubhan lamps came. Known for its blue hill and bee-keeping.

**Cnoc ghorm** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 24 an t-Sultain, LE 1,191 by herders of Cathair mhòr. A blue-grey hill town just north of Cathair mhòr, pasturing the garrison's horses. It follows the order of Macha and has always been the city's stable. Known for its horse pastures of Cathair mhòr.

**Cnoc ghorm** (Ceann mhin). Founded 30 am Faoilleach, FE 2,292 by Dia-thìrich keepers of Calbh Cnoc ghorm. The blue hill grew up around Calbh Cnoc ghorm, the standing column carved with the doctrine itself: Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann. If the doctrine has a birthplace it may be here, and the town has never let the island forget it. It is a large town now, and pilgrims of all three faiths climb to the stone. Known for the doctrine stone.

**Cnoc ìseal** (Doire chiar). Founded 7 an t-Samhain, LE 1,261 by flax-growers of the north. Cnoc ìseal, the low hill, is a small town of the north-east given to flax and linen. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and has changed little since. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its flax fields and linen.

**Cnoc ìseal** (Doire mhin). Founded 31 an Cèitean, LE 43 by farmers of Doire mhin. Cnoc ìseal of Doire mhin is a small town of hill farms east of the capital, founded in the long quiet centuries. The field of Muileann ghlas, where An Cogadh Fada ended, lies just to the west, and the town's barns sheltered the wounded after the battle. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its hill farms by Muileann ghlas field.

**Cnoc ìseal** (Baile chiar). Founded 4 an Dàmhair, LE 870 by the garrison of the capital's south road. Cnoc ìseal of Baile chiar is a walled hill on the capital's south road, founded in the long quiet centuries as a watch-post over the southern farms. Its walls were strengthened in the war of the Severance. It is a small town now. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha, and a toll it no longer collects. Known for its walled hill on the capital's south road.

**Cnoc ìseal** (Ros bheag). Founded 18 an Lùnastal, FE 2,606 by Dia-thìrich fishers of the west. A low harbour on the western coast, sheltered by Ros bheag, which it has always served as a lesser port. Its people follow the order of Manannan, the order that runs along the west. The fighting of the Long War at Àth leathan was near enough that the harbour carried supplies for the crown's regiments. Known for its western fishing and war-supply landing.

**Cnoc ìseal** (Caol shean). Founded 23 an Giblean, FE 1,825 by Dia-thìrich pilgrims to Allt an Àigh. Cnoc ìseal began as a halt for pilgrims going down to Allt an Àigh, and its inns still fill at the phase of the moon when the stream is said to give fortune. Its nearness to Muileann chaol has drawn scholars as well, and many readers of the library lodge here. The town keeps the druid schools' habit of arguing a question before answering it. Known for its pilgrim lodgings on the Allt an Àigh road.

**Cnoc leathan** (Cnoc leathan). Founded 11 am Màrt, FE 172 by innkeepers of the south road. Cnoc leathan is a large town and the seat of its province, on the south road of the east. An Taigh-òsta Grianach, one of the great inns of the old circuit, stands to its south. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Slighe Cnoc leathan, the road south past An Taigh-òsta Grianach, has been kept up by the inn's own toll since Anna Ruadh's charter. Known for An Taigh-òsta Grianach on the south road.

**Cnoc leathan** (Dùn chrom). Founded 12 an Dàmhair, LE 1,189 by Dia-thìrich herders of Dùn chrom. A modest town on the broad hill beside Muileann òg, whose people live for most of the year on herding and for one season on the fair. Since Fèill Muileann òg became the island's greatest gathering, Cnoc leathan has lodged the traders the fair town cannot hold and stabled their animals. It stood near the lines at Muileann ghlas and was emptied for the battle. Known for its lodgings and horse-lines for Fèill Muileann òg.

**Cnoc leathan** (Muileann leathan). Founded 9 an t-Samhain, AE 14 by the human administration, as a coast fort. Cnoc leathan was built by the human administration as a fort on the northern coast road, not far from the lighthouse at Muileann bheag. The Tuathaich have held it since the Severance and keep its citadel manned. Its small garrison follows the Tuathaich Church. Known for its Tuathaich-held fort on the north coast.

**Cnoc mhòr** (Cnoc mhòr). Founded 8 am Màrt, FE 1,210 by cattle-drovers of the interior. Cnoc mhòr is the market hill on the Abhainn chiar below Cathair mhòr, where the interior drove roads meet. It was walled in the Age of Strangers, when the city's markets spilled out to it. It is a prosperous town. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha, and sells the gulf its beef. Known for its cattle market below Cathair mhòr.

**Cnoc mhòr** (Doire ghlas). Founded 5 an t-Sultain, LE 1,233 by Dia-thìrich herders; resettled by the Tuathaich. Cnoc mhòr of Doire ghlas is a Tuathaich town of the north coast, founded by Dia-thìrich herders in the long quiet centuries and resettled after the Severance. Its people supply the keepers of Taigh-solais Muileann bheag. It keeps the faith of the Church. Known for its keepers of the Muileann bheag light.

**Cnoc mhòr** (Àth dhomhain). Founded 11 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,375 by hill-farmers of the Àth dhomhain country. The great hill above Baile gheal, farmed since the Holy Age and never walled, since Baile gheal's walls stand close below. The two towns share a market and a long quarrel over which is the elder. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its hill farms and its quarrel with Baile gheal.

**Cnoc mhòr** (Muileann bhàn). Founded 31 an Cèitean, LE 1,645 by hill-lords of Muileann bhàn. A great hill in the south, above the harbour of Seann Warr and the large mill town of Muileann bhàn. It keeps the Old Spirits, and its hill-farms supply both. Known for its hill-farms above Seann Warr.

**Cnoc naomh** (Cnoc naomh). Founded 10 an t-Samhain, VE 8,217 by households who came for the spring of the holy hill. A holy hill with a citadel south of the capital, the seat of Siorrachd Cnoc naomh and a house of the order of Macha since the Age of Sundering. It lies close by the battlefield of Muileann ghlas, and its druids buried the dead of both sides after the Long War's last battle. It is a large town of druids, soldiers and pilgrims. Known for the druids who buried Muileann ghlas's dead.

**Cnoc naomh** (Inis mhòr). Founded 29 an Cèitean, FE 1,142 by a custodian house of Inis mhòr. The holy hill carried a shrine before it carried a citadel; the citadel was added to guard Inis mhòr from the hills. The shrine still stands inside the walls. The fourth regiment from Caol bheag drills on the plain below it. On the moor above the town is Coinneachadh a' Mhonaidh, the cairn where the crew-leaders of the northern pits fixed the week of their rising. Known for its citadel on the holy hill.

**Cnoc òg** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 8 an Dùbhlachd, AE 81 by miners' families from Cnoc dhubh. The 'young hill' was settled by families spilling out of Cnoc dhubh when the great diggings drew workers to the eastern hills. It has little of its own beyond houses and a meeting-hall of the druid schools, and its people work in the fields and shops of its larger neighbour. Known for housing the overflow of Cnoc dhubh.

**Cnoc òg** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 7 an t-Iuchar, AE 80 by silver miners of Muileann chiar. A young hill-town with a citadel beside the silver mine of Muileann chiar, raised when the Dia-thìrich held the silver seam against the human claims. The citadel was built to guard the seam, and the town grew as the silver town grew. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for the citadel over the silver seam.

**Cnoc òg** (Àth shean). Founded 24 an Cèitean, LE 124 by farmers from Àth shean. A young hill town close to Muileann òg, whose fair is the largest gathering on the island. It lodges traders and their beasts during the fair and is quiet the rest of the year. It follows the order of Macha. Known for its lodgings for the Fèill Muileann òg.

**Cnoc òg** (Muileann naomh). Founded 31 am Faoilleach, SE 2 by the restored kingdom, as a border post. Cnoc òg, "the young hill", was walled by the restored kingdom soon after the Severance, on the Dia-thìrich side of the line facing the Tuathaich towns to the north and west. It has never been more than a small town of soldiers' families and carters. In An Cogadh Fada it lay a short march behind the field at Àth leathan, and its walls held the wounded after that first battle. Known for its border walls facing the Tuathaich.

**Cnoc òg** (Àth shean). Founded 17 an t-Sultain, AE 43 by suppliers to the garrison at Inis mhòr. Cnoc òg grew up in the Age of Strangers to supply the garrison at Inis mhòr, where the first regiment is now stationed. It is a town of bakers and harness-makers. It follows the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its supplies for the first regiment.

**Cnoc ruadh** (Cathair fhada). Founded 9 an Dàmhair, LE 1,619 by herders of the south road. Cnoc ruadh of Cathair fhada is a town on the south road, a hill only in name, founded in the long quiet centuries by herders who grazed the red ground there. It grew as a stopping place between the southern ford towns and the capital. Its people keep the capital's order, the order of Macha, and sell hides at the market of Àth shean. Known for its red pasture on the south road.

**Cnoc ruadh** (Achadh chaol). Founded 14 am Màrt, FE 37 by shepherds of the eastern uplands. Cnoc ruadh of Achadh chaol is a hill town of the eastern uplands, a sheep town since the Holy Age. Its wool goes down to Cuan ruadh for shipping. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Known for its red-hill sheepwalks and Cuan ruadh wool.

**Cnoc shean** (Doire fhiadhaich). Founded 6 an t-Sultain, FE 1,217 by Dia-thìrich herders of the south. Cnoc shean, the old hill, is a small town of the south, settled since the Holy Age. Its common holds the market of the farms around it. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its market common on the old hill.

**Cnoc shean** (Inis chrom). Founded 19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 202 by the lords of the old hill. A small old hill-town with a citadel in the west, commanding the road between Baile Mòr fhionn and the harbours of the south-west. It follows the order of the Stone and has kept a garrison since the war before the Severance. Known for the old hill citadel.

**Cnoc shean** (Cnoc shean). Founded 18 am Màrt, FE 3 by Dia-thìrich traders of the eastern plain. Cnoc shean is the old hill market for the granary fields of Achadh mhòr, and the seat of its province. It is a town of more than twenty thousand, with grain-halls and a weighing-house older than any coinage on the island. The tavern An Sligeanach Fad' às lies on the road to Achadh mhòr, and its dried deer is sold in Cnoc shean's market. Known for its old hill market of the granary fields.

**Cnoc thais** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 84 by shepherds of the Cuan ghlas hills. A damp hill-town above the river port of Cuan ghlas, its name taken from the mists that sit on it most mornings. It was never walled and never fought over, and its people send wool and cheese down to the river quays and to Cnoc chiar. A small house of the druid schools keeps the only books in the place. Known for its mist, its wool and its hill cheese.

**Cnoc thais** (Cnoc thais). Founded 19 an t-Sultain, VE 9,651 by Dia-thìrich hill-farmers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A damp hill in the north-west, seat of Siorrachd Cnoc thais, and one of the larger Tuathaich towns since the Severance. It follows the faith of the Church and is the market of the two Muileann àrsaidhs. Known for the market of the two ancient mills.

**Cnoc thais** (Ceann mhin). Founded 3 an t-Iuchar, LE 536 by hill-farmers of the south-east. A damp hill above the small harbour of Caol dhomhain in the south-east. It keeps the Old Spirits and sends its cattle to Baile gheal. Known for its cattle on a misty hill.

**Cnoc thais** (Cnoc leathan). Founded 20 an Dùbhlachd, LE 274 by reed-cutters of Cnoc leathan. Cnoc thais is a damp hill whose reed-beds thatch the roofs of the eastern plain. It is a town of eleven thousand. Its cutters work the beds in the dry months and its thatchers travel in the wet. Known for its reed-cutters and thatch.

**Cnoc uaine** (Caol ìseal). Founded 17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,305 by the garrison of the north-coast road. Cnoc uaine of Caol ìseal is a hill fort over the north-coast road, raised in the long quiet centuries and walled since. Its garrison watched the road through the Age of Strangers. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Known for its hill fort over the north-coast road.

**Cnoc uaine** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 9 an Dàmhair, LE 938 by Dia-thìrich herders; resettled by the Tuathaich. Cnoc uaine of Muileann àrsaidh is a green hill of the north-west, founded by Dia-thìrich herders in the long quiet centuries. It was resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It is a grazing town and keeps the faith of the Church. Known for its green hill grazing.

**Cnoc uaine** (Cnoc àrsaidh). Founded 31 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,155 by hill-lords of the south-west. A green walled hill in the south-west, fortified against pirates who raided the coast in the centuries after the Sundering. It follows the order of the Stone and sends its young to the first fleet at Àth gharbh. Known for the walled green hill.

**Cnoc uaine** (Baile chaol). Founded 21 an Cèitean, FE 2,852 by Dia-thìrich keepers of the holy wood. Cnoc uaine is a green hill on the Abhainn mhin at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar. It is a large town of nearly seventeen thousand, and its people share the keeping of the wood with Àth dhearg. It keeps the Old Spirits, though the wood itself is sacred to Flidais and held by the druid schools. Known for its green hill on the holy wood's edge.

**Cuan àrsaidh** (Achadh naomh). Founded 28 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,483 by the river-lords of the Abhainn ìseal. An ancient river port a little below Cuan bheag on the Abhainn ìseal, trading grain from the fields around Baile fhiadhaich since the Holy Age. The Green Death, A' Phlàigh Uaine, struck the town in the Age of Strangers. It follows the capital's order, the order of Macha. Its stone jetty is held to be the oldest on the island still in use, and it is patched each generation rather than rebuilt. Known for the island's oldest working jetty.

**Cuan bheag** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 1 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,554 by river traders of the northern country. Cuan bheag, the small harbour, is a river port on the upper Abhainn ìseal. It was a fishing water until the Age of Strangers, when human traders wanted a sheltered mooring on this side of the island, with the river open to the sea at Ros gheal, and it grew busy. The restored kingdom built its citadel to watch the northern approaches, and the town has since become one of the larger river ports of the province. Its people keep the Old Faith in the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its sheltered river mooring and the northern watch.

**Cuan bheag** (Caol mhòr). Founded 10 am Màrt, SE 17 by Tuathaich fishing families. Cuan bheag of the north-west was built by Tuathaich fishing families in the first years after the Severance, on a shore the Dia-thìrich had never settled. It is a village of boats and drying racks. It sells its catch through Caol mhòr. Known for its Tuathaich fishing boats and drying racks.

**Cuan chrom** (Seann Vell). Founded 10 am Faoilleach, LE 1,231 by Dia-thìrich innkeepers of Seann Vell. Cuan chrom is a river town on a bend of the Abhainn fhionn, and An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, one of the great houses of the old tavern circuit, stands at its river quay. The tavern was a waypoint on the mining roads and doubled as a militia halt in the years before the war. It is known across the island for its steamed carp and green brandy. Known for An Taigh-seinnse Mòr and steamed carp.

**Cuan dhearg** (Muileann chrom). Founded 12 an Dàmhair, LE 1,789 by river fishers of the Abhainn uaine. Cuan dhearg is one of the ring of small river towns on the Abhainn uaine above Cathair mhòr, named for the red cliffs over its landing. It lives on the river fish and the short ferry runs between the river towns, and sends what it has for the sea down to Ceann leathan at the river mouth. It has never been walled. It is not the southern Cuan dhearg that Tonn Mhòr destroyed; the chroniclers have confused the two more than once. Its inn, An Cupa Dàna, is where Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, the Leaden Hawk company, gathered in the first spring of the Severance war before walking to the Hawk coast. Known for its red-cliffed river landing and ferries.

**Cuan dhearg** (Seann Vell). Founded 31 am Faoilleach, FE 1,384 by fishing clans of the southern shore. A red-cliffed harbour on the southern coast that was a fishing town for three ages. The Great Wave, Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol, struck it in a single night in the first years of the new kingdom and destroyed the lower town with its fleet, and the harbour was rebuilt higher up the cliff. Its people keep the Old Spirits of the Dia-thìrich, and every house facing the sea keeps a lamp in the upper window. The harbour is on Eilean bhàn, the largest island off the south coast, which it shares with Cnoc chaol. Known for its rebuilding after the Great Wave.

**Cuan ghlas** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 15 an t-Ògmhios, FE 221 by grey-water fishers of the north-east. A grey river port on the Abhainn ghorm in the north-east with a citadel, the seat of Siorrachd Cuan ghlas, and a large village, whose barges go down to Ros chiar at the river mouth. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and is served by the hill town of Cnoc thais above it. Known for the grey river port and its citadel.

**Cuan ruadh** (Cuan ruadh). Founded 1 an t-Sultain, VE 7,710 by Dia-thìrich fishers of the east. Cuan ruadh is the easternmost harbour of the island and the seat of its province, a port since the Ancient Age. Its boats go out further than any on the coast, and it has lost more to pirates than any other eastern town. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Known for the island's easternmost harbour.

**Cuan shean** (Cuan shean). Founded 18 an t-Ògmhios, VE 8,078 by Dia-thìrich households who took up the old landing. The old harbour of the west, the seat of Siorrachd Cuan shean and one of the largest towns on the island. It shipped western grain and timber through the Holy Age and served the human traders after the Crossing. Since the Long War it has been home to An ceathramh cabhlach, the fourth fleet. It follows the order of Manannan. Known for the fourth fleet's harbour.

**Cuan uaine** (Doire fhada). Founded 23 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,534 by Dia-thìrich custodians of the capital's east. Cuan uaine, whose name means the green harbour, is a walled temple city on the Abhainn fhionn east of the capital, fortified in the Holy Age to guard the river road to the eastern shore. Its temple of Macha is much visited by those who cannot reach the capital's. The barracks town of Inis mhòr lies just upriver to the north. Its copyists and tailors work for the capital. Known for the temple of Macha on the Abhainn fhionn.

#### D

**Doire bhàn** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 14 an t-Iuchar, LE 27 by the oak-cutters of Seann Dunn. A white oak grove between Seann Dunn and Seann Mhorn, cut for charcoal and ship-timber. It keeps the Old Spirits and is a large, quiet village with no walls. Known for its timber for the coast harbours.

**Doire bhàn** (Àth ghlas). Founded 7 an t-Sultain, LE 1,287 by Dia-thìrich woodwards of Àth ghlas. A small village in a copse of white-barked trees across the river from Àth ghlas, cutting firewood and poles for the town. It keeps clear of the ruin of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire to the east, as its elder neighbour does. It follows the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its white-barked copse by Àth ghlas.

**Doire bheag** (Muileann mhin). Founded 4 an t-Samhain, LE 1,560 by Dia-thìrich woodcutters of the capital. A small village in an oak copse north-east of Cathair dhearg, which has cut firewood and charcoal for the capital for as long as there are accounts. It has never grown past seven hundred people. Its people follow the capital's order, the order of Macha, and take their wood into the city on market days. Known for its firewood for the capital.

**Doire chaol** (Doire chaol). Founded 3 an Giblean, AE 17 by carters of the capital's road. Doire chaol was a carters' village outside the capital in the Age of Strangers, and after the Severance it was laid out anew on a narrow oak strip by the Abhainn dhomhain south of the capital, to house the families of the royal household. It grew into a large village, and in the kingdom's fourth decade it was cut out of the shire of Baile chiar as a shire of its own, the only shire made since the shires were first drawn. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for the capital's household village.

**Doire chaol** (Ceann mhòr). Founded 28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,234 by Dia-thìrich charcoal-burners; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. A charcoal village in a narrow oakwood, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. The newcomers made the Dia-thìrich shrine of Manannan they found there their church rather than raising their own, as several villages of this coast did. It still burns charcoal for the smiths of Àth fhionn and Àth dhearg. Known for its narrow oakwood and charcoal.

**Doire chaol** (Caol gharbh). Founded 22 an Lùnastal, LE 762 by woodwards for Caol gharbh's yards. A village in a narrow oakwood that has sent timber to the boatyards of Caol gharbh since the yards were opened. It has always been small and has always been owed money by the yards. Its families also hunt the oakwood, and their venison goes down to Caol gharbh with the timber. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its oak for Caol gharbh's boatyards.

**Doire chaol** (Baile àrsaidh). Founded 16 an t-Ògmhios, LE 123 by Dia-thìrich woodwards of Baile àrsaidh. A village in a narrow oakwood south of Baile àrsaidh, felling for the yards at Cuan shean as the larger Doire gharbh does. The two oakwood villages have argued over the same buyers in every age. It follows the order of Manannan. Known for its narrow oakwood of Baile àrsaidh.

**Doire chiar** (Doire chiar). Founded 8 an Giblean, VE 9,506 by oak-keepers of the north-east. A dusky oak grove grown into a large village, the seat of Siorrachd Doire chiar. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith, and its druids are said to hold their disputations under the oldest trees. Known for its disputations under the oaks.

**Doire dhearg** (Muileann bhàn). Founded 21 an t-Iuchar, AE 32 by Dia-thìrich miners bound by the strangers' contracts. Doire dhearg began as a mining camp in the Age of Strangers, when the interior was first worked by the ton. Its red spoil-heaps are still visible above the village. Many of its people left when the workings moved on, and the village that remains keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Known for its red spoil-heaps of the camp years.

**Doire dhìreach** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 1 an Dàmhair, FE 647 by Dia-thìrich woodwards of the Baile Mòr dhomhain plain. An oak grove kept by woodward families, whose trees grow tall and true beyond the common run. It is told of the Sundering that the shipwrights sent to Doire dhìreach for keels when the ocean ships were built, and the village has told that tale of itself ever since. It has grown into a large village of timber-yards and cooperages, serving Àth mhòr and Baile Mòr àrsaidh. Known for its straight-grown oak for keels.

**Doire dhubh** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 26 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,523 by Dia-thìrich woodwards of Cnoc bhàn. A village in a dark oak grove a short way north of Muileann chaol. When the library was founded its oak was cut for the shelves and reading-tables, and the woodwards still claim a right to repair them. It sends its remaining timber to Cnoc bhàn and Baile thais. Known for its dark oak for the library's shelves.

**Doire fhada** (Baile ghlas). Founded 3 an t-Sultain, LE 360 by woodsmen of the capital shore. Doire fhada, the long grove, is a walled village on the shore of Loch chrom near the capital, founded in the long quiet centuries. It was walled in the Age of Strangers to protect its grain stores. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its walled long grove.

**Doire fhada** (Doire fhada). Founded 27 am Faoilleach, FE 2,013 by oak-cutters of the capital's forests. A long oak grove east of the capital cut for ship-timber since the Holy Age, and the shipwrights who built the Sundering fleet are said to have taken their keels here. The village grew enormous without changing its name, and it is now the seat of Siorrachd Doire fhada and a river port of the capital's order, Macha's, on the Abhainn fhionn. The grove itself is mostly gone, and the village keeps one old oak fenced by the river quay. Known for its ship-timber and the fenced oak.

**Doire fhiadhaich** (Ros dhomhain). Founded 18 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,506 by woodcutters of the wild oak wood. Doire fhiadhaich was a wild oak wood on the capital shore, and tradition holds that timber for the Sundering fleet was felled here. The wood is long gone and the village is now a fishing quarter between Ros dhomhain and the capital's harbours. It has kept its village rank and its own fishing rights. Known for its oaks said to have built the Sundering fleet.

**Doire fhiadhaich** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 13 an t-Samhain, FE 1,348 by custodians of Cnoc dhubh. Doire fhiadhaich of Cnoc dhubh is a village only by the old rank; it is large, and it has a citadel raised by the Holy Age custodians who held these hills. Làrach an Teampaill lies in the hills to its east. Its people keep the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits and will not cut the oaks nearest the ruin. Known for its citadel above Cnoc dhubh.

**Doire fhiadhaich** (Doire fhiadhaich). Founded 19 an Lùnastal, FE 1,981 by the oak-keepers of the south. A wild oak grove in the south, grown into a very large village and the seat of Siorrachd Doire fhiadhaich. It follows the order of Macha and supplies timber to the city of Cathair fhada close by. Known for its timber for Cathair fhada.

**Doire fhiadhaich** (Seann Tarr). Founded 11 am Màrt, LE 1,117 by Dia-thìrich woodwards of Seann Tarr. A village in a wild oakwood between Baile Mòr ruadh and the east coast. It lives on timber and on the boar hunts that the city's families come out for. It keeps the Old Spirits. Known for its wild oakwood and boar.

**Doire fhionn** (Caol shean). Founded 19 an Lùnastal, FE 669 by woodsmen of the eastern hills. Doire fhionn of Caol shean is an oak-grove village on the way to Allt an Àigh. Pilgrims to the stream have lodged in its houses since the Holy Age, and the Library at Muileann chaol stands on the road to the north. Its people follow the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its oak grove on the pilgrims' way.

**Doire fhionn** (Doire fhionn). Founded 20 am Màrt, FE 397 by Dia-thìrich woodsmen of the east. Doire fhionn of the east is the seat of its province, a great village of the Holy Age in an oak grove; for all its size it has never been raised to the rank of a town. Its oaks are felled and planted under rules older than the kingdom. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits, and the old field-village of Achadh àrsaidh lies to its north. Known for its great oak grove of the east.

**Doire fhionn** (Doire fhionn). Founded 4 an t-Samhain, FE 1,149 by the oak-keepers of the Old Spirits. A fair oak grove in the north, the seat of Siorrachd Doire fhionn and a large village of the Old Spirits. The grove has never been cut for ship-timber, its keepers holding it for the ancestors, and it lies on the road between Cathair naomh and the Tuathaich line. Known for an uncut grove of the ancestors.

**Doire fhionn** (Doire ghlas). Founded 5 an Dàmhair, LE 482 by Dia-thìrich woodwards; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance.
