A Dia-thìrich village in a grove of pale oaks, left empty at the Severance and resettled by Tuathaich families sent north. Its people keep the Tuathaich Church, and it is one of the northern households where the voyage of Naomh Breandan is still told at the hearth, a telling the Dia-thìrich druids call superstition. It lives on timber and on the fort at Cnoc leathan nearby. Known for its pale oaks and Tuathaich hearth-tellings.

**Doire gharbh** (Cnoc dhìreach). Founded 5 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,269 by Dia-thìrich woodwards of Cnoc dhìreach. A large village in rough oakwood below the Doire uaine hills, walled against the thing that the old inscriptions say walks in those hills. The rolls give a plainer reason: the walls went up in the Age of Strangers, when the strikes in the eastern district reached its gates. The warm springs of Muileann ruadh lie a short walk east. Known for its palisade under the Doire uaine hills.

**Doire gharbh** (Cuan shean). Founded 2 an Dàmhair, FE 1,695 by Dia-thìrich shipwrights' woodwards. A large walled village in rough oakwood that has supplied timber to the yards at Cuan shean since the Holy Age. When the fleet of Cuan shean was raised in the Long War its hulls were cut here. It follows the order of Manannan, as does most of the west. Known for its rough oak for the western fleet.

**Doire gheal** (Baile ìseal). Founded 10 an Dàmhair, AE 65 by human settlers of the Age of Strangers. A small white oak grove settled by humans in the early years after the Crossing, one of the few human foundations of the north-west. Its people stayed through the Severance and are among the oldest human families on the island. It follows the faith of the Church. Known for its house of one of the oldest human families.

**Doire ghlas** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 14 an Gearran, FE 503 by woodsmen of Cnoc dhubh. Doire ghlas of Cnoc dhubh is a village of grey oaks near Làrach an Teampaill. It was founded in the Holy Age, and its people have guided visitors to the ruin ever since. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Known for its grey oaks by Làrach an Teampaill.

**Doire ghlas** (Doire ghlas). Founded 26 an Giblean, VE 7,793 by Dia-thìrich oak-cutters, resettled by the Tuathaich. The grey oak grove of Doire ghlas is the grove of the Keeper. Here, the Line of the Mason tells, Coimhdeach na Fine, the kin's keeper, came as a figure of grey smoke to Diarmad of that line and told him the making of the world and gave him the riddle of the coal; here Cormac of the Misstrike lit the coal of life with his own blood; and here Ailean son of Suibhne brought the six lit coals, saw the Keeper light the seventh, and after a vigil of seven nights was crowned by Caoran and the Tuath Dè. It was a small Dia-thìrich village in the grove until the Severance, when the families shepherded north were gathered here before being sent on, and so many stayed that it became the largest settlement in the Tuathaich homeland almost at once. It never took a town's name, and the Tuathaich keep it a village in speech on purpose. It is the seat of Siorrachd Doire ghlas and the heart of the Tuathaich Church, whose priests are said to hold the oldest copy of the voyage of Naomh Breandan here; the library has asked to copy it and been refused. The priests keep no telling of the Keeper, and the Old Faith's households that still come to walk under the oaks keep to the edge of the churchyard. Its wool mills, built with the Moot's money, make the grey twill of the north. Known for the great Tuathaich gathering-village.

**Doire ghorm** (Seann Skell). Founded 26 an t-Sultain, LE 1,794 by charcoal-burners of the south-east. Doire ghorm is a grove village of the south-east, founded by charcoal-burners in the long quiet centuries. Its charcoal once fed the smithies of the south coast. It keeps the orthodox rite of Brìde's flame, like its neighbours. Known for its charcoal for the south-coast smithies.

**Doire mhin** (Caol mhòr). Founded 3 an Giblean, FE 2,743 by Dia-thìrich woodsmen of the Holy Age. An oak-grove village of the Holy Age, Doire mhin was emptied of its Dia-thìrich families in the years of the Severance and filled by Tuathaich households moved north. It is a large village for its kind, living on the smooth-barked oaks that name it. Its timber goes down to the yards of Caol mhòr, and its people keep the faith of the Church. Known for its oak timber for the Caol mhòr yards.

**Doire mhin** (Doire mhin). Founded 10 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,260 by the oak-keepers of the capital's north. A smooth-barked oak grove north of the capital, grown into one of the largest settlements on the island while keeping its village name and customs. It is the seat of Siorrachd Doire mhin and follows the order of Macha. Its people farm for Cathair mhòr and send much of their grain to the tithe-granaries at Baile chrom. Known for the great grove-village of the north road.

**Doire mhòr** (Muileann chrom). Founded 24 an Giblean, LE 568 by Dia-thìrich hill households above Muileann chrom. Doire mhòr, the great oak grove, was a hill village above Muileann chrom when the humans came, and the first settlement to refuse the Company's contract: its custodian Beathag Dhubh told the agent that the hill was not hers to sell. The Company turned its stream to wash coal, and at last took the village itself for a shaft beneath the hill, and its last households were carried out by constables. The beacon of the day the pits stopped was lit on its hill. The oak wood went long ago to pit-props, and a few families farm the clearing. Known for its refusal of the first contract.

**Doire mhòr** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 24 an t-Sultain, FE 1,316 by Dia-thìrich woodwards; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. A great oakwood village, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance and now one of the largest places they hold, with fourteen thousand people. It lives on timber and charcoal, and its charcoal fed the northern smithies when the coloured coal was no longer theirs to burn. It follows the faith of the Church. Known for its great oakwood and charcoal.

**Doire naomh** (Seann Skell). Founded 14 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,785 by Dia-thìrich druids of the west coast. A holy oak grove in the west near Àth leathan, where the Long War's first battle was fought. It stayed Dia-thìrich and kept the order of Manannan, and it buried many of the dead of that battle in its grove. The grove is closed to strangers. Known for its graves of the Àth leathan dead.

**Doire ruadh** (Inis bhàn). Founded 24 an Cèitean, LE 1,491 by hawk-keepers of the north. Doire ruadh is a village of red oaks inland of the Hawk bay, founded in the long quiet centuries by families who kept hawks for the rite of Mòd, the hungry hawk of Acaill. Its birds are still flown at the Hawk order's gatherings in Cnoc bheag. Since the Severance it has lain close to the Tuathaich border and has seen more soldiers than it wishes. Known for its red oak grove and hawk-keepers.

**Doire shean** (Doire shean). Founded 14 an Lùnastal, VE 6,018 by potters of the south-west coast. An old oak grove in the south-west, grown into one of the largest villages on the island and the seat of Siorrachd Doire shean. At its heart is Am Buabhall Fortanach, the most famous tavern on the old roads, which serves jugged buffalo and has stood since the Holy Age. It is a harbour as well, where the hulls of the first fleet of Àth gharbh lie, and follows the order of the Stone. Rathad na Banrighinn, Queen Catrìona's stone road from the capital to Inis thais, runs through the village past the tavern. Known for Am Buabhall Fortanach and jugged buffalo.

**Doire uaine** (Muileann chiar). Founded 13 an Gearran, FE 2,879 by herders of the Doire uaine hills. Doire uaine is a small village in the hills where inscriptions describe the Hollow Man, something that walked without breathing and attacked anyone who lit a fire in its sight. The village was founded in the Holy Age. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for the Hollow Man of the hills.

**Doire uaine** (Muileann bheag). Founded 16 an Lùnastal, FE 1,738 by the grove-keepers of the Old Spirits. A green oak grove in the north-east, not the Doire uaine of the Hollow Man's hills, a confusion the library records note with some weariness. It keeps the Old Spirits and cuts its oak for Muileann bheag. Known for its oak for Muileann bheag.

**Dùn chiar** (Achadh àrsaidh). Founded 2 an Cèitean, FE 862 by a custodian house guarding the capital's east. Dùn chiar is a hill fort of dusky stone east of Cathair dhearg, called a city for its rank rather than its people, who are few. Its citadel and walls were rebuilt in every age, and it has served as the eastern guard of the capital since the kings of the Holy Age. It follows the capital's order, the order of Macha, and its garrison takes part in the rites of Cathair dhearg. Known for its dusky hill fort east of the capital.

**Dùn chrom** (Dùn chrom). Founded 7 am Faoilleach, VE 8,124 by the lords of the bent hill. A fortified city on a crooked hill in the midlands, seat of Siorrachd Dùn chrom, with a citadel that commands the roads south of the capital. The last battle of the Long War, at Muileann ghlas, was fought within sight of its citadel, and the crown's commanders used its citadel as their headquarters. It follows the order of Macha and is served by the stockyard town of Baile chrom and the ford at Àth mhin. Known for the citadel above Muileann ghlas.

**Dùn dhearg** (Dùn dhearg). Founded 9 an Gearran, VE 9,597 by households who owed nothing to Dùn ìseal. Dùn dhearg is the red hill-fort city of the east and the seat of its province, a city of more than twenty-five thousand. The mills of Muileann dhomhain grind its bread and the quarries of Cnoc ghlas built its houses. It keeps the Old Spirits, and its old fort is the site of the province's ancestor feasts. Known for its red hill-fort.

**Dùn dhubh** (Muileann bheag). Founded 26 an Cèitean, FE 1,182 by a custodian house of Muileann bheag. Dùn dhubh is a walled hill fort of dark stone, ranked a city though it holds under three thousand people. It commands the coast road above Muileann bheag and the harbour of Seann Toll. Its walls were raised in the Holy Age and repaired in every age after. A dubhan works stands under its walls, on the old charcoal-burners' ground. Known for its black fort over the coast road.

**Dùn fhiadhaich** (Cnoc naomh). Founded 20 an Giblean, FE 1,384 by the lords of the wild hill. A small wild city on a hill south of the capital, near Achadh mhin, which the Great Wave struck. Its hill kept it clear of the water, and it took in the survivors of the villages below. It follows the order of Macha. The clay of its hill makes it the largest pottery on Dia-thìr, and Cathair fhada sells its ware to the north. Known for its refuge from the Great Wave.

**Dùn gheal** (Àth shean). Founded 26 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,934 by a custodian house of the southern approach. The white fort is ranked a city though it holds only a few thousand people, a hill fort limed white so that it could be seen from the capital. It watched the southern road in the Holy Age and has done so since. It is now the market for Baile uaine and the farms of Àth shean. Known for its white-limed hill fort.

**Dùn ìseal** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 9 an Lùnastal, VE 5,324 by the hill-folk of the first Stone King. A low fort-city in the east with walls, a citadel and a temple, the seat of Siorrachd Dùn ìseal. It is the hill of the first kingdom: Ailean Mòr, crowned in the grove at Doire ghlas, came here and took the hill and the valleys about it, and threw up its first bank, and the Stone Kings held it after him. Its temple is the Hall where Brìde's undying flame was first bound, kept by the Dia-thìrich custodians through every age; the townsfolk themselves keep the Old Spirits, and their ancestor hall beside it is the chief spirit-house of the eastern hills. It stands between the silver seam of Muileann chiar and the hot springs of Muileann ruadh, and it was held by the Dia-thìrich in the dispute over the silver. It is the market town of the eastern hills and plain, and the market under the Hall is older than the kingdom. The silver, gold and copper of its hills pass through it as blanks for the mint, and the town salts venison and binds books. Known for the Hall of Brìde's flame.

**Dùn thais** (Ros bheag). Founded 23 an Gearran, FE 2,142 by custodians of the western hills. Dùn thais, the damp fort, is a hill stronghold above the western coast, held by custodians of the vein's western road since the Holy Age. Its walls were rebuilt in the Age of Strangers, when the western harbours began shipping coal, and its citadel has never stood empty since. In An Cogadh Fada its garrison marched to the field of Àth leathan, a short road to the north-east. Known for its hill citadel of the western coast.

**Dùn thais** (Dùn thais). Founded 28 am Màrt, VE 7,796 by hill-folk pushing east. Dùn thais of the north-east is a great hill city with a citadel and a temple, the chief place of its province. It lies close to Leabharlann Muileann chaol, and many of the Library's clerks and copyists live in it. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith, and its temple is sacred to Flidais, lady of the deer. Its tailors and smiths work for the library's clerks and the hill towns, and its own woods give timber. Known for its place as the great hill city near the Library.

**Dùn thais** (Baile Mòr mhòr). Founded 10 an Dàmhair, FE 1,454 by custodians of the northern coast. Dùn thais of the north is the northernmost Dia-thìrich citadel, raised by the Holy Age custodians on the northern coast. Since the Severance it has watched the Tuathaich country. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Known for the northernmost Dia-thìrich citadel.

#### I

**Inis àrsaidh** (Seann Skell). Founded 28 am Faoilleach, FE 76 by Dia-thìrich fishers of the west. Inis àrsaidh is an island town on the Abhainn naomh in the west, founded in the Holy Age; its ships put to sea from Ros àrsaidh at the river mouth. It was the nearest river port to the field of Àth leathan, and in An Cogadh Fada it victualled the kingdom's host for the first battle. Its fairground is one of the two grounds where the travelling circus, An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn, pitches. Known for its river port near the field of Àth leathan.

**Inis àrsaidh** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 28 an t-Sultain, FE 242 by Dia-thìrich island-lords, resettled by the Tuathaich. An ancient island city on the north-west coast, all but joined to Ceann dhubh. It was a Dia-thìrich harbour-city until the Severance and has been Tuathaich since. It follows the faith of the Church and is one of the few Tuathaich harbours with a fleet of its own. Known for the Tuathaich island harbour.

**Inis bhàn** (Inis bhàn). Founded 16 an Giblean, VE 9,239 by seal-taking households of the lower river. Inis bhàn is the great river port of the north-west Dia-thìrich country and the seat of its province, a town of nearly forty thousand on the Abhainn ìseal whose barges run down to Ros gheal on the coast. It is a town of the Hawk order, and its shrines face down the river toward the sea. The Green Death, A' Phlàigh Uaine, struck it in the Age of Strangers. It is one of several towns that claim the dock from which the ships of the Sundering set out, a claim the others dispute and no roll can settle. Known for its white-island river port and Hawk-order shrines.

**Inis bheag** (Inis bheag). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,435 by boat-builders of the north-east. Inis bheag is an island town on the Abhainn bheag in the north-east and the seat of its province. Its boatyards have built fishing craft for the coast since the Holy Age and send them down the river to the sea at Caol chrom. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and shares its river with Ros fhionn of the old bridge. Known for its boatyards of the small isle.

**Inis bheag** (Seann Toll). Founded 4 an Dàmhair, FE 2,244 by the island-keepers of Seann Toll. A small walled harbour on a tidal islet of the north coast, near the holy city of Cathair naomh. It ferries pilgrims from the sea to the holy city and keeps the Old Spirits. Known for the pilgrims' ferry to Cathair naomh.

**Inis chrom** (Inis chrom). Founded 25 an Giblean, FE 1,601 by sailors of the south-west. Inis chrom is a large walled harbour on a bent island in the mouth of the Abhainn ghorm in the south-west. It has been a port since the Holy Age and its sailors keep the order of the Stone. It lies close to Am Buabhall Fortanach and Àth gharbh. Known for its bent isle harbour and its sailors of the Stone.

**Inis ìseal** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 9 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,060 by Dia-thìrich river-folk of the Abhainn ìseal. Inis ìseal is a low island in the Abhainn ìseal above Cnoc bheag, fortified in the long quiet centuries to guard that town's river and walled again in the Age of Strangers. Since the Severance it has been a frontier fortress facing the Tuathaich border, supplied by boats that come up the river from Ros gheal. The Green Death, A' Phlàigh Uaine, struck its garrison in the Age of Strangers, It ranks as a city, but it is a barracks. The fortress keeps its own boatyard and weaving-sheds, and its cheese goes down the river to Ros gheal. Known for its island fortress guarding Cnoc bheag.

**Inis ìseal** (Muileann chrom). Founded 12 an Giblean, LE 1,110 by Dia-thìrich river boatmen. Inis ìseal is a river port on a low island in the Abhainn uaine, a short way from the landing at Cidhe Beag. It is the rival of Ceann fhada a short way upstream, and the two have disputed tolls in every age. It prospered in the Age of Strangers carrying coal and has kept its trade by carrying grain. Known for its river-island port on the Abhainn uaine.

**Inis leathan** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 29 an Giblean, LE 1,298 by ferrymen of the broad isle. Inis leathan is a village on a broad island in the lower Abhainn fhionn near the north coast, founded in the long quiet centuries by ferrymen who ran boats to either bank. In the Age of Strangers its ferry carried supplies to the tavern and mill at Muileann fhada. It still keeps the ferry, and little else. Known for its ferrymen of the broad isle.

**Inis mhin** (Inis mhin). Founded 5 an Lùnastal, FE 2,644 by Dia-thìrich harbour-folk; resettled by the Tuathaich. Inis mhin was a Dia-thìrich harbour of the Holy Age on a tidal islet of the north coast, and its citadel was raised in the Age of Strangers by human administrators guarding the northern landing. After the Severance it passed wholly to the Tuathaich, and it is now one of their chief ports. It is among the coastal towns where the voyage of Naomh Breandan is still told, and its church keeps the old Tuathaich telling more closely than the churches of its neighbours. In the first spring of the Severance war the Leaden Hawk company, Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, lay twelve hours in the town and heard of the constables riding the western roads. Known for the telling of Naomh Breandan's voyage in its Tuathaich port.

**Inis mhin** (Achadh naomh). Founded 20 an Cèitean, VE 8,495 by fowlers of the eastern cliffs. A smooth low island joined to the shore by a causeway, walled, with a small harbour. The fowlers who settled it in the Ancient Age became traders and then wall-builders, since the eastern waters were a haunt of pirates in the Age of Strangers. It keeps the Old Spirits and is the harbour for Àth chaol and Achadh naomh. Known for its causeway harbour and seal-oil.

**Inis mhòr** (Seann Vell). Founded 12 an t-Sultain, LE 730 by boatmen of Seann Vell. An island town on the Abhainn fhionn, settled in the long quiet centuries by boatmen from Seann Vell upriver, Inis mhòr was walled once the capital's eastern approaches became worth defending. A' chiad rèisimeid, raised in the campaign of An Cogadh Fada, is stationed here and bears the town's name. Its barracks are now larger than the old fishing quarter. The temple town of Cuan uaine can be seen a little way downriver, and what the town ships goes down the river to Cathair dhomhain. The white sand of its river banks goes to its glass-house. Known for its barracks of the first regiment.

**Inis mhòr** (Inis mhòr). Founded 16 an Dàmhair, VE 9,651 by net-fishers of the Abhainn ghorm. Inis mhòr of the north-east is the great river port of its province, on the Abhainn ghorm, a fishing town of the Ancient Age that the trade of the Age of Strangers made a city; its barges run down the river to Ros chiar at the mouth. Its people follow the druid schools of the Old Faith, and the town's debating halls were among the first to reopen at the schools' revival. It shares the river and coastal trade with Ceann bheag and the walled town of Baile Mòr dhìreach inland. Known for its north-eastern river fleet and debating halls.

**Inis naomh** (Tobar ghorm). Founded 9 am Faoilleach, FE 2,521 by keepers of the holy isle. Inis naomh is a walled harbour on a holy tidal isle of the north coast, reached on foot at low water, founded in the Holy Age. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Its walls were built to keep the isle's shrine safe from raiders. Known for its holy isle and its walled landing.

**Inis thais** (Inis thais). Founded 21 an Lùnastal, VE 7,731 by Dia-thìrich fishing households of the western coast. Inis thais is a walled temple city of the south-west and the seat of its province. Its temple of Lia Fàil, the stone called Clach that cries out under the rightful king, is the chief house of the order of the Stone, and pilgrims come to it from Caol leathan and the whole western coast. It has been a holy city since the Holy Age. Besides its pilgrims it lives on its shipyard, which builds seagoing hulls for the western coast, and on its cheese and books. Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, the Leaden Hawk company sent by the council in the Severance war, ended its road at the temple here; the druids of Lia Fàil kept the city out of the war but shut its harbour to the Company's ships. Known for the temple of Lia Fàil and its pilgrims.

**Inis uaine** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 3 an t-Ògmhios, LE 980 by boatmen of the Abhainn chaol. Inis uaine is a river town on a green island in the Abhainn chaol in the east, founded in the long quiet centuries; its boats go down to the sea at Seann Mhorn. In An Cogadh Fada, An t-ochdamh rèisimeid was raised here to guard the eastern dubhan tanks and took the town's name, and the barracks have changed the town's trade from fish to soldiers' wants. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Known for its barracks of the eighth regiment.

#### M

**Muileann àrsaidh** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 10 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,444 by Dia-thìrich millers; resettled by the Tuathaich. Muileann àrsaidh, the ancient mill, is the younger of the two Muileann àrsaidh in the Tuathaich north-west, founded as a Dia-thìrich mill town in the Holy Age; the seat of the shire is the elder town close by. It was walled in the Age of Strangers and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. The mill still grinds for the surrounding villages. Known for the old mill of the north-west.

**Muileann àrsaidh** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 3 an t-Samhain, VE 7,789 by Dia-thìrich millers, resettled by the Tuathaich. An ancient mill town of the north-west, and seat of Siorrachd Muileann àrsaidh, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. A second Muileann àrsaidh lies close by, and the two are called the elder and the younger. It follows the faith of the Church. Known for the elder of the two ancient mills.

**Muileann àrsaidh** (Cnoc thais). Founded 20 an Giblean, LE 1,779 by Dia-thìrich millers, resettled by the Tuathaich. The younger of the two Muileann àrsaidhs, walled, a short distance from the elder. Gorta Baile chrom, the Great Hunger, struck it in the Age of Strangers, and it was resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It follows the faith of the Church. Known for the younger ancient mill.

**Muileann àrsaidh** (Dùn thais). Founded 19 am Faoilleach, FE 1,670 by a custodian house of Dùn thais. Muileann àrsaidh is an ancient mill fortified with a citadel, a short way from Muileann chaol. The citadel guarded the road to the coal in the Holy Age and now guards the road to the library. It is a small place of fewer than two thousand. Known for its fortified ancient mill.

**Muileann bhàn** (Muileann bhàn). Founded 24 an Dàmhair, VE 7,701 by herders of the eastern plain. Muileann bhàn is a town of thirty-four thousand with a citadel, the seat of its province, standing where the coal road from the eastern diggings met the mills. In the Age of Strangers its citadel held the human administration's weighing-house and its guards. The mills have turned to grain since the Severance, and the Old Spirits, the old rite of the ancestors, which were never lost here, have come back to the square. Known for its white mills and citadel of the coal road.

**Muileann bheag** (Muileann bheag). Founded 23 an Giblean, FE 1,789 by grain-millers of the north-east. A small mill that grew into a sizable town and the seat of Siorrachd Muileann bheag. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and grinds for the harbour at Ros chiar. It shares its name with three others on the island, including the Tuathaich lighthouse town. Known for its flour for the north-east harbours.

**Muileann bheag** (Muileann leathan). Founded 14 an Giblean, LE 1,530 by Dia-thìrich millers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A small mill town on the north coast beside Taigh-solais Muileann bheag, one of the five lighthouses built in the Age of Strangers. It became Tuathaich at the Severance, and the Tuathaich lighthouse-keepers tended the beacon for the kingdom until it was converted to dubhan. It follows the Tuathaich Church. Known for Taigh-solais Muileann bheag.

**Muileann bheag** (Caol fhiadhaich). Founded 31 an Cèitean, LE 1,295 by wardens of the panther roads. Muileann bheag is a fort with a citadel north of Baile dhomhain, whose fields the panthers of Imrich nam Pantar cross. It is not the Muileann bheag of the northern lighthouse. Travellers stop at Am Buabhall Fortanach nearby, and the first fleet lies at Àth gharbh a short way west. Known for its citadel north of the panther roads.

**Muileann bheag** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 23 an t-Sultain, LE 728 by millers of Cuan ghlas. Muileann bheag is a mill town of fourteen thousand grinding for Inis mhòr and Caol bheag. Its mills are among the busiest in the north. It is one of several places named Muileann bheag, and not the fort above the panther roads nor the town of the northern lighthouse. Known for its mills for Inis mhòr and Caol bheag.

**Muileann chaol** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 12 am Màrt, FE 2,570 by grain-millers of the Holy Age. The smaller and older of the two Muileann chaols, a narrow mill beside a small keep in the eastern hills. The great library stands in its namesake to the south-east, and the library's carriers are said still to bring misaddressed parcels here. It is a town of the druid schools, and its mill feeds the villages of Achadh gharbh and Tobar dhubh. Known for the library's misaddressed parcels.

**Muileann chaol** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 18 an t-Ògmhios, VE 8,541 by households of the hill. A narrow mill town in the eastern hills, and the home of Leabharlann Muileann chaol, the library that keeps the fullest record of the island. The library was founded in the new kingdom and has since taken in the provincial archives, and its war archive is sealed. The town lives on the library and on the river landing at Ceann dhomhain, and to put a thing in the Library is to settle it. Paper has been made here since the Age of Sundering, and its copyists and binders work for the library. Known for Leabharlann Muileann chaol, the great library.

**Muileann chiar** (Achadh shean). Founded 10 an Gearran, FE 98 by keepers of the sacred forest. Muileann chiar of Achadh shean stands at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, the forest marked sacred before any faith claimed it. Its people were party to the holy-wood dispute of the Holy Age and have kept the forest's edge since. Tiormachd Achadh shean, the Long Drought, struck it in the Age of Strangers. It is not the silver town of the same name. Its smiths make arms for the east coast. Known for its keepers of the sacred forest's edge.

**Muileann chiar** (Seann Bhral). Founded 10 an t-Iuchar, LE 239 by millers of the Seann Bhral country. A dusky mill town with a citadel in the south-east, not the silver town of the same name further north; the confusion of the two is an old grievance here. It grinds for Àth chiar and the harbour of Seann Bhral. It keeps the Old Spirits. Known for the other Muileann chiar.

**Muileann chiar** (Muileann chiar). Founded 23 an t-Iuchar, LE 365 by coal-breakers of the eastern diggings. Muileann chiar, seat of the province of the same name, began as a coal-breaking mill for the diggings in the hills east of the capital. It grew large in the Age of Strangers, when the district was worked by the ton, and lost its trade when Scàineadh Cill ghlas, a short way west, closed the district for a generation. It is not the silver town of the same name further east, and the two are often confused in the older records. Known for its coal mills of the eastern district.

**Muileann chiar** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 10 an Lùnastal, FE 7 by Dia-thìrich custodians who found the silver seam. Muileann chiar was founded when a seam of silver was found near the great vein but not of it, the first wealth proved in the island's rock that was not the coloured coal. In the Age of Strangers the humans' concerns tried to claim the silver too, and the Dia-thìrich kept it; the town grew beside the coal workings as the call for both rose. It is smaller now than in its great years. Known for the island's silver seam.

**Muileann chrom** (Seann Skell). Founded 22 an Cèitean, LE 1,226 by Dia-thìrich millers of the Seann Skell country. A crooked mill on the edge of the north-west, left in Dia-thìrich hands when the Tuathaich homeland was fixed around it. It keeps the order of Manannan, whose sea-feasts its Tuathaich neighbours keep beside their church's, and its millers have ground for both peoples since the Severance. Cnoc ghlas and Àth àrsaidh over the line buy its flour. Known for a Dia-thìrich mill on the Tuathaich line.

**Muileann chrom** (Muileann chrom). Founded 11 an Gearran, FE 1,556 by Dia-thìrich millers on the river bend. The mill on the bend of the river gave its name to the town and then to the province, of which it is the seat and the largest place. It ground grain for the whole central country and, in the Age of Strangers, for the camps east of it as well. It is a busy town and has never needed walls, standing between Cathair mhòr and Ceann leathan on the road that joins them. In the last years of the humans' rule the Company laid the coal line from its yards, and the railway ran from its pits by Cathair dhearg down to the quay at Ros dhomhain; the kingdom's Rail Board keeps its yards here still. Known for the great mill on the river bend.

**Muileann chrom** (Tobar fhiadhaich). Founded 27 an Gearran, LE 471 by millers of Tobar fhiadhaich. A mill town on the north coast, grinding for Tobar fhiadhaich and the upland farms behind it. It is one of several places named Muileann chrom and is not the great mill town of the central country. It is a quiet town of millers and inshore fishers. Known for its north-coast mill of Tobar fhiadhaich.

**Muileann dhearg** (Inis bheag). Founded 15 an Giblean, LE 1,566 by red-stone millers. A red mill town beside Muileann fhada in the north-east, the two together grinding for Doire chiar. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its red mill beside Muileann fhada.

**Muileann dhearg** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 2 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,179 by Dia-thìrich millers of the central country. The red mill is the seat of its province and one of the largest towns of the centre, standing between Seann Chwen and Cnoc ghorm. Its mills broke coal in the Age of Strangers and turned back to grain after the Severance. It is a town of the capital's order, the order of Macha, busy and unwalled. Known for its stamping mills turned to grain.

**Muileann dhearg** (Muileann chrom). Founded 26 an Gearran, LE 797 by millers of Muileann chrom. A walled mill town on the road north of Muileann chrom, one of three places named Muileann dhearg. It was walled in the Age of Strangers to protect its stores. It follows the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its walled red mill.

**Muileann dhearg** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 30 an t-Sultain, LE 2 by coal-breakers of the central diggings. Muileann dhearg, seat of its province, is a mill town a short way from Cill ghlas. Scàineadh Cill ghlas tore open the hills nearby and killed dozens, and the town's mills stood idle for a generation after. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its red mill beside Cill ghlas.

**Muileann dhìreach** (Achadh chaol). Founded 17 an Lùnastal, FE 1,432 by the custodian house of Achadh chaol. Muileann dhìreach was raised to grind the barley of Achadh chaol, and its mill-race still runs straight as a ruled line from the stream above the town. In the Age of Strangers it ground for the camps as well as for its own people, and the tithe clerks kept a counting-room beside the wheel. A reading-house of the druid schools stands on the square, and the miller's guild and the school have shared its bell time out of mind. Known for its grain mills on the straight race.

**Muileann dhomhain** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 8 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,747 by the millers of the deep race. A mill on a deep, fast race in the central country and the seat of Siorrachd Muileann dhomhain. It was a milling town for centuries and grew rich carrying grain to the mining settlements in the Age of Strangers, when the camps could no longer feed themselves. It keeps the Old Spirits of the Dia-thìrich, and its grain-exchange still sets the price of flour for the south-east. Known for the grain-exchange of the south-east.

**Muileann dhomhain** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 23 am Màrt, FE 2,637 by Dia-thìrich millers of Dùn ìseal. The deep mill takes its name from a mill-race cut far down into the rock to reach a steady flow. It grinds for Dùn dhearg and the villages around it and has done so since the Holy Age. The Old Spirits, the old rite of the ancestors, hold here, and each new millstone is blessed at the hearth before it is set. Known for its deep-cut mill-race.

**Muileann dhomhain** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 9 an t-Samhain, FE 1,417 by Dia-thìrich millers of the south-east. Muileann dhomhain, seat of its province, is a town of twenty thousand built around deep mill-pools fed from the hills. Its flour goes down to the quays of Ceann chaol and out by sea, and the two towns have leaned on each other since the Holy Age. It is not the smaller Muileann dhomhain of Dùn ìseal to the north. Known for its deep mill-pools feeding Ceann chaol's ships.

**Muileann dhubh** (Achadh naomh). Founded 27 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,019 by millers of Achadh naomh. The black mill stands on the northern road near Tobar ghorm, grinding for the villages of Achadh naomh province. Its wheel was darkened, the old telling says, by coal dust carried downstream from the mining roads. It is a small town and has always been one. Known for its black mill of the northern road.

**Muileann fhada** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 8 an Dàmhair, FE 550 by millers of the northern mining road. Muileann fhada, the long mill, is a small walled town on the old mining road of the north. An Taigh-seinnse Reòta stands at its edge, one of the great taverns of the old circuit. Colbh Cnoc chiar stands to the west, and the town's people say the stone's two words are older than any mill. Known for An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the mining road.

**Muileann fhada** (Baile ghorm). Founded 16 an t-Samhain, LE 617 by millers of the house of Tormod mac Ruairidh. A long mill-race cut beside a south-eastern stream gave the town its name and its living, grinding the grain of the farms about the other Baile ghorm. Its walls were raised in the Age of Strangers, when the roads past Làrach an Dùin carried coal-wagons and the thieves who followed them. It keeps the Old Spirits, and the millers still leave the first sack of each season at the race-head for the ancestors. Cnoc bhàn on the hill above buys most of its flour. Known for the long mill-race and first-sack offering.

**Muileann fhada** (Doire chiar). Founded 10 am Màrt, LE 785 by millers of Doire chiar. A long mill in the north-east beside Muileann dhearg, grinding for the large village of Doire chiar. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its flour for Doire chiar.

**Muileann fhada** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 21 an Giblean, FE 1,240 by millers of the Ros fhionn river. A long mill-house on the Ros fhionn gave the place its name, and a river quay below it made it a port, sending flour downstream by barge. Its walls date from the Age of Strangers, when a tithe store was kept here and needed guarding. The river trade failed when the carts took the traffic, and the crossing of Drochaid Ros fhionn just upstream is now rarely used; the town has shrunk to its walls. Known for a river port gone quiet.

**Muileann fhionn** (Caol mhòr). Founded 12 an t-Iuchar, AE 23 by human administrators of the northern landing. Muileann fhionn was built as a fort and mill by human administrators in the Age of Strangers, to guard the northern landing. After the Severance it became a Tuathaich town. It keeps the faith of the Church, and it has since been the market town of the north-western interior and the greatest cattle-market on Dia-thìr. Its own trade is in paper and books. Known for its strangers' fort of the north.

**Muileann fhionn** (Seann Chwen). Founded 1 an Cèitean, LE 1,404 by millers of the Ceann leathan country. A fair-stoned walled mill town between Ceann leathan and Cuan dhearg, grinding grain landed at Ceann leathan's harbour and Cuan dhearg's river landing. Its walls went up in the Age of Strangers. It follows the order of Macha. Known for its grain milled for two landings.

**Muileann gharbh** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 12 am Màrt, AE 33 by a human coal concern. Muileann gharbh, the rough mill, was built in the Age of Strangers to break coal on the road down to the eastern harbours. When the mountain was worked day and night the mill never stopped, and the town grew no larger than the mill needed. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith, whose teachers found many hearers among the mill hands. Known for its rough mill of the coal road.

**Muileann gheal** (Dùn dhearg). Founded 7 an Dàmhair, LE 1,082 by white-stone millers. A white stone mill in the south-east that grinds for the city of Dùn dhearg. It keeps the Old Spirits and is a large mill-town with a guild of millers older than the city's walls. Known for its flour for Dùn dhearg.

**Muileann gheal** (Muileann chiar). Founded 20 an Lùnastal, FE 2,347 by mountain households of the carriers' country. Above Muileann gheal rises Binnean a' Chlachair, the Mason's Point, the highest ground of Dia-thìr, from which Fearghas of the Mason's line let the six unlit coals fall and saw the snowflake coal take fire in the air; the herders of the town leave a stone on its top when they pass. Muileann gheal was a mountain settlement of the Holy Age whose common granary was opened in the poor season, and in the Age of Strangers it was walled as a mill-camp under the Doire uaine hills to break coal from the eastern diggings. It is small, fewer than seven hundred people. The warm springs of Muileann ruadh lie a short walk away, and the camp's miners bathed there. Known for its walled mill-camp under Doire uaine.

**Muileann ghlas** (Dùn chrom). Founded 16 an t-Samhain, FE 748 by Dia-thìrich millers of Dùn chrom. The grey mill is an old grain town near the fair at Muileann òg and within a day of the capital. It is remembered above all for the Battle of Muileann ghlas, the second and last great battle of An Cogadh Fada, fought on its fields, in which the Tuathaich holdouts were broken. The battlefield, Àraich Muileann ghlas, lies just north-west of the town. Known for the last battle of the Long War.

**Muileann leathan** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 23 an Lùnastal, SE 13 by Tuathaich millers. Muileann leathan of the north-west was built by Tuathaich settlers soon after the Severance to grind grain for the northern villages, which had lost the Dia-thìrich mills to the south. It is a small town, and its mill-race was dug by hand by the first households. It keeps the faith of the Church. Amber washed up on the nearby shore is its other trade. Known for its Tuathaich grain mill.

**Muileann leathan** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,746 by the millers of the wide stream. A broad mill on a slow river, old enough that its founding is recorded only in the king-lists of the Holy Age. It grinds for the coast-town of Seann Mhorn and for the villages round Àth àrsaidh, and its people keep the Old Spirits. The temple ruins of Làrach an Teampaill lie in the hills behind it, and the millers will not quarry them. Known for its wide mill-wheels and grain for Seann Mhorn.

**Muileann leathan** (Muileann leathan). Founded 24 an Giblean, VE 6,933 by weaving households of the north; resettled by the Tuathaich. A wide mill on a northern stream, walled with a citadel, and the seat of Siorrachd Muileann leathan. It was a Dia-thìrich town until the Severance, when the Tuathaich took it over as one of the principal towns of their homeland. It is a centre of the Tuathaich Church, and its keep is where the Tuathaich northern coast is governed. Known for the Tuathaich mill-citadel.

**Muileann leathan** (Ceann mhin). Founded 16 an Dàmhair, LE 1,423 by millers of Ceann mhin. A walled mill town a short way inland from Ceann mhin, whose broad mill-pool is the largest on that coast. It was walled when Ceann mhin was, in the Age of Strangers, to protect its stores. Its flour goes to the ships at Ceann mhin and never to the rival quays of Ceann chaol. Known for its broad mill serving Ceann mhin.

**Muileann mhin** (Baile fhiadhaich). Founded 18 an Gearran, LE 1,599 by millers of the west. Muileann mhin of Baile fhiadhaich is a mill town of the west, founded in the long quiet centuries on a stream that turns smooth stones. It grinds for the harbour at Baile fhiadhaich. It keeps the order of Manannan, and its millers are known for honest measures. Known for its smooth-stone mill of the west.

**Muileann mhin** (Muileann mhin). Founded 20 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,458 by millers of the capital country. Muileann mhin is a large river town on the Abhainn fhionn east of the capital and the seat of its province. Its flour mills have fed the capital since the Holy Age. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha, and ships its flour down the river to Cathair dhomhain and along the shore to Cathair dhearg and Ros dhomhain. Known for the capital's flour mills.

**Muileann mhin** (Tobar ghorm). Founded 8 an t-Iuchar, LE 656 by millers of Tobar ghorm. Muileann mhin grinds the fine flour of Tobar ghorm, a short way east, and has risen and fallen with the larger village's harvests in every age. Its wheels are the oldest still turning in the province, and the miller families keep a roll of their masters going back to the Age of Sundering. In fair season the carts from the wool fairs come back loaded with its flour. Known for its fine flour for Tobar ghorm.

**Muileann naomh** (Muileann naomh). Founded 4 an t-Ògmhios, FE 599 by Dia-thìrich millers of the west coast. A holy mill in the west, the seat of Siorrachd Muileann naomh, whose wheel is said to have been consecrated to Manannan mac Lir. It lies near the Àth leathan battlefield and was taken over by crown regiments in the Long War. It follows the order of Manannan. Known for the consecrated mill-wheel.

**Muileann naomh** (Muileann naomh). Founded 24 am Faoilleach, VE 8,309 by Dia-thìrich households of the south coast. A holy mill in the south, the seat of Siorrachd Muileann naomh, whose druids of the orthodox order of Brìde's flame bless the grain before it is ground. It is one of the few towns of Òrd Bhrìde and trades with Caol ruadh and Seann Skell. Its hawk-house was the southernmost of Òrd an t-Seabhaig, the first on Dia-thìr to hang a bronze bell, until it took Òrd Bhrìde's written order in the first years of the restored kingdom; the bell now rings for Brìde's flame. Known for its grain blessed by the druids of Brìde's flame.

**Muileann òg** (Dùn chrom). Founded 10 am Faoilleach, FE 905 by carriers of the western road. Muileann òg, the young mill, stood beside the old ford-ground of the gathering in the Holy Age; it was burned in the War of the Roads and rebuilt as a market town. Its annual fair, Fèill Muileann òg, became the island's largest gathering. The field of Muileann ghlas, where An Cogadh Fada ended, lies close by. Rathad na Fèille, the fair road, was metalled from Cathair dhearg in the fair's first years. Known for Fèill Muileann òg, the great fair.

**Muileann ruadh** (Doire fhionn). Founded 29 an Giblean, FE 1,583 by Dia-thìrich millers of the north. Muileann ruadh of Doire fhionn is a mill town of the north-central country, founded in the Holy Age. Its citadel was raised after the Severance to watch the Tuathaich border. It keeps the Hawk order of the Old Faith. Known for its red mill and border citadel.

**Muileann ruadh** (Cnoc naomh). Founded 14 an Lùnastal, LE 1,385 by red-sandstone millers. A small mill-town built of red sandstone, grinding for Baile chrom and the village of Cill fhada. It was never walled, relying on Baile chrom's walls in hard times. Its people keep the order of Macha, and the mill-house has a small shrine to Macha's black horse above the wheel. Known for its red sandstone mill-house.

**Muileann ruadh** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 11 an t-Ògmhios, FE 405 by keepers of the hot springs. A red walled mill town beside Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, the hot springs whose warm water drives its wheel through winter. The keepers of the Old Spirits held the springs sacred, and the healers of the Old Faith call them Dian Cècht's. The town walled them against the claims of the human administration. It is a place for the sick and the old to bathe. Known for the hot springs of Muileann ruadh.

**Muileann ruadh** (Cnoc leathan). Founded 15 am Faoilleach, LE 190 by Dia-thìrich millers of Cnoc leathan. Muileann ruadh is a walled mill town near An Taigh-òsta Grianach, the great inn of the eastern road. Its walls were raised when the inns fortified before the war, and the town and the inn have shared a watch ever since. The eastern Toll-dubh, the shaft of the Old Ones that charcoal-burners found again in the Age of Sundering and the custodians walled up, lies close by, and the townsfolk keep away from it. It is not the Muileann ruadh of the warm springs to the west. Known for its red mill on the inn road.

**Muileann shean** (Muileann shean). Founded 1 an t-Samhain, FE 1,093 by the first millers of the northern river. The old mill of the north, whose wheel the Holy Age king-lists already call ancient, and the seat of Siorrachd Muileann shean. Its walls went up in the Age of Strangers, when it ground grain for the mining camps on contract and was raided for it. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and owns the well-village of Tobar ìseal below it. Known for the oldest mill-wheel in the north.

**Muileann uaine** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 8 am Màrt, AE 48 by a human milling concern with Dia-thìrich labour. Muileann uaine was built in the Age of Strangers as a breaking mill for coal from the interior workings. It is not the Muileann uaine of the Cnoc bheag country that the Green Death struck, though the two are often confused. It is a small town now and keeps the orthodox rite of Òrd Bhrìde. Known for its coal-breaking mill of the interior workings.

**Muileann uaine** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 3 an t-Sultain, FE 2,593 by millers of the green wood. A green mill in the wooded middle west, one of the few towns where Òrd an t-Seabhaig, the Hawk order, whose rite is the older form of Òrd Bhrìde's, still holds. The carved hawk over the mill-door is said to be as old as the Binding of the First Flame. A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death, struck it in the Age of Strangers, and since then the second sense of 'uaine' has clung to its name. Known for the Hawk-order mill.

#### R

**Ros àrsaidh** (Ros bheag). Founded 16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,221 by custodians of the western headland. Ros àrsaidh is a small walled harbour on an ancient headland of the west, fortified by the Holy Age custodians. It lies within the province of Ros bheag and has always stood in the shadow of that citadel. It keeps the order of Manannan. The coast road north from Ros bheag, Ceum Ros àrsaidh, starts below its walls; Strake's constables held it in the last months of the Severance war. Known for its walled harbour on the ancient headland.

**Ros bhàn** (Seann Chwen). Founded 24 an Lùnastal, LE 104 by the garrison of the gulf mouth. Ros bhàn is a fortified headland at the mouth of the gulf, walled and given a citadel in the long quiet centuries to guard the harbours within. It is a city by rank, though most of its people are soldiers, customs clerks and their families. The white stone of its headland gives it its name. The customs town also boils soap and blows glass for the gulf. Known for its fortified headland at the gulf mouth.

**Ros bheag** (Ros bheag). Founded 2 an Dàmhair, VE 6,597 by hill-folk households come down to the western shore. Ros bheag is the citadel harbour and provincial seat of the western coast, holding Dùn thais and Ros àrsaidh within its province. It was fortified in the Holy Age and has been the western sea's naval station through every age since. Its people keep the order of Manannan. It is the market town of the west coast, and its own trade is in books, boots and salted food. Known for its citadel harbour of the western coast.

**Ros chiar** (Ceann bheag). Founded 1 an t-Iuchar, FE 7 by the headland-lords of Ceann bheag. A dusky headland city on the north coast, walled, with a citadel on the rock and a harbour below. It was one of the harbours the human traders first used after the Crossing, and its citadel was taken and retaken in the war before the Severance. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and competes with Caol bheag for the northern trade. Slighe-uisce fhuar, the cold way along the north coast to Caol mhin, begins at its harbour; the grain barges of Inis mhòr sailed it until the roads took their trade. Known for the fortified headland harbour.

**Ros chiar** (Muileann bheag). Founded 19 an Lùnastal, LE 1,488 by fishers of Muileann bheag. A dusky headland harbour village on the north-east coast that ships the flour of Muileann bheag. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and competes with Seann Toll for the coast trade. Known for the flour harbour of Muileann bheag.

**Ros dhìreach** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 30 an Lùnastal, LE 625 by fishers of the Hawk coast. Ros dhìreach of Cnoc bheag is a walled fishing village on the north-central coast, founded in the long quiet centuries. A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death, struck it in the Age of Strangers. It was walled after the Severance, when the Tuathaich coast became a frontier. It keeps the rite of the Hawk order. Known for its walls and its fishing boats on the Hawk coast.

**Ros dhìreach** (Cnoc mhòr). Founded 22 an t-Ògmhios, LE 76 by Dia-thìrich harbour-folk of the gulf. Ros dhìreach of Cnoc mhòr is a harbour on a straight headland of the gulf, founded in the long quiet centuries. It is a city by rank and the harbour of Cnoc mhòr's cattle trade. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. Its clay-pits feed its potteries, and its soap-boilers serve the gulf. Known for its straight headland harbour.

**Ros dhomhain** (Ros dhomhain). Founded 19 an t-Iuchar, VE 7,017 by fishers of Loch chrom. Ros dhomhain is the most populous place of the capital country, a merchant port that outgrew every wall it was ever given until no one built another. The first human traders lodged here after the Crossing, and its counting-houses have served every master of the island's trade since. It sits between the capital and the old harbour of Seann Vell, and the three have run together into one shore. The Company's railway, the coal line, came down to its deep-water quay from the pits at Muileann chrom in the last years of Edward Vane's commission, and the first steamer seen on Dia-thìr had come into its harbour half a century before. In the present year its quay became the one place on the island where dubhan may be loaded for beyond the island, under the charter Dubhan won from the council: a clerk of the Treasury takes the tithe on every barrel, and the custodians of Brìde's order seal every hold. Known for the capital country's great merchant port.

**Ros fhionn** (Caol shean). Founded 10 am Màrt, FE 1,262 by Dia-thìrich river-folk of the east. Ros fhionn of Caol shean is a small citadel city on the Abhainn chaol in the east, near the stream of Allt an Àigh. It is where most pilgrims to the stream come ashore from the river boats that bring them up from Seann Mhorn, and its citadel was raised in the Age of Sundering to guard them. It is not the Ros fhionn of the old bridge, which lies to the north. Known for its river landing of the Allt an Àigh pilgrims.

**Ros fhionn** (Inis bheag). Founded 29 an Lùnastal, FE 41 by custodians of the river crossing. Ros fhionn of Inis bheag is a walled city on a headland over the Abhainn bheag, founded in the Holy Age where the first bridges crossed the river. Drochaid Ros fhionn, the old crossing, is still standing. Little has crossed it since the salt went by sea, save in the century when the Company's coal carts used it on the eastern coal road; it fell silent again when the eastern pits flooded in the Severance war. The salt-boats' lane round the east cape, Seòlaid Ros fhionn, is named for the town. Its temple is a hall of the druid schools, sacred to Flidais. The salt trade that built the bridge is gone, but the market-court the salt-masters set up stayed on the headland. The town is still the market of fifty-three towns of the north-eastern hills, and no market on the island reaches further. Its yards on the river build barges and hulls, and it makes cheese for the hill towns. Known for Drochaid Ros fhionn, the old bridge.

**Ros gharbh** (Ros gharbh). Founded 3 am Faoilleach, LE 255 by fishers of the rough headland. Ros gharbh is a harbour town on a rough headland of the gulf and the seat of its province. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and grew with the gulf's fishing fleet. Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol, the Great Wave, ran up the gulf in SE 4, broke its quays and threw the fleet onto the headland, though the town on its height lost few people. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for the gulf's fishing fleet.

**Ros gheal** (Ros gheal). Founded 29 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,009 by Dia-thìrich fishers of the white headland. Ros gheal, Ros leathan and Seann Skell share one bay on the north-central coast, and have quarrelled over its moorings for as long as the rolls run. Ros gheal is the largest of the three and the seat of its province. Its people keep the Hawk order's rite of Mòd, and its white headland is the first land the northern fishing boats see coming home. Known for its white headland and the disputed bay.

**Ros leathan** (Ros gheal). Founded 30 am Faoilleach, LE 1,774 by Dia-thìrich fishers of the Hawk bay. Ros leathan is a harbour town on the Hawk bay, sharing it with Ros gheal and Seann Skell. It was founded in the long quiet centuries by fishers who would not pay Ros gheal's mooring dues. It keeps the Hawk order of the Old Faith. Known for its rival wharves of the Hawk bay.

**Ros mhòr** (Caol mhòr). Founded 15 an t-Ògmhios, LE 432 by Dia-thìrich fishers; resettled by the Tuathaich. Ros mhòr of the north-west is a harbour on a great headland, founded by Dia-thìrich fishers in the long quiet centuries. After the Severance it was resettled by the Tuathaich and grew with the northern trade. It lies between the harbours of Caol mhòr and Caol naomh. Known for its great headland harbour.

**Ros ruadh** (Seann Chwen). Founded 27 am Faoilleach, LE 100 by quarrymen of the red headland. Ros ruadh is a small harbour on the gulf, founded by quarrymen who shipped its red stone to the gulf cities. Much of Ceann leathan and Ros bhàn is built of it. It keeps a ferry to the harbours across the water. Known for its red stone for the gulf cities.

**Ros ruadh** (Ceann mhòr). Founded 21 an Dùbhlachd, VE 3,075 by fishing households of the north-west coast; resettled by the Tuathaich. A red headland harbour on the north-west coast, one of the Dia-thìrich harbours given to the Tuathaich after the Severance. The fishing families of Ros ruadh are among those who keep the voyage of Naomh Breandan alive in speech, and some say the saint's boat put out from this headland. It follows the faith of the Church. Known for the Naomh Breandan telling of the north-west.

#### S

**Seann Bhral** (Baile àrsaidh). Founded 5 an Dàmhair, VE 196 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Bhral of the west coast is a Seann-Dhaoine site the Dia-thìrich resettled in the Holy Age. It grew into a large port on the western sea roads and took up the order of Manannan, the Old Faith's order of the sea, which is strong along this coast. Its harbour is unwalled, trusting to the citadel at Ros bheag to the north. Known for its west-coast harbour of the order of Manannan.

**Seann Bhral** (Seann Bhral). Founded 30 an Lùnastal, VE 1,005 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Bhral of the south-east is a Seann-Dhaoine site that the Dia-thìrich resettled in the Holy Age, and it has grown into the greatest harbour of that coast and the seat of its province. It was walled in the Age of Strangers, when its quays shipped coal from the interior. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. Known for the south-east's great walled harbour.

**Seann Bhral** (Ros gharbh). Founded 9 an t-Samhain, VE 7,400 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Bhral is a walled harbour on a Seann-Dhaoine site, settled by the Dia-thìrich and named by them for the Old Ones. It lies near Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, the ruined outpost no one can date. It is a port town of four thousand. Known for its walled old harbour of Ros gharbh.

**Seann Bhrenn** (Seann Bhrenn). Founded 12 an Giblean, VE 321 by the Seann-Dhaoine. A Seann-Dhaoine harbour on the north coast, called Seann Bhrenn by the Dia-thìrich, and the seat of the shire of the same name. It is a large village of the Old Spirits, and its fishers tell that the harbour-stones were laid by people who had no need of the Dia-thìrich's tides. Known for the northern Seann-Dhaoine harbour.

**Seann Bhrenn** (Ceann mhin). Founded 15 an Lùnastal, VE 23 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Bhrenn is an old harbour of the Seann-Dhaoine, settled by the Dia-thìrich in the Holy Age. It lies hard beside Caol gharbh, and the two harbours have quarrelled over the same water for as long as there are records, each claiming the other was built on its fishing ground. It is a port town of nearly nine thousand and the older of the two by its name. Known for its old harbour quarrelling with Caol gharbh.

**Seann Chwen** (Seann Dunn). Founded 1 am Faoilleach, VE 1,236 by the Seann-Dhaoine. The landing stones at Seann Chwen are of the Seann-Dhaoine, and the name was given by the Dia-thìrich who resettled the site in the Holy Age. It is a small harbour on the south shore, but its citadel guards the capital's southern sea road, and it has been garrisoned more often than its size would suggest. Its people keep the order of Macha, the capital's order of the Old Faith, and its green is one of the two grounds where the travelling circus, An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn, pitches. Known for its citadel on the capital's southern sea road.

**Seann Chwen** (Seann Chwen). Founded 19 an Giblean, VE 32 by the Seann-Dhaoine. The larger Seann Chwen is the chief harbour of the gulf and the seat of the province that bears its name, built on a Seann-Dhaoine site the Dia-thìrich resettled in the Holy Age. It takes the fish of the gulf and the goods of Cathair mhòr. It has no walls; the fortified headlands of Ros bhàn and Ceann leathan stand to either side of it. Known for the gulf's chief harbour and fish-market.

**Seann Chwen** (Àth shean). Founded 29 an Lùnastal, VE 3,488 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Chwen of Àth shean is a harbour on the south coast, on a Seann-Dhaoine site. It was resettled by the Dia-thìrich in the Holy Age and is the port for the southern Àth shean. It keeps the capital's order, the order of Macha. Known for its south-coast old harbour.

**Seann Dunn** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 5 an Cèitean, VE 642 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Dunn keeps a Seann-Dhaoine name, and its citadel stands on footings no Dia-thìrich mason laid. It stands on the Abhainn chaol a little above the river mouth, and is the river landing and lodging-place for those who visit Làrach an Teampaill in the hills to the north, whose ships put in at Seann Mhorn down the coast; its own ancestor hall serves the Old Spirits. An Taigh-seinnse Òir, one of the great taverns of the old mining circuit, stands in the town itself. Its yards are the largest shipyard on Dia-thìr, and the town cuts the sails and makes the cheese of the east coast. Slighe-mhara àrsaidh, the ancient sea-way of the Old Ones, begins at the river mouth below the town and runs round the south-east cape to Ceann chaol. Known for An Taigh-seinnse Òir and the temple road.

**Seann Dunn** (Seann Dunn). Founded 28 am Faoilleach, VE 601 by the Seann-Dhaoine. The Seann-Dhaoine left the harbour-mole and the name Dunn; the Dia-thìrich called it Seann Dunn and built a citadel over the mole. It is the seat of the shire of the same name and follows the order of Macha. It is a village in form but large in number, with the ford-town of Àth ghorm under its protection. Known for the Seann-Dhaoine harbour-mole.

**Seann Dunn** (Baile chaol). Founded 22 an Dùbhlachd, VE 320 by the Seann-Dhaoine. The harbour stones of Seann Dunn are older than any Dia-thìrich work, and the name the Dia-thìrich gave the place keeps a root that is not their own. It became a Dia-thìrich port in the Holy Age, and its citadel was raised above the harbour to guard the eastern approaches. It is now a city of shipping and salt-fish, and its oldest families still claim that the harbour wall was only repaired, never built, by their ancestors. Its yards build seagoing hulls and cut their sails. Known for its Seann-Dhaoine harbour stones and its citadel.

**Seann Mhorn** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 5 an t-Iuchar, VE 80 by the Seann-Dhaoine. The Seann-Dhaoine left the harbour-stones and the name Morn; the Dia-thìrich, finding both, called the place Seann Mhorn and built on top. It is a walled port with a citadel over the harbour mouth, fought over more than once in the troubles before the Severance, and it keeps the Old Spirits of the Dia-thìrich. Stones of the older builders are set into the harbour wall, and the fishermen touch one before they sail. Known for the Seann-Dhaoine stones in its harbour wall.

**Seann Mhorn** (Àth chiar). Founded 31 an Cèitean, VE 784 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Mhorn is a small old harbour, one of several Seann names on this stretch of the southern coast, and was settled by the Dia-thìrich in the Holy Age. It lies between Seann Skell and Seann Vell. It is a fishing village of three thousand. Known for its small old harbour.

**Seann Skell** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 10 an Gearran, VE 1,404 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Skell is a Seann-Dhaoine harbour on the far north-west coast, named by the Dia-thìrich who resettled it; it passed to the Tuathaich after the Severance. Its citadel looks out over the waters where pirate ships are still reported and where old sailors place the Sea-Watcher. It is not the Seann Skell whose name the regiments carry, which lies far to the south-east. Known for its watch over the pirate waters.

**Seann Skell** (Seann Skell). Founded 19 an t-Samhain, VE 1,833 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Skell of the Hawk bay is a walled harbour city on a Seann-Dhaoine site, sharing its bay with Ros gheal and Ros leathan. It was resettled by the Dia-thìrich in the Holy Age and walled in the Age of Sundering. It keeps the Hawk order of the Old Faith. It is the market town of the Hawk bay and the north-central coast. Amber from the bay's strands is the one good it sells to other markets, and its yards build seagoing hulls. Known for its walled old harbour of the Hawk bay.

**Seann Skell** (Seann Skell). Founded 29 am Faoilleach, VE 7,987 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Skell is the great southern port, a town of nearly sixty thousand whose harbour lies on a site the Seann-Dhaoine used before the Dia-thìrich; the name keeps their root. It is the seat of its province and a centre of Òrd Bhrìde, the order of Brìde's flame. The ninth regiment and the second fleet, raised in the Long War, are stationed here. It shares its name with the great western river port. Glass is blown there from the white sand of its own shore. Known for the southern fleet harbour.

**Seann Skell** (Seann Skell). Founded 6 an Gearran, VE 173 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Skell is the great river port of the west, a city of seventy-four thousand and the largest place on the island, whose barges run down the Abhainn naomh to Ros àrsaidh; its river harbour is a Seann-Dhaoine site and the name keeps their root. It is walled by its citadel rather than by curtain walls, and the seventh regiment, raised in the Long War, is stationed here. The first battle of that war was fought at Àth leathan, a short march north. Known for the great western river port.

**Seann Tarr** (Muileann bheag). Founded 30 an Cèitean, VE 884 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Tarr is a Seann-Dhaoine site on the north-eastern coast, resettled by the Dia-thìrich in the Holy Age, and its ancestor hall is one of the oldest spirit-houses of the Old Spirits still in use. A citadel was raised over the harbour in the Age of Sundering. It is small for a city, but the shrine draws the whole north-east at the great feasts. It is the market town of the north-eastern coast, whose market began at the shrine's feasts. Honey from its heather and wax for the shrine lights are its own goods, with cheese and books, and its rope-makers are a chartered guild. Known for its north-eastern ancestor shrine.

**Seann Tarr** (Seann Tarr). Founded 25 an Giblean, VE 1,212 by the Seann-Dhaoine. A harbour of the Seann-Dhaoine on the eastern coast, named Seann Tarr by the Dia-thìrich, and the seat of the shire of the same name. It is a large village that follows the Old Spirits. The eastern pirates made it unsafe in the Age of Strangers, and it has a small fleet of its own. Known for the old eastern harbour and fleet.

**Seann Tarr** (Cnoc gheal). Founded 17 an Lùnastal, VE 4,706 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Tarr is a small harbour whose landing stones are older than any Dia-thìrich work, and the root in its name is not of the Dia-thìrich tongue. Dia-thìrich fishers settled it in the Holy Age and gave it the name it bears, and the name marks it as a place of the Old Ones. On clear nights the lighthouse of Àth dhearg can be seen from its quay, and its boats steer by it. Known for the Old Ones' landing stones.

**Seann Toll** (Seann Toll). Founded 8 an t-Samhain, VE 1,033 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Toll, old hollow, is named for the sea-caves under its headland, where Seann-Dhaoine marks are said to be cut into the rock. The Dia-thìrich resettled it in the Holy Age and it has been a fishing port ever since. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits and the northern herring fleet. Known for its sea-caves and the north-coast herring.

**Seann Toll** (Muileann chrom). Founded 8 an Gearran, VE 92 by the Seann-Dhaoine. A Seann-Dhaoine river port on the Abhainn uaine in the midlands, called Seann Toll by the Dia-thìrich for the hollow in the rock where its boats lie. It is walled and follows the order of Macha, and it stands a short way west of Cill ghlas, where the Rending opened. It lies close to Ceann leathan at the river mouth, where the Còmhrag is fought each year, and fighters from the tournament fill its taverns. Known for the rock-hollow landing and Còmhrag crowds.

**Seann Toll** (Muileann bheag). Founded 19 an Giblean, VE 2,319 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Toll is a harbour in a cleft of the rock, and its lowest quay is cut in a manner the Dia-thìrich did not use; it is held to be the work of the Seann-Dhaoine, and nothing more is known of it. The Dia-thìrich settled it in the Holy Age as the nearest harbour for Dùn dhubh and Muileann bheag. It is a small port town of fishers and lightermen. Known for its cleft-rock harbour of the Old Ones.

**Seann Vell** (Ros dhomhain). Founded 29 an Lùnastal, VE 8,883 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Vell on the capital shore stands on Seann-Dhaoine quay stones, still visible at low water beneath the later harbour. The Dia-thìrich resettled it in the Holy Age and walled it in the long quiet centuries. It has since been drawn into the sprawl of Ros dhomhain, but keeps its own walls and its own harbour-master. Its scent-makers distil the best-known scent on the island. Known for its old quay stones of the capital shore.

**Seann Vell** (Seann Vell). Founded 4 an t-Ògmhios, VE 396 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Vell of the south-east is a citadel harbour on a Seann-Dhaoine site, resettled by the Dia-thìrich in the Holy Age. Its citadel guards the south-eastern coast and the approach to Seann Bhral, its larger neighbour and old rival. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits. The town stands on Eilean dhearg, the island where the Seann-Dhaoine of the older Seann Vell laid their dead. Known for its south-eastern citadel harbour.

**Seann Vell** (Baile mhin). Founded 1 an Gearran, VE 1,698 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Vell of Baile mhin is a small river landing on a Seann-Dhaoine site on the Abhainn bheag in the north-east, a short way above the river mouth at Caol chrom, resettled by the Dia-thìrich in the Holy Age. It lives on the seal-hunt at the river mouth and the fishing. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for its old landing stones and seal-hunters.

**Seann Vell** (Seann Vell). Founded 16 an Dàmhair, VE 1,197 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Vell of the west coast is a small harbour on a Seann-Dhaoine site, the seat of its province. It was resettled by the Dia-thìrich in the Holy Age and took up the order of Manannan with the rest of the coast. An ceathramh cabhlach is stationed at Cuan shean, a short way up the coast. Its shire is the humans' old district of the outer coasts, kept whole: the islands of the west and south, Eilean bhàn with Cuan dhearg and Cnoc chaol, and the southern edge of the windy coast in the far north-west. Known for its old harbour of the west coast.

**Seann Vell** (Seann Vell). Founded 1 an t-Ògmhios, VE 3,673 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Vell of the capital's east is a walled river town on a Seann-Dhaoine site on the Abhainn fhionn and the seat of its province. It was resettled by the Dia-thìrich in the Holy Age. An Taigh-seinnse Mòr stands just east of it, at the river quay of Cuan chrom. Known for its walls on the Cuan chrom road.

**Seann Warr** (Seann Warr). Founded 27 am Màrt, VE 725 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Warr is a Seann-Dhaoine harbour on the capital's western shore, resettled by the Dia-thìrich and walled in the Holy Age. Its citadel guards the western approaches to the capital. An còigeamh rèisimeid, raised in An Cogadh Fada, is stationed here and carries its name. Its salt-pans have sold salt since the first years of the humans' trade, and the flax of its lake-shore fields, pressed for linseed oil, is grown nowhere else on the island. Loch chrom is fresh, and the town's salt is boiled from brine springs that rise in the reed marsh behind it. Known for the fifth regiment's walled harbour.

**Seann Warr** (Àth chiar). Founded 15 an Gearran, VE 2,245 by the Seann-Dhaoine. Seann Warr of Àth chiar is a small harbour on a Seann-Dhaoine landing on the south shore of the gulf. The Dia-thìrich resettled it in the Holy Age. It keeps the ancestor rite of the Old Spirits and a few boats, and pays its dues to the larger harbours across the water. Known for its old landing on the gulf's south shore.

#### T

**Tobar bhàn** (Cnoc gheal). Founded 13 an Cèitean, FE 968 by well-keepers of the north-eastern shore road. Tobar bhàn is a well village on the north-eastern shore road, named for a spring whose water runs white with chalk. The beacon of Taigh-solais Àth dhearg stands on the coast beyond it, and through the later Age of Strangers the village kept the lamp-keepers in bread and peat. Its people hold to the Old Spirits, the ancestors and the weather, and still leave a cup at the well before a sea-journey. Known for its white well and the lighthouse keepers.

**Tobar dhearg** (Tobar dhearg). Founded 12 an Dàmhair, VE 8,270 by the keepers of the southern beacon. Tobar dhearg is a large village around a well of red water, the seat of its province. Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, one of the five lighthouses of the Age of Strangers, stands on the shore below it; it burned a coal flame for over a century before it was converted to dubhan. The village holds to Òrd Bhrìde, and its druids, keepers of Brìde's flame, keep the light's log. Known for the southern lighthouse and red well.

**Tobar dhearg** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 16 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,150 by Dia-thìrich well-keepers; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. A Dia-thìrich village around a well of red water, resettled by Tuathaich families after the Severance. Like several villages of this coast it made the shrine of Manannan that it inherited its church rather than raising its own. It lives on sheep and on the market at Cathair gheal. Known for its red well of the western Tuathaich.

**Tobar dhìreach** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar, VE 42 by well-diggers of the high valleys. A large well village in the central-east, laid out along a straight channel that carries its water. It is the eldest of the three wells that claim the mason's crack, and the only one that can show a capped shaft, scorched at the lip, where it says the lightning fell into the vein and the first fire was taken. The slab laid over the burnt vein lies beside it, and the keepers' house faces the slab. The Mason's line lived here through the long generations of the Seven Coals: Brian buried the five coals beside the slab and found the black one warm on the next day, and Seathan snapped the fire out of his own fingers in a doorway of the village. It follows the druid schools of the Old Faith and supplies water and vegetables to Baile Mòr uaine and Baile thais. Its paper-mill makes the paper of the royal chronicle. Known for the straight water-channel.

**Tobar dhomhain** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 17 am Màrt, AE 32 by miners of the western hills. A deep well-village in the western hills, dug to supply a mining camp that has since been abandoned. It is one of the smallest villages on the island and follows the order of Manannan. The grassland above the village is where the Leaden Hawk company kept its watch on the road from Ros bheag in the first spring of the Severance war. Known for the well of a lost camp.

**Tobar dhubh** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 7 an t-Samhain, FE 1,590 by Dia-thìrich well-keepers of Cnoc bhàn. A village around a deep well whose water runs dark, said in the old telling to rise from near the vein. It has never been proved so, and the druid scholars of Cnoc bhàn have argued it both ways. The well still draws visitors who drink from it for luck. Known for the dark well of old telling.

**Tobar fhiadhaich** (Tobar fhiadhaich). Founded 10 an t-Samhain, VE 7,202 by herders of the northern moor. Tobar fhiadhaich is a large village around a wild spring on the moor, and the seat of its province. It lives on grazing and on the peat of Achadh gharbh. Its herders have walked the same moor paths since the Ancient Age, and its spring is said never to have failed, even in the driest years. Known for its wild spring and moorland grazing.

**Tobar ghorm** (Doire fhionn). Founded 27 am Faoilleach, FE 2,921 by Dia-thìrich well-keepers of the northern road. A village around a blue spring on the road running north toward the Tuathaich country, and the last Dia-thìrich water on that road. Since the Severance it has traded with both sides of the line and has been trusted by neither. It is not the larger Tobar ghorm of the wool fairs, and it resents the confusion. Known for its blue spring on the northern road.

**Tobar ghorm** (Tobar ghorm). Founded 31 am Faoilleach, FE 950 by Dia-thìrich herders of the northern plain. Tobar ghorm is a large village around a blue spring, the seat of its province, and home to the greatest wool fairs of the north. The fairs were old before the humans came, and the humans' wool-buyers made them larger. The mills of Muileann mhin grind its grain. Known for its blue spring and wool fairs.

**Tobar ìseal** (Tobar fhiadhaich). Founded 26 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,494 by the well-keepers of Muileann shean. A low well in a hollow below Muileann shean, ringed with stone in the Holy Age and watched ever since. The small keep that gives it a citadel was built to guard the water for the mill town in dry years, and the dry summers since have shown the builders wise. It is still a village, and the millers upstream own it in all but name. Known for the guarded low well.

**Tobar ìseal** (Dùn dhearg). Founded 26 am Faoilleach, LE 508 by well-keepers of Dùn dhearg. A low well-village in the east that waters the city of Dùn dhearg in dry seasons. It keeps the Old Spirits, and its well-keepers still bless the water before it is carted up the hill. Known for the well that waters Dùn dhearg.

**Tobar òg** (Inis bheag). Founded 21 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,395 by well-diggers of Inis bheag. A young well village in the north-east, dug to water the fields behind Inis bheag when those fields were first broken. It has grown into a sizeable village and follows the druid schools of the Old Faith. Known for the young well behind Inis bheag.

**Tobar shean** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 29 an Lùnastal, LE 822 by well-keepers of Baile òg. An old well-village in the eastern hills, walled in the troubled years because its well was the only sure water on the road past Làrach an Teampaill. It keeps the Old Spirits, and the well-keepers still close the gate in dry seasons and ration the water by the bucket. Known for the walled well on the temple road.
